frq.title: SAQ 1 · The Populists reconsidered (secondary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

"The Populists have too often been remembered as backward-looking farmers, nostalgic for a vanishing world of yeoman independence and quick to blame distant bankers and foreigners for their troubles. The record of the 1880s and 1890s suggests something different. Through the Farmers' Alliances, hundreds of thousands of farmers built cooperatives, attended lectures on money and credit, and drafted detailed plans for federal loans on stored crops, a flexible national currency and public ownership of the railroads. Far from rejecting the modern economy, they sought to use a stronger national government to give ordinary producers a fair place within it. Their proposals were not the complaints of a dying class but a blueprint that later reformers would borrow."

Miriam Ostrander, historian, The Cooperative Commonwealth Reconsidered, 2019. (The historian and the book are fictional, written for this exercise.)

parts.q: Describe the historian's argument about the Populist movement.
parts.a: The historian argues that the Populists were forward-looking reformers, not nostalgic victims: through cooperatives, economic education and concrete proposals for federal credit, currency reform and railroad ownership, they tried to use a stronger national government to secure farmers a fair place in the modern industrial economy, and their program anticipated later reforms.
parts.n: Quoting 'not the complaints of a dying class' or writing 'the historian talks about farmers' earns nothing; describe the claim, modern reformers using the state, in your own words.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1865 to 1898, not directly mentioned in the excerpt, supports the historian's argument.
parts.a: The Omaha Platform (1892) supports it. Beyond the currency and railroad planks, the People's Party demanded a graduated income tax and endorsed the secret ballot and direct election of senators, modern reforms meant to make government answer to ordinary voters and tax concentrated wealth; the income tax and direct election became the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Amendments in 1913. (Also accepted: the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887, won partly by farmer pressure after the Granger laws, as evidence that agrarian demands shaped modern regulation.)
parts.n: Reusing the excerpt's own examples (cooperatives, the subtreasury loans, railroad ownership) earns nothing; the development must be new and tied to 'forward-looking'.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1865 to 1898 could be used to challenge or modify the historian's argument.
parts.a: The 1896 fusion modifies it. The Populists endorsed the Democrat William Jennings Bryan and let free silver, a single inflationary remedy, stand for their whole program, which suggests that much of the movement's appeal was a narrower debtor's grievance rather than a broad modern blueprint; after Bryan's defeat the party collapsed. (Also accepted: the Omaha Platform's resolutions calling for tighter restriction of 'undesirable' immigration, which fit the older image of Populists blaming foreigners.)
parts.n: Simply disagreeing ('the Populists were backward') earns nothing; name a specific development and explain how it limits the historian's claim.

frq.title: SAQ 2 · Carnegie's 'Wealth' (primary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

"The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer measures how far civilization has advanced. We need not regret it; it is essential to progress. The law of competition may be hard on the individual, but it is best for the race, because it ensures the survival of the fittest in every field. We must therefore accept great inequality of wealth and the concentration of business in the hands of a few. The only question is what the rich should do with their surplus. The best answer is that a man of wealth should live modestly and administer his surplus, during his lifetime, as a trust for the community, founding libraries, parks and institutions that help those who will help themselves. Charity given without discrimination does more harm than good."

Described period document: an essay by Andrew Carnegie, owner of the largest American steel company, titled 'Wealth', published in the North American Review in June 1889 and later known as 'The Gospel of Wealth'. The wording is a paraphrase composed for this exercise from the essay's arguments; it is not a quotation.

parts.q: Describe the historical situation in which Carnegie wrote this essay.
parts.a: By 1889 industrial capitalism had created giant firms and fortunes, such as Carnegie's steel empire and Rockefeller's Standard Oil Trust, while workers faced wage cuts and long hours and a widening gap between rich and poor. The Great Railroad Strike (1877), the Haymarket affair (1886) and Henry George's best-selling Progress and Poverty (1879) had made many Americans ask whether such concentrated wealth was legitimate, the question Carnegie set out to answer.
parts.n: Summarizing the excerpt ('he says the rich should give money away') describes content, not situation; the point needs the industrial inequality and conflict behind it.

parts.q: Explain how Carnegie's argument reflects ONE intellectual development of the period 1865 to 1898.
parts.a: It reflects Social Darwinism. Writers such as Herbert Spencer and William Graham Sumner applied 'survival of the fittest' to society, arguing that competition rewarded the able and that interfering with it would harm progress; Carnegie uses the same logic to call inequality natural and beneficial, and he rejects indiscriminate charity because it would sustain the 'unfit'. His call to give, though, goes beyond Sumner's laissez-faire, which is what makes it the Gospel of Wealth.
parts.n: Naming Social Darwinism without linking it to a line in the excerpt ('survival of the fittest', inequality as progress) earns nothing.

parts.q: Explain ONE way other Americans challenged ideas like those in the excerpt between 1865 and 1898.
parts.a: Social Gospel ministers such as Washington Gladden argued that poverty came from unjust social conditions, not unfitness, and that Christianity required reforming wages, housing and child labor rather than relying on the rich to give. (Also accepted: the Homestead Strike of 1892, in which Carnegie's own steelworkers fought wage cuts and the destruction of their union; the Populists' 1892 demand for a graduated income tax; or Bellamy's Looking Backward, which imagined an economy without private fortunes.)
parts.n: A challenger named without the contrast ('the Social Gospel disagreed') earns little; say what the challenger rejected in Carnegie's argument.

frq.title: SAQ 3 · 'The Bosses of the Senate' (non-text source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the image described below.

Described image: a color cartoon by Joseph Keppler titled 'The Bosses of the Senate', published in the humor magazine Puck in January 1889. The scene is the chamber of the U.S. Senate. Small, ordinary-looking senators sit at their desks. Along the back of the chamber, towering over them, stand enormous, bloated men in top hats whose bodies are money bags, each labeled with the name of a trust, such as the Standard Oil, sugar, copper, steel and coal trusts. A sign on the wall reads: 'This is a Senate of the Monopolists, by the Monopolists and for the Monopolists!' One door, marked 'Entrance for Monopolists', stands open; another, the 'People's Entrance' to the public gallery, is shut and marked 'Closed'. (The description summarizes the cartoon's layout and labels for this exercise.)

parts.q: Describe the point of view the artist expresses about the relationship between business and government.
parts.a: Keppler argues that large trusts controlled the federal government: the monopolists' giant size and position above the senators show that the Senate served business combinations rather than voters, and the open monopolists' door beside the closed people's entrance shows ordinary citizens shut out of lawmaking. The sign's parody of Lincoln's Gettysburg phrase says democracy had been captured by concentrated wealth.
parts.n: Listing what is in the picture (money bags, senators, doors) is description, not point of view; state the claim the images make about who controlled government.

parts.q: Explain ONE historical development from the period 1865 to 1898 that supports the artist's point of view.
parts.a: The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) supports it: Congress wrote it vaguely and enforced it weakly, and in United States v. E.C. Knight Co. (1895) the Supreme Court exempted the sugar trust, which controlled most American refining, because manufacturing was not commerce. The law that answered public anger at monopolies left the trusts in the cartoon largely untouched. (Also accepted: senators were chosen by state legislatures, where railroad and corporate money shaped the choice, so the Senate was nicknamed a millionaires' club.)
parts.n: A development that merely shows trusts existed (Standard Oil was big) does not support the claim; it must show business influence over government.

parts.q: Explain ONE way Americans attempted to reduce the influence of business on government between 1865 and 1898.
parts.a: The Populists' Omaha Platform (1892) endorsed the direct election of senators so that voters, not state legislatures open to corporate influence, would choose them, alongside demands for government ownership of railroads and a graduated income tax. The reform was achieved in the Seventeenth Amendment (1913). (Also accepted: the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887, which created the first federal regulatory commission to police railroad rates, though its weakness showed the limits of reform.)
parts.n: Naming a reform without explaining how it would reduce business influence earns nothing; tie it to the cartoon's complaint that the people were shut out.

frq.title: DBQ · Why organized labor struggled, 1877-1898
frq.stem:
Evaluate the relative importance of the factors that limited the success of organized labor in the United States from 1877 to 1898.

The documents are paraphrased for this exercise from the sources named in each source line; the wording is not a direct quotation. Document 3 is a described image and Document 4 is a labelled composite.

Document 1
Source: Preamble of the Knights of Labor, adopted at the order's 1878 national assembly (paraphrase).
The rapid growth and aggression of great capitalists and corporations will, unless checked, reduce the toiling masses to poverty and degradation. We therefore organize every branch of honest labor to secure to workers the full share of the wealth they create. We seek cooperative institutions that will replace the wage system, an eight-hour day, an end to the labor of young children, and arbitration in place of strikes wherever possible.

Document 2
Source: Samuel Gompers, leader of the cigar makers' union and later president of the American Federation of Labor, testimony before a U.S. Senate committee on relations between labor and capital, 1883 (paraphrase of his arguments).
A single worker cannot bargain with a great employer; only the trade union gives him any strength. Our fight is for higher wages and shorter hours now, not for some plan of the distant future. Our wages are undercut when whole families, many of them newly arrived immigrants with their children, roll cigars at home in the tenements for whatever the manufacturer will pay.

Document 3
Source: Engraving on the cover of Harper's Weekly, a national magazine read mainly by middle-class Americans, May 1886 (described image).
In a crowded Chicago street at night, a bearded speaker stands on a wagon with his arm raised. In the foreground a bomb explodes in a burst of light among a line of uniformed policemen, several of whom fall; other officers fire revolvers into a crowd of men in workers' caps who scatter in panic.

Document 4
Source: Composite of employment agreements required by manufacturers and mine owners in the 1880s and 1890s, written for this exercise.
I, the undersigned, declare that I am not a member of any labor union and agree not to join one while employed by this company. I understand that joining a union, or taking part in any strike, is cause for my immediate discharge without further notice.

Document 5
Source: Federal court injunction obtained by U.S. Attorney General Richard Olney against Eugene V. Debs and the officers of the American Railway Union, Chicago, July 1894 (paraphrase).
The defendants are commanded to stop interfering in any way with trains carrying the United States mail or engaged in interstate commerce, and to stop compelling or inducing, by threats, persuasion, force or any other means, any railroad employee to refuse or neglect his duties.

Document 6
Source: Eugene V. Debs, president of the American Railway Union, testimony before the U.S. Strike Commission appointed to investigate the Pullman Strike, August 1894 (paraphrase).
It was not the soldiers that ended the strike, and it was not the older railroad brotherhoods that refused to join us. It was the federal courts. Once we were restrained from acting as officers of the union and then arrested, our men were left without leadership, and the strike collapsed.

Document 7
Source: Manifesto of the Workingmen's Party of California, led by Denis Kearney, 1877 (paraphrase).
The railroad and land monopolists have filled our state with cheap Chinese labor to grind down the wages of white workingmen. We declare that the Chinese must go, and we will use the ballot to drive out both the Chinese laborer and the monopolists who import him.

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: The most important factor limiting organized labor from 1877 to 1898 was the alliance of government and courts with employers, because troops and especially federal injunctions turned strikes that workers might win against one company into contests they could not win against the state (Docs 5, 6); employers' own weapons (Docs 3, 4) and divisions among workers by skill, race and nationality (Docs 2, 7) mattered too, but chiefly by leaving unions too weak to withstand that state power.
parts.n: A list of factors with no ranking restates the prompt; the thesis must weigh the factors and set up the line of reasoning the essay follows.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Describe the rise of industrial capitalism after the Civil War: railroads, steel and other industries consolidated into national corporations employing thousands of wage workers, many of them immigrants, as machines deskilled crafts. The depressions after the panics of 1873 and 1893 brought repeated wage cuts and layoffs, while laissez-faire ideas and Social Darwinism taught that unions interfered with natural economic law, setting the stage for bitter conflict.
parts.n: 'The Gilded Age was a time of industrialization' is a phrase, not a description; context must describe developments and lead into the prompt.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence from the documents: plan which documents support which part of the argument.
parts.a: Paragraph 1, government and courts as the decisive factor: Doc 5 (the injunction forbids even persuading workers to strike), Doc 6 (Debs says the courts, not soldiers, ended the strike). Paragraph 2, employer power: Doc 4 (yellow-dog agreements make union membership grounds for firing), Doc 3 (Harper's portrays labor protest as bomb-throwing violence, turning middle-class opinion against unions). Paragraph 3, divided workers: Doc 2 (skilled unionists see immigrant families as undercutting them), Doc 7 (California workers target Chinese laborers), Doc 1 (the Knights' broad cooperative goals contrast with the AFL's narrow aims).
parts.n: Quoting or listing documents earns at most 1 point; for 2 points, at least four documents must be described and used to support the argument about relative importance.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents: choose one piece and say where it goes.
parts.a: In paragraph 1 or 2: the Homestead Strike (1892), where Henry Clay Frick locked out the Amalgamated Association, brought in about 300 Pinkerton guards, and, after a deadly battle, the Pennsylvania governor sent some 8,000 militia who let strikebreakers reopen the mill, destroying the union. It shows private force and state power working together. (Also usable: President Hayes's use of federal troops in the Great Railroad Strike of 1877.)
parts.n: The outside evidence must be described, not just named, and must differ from the evidence used for contextualization.

parts.q: Row D · Sourcing: plan two sourcing explanations.
parts.a: Doc 3: Harper's Weekly addressed a middle-class national audience, and its purpose was to depict the Haymarket events as anarchist violence, so the image shows how the press shaped public opinion against unions, a reason labor lost public sympathy. Doc 6: Debs spoke to a federal commission shortly after defeat, and as union president he had a reason to blame the courts rather than his own strategy of a national boycott; yet Doc 5 corroborates his claim that the injunction was the decisive weapon.
parts.n: Identifying the author or audience alone earns nothing; explain how that point of view, purpose, situation or audience matters to the argument.

parts.q: Row D · Complexity: plan how the essay shows a complex understanding.
parts.a: Show change over time in the decisive factor: in 1877 and 1892 labor lost mainly to troops, militia and private guards, but by 1894 the federal injunction (Doc 5) let courts defeat a strike without a battle, a shift confirmed by In re Debs (1895). Then qualify: the AFL, organizing skilled workers with narrow goals (Doc 2), survived where the Knights (Doc 1) and the American Railway Union collapsed, so labor's own strategy and divisions shaped which unions endured.
parts.n: A single sentence of 'however' or a one-line mention of another cause is not complexity; it must be developed as part of the argument.

rows.earns: A defensible claim that weighs the factors and establishes a line of reasoning, in one place, e.g.: government and court support for employers mattered most, because injunctions and troops made strikes unwinnable, while employer tactics and worker divisions mattered mainly by weakening unions.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('many factors limited labor'), or listing factors with no judgment of relative importance.

rows.earns: Describes a broader development relevant to the prompt, beyond a phrase: e.g., the post-Civil War rise of national corporations, deskilling and wage labor, and the depressions after 1873 and 1893 that brought wage cuts.
rows.loses: A single phrase ('it was the Gilded Age'), or context that has nothing to do with labor.

rows.r: Row C · Evidence from the documents
rows.earns: 2 points: uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument about which factors mattered most (e.g., Docs 5 and 6 for courts, Doc 4 for employers, Doc 7 for racial division). 1 point: accurately describes the content of at least three documents on the topic.
rows.loses: Quoting or listing documents without describing them, or describing them without tying them to the argument (caps at 1 point).

rows.r: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents
rows.earns: One specific, described piece of evidence not in the documents and different from the context, used for the argument: e.g., the Homestead Strike (1892) and the state militia, the Great Railroad Strike (1877), In re Debs (1895), or the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882).
rows.loses: A name with no description ('Homestead'), or evidence already used as context.

rows.earns: For two documents, explains how or why point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience is relevant to the argument: e.g., Harper's middle-class audience and the press's role in turning opinion against unions; Debs's position as defeated union leader and why he blamed the courts.
rows.loses: Identifying the source ('Debs was a union leader') without explaining why it matters to the argument.

rows.earns: A complex understanding woven into the argument, e.g.: explains how the decisive factor changed from troops and private guards to the court injunction; or weighs outside forces against labor's own strategies (the AFL's survival versus the Knights' collapse); or uses all seven documents effectively.
rows.loses: A passing mention of another view or a single 'however' sentence.

frq.title: LEQ · Federal policy toward American Indians, 1865-1898
frq.stem: Evaluate the extent to which federal policy toward American Indians changed from 1865 to 1898.

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: Federal policy changed substantially in its methods, from making treaties and forcing Plains nations onto reservations by war in the 1860s and 1870s to dissolving tribal landholding and culture through allotment and boarding schools in the 1880s and 1890s, but its underlying goal did not change: transferring Native land to settlers and ending tribal independence.
parts.n: 'Policy changed a lot' restates the prompt; the thesis must judge the extent and name what changed and what stayed the same.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Describe the pressures behind policy: after the Mexican War and the gold rushes, and with the Civil War over, the transcontinental railroad (1869), mining strikes and the Homestead Act drew hundreds of thousands of settlers onto the Plains, while commercial hunters destroyed the bison. Earlier removal of eastern nations in the 1830s had pushed Native peoples west of the Mississippi, and now there was no farther west to move them to.
parts.n: Context must be described, not named; 'Manifest Destiny' as a phrase earns nothing without the developments that brought settlers west.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence: plan the body paragraphs and their evidence.
parts.a: Paragraph 1, changes in method: the Fort Laramie Treaty (1868) still dealt with the Lakota as a nation, but the Indian Appropriations Act (1871) ended treaty-making; after Little Bighorn (1876) the U.S. seized the Black Hills; the Carlisle school (1879) and the Dawes Act (1887) replaced confinement with assimilation, allotting 160-acre parcels and selling 'surplus' land. Paragraph 2, continuity of aim and force: gold in the Black Hills broke the 1868 treaty just as earlier treaties had been broken, army campaigns continued to Wounded Knee (1890), and Native land fell from about 138 million acres (1887) toward 48 million by 1934.
parts.n: Two named events earn 1 point; 2 points require specific evidence used to support the argument about extent of change.

parts.q: Row D · Analysis and reasoning: plan the reasoning and the complexity.
parts.a: Frame the essay as continuity and change: the method moved from war and reservations to legal and cultural assimilation, while the goal of land transfer stayed constant. For complexity, explain multiple perspectives: reformers such as Helen Hunt Jackson (A Century of Dishonor, 1881) saw allotment as humane, yet it cost more land than the wars; and Native peoples shaped the outcome, preserving cultures through movements like the Ghost Dance and by keeping languages and kinship alive under assimilation pressure.
parts.n: Mentioning reformers or Native resistance once is not complexity; it must be explained as part of the argument about extent.

rows.earns: A defensible claim about the extent of change that sets up a line of reasoning, e.g.: methods shifted from war and treaties to allotment and assimilation, but the goal of taking Native land and ending tribal sovereignty stayed the same.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt, or a claim with no judgment of extent.

rows.earns: Describes the broader situation, beyond a phrase: e.g., railroads, mining and homesteading drawing settlers onto the Plains after the Civil War, the destruction of the bison, and the legacy of earlier removal.
rows.loses: A single phrase ('westward expansion was happening') or unrelated context.

rows.earns: 2 points: uses at least two specific pieces of evidence to support an argument about extent (e.g., the 1871 end of treaty-making and the Dawes Act as change; broken treaties and Wounded Knee as continuity). 1 point: identifies specific relevant examples without using them for an argument.
rows.loses: Vague generalities ('the government was unfair to Native Americans') with no specific examples.

rows.earns: 1 point: uses continuity and change to structure the argument. 2 points: a complex understanding, e.g., explains both what changed and what continued, the gap between reformers' intentions and results, or Native agency in preserving culture, as part of the argument.
rows.loses: A narrative of events with no reasoning, or a one-line nod to complexity.

units.title: Period 7: 1890–1945
units.blurb: The Spanish-American War, muckrakers and the Square Deal, the Fourteen Points, the Harlem Renaissance, the New Deal agencies, Pearl Harbor, Korematsu and the atomic bomb. Contrasts and contextualization openers recur.
keys: Mahan's sea power and the hunt for markets produced the 1898 war with Spain, the Platt Amendment, the Philippine war and the Roosevelt Corollary.
Muckrakers spurred Progressive reforms from the 1906 Meat Inspection Act to the Federal Reserve and the 16th through 19th Amendments.
Submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram brought U.S. entry in 1917, but Lodge's Senate rejected Wilson's League of Nations.
War brought the Espionage and Sedition Acts, Schenck's clear and present danger test, the Great Migration and the 1919 Red Scare.
The 1920s set installment-plan consumerism, the Harlem Renaissance and flappers against nativist quotas, Scopes and Prohibition.
Margin speculation, weak banks and unequal incomes turned the 1929 crash into a Depression that Hoover's voluntarism could not stop.
FDR's New Deal, from the CCC and AAA to Social Security and the Wagner Act, built the modern welfare state and the Democratic coalition.
Pearl Harbor ended neutrality, and wartime mobilization ended the Depression, interned Japanese Americans (Korematsu) and built the atomic bomb.

units.title: Period 8: 1945–1980
units.blurb: Containment from the Truman Doctrine to detente, Korea and Vietnam, McCarthyism, Levittown, Brown through the Voting Rights Act, the Great Society, Friedan and Roe, Watergate and stagflation. Comparisons recur.
keys: Kennan's containment produced the Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan and NATO, and NSC-68 and Korea turned it into a global military commitment.
After the 1949 loss of China and the Soviet bomb, McCarthyism and HUAC hunted subversives until the 1954 Army-McCarthy hearings.
The GI Bill, Levittown and the 1956 Interstate Highway Act built a white suburban middle class and left cities segregated.
Brown v. Board (1954), the Montgomery boycott and Birmingham's televised violence forced the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Johnson's Great Society added Medicare, Medicaid and the War on Poverty while the Warren Court expanded rights from Gideon to Griswold.
Domino theory and the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution escalated Vietnam until Tet in 1968 broke public trust and Johnson's presidency.
After 1965 Black Power, the Chicano movement, AIM, Stonewall and second-wave feminists (NOW, Roe v. Wade) widened the rights revolution.
Watergate, stagflation and the 1973 oil embargo shattered trust in government, while Nixon's detente and Carter's Iran crisis closed the era.

units.title: Period 9: 1980–Present
units.blurb: Reagan's New Right and supply-side economics, the end of the Cold War, NAFTA, September 11 and Iraq, the 2008 crisis, immigration and marriage debates, and polarization. Comparisons with earlier eras recur.
keys: Stagflation, Watergate and backlash against Roe and busing built the New Right coalition that elected Reagan in 1980.
Reagan's supply-side tax cuts, deregulation and PATCO firings brought growth with a tripled debt, weaker unions and wider inequality.
Reagan's rearmament and SDI plus Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika ended the Cold War with the Wall's fall in 1989 and the USSR's in 1991.
NAFTA in 1994, the WTO and the internet drove globalization, boosting growth while hollowing out Rust Belt manufacturing.
Clinton's welfare reform and impeachment, then Bush v. Gore in 2000, showed partisan polarization hardening before September 11.
September 11 brought the Afghanistan and Iraq wars, the PATRIOT Act and DHS, and reopened the security-versus-liberty debate.
Subprime mortgages and deregulation caused the 2008 crisis, answered by TARP, stimulus, Dodd-Frank and Obama's Affordable Care Act.
Post-1965 immigration, the marriage fight from DOMA to Obergefell and the culture wars deepened polarization in a more diverse nation.

Migration and immigration in the 1990s and 2000s

frq.title: SAQ 1 · Why did the Cold War end? (secondary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

"Americans like to say that Ronald Reagan won the Cold War. The claim flatters us but misreads the evidence. By 1980 the Soviet economy was stagnating under central planning, a costly war in Afghanistan, and a military budget that consumed perhaps a sixth of national output. When world oil prices collapsed in the mid-1980s, the regime lost its main source of hard currency. The decisive choices were made in Moscow and in the streets of Eastern Europe: Mikhail Gorbachev opened political debate, loosened economic controls, and, above all, refused in 1989 to send tanks into Eastern Europe as his predecessors had in 1956 and 1968. American pressure raised the costs of a contest the Soviets were already losing, but the Cold War ended because Soviet leaders and East European citizens chose to end it."

Source: Miriam Calder, a fictional historian; the excerpt was written for this exercise and summarizes one side of a real historical debate.

parts.q: Describe the historian's argument about the end of the Cold War.
parts.a: The historian argues that the Cold War ended mainly because of Soviet internal weakness, a stagnant planned economy, the Afghan war, heavy military spending and falling oil revenue, and because of choices made by Gorbachev and East Europeans, above all his refusal to use force in 1989; U.S. pressure only raised the costs of a contest the Soviets were already losing.
parts.n: Quoting a sentence or saying 'the historian talks about the Cold War' earns nothing; the point needs the claim about which causes mattered most.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1980 to 1991, not directly mentioned in the excerpt, could be used to support the historian's argument.
parts.a: Poland's Solidarity movement supports it. The independent union, formed in 1980, survived martial law and won the partly free elections of June 1989, forming the first non-communist government in the bloc; once Gorbachev let that result stand, citizens in East Germany, Czechoslovakia and elsewhere toppled their regimes, showing the Cold War ending through East Europeans' choices rather than U.S. pressure.
parts.n: Naming Solidarity (or the Baltic independence movements, or the failed August 1991 coup) without explaining how it shows internal or East European causes earns nothing; the excerpt's own examples do not count.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1980 to 1991 could be used to challenge or modify the historian's argument.
parts.a: Reagan's military buildup and the Strategic Defense Initiative (1983) challenge it. Soviet leaders feared a high-technology arms race they could not afford, and after Reagan refused to give up SDI at Reykjavik (1986), Gorbachev accepted the INF Treaty (1987) on largely American terms, which suggests U.S. pressure shaped Soviet choices rather than only adding costs. U.S. aid to the Afghan mujahideen, which raised the cost of that war, is another answer.
parts.n: 'Reagan was a strong leader' is not a development; the answer needs a specific U.S. action and how it influenced Soviet decisions.

frq.title: SAQ 2 · Mobilizing the religious right (primary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the source below.

"Dear Friend, America is in trouble. For two decades judges and bureaucrats in Washington have driven prayer out of our public schools, legalized the killing of unborn children, and pushed an Equal Rights Amendment that would draft our daughters and weaken the family. Pornography fills our newsstands, and secular humanists write our children's textbooks. Millions of Christians have stayed home on Election Day, believing politics was not their concern. That must end. Please register to vote, register your neighbors, and send a gift today so that every member of Congress will know where moral Americans stand."

Source: A labeled composite paraphrase of fund-raising and voter-registration letters sent to supporters by national religious-conservative organizations, 1980-1981. It was written for this exercise and is not a quotation from any single letter.

parts.q: Describe the historical situation in which letters like these were written.
parts.a: They came from the conservative reaction to the changes of the 1960s and 1970s: Engel v. Vitale (1962) had barred state-sponsored school prayer, Roe v. Wade (1973) had legalized abortion nationwide, and the ERA, passed by Congress in 1972, was still being fought over in state legislatures. Evangelical leaders had just founded groups such as the Moral Majority (1979) to mobilize believers, and the 1980 campaign offered a candidate, Reagan, who embraced their agenda.
parts.n: 'It was the 1980s' only restates the date; the point needs the specific developments the letters react to.

parts.q: Explain how the purpose or the audience of the letters shaped their content.
parts.a: Written to evangelical supporters to raise money and register voters, the letters use alarm ('America is in trouble'), a list of threats to the family, and a villain (Washington judges and bureaucrats) to move readers to act; they overstate, for example claiming the ERA would draft daughters, because fear and moral urgency motivate donations and turnout better than balanced argument.
parts.n: Saying the letters are 'biased' earns nothing; explain how the goal of raising money and votes from believers produced the alarmed tone and chosen issues.

parts.q: Explain ONE way the religious right influenced U.S. politics in the period 1980 to 2001.
parts.a: It became a core Republican constituency. Evangelical voters helped elect Reagan in 1980, and in the 1990s the Christian Coalition's church-distributed voter guides helped Republicans win Congress in 1994; its issues, opposition to abortion and to same-sex marriage, entered the Republican platform and shaped laws such as the Defense of Marriage Act (1996).
parts.n: Naming the Moral Majority again describes the source; the point needs a specific political result with its link to religious conservatives.

frq.title: SAQ 3 · Where immigrants came from, 1970 and 2000 (non-text source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the chart described below.

Described chart: two stacked bars titled 'Foreign-Born Population of the United States by Region of Birth, 1970 and 2000.' The 1970 bar stands for about 9.6 million people; the 2000 bar for about 31 million. Shares are rounded from U.S. Census Bureau figures:
Region of birth · 1970 · 2000
Europe · about 62% · about 16%
Latin America · about 19% · about 52%
Asia · about 9% · about 26%
All other regions · about 10% · about 6%

parts.q: Identify ONE change shown in the chart.
parts.a: The foreign-born population more than tripled, from about 9.6 million in 1970 to about 31 million in 2000, and its main origin shifted from Europe (about 62 percent in 1970) to Latin America (about 52 percent in 2000) and Asia (about 26 percent).
parts.n: 'Immigration changed' is too vague; the point needs the direction of the change and at least one figure or region.

parts.q: Explain ONE cause of the change shown in the chart.
parts.a: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 ended the national-origins quotas that had favored Europeans since the 1920s and made family reunification the main basis for admission, so each Latin American or Asian immigrant could later sponsor relatives; wars in Central America and Southeast Asia and economic crises in Mexico pushed migrants toward U.S. jobs.
parts.n: Naming the 1965 law without explaining how it changed who could come (quotas ended, family preferences) earns nothing.

parts.q: Explain ONE effect of the change shown in the chart on U.S. politics or society in the period 1980 to 2001.
parts.a: Immigration became a political flashpoint. California voters passed Proposition 187 (1994) to deny public services to undocumented immigrants, Congress tightened enforcement in the 1996 immigration law, and the backlash in turn mobilized Latino voters, who swung toward the Democrats in California and grew into a force both parties courted.
parts.n: The effect must be tied to the change in the chart and fall within 1980-2001; 'America became diverse' without evidence earns nothing.

frq.title: DBQ · Conservatism and the federal government, 1980-2000
frq.stem:
Practice. The exam draws its DBQ from 1754 to 1980, so none comes from Period 9; this one practises the same seven-point skills on Period 9 content.

Evaluate the extent to which the conservative movement changed the role of the federal government in the United States from 1980 to 2000.

The documents are paraphrased for this exercise from the sources named in each source line; apart from the short passages in quotation marks in Documents 1 and 6, the wording is not a direct quotation.

Document 1
Source: Ronald Reagan, First Inaugural Address, January 20, 1981.
"In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem." The new president says he intends to curb the size and influence of the federal establishment, to respect the distinction between the powers granted to the national government and those reserved to the states or the people, and to lighten the tax burden so that Americans can work, save and invest.

Document 2
Source: A labeled composite paraphrase of speeches and leaflets at Solidarity Day, a march in Washington organized by the AFL-CIO, September 19, 1981.
The administration fired thousands of air traffic controllers for asking for a fair contract, and its budget cuts school lunches, job training and unemployment benefits while cutting taxes for the wealthy. We march to defend what working people won over fifty years: Social Security, the minimum wage, safety laws and the right to organize.

Document 3
Source: Federal spending and the top income-tax rate, compiled from Office of Management and Budget and Internal Revenue Service historical tables (figures rounded; outlays for fiscal years).
Year · Federal outlays (% of GDP) · Top federal income-tax rate (%)
1980 · 21 · 70
1985 · 22 · 50
1990 · 21 · 28
1995 · 20 · 39.6
2000 · 18 · 39.6

Document 4
Source: Ronald Reagan, remarks on signing the Social Security Amendments of 1983, April 20, 1983.
The president calls the law proof of the nation's ironclad commitment to Social Security. He says the bipartisan compromise rescues the system from insolvency and assures the elderly that their checks will keep coming, and that both parties accepted sacrifices, higher payroll taxes, a delayed cost-of-living increase and a gradual rise in the retirement age, to save it.

Document 5
Source: Contract with America, a platform signed by Republican candidates for the House of Representatives, September 1994.
The signers promise to end government that is too big, too intrusive and too free with the public's money, and pledge that within the first hundred days of a Republican Congress the House will vote on a balanced-budget amendment, a line-item veto, welfare reform with work requirements, tax cuts for families, and limits on federal mandates imposed on the states.

Document 6
Source: Bill Clinton, State of the Union Address, January 23, 1996.
"The era of big government is over." The president adds that the nation cannot go back to a time when citizens were left to fend for themselves, and calls for a smaller, less bureaucratic government that still protects Medicare, Medicaid, education and the environment.

Document 7
Source: Marian Wright Edelman, president of the Children's Defense Fund, an advocacy group for poor children, open letter to President Clinton urging him to veto the Republican welfare bill, 1995.
Ending the sixty-year federal guarantee of aid to poor children would be a moral and practical disaster. Block grants would let states cut benefits in hard times, and many more children would fall into poverty. She urges the president, a Democrat, not to sign away the safety net his party built.

rows.earns: A defensible claim about extent that sets up a line of reasoning, in one place, e.g.: conservatives changed the federal government's priorities, cutting top tax rates, deregulating, confronting unions and ending the welfare entitlement, and moved even Democrats to their terms, but they did not shrink its overall size or dismantle Social Security and Medicare, which proved too popular to cut.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('conservatives changed the government to some extent'), a claim with no line of reasoning, or a thesis split between introduction and conclusion.

rows.earns: Describes, beyond a phrase, the setting: the expansion of federal power from the New Deal through the Great Society, then the 1970s crises (stagflation, Watergate, tax revolts such as Proposition 13, backlash against busing and Roe) that discredited liberalism and built the New Right coalition that elected Reagan.
rows.loses: A phrase such as 'in the 1980s people wanted less government,' or context that describes Reagan's own policies (the topic itself) rather than the setting.

rows.r: Row C · Evidence from the documents
rows.earns: 2 points: uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument about extent (e.g., Doc 1's goal of curbing federal power against Doc 3's steady outlays; Doc 4's rescue of Social Security; Doc 5's program; Doc 6's Democratic acceptance of smaller government; Doc 7's warning about the welfare entitlement's end). 1 point: accurately describes the content of at least three documents.
rows.loses: Quoting or listing documents without describing their content, or describing them without tying them to the claim about extent.

rows.r: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents
rows.earns: One specific piece of evidence not in the documents, described and tied to the argument, e.g., deregulation from airlines (1978) to the Garn-St Germain Act (1982) and the savings and loan collapse; the 1996 welfare law's work requirements and time limits; the 1995-96 government shutdowns over Medicare; Gramm-Leach-Bliley (1999). It must differ from the evidence used for context.
rows.loses: A name dropped without description, or the same evidence used for the contextualization point.

rows.r: Row D · Sourcing (point of view, purpose, historical situation, audience)
rows.earns: For at least two documents, explains how or why the sourcing matters to the argument, e.g., Doc 4: Reagan, facing the 1984 election, wanted credit for protecting Social Security, which shows conservatives' limits; Doc 6: Clinton, after the 1994 Republican sweep and before his reelection, adopted conservative language to win the center, which shows how far the terms of debate had moved.
rows.loses: Merely identifying the author or date ('Doc 6 is by Clinton') without explaining how the sourcing affects the argument.

rows.earns: Demonstrates a complex understanding, e.g., distinguishes rhetoric from results (Docs 1 and 3: tax rates fell sharply while spending barely moved), explains both change and continuity, or connects the era to the Gilded Age's laissez-faire or to the New Deal it tried to roll back, with evidence woven into the argument.
rows.loses: A single sentence saying 'there were both changes and continuities' with no explanation or evidence.

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: From 1980 to 2000 the conservative movement changed the federal government's direction more than its size: it cut top tax rates from 70 to under 40 percent, deregulated industries, weakened unions and ended the federal welfare entitlement, and it pushed even Democrats to declare big government over, yet federal spending stayed near a fifth of GDP and Social Security and Medicare survived because voters defended them.
parts.n: 'Conservatives changed government a lot' sets up no line of reasoning; the thesis must name what changed and what did not.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Describe how federal power grew from the New Deal (Social Security, regulation, union rights) through the Great Society (Medicare, Medicaid, the War on Poverty), then how the 1970s undermined confidence in it: stagflation defied Keynesian fixes, Watergate bred distrust, Proposition 13 (1978) showed a tax revolt, and backlash against busing, Roe and the ERA mobilized evangelicals, so a New Right coalition was ready to elect Reagan in 1980.
parts.n: Several sentences that describe the setting and link it to the prompt; a one-line mention of stagflation is a phrase, not context.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence from the documents: plan the body paragraphs.
parts.a: Change: Doc 1 announces the goal of curbing federal power and taxes, and Doc 3 shows the top rate falling from 70 to 28 percent by 1990; Doc 5 pledges a balanced budget and welfare reform; Doc 6 shows a Democratic president accepting that 'the era of big government is over'; Doc 7 shows the welfare entitlement under threat and its defenders' fears. Limits: Doc 3 shows outlays near 21 to 22 percent of GDP through the 1980s, and Doc 4 shows Reagan rescuing Social Security rather than cutting it; Doc 2 shows organized labor resisting.
parts.n: Use at least four documents to support the argument, describing their content in your own words rather than quoting.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents: choose one piece.
parts.a: The 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Act, signed by Clinton after two vetoes, replaced AFDC with TANF block grants, work requirements and a five-year lifetime limit, the clearest case of conservative ideas changing a New Deal-era program. Alternative: the Garn-St Germain Act (1982) and the savings and loan collapse that cost taxpayers roughly 124 billion dollars.
parts.n: Describe it and tie it to the argument; it must differ from the evidence used for context.

parts.q: Row D · Sourcing: plan two sourcing explanations.
parts.a: Doc 4: signing the bill a year before his reelection campaign, Reagan had a political purpose in stressing his 'ironclad commitment' to the elderly, which shows how popular programs limited conservative cuts. Doc 6: speaking to a national audience in an election year, after Republicans had swept Congress in 1994, Clinton had reason to adopt conservative language, which shows how far conservatives had shifted the terms of debate.
parts.n: Each sourcing move must explain how the purpose, audience, situation or point of view matters to the argument, not merely name it.

parts.q: Row D · Complexity: plan the complexity move.
parts.a: Distinguish rhetoric from results: Docs 1 and 3 together show that tax rates fell sharply while spending barely changed, because defense rose and entitlements proved untouchable; then connect across periods, since the conservative program echoed Gilded Age laissez-faire, yet unlike the 1890s the New Deal state's core survived, which is why the change was one of direction more than size.
parts.n: The complexity must be part of the argument and explained with evidence; a closing line that the question is 'complicated' earns nothing.

frq.title: LEQ · The end of the Cold War and U.S. foreign policy, 1980-2011
frq.stem: Evaluate the extent to which the end of the Cold War changed United States foreign policy in the period from 1980 to 2011.

rows.earns: A defensible claim about extent that sets up a line of reasoning, e.g.: the end of the Cold War changed the targets and justifications of U.S. foreign policy, from containing the Soviet Union to regional wars, humanitarian interventions and then terrorism, but it did not change the underlying pattern of global military presence and willingness to intervene that ran from Reagan through Obama.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('the end of the Cold War changed foreign policy in many ways') or a claim that sets up no line of reasoning.

rows.earns: Describes the broader setting beyond a phrase: e.g., the Cold War framework built after 1945 (containment, NATO, nuclear deterrence, proxy wars from Korea to Vietnam) and the collapse of detente after the 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iranian revolution.
rows.loses: A phrase such as 'the Cold War was a long conflict' or context unconnected to the question of change.

rows.earns: 2 points: uses at least two specific pieces of evidence to support an argument about extent (e.g., the Reagan Doctrine and the military buildup; the 1991 Gulf War coalition; Somalia and Rwanda; Bosnia, Dayton and Kosovo; NATO expansion in 1999; the 2001 invasion of Afghanistan and the 2003 Bush Doctrine war in Iraq). 1 point: identifies two specific, relevant examples without using them to support an argument.
rows.loses: General statements ('America fought many wars') with no specific example.

rows.earns: 1 point: uses continuity and change to frame the argument. 2 points: demonstrates a complex understanding, e.g., explains both change (new enemies, humanitarian missions, preemption) and continuity (global bases, alliances, interventionism), or connects the post-1991 debates over using American power to earlier debates such as those after World War I or Vietnam.
rows.loses: Listing events in order without explaining what changed and what persisted, or a one-line nod to complexity.

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: The end of the Cold War changed the enemies and stated purposes of U.S. foreign policy, from containing the Soviet Union to reversing regional aggression, stopping ethnic cleansing and, after 2001, fighting terrorist networks, but it changed little in the habit of global intervention, since presidents from Reagan to Obama kept worldwide forces and used them repeatedly.
parts.n: 'To a large extent' without saying what changed and what did not sets up no line of reasoning.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Describe the Cold War framework: after 1945 the United States built containment around NATO, nuclear deterrence and interventions from Korea to Vietnam; detente in the 1970s collapsed after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (1979), and the Iranian revolution and hostage crisis left Americans feeling weak, the setting Reagan's policies answered.
parts.n: Must describe, in a few sentences, the situation the essay measures change against.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence: plan the body paragraphs and their evidence.
parts.a: Cold War policy, 1980-1991: the Reagan Doctrine (aid to the mujahideen and Contras), the buildup and SDI, Grenada, then the INF Treaty and the Soviet collapse. Change after 1991: the UN-backed Gulf War, humanitarian missions in Somalia and the Balkans, inaction in Rwanda, NATO expansion (1999). Change after 2001: the war on terror, Afghanistan, the Bush Doctrine of preemption and the Iraq War. Continuity: global bases, alliances and repeated interventions, through bin Laden's killing in 2011.
parts.n: Each piece must be specific and explicitly tied to the claim about extent.

parts.q: Row D · Analysis and reasoning: plan the reasoning and the complexity.
parts.a: Frame each paragraph as change or continuity and explain why: the Soviet collapse removed the organizing enemy and the Soviet check, so new missions appeared, while the institutions and assumptions of the Cold War, alliances, forward bases and faith in American power, carried over. For complexity, explain both, and connect the 1990s debate over when to use force (Somalia, Rwanda, Kosovo) to the earlier post-Vietnam debate and the War Powers Resolution.
parts.n: The complexity must be explained with evidence; a final sentence that 'there was both change and continuity' earns nothing.

units.ced: AP United States History Course and Exam Description, Effective Fall 2026

units.title: Exam Craft
units.blurb: Exam format and timing, the SAQ, DBQ and LEQ rubrics point by point, causation, comparison and continuity essays, then practice theses, sourcing sentences and contextualization openers. Includes the May 2027 changes.
keys: The 3-hour-15-minute Bluebook exam weighs 55 multiple-choice questions (40%), three SAQs (20%), the DBQ (25%) and the LEQ (15%).
From May 2027 all three SAQs are required, each with a source, and everyone answers one LEQ prompt, while the rubrics are unchanged.
A multiple-choice answer must trace back to the stimulus, so read the whole set first and skip any question you cannot narrow.
Each SAQ part scores independently, and briefly explain demands one specific fact plus a sentence tying it to the question.
A thesis earns its point only by taking a defensible position with a line of reasoning, never by restating the prompt.
Contextualization needs two or three sentences describing broader developments before, during or after the prompt's time frame.
The DBQ rewards using six documents to support an argument, one piece of outside evidence and HIPP sourcing on three documents.
Complexity is earned across the essay by qualifying, corroborating or linking periods, and the LEQ must run on causation, comparison or CCOT.

cards.q: Date the boundary years of AP Period 1 and name the event that marks each end.
cards.a: 1491 to 1607. The period opens in 1491, the last year before Columbus's 1492 voyage began sustained contact, so that it starts with Native societies on their own terms rather than as a prologue to Europe; it closes in 1607 with the founding of Jamestown, England's first permanent colony, which opens Period 2 (1607-1754).
cards.h: → two years, each tied to one event
cards.n: Writing 1492 as the start earns nothing on a periodization question: the CED deliberately begins one year before contact.

cards.q: State the three developments the College Board identifies as defining Period 1.
cards.a: (1) Native populations migrated across North America and built distinct, increasingly complex societies by adapting to and transforming diverse environments (KC-1.1). (2) Contact among Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans produced the Columbian Exchange and social, cultural, and political change on both sides of the Atlantic (KC-1.2). (3) Within that contact, Europeans and Native Americans asserted divergent worldviews on religion, gender, family, land use, and power.
cards.h: → three key concepts, one sentence each
cards.n: 'Columbus discovered America' as the defining development earns nothing; the CED frames the period around Native adaptation, exchange, and divergent worldviews.

cards.q: Place these early colonial events in order: Treaty of Tordesillas, Columbus's first voyage, founding of Jamestown, Pueblo Revolt.
cards.a: Columbus's first voyage (1492) → Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) → founding of Jamestown (1607) → Pueblo Revolt (1680). The first two fall in Period 1; Jamestown closes it; the Pueblo Revolt is a Period 2 event that grew out of Period 1 Spanish colonization of New Mexico.
cards.h: → four events, earliest first, with years
cards.n: Borrows from u2: Jamestown and the Pueblo Revolt sit in Period 2. Placing Tordesillas before Columbus earns nothing; the treaty divided lands his voyage had just claimed.

cards.q: Describe the historical context of the Americas in 1491 that a contextualization paragraph for a Period 1 prompt should establish.
cards.a: The Americas in 1491 were densely and diversely peopled, not empty. Tens of millions of Native people lived in societies ranging from the Aztec and Inca empires to Pueblo irrigation towns, Mississippian mound cities, Eastern Woodland farming villages, mobile Great Basin bands, and salmon-rich Northwest villages. These societies had adapted to and transformed their environments through maize agriculture, irrigation, trade networks, and varied social structures.
cards.h: → population + range of societies + tie to environment
cards.n: 'Before Columbus the land was untouched wilderness' earns nothing and is historically wrong; the point requires describing settled, varied, environment-shaping societies.

cards.q: Describe the developments within Europe before 1492 that set the context for its expansion into the Western Hemisphere.
cards.a: Late-medieval Europe was recovering population and trade after the Black Death, and its monarchs were centralizing power. Renaissance curiosity and the Crusades fed demand for Asian spices and silks; Italian and Muslim middlemen controlled the overland routes, so Atlantic states sought sea routes. Portugal had pushed down Africa's coast (Dias rounded the Cape in 1488), and Spain completed the Reconquista in 1492 with a crusading, conversion-minded monarchy.
cards.h: → four European developments, each tied to expansion
cards.n: Naming 'the Renaissance' as a phrase earns nothing; contextualization must describe how these developments pushed Europeans outward.

cards.q: Describe the West African context that shaped the Atlantic world before and after 1492.
cards.a: West Africa held powerful, commercially connected states. Trans-Saharan caravans had long carried gold, salt, and captives between empires such as Mali and Songhai and the Mediterranean, and slavery existed as an African institution. From the 1440s Portuguese ships traded on the coast for gold and enslaved people, building forts such as Elmina (1482) and sugar colonies on Atlantic islands. That existing trade is what European merchants later redirected toward the Americas.
cards.h: → African states + trade before and after the Portuguese
cards.n: Describing Africa only as a source of slaves earns nothing for context; the point requires the pre-existing states, trade, and Portuguese partnership that KC-1.2.II.C builds on.

cards.q: Explain how a response earns the contextualization point on a Period 1 prompt about the Columbian Exchange, and what falls short.
cards.a: The point requires describing a broader development before, during, or after 1492-1607 that is relevant to the topic, in more than a phrase. For example: two sentences on Portugal's fifteenth-century Atlantic voyages, its sugar-and-slave plantations on Madeira and Sao Tome, and the search for a sea route to Asia, then a link to the exchange of crops, animals, disease and people after 1492. Restating the prompt's dates or dropping the phrase 'Age of Exploration' earns nothing.
cards.h: → describe a broader development + link it to the prompt
cards.n: Contextualization that only restates the prompt's period ('in the 1500s Europeans explored') is the classic zero; the rubric says a phrase or reference is not enough.

cards.q: Describe the continuities in Native American life across North America that persisted through the first century of European contact.
cards.a: Across most of North America Native societies kept their basic patterns to 1607. Maize-beans-squash farming with seasonal hunting continued in the Eastern Woodlands, mobile bison hunting and foraging on the western Plains and Great Basin, and salmon-based villages in the Northwest. Native nations still controlled almost all land north of Mexico, governed themselves, and traded along existing networks; Europeans held only Spanish Florida, New Mexico and coastal contacts.
cards.h: → three kinds of continuity, with where
cards.n: 'Everything changed after 1492' earns nothing on a continuity task; the answer must name specific patterns that lasted and where.

cards.q: Compare the Americas of 1491 with the Americas of 1607 in population, political control, and economy.
cards.a: Change: Native population fell by an estimated 50-90 percent in contacted regions from epidemics, warfare and forced labor; Spain ruled the Caribbean, Mexico, Peru, Florida and New Mexico, and silver mining, encomienda and enslaved African labor tied the Americas to a global economy. Continuity: outside Spanish zones, Native nations still governed themselves by the same maize, hunting and fishing economies, and European settlement north of Mexico was a few outposts.
cards.h: → change on three axes, then the continuity
cards.n: A comparison that lists 1491 and 1607 facts without stating what changed and what stayed the same earns nothing; the similarity or difference must be stated.

cards.q: Identify the pattern of migration and settlement that produced the diversity of Native societies Europeans met after 1492.
cards.a: Ancestors of Native Americans entered the continent from Asia, most likely across the Bering land bridge and along the Pacific coast during the last Ice Age (commonly dated to at least 15,000 years ago), then spread south and east over millennia. As groups settled deserts, grasslands, woodlands, river valleys and coasts, they developed distinct languages, subsistence systems and social structures adapted to each environment, so 1491 America held hundreds of nations.
cards.h: → entry route + spread + adaptation → diversity
cards.n: The migration dating is approximate and debated among archaeologists; the CED tests the adaptation-to-environment pattern, not a date.

cards.q: Classify each development in the Americas across 1491-1607 as a CONTINUITY or a CHANGE, with one phrase of reasoning: maize-beans-squash farming in the Eastern Woodlands · Native control of the North American interior · population of the Caribbean islands · labor system on Hispaniola · animals used on the Great Plains · religion in central Mexico · trade networks of the Mississippi and Great Lakes · political rule in Peru · European settlement north of Mexico · the Atlantic as a highway for people, crops and disease · social structure of Spanish colonial towns · subsistence in the Great Basin
cards.a:
Eastern Woodlands farming → continuity (same crops and seasonal round to 1607)
Native control of the interior → continuity (Europeans held only coastal and Southwest outposts)
Caribbean population → change (Taino collapse from disease and forced labor)
Hispaniola labor → change (encomienda, then enslaved Africans)
Plains animals → change beginning (horses spread after Spanish arrival, mostly after 1607)
Religion in central Mexico → change (Catholic missions, syncretism with Native practice)
Mississippi and Great Lakes trade → continuity (networks persisted, now carrying some European goods)
Rule in Peru → change (Inca replaced by Spanish viceroyalty after 1533)
European settlement north of Mexico → change but small (St. Augustine 1565, New Mexico 1598)
The Atlantic → change (Columbian Exchange makes it a two-way route)
Spanish colonial society → change (casta hierarchy created)
Great Basin subsistence → continuity (mobile foraging unchanged)
cards.h: → label each, then the one-phrase reason
cards.n: Labeling without the reason earns nothing on a continuity-and-change task; the reasoning phrase is the scored move.

cards.q: Explain why historians treat 1491 as a meaningful starting point for United States history rather than 1492.
cards.a: Starting in 1491 makes Native societies the baseline rather than a prologue to Europe. The story then begins with tens of millions of people in complex, environment-adapted societies, so change after 1492 is measured against what existed and Native peoples appear as actors, not as an empty stage.
cards.h: → Native baseline first → contact measured as change to existing societies → Natives as actors
cards.n: 'Because that is the year before Columbus' restates the date and earns nothing; the point is what the baseline does for the analysis.
o: A 1492 start would define Native peoples by European arrival, while 1491 lets their own migrations, adaptations and political systems count as history.
Beginning before contact turns the Columbian Exchange into a measurable transformation of existing societies rather than a discovery of new land.

w.a: Historians start in 1491 because that is the last year before Columbus sailed.
w.why: restates the date without saying why a pre-contact baseline matters

w.a: Historians start in 1491 because nothing important happened in the Americas before Europeans arrived.
w.why: false and the opposite of the CED's point about complex Native societies

w.a: Historians start in 1491 because the Aztec Empire was founded that year.
w.why: invented fact; Tenochtitlan dates to about 1325 and the Triple Alliance to 1428

cards.q: Explain why Europe, rather than a Native American or West African power, initiated sustained transatlantic contact in the 1490s.
cards.a: Europeans combined means and motive. Portugal and Spain had a generation of Atlantic sailing experience, caravels, compasses and charts, and monarchs willing to fund voyages. They had reasons to sail: a sea route to Asian wealth around Muslim and Italian middlemen, rivalry, and a crusading drive to spread Christianity.
cards.h: → Atlantic experience + ships and instruments + royal funding → plus wealth, rivalry, religion motives → voyages
cards.n: 'Because Europeans were more advanced' earns nothing; the answer must name the specific maritime means and the specific motives.
o: Iberian states had spent the fifteenth century learning Atlantic winds and currents on the African coast, so the westward crossing was an extension of an existing enterprise.
West African and Native American states were oriented toward land-based or coastal trade networks and had no comparable incentive to seek an ocean route to Asia.

w.a: Europe initiated contact because Columbus was the first person brave enough to sail into the unknown.
w.why: individual bravery explains nothing about why Iberian states funded and repeated such voyages

w.a: Europe initiated contact because Native Americans had no boats.
w.why: false; coastal and river peoples used sophisticated canoes, and it ignores Europe's means and motives

w.a: Europe initiated contact because the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 completely cut off all trade with Asia.
w.why: overstated; Asian goods still reached Europe, and the claim omits ships, funding and religion

cards.q: Explain why the century after 1492 brought far greater change to the Caribbean, Mexico, and Peru than to the interior of North America.
cards.a: Spain went where dense populations and silver promised wealth and labor. Taino, Aztec and Inca lands were conquered, emptied by epidemics, and reorganized under encomienda, mining and missions. The North American interior held no such prize, so Europeans touched it only by disease, trade goods and expeditions.
cards.h: → wealth and labor draw Spain south → conquest, disease, encomienda there → interior untouched except indirectly
cards.n: 'Spain just did not get there yet' earns nothing; the point requires the pull of silver and dense populations and the resulting uneven change.
o: Change followed conquest, and conquest followed wealth: where there was silver and tribute-paying populations, Spanish institutions were built; elsewhere Spanish expeditions such as Coronado's found nothing worth holding.
Epidemics spread ahead of settlers, so even the interior changed demographically, but its political and economic structures survived because no colonial state replaced them.

w.a: The interior changed less because its Native peoples were stronger warriors than the Aztecs.
w.why: ignores that Spain chose targets by wealth and population, not by weakness

w.a: The interior changed less because Europeans did not know it existed until the 1700s.
w.why: false; Coronado and de Soto crossed it in the 1540s

w.a: The interior did not change at all because no Europeans settled there.
w.why: overstates the continuity; disease and trade goods reached the interior before settlers

cards.q: Explain why the Columbian Exchange is a turning point in world history rather than only in the history of the Americas.
cards.a: The exchange ran both ways, worldwide. American maize and potatoes fed population growth in Europe, Africa and Asia; American silver flowed via Spain and Manila to China; Eurasian animals, crops and diseases remade American populations; and demand for labor redirected the African slave trade across the Atlantic.
cards.h: → two-way flows → Old World crops and silver effects, American disease and animal effects, slave trade redirected
cards.n: 'The Columbian Exchange changed everything' with no specific exchange named earns nothing; each direction needs a named item and its effect.
o: European societies shifted from feudalism toward capitalism partly on American mineral wealth, so the exchange changed Europe's economic structure, not just its diet.
The demographic effects alone were global: the Americas lost most of their people while Old World populations grew on American crops.

w.a: The Columbian Exchange was a world turning point because Columbus proved the earth was round.
w.why: myth; educated Europeans already knew the earth was round, and it names no exchange

w.a: The Columbian Exchange mattered to the world because Europeans brought civilization to the Americas.
w.why: a value judgment, not a described exchange, and it ignores the flows toward Europe, Africa and Asia

w.a: The Columbian Exchange was mainly about Native Americans catching smallpox.
w.why: one effect in one direction; it misses crops, silver, animals and the slave trade

cards.q: Explain why most Native nations north of Mexico still governed themselves in 1607 despite a century of European contact.
cards.a: European presence north of Mexico was tiny and coastal. Spain held only St. Augustine (1565) and a few New Mexico settlements (1598); French and English efforts were voyages, fishing stations and the failed Roanoke colony. With no settlers, soldiers or missions inland, Native nations kept land, leaders and economies.
cards.h: → few Europeans, only coastal outposts → no colonial state inland → Native sovereignty persists
cards.n: 'Native Americans resisted successfully' alone earns nothing here; the continuity came mostly from the absence of a colonial presence, which the answer must describe.
o: Spanish colonization followed silver and dense populations, and North America offered neither, so the interior was left to Native control by default.
The tools that later broke Native sovereignty, permanent settler colonies and sustained warfare, only began with Jamestown and its successors after 1607.

w.a: Native nations still governed themselves in 1607 because Europeans respected their sovereignty.
w.why: false; Spain claimed everything by papal grant and conquered wherever it chose

w.a: Native nations still governed themselves because no European had yet reached North America.
w.why: false; Spain had Florida and New Mexico, and French and English ships had visited for a century

w.a: Native nations still governed themselves in 1607 because the Pueblo Revolt had driven the Spanish out.
w.why: wrong period; the revolt came in 1680, seventy-three years later

cards.q: Identify the Pueblo peoples and how they adapted to the arid Southwest.
cards.a: Pueblo peoples (Hopi, Zuni, Acoma, Rio Grande towns) were sedentary maize farmers of the arid Southwest. They met aridity with irrigation canals, terraces, check dams and dry-farming, and built permanent multi-story adobe and stone towns. Maize surpluses supported dense settlement, craft specialization and religious hierarchy, the KC-1.1.I.A chain from maize to economic development, settlement and social diversification.
cards.h: → environment → techniques → settlement and society
cards.n: 'They lived in adobe houses' describes without connecting to aridity; the point requires the adaptation (irrigation) and its social result.

cards.q: Identify the subsistence pattern of Great Plains and Great Basin peoples before contact.
cards.a: Largely mobile hunting and gathering. Great Basin peoples (Ute, Shoshone, Paiute) moved in small bands through a seasonal round of pine nuts, seeds, roots and small game because the desert could not feed large settled groups. Western Plains peoples (such as the Apache) followed bison herds on foot, using dogs to haul goods; some eastern Plains groups (Mandan, Pawnee) also farmed maize in river valleys. Mobility was the adaptation to aridity and grassland (KC-1.1.I.B).
cards.h: → mobility + resource base, two regions
cards.n: Describing Plains peoples as horse-mounted buffalo hunters earns nothing for 1491: horses arrived with the Spanish and spread mostly after 1600.

cards.q: Identify the Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) and their form of political organization.
cards.a: An Iroquoian-speaking people of present-day New York who combined maize-beans-squash farming with hunting and lived in palisaded longhouse villages. Five nations (Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca; the Tuscarora joined in the 1720s) formed the Iroquois Confederacy, a council of chiefs chosen by clan mothers in a matrilineal society where women controlled fields and households. It illustrates complex social structure among mixed-economy villages (KC-1.1.I.C).
cards.h: → region + subsistence + council + women's role
cards.n: The founding date of the Confederacy is debated (before 1600, possibly as early as the 1100s); do not invent one. Illustrative example, not a required name.

cards.q: Identify the Algonquian peoples of the Atlantic seaboard.
cards.a: A large family of Algonquian-language peoples of the Eastern Woodlands and coast (Powhatan, Wampanoag, Narragansett, Pequot, Lenape). They mixed maize, beans and squash farming with hunting, fishing and shellfish gathering, moving seasonally between villages, fields and hunting grounds; this mixed economy favored semi-permanent villages under sachems (KC-1.1.I.C). They were the first peoples the English met at Roanoke, Jamestown and Plymouth.
cards.h: → what the name covers + economy + settlement
cards.n: Illustrative example. 'Algonquian' names a language family, not one nation; treating Powhatan and Wampanoag as one people earns nothing on a comparison task.

cards.q: Identify Cahokia and the Mississippian culture.
cards.a: The Mississippian culture (roughly 800-1500 CE) of the Mississippi and Ohio valleys built maize-based chiefdoms with earthen platform mounds, ranked societies and long-distance trade. Its largest center, Cahokia near present-day St. Louis, peaked around 1050-1150 CE at a population commonly estimated at 10,000-20,000, the largest settlement north of Mexico, and was largely abandoned by about 1350-1400: farming producing complex settlement (KC-1.1.I.C).
cards.h: → culture + city + scale + dates
cards.n: Population estimates vary (some run to 30,000) and the decline's causes are debated; give a range, not a single confident number.

cards.q: Identify the Chinook and other Pacific Northwest peoples.
cards.a: Peoples of the Northwest coast and Columbia River (Chinook, Kwakwaka'wakw, Haida, Tlingit) who did not farm but lived in permanent cedar plank-house villages on the ocean's wealth: salmon runs, shellfish, sea mammals and timber. Stored surpluses supported dense populations, craft specialization (canoes, totem poles), hereditary rank and the potlatch gift-feast. They show settled, stratified society built on ocean resources rather than agriculture (KC-1.1.I.D).
cards.h: → resource + settlement type + rank
cards.n: Saying they were 'simple hunter-gatherers' earns nothing; the KC's point is settled communities supported by ocean resources.

cards.q: Identify the Chumash and other Native peoples of present-day California before contact.
cards.a: California peoples (Chumash, Pomo, Miwok, Yokuts and many others) lived by hunting and gathering, above all acorns ground into meal, plus fish, shellfish and game. Mild climate and varied resources let them live in relatively dense, semi-permanent villages with great linguistic diversity; the coastal Chumash built plank canoes, used shell-bead money and traded with the Channel Islands. Like the Northwest, California shows settled life without farming (KC-1.1.I.D).
cards.h: → staple food + other resources → settlement type
cards.n: Specific nation names are illustrative; the scored idea is hunting and gathering supporting settled communities, which contradicts 'no farming means nomadic'.

cards.q: Describe how the Ancestral Puebloans and the Hohokam transformed the Southwest environment before 1491.
cards.a: They engineered water. The Hohokam of the Salt and Gila valleys (present-day Arizona) dug hundreds of miles of irrigation canals to grow maize, beans, squash and cotton in the desert. Ancestral Puebloans at Chaco Canyon built multi-story great houses, roads and water-control systems around 850-1150 CE, then dispersed during drought to the Rio Grande and Hopi mesas. Both cases show societies transforming, not merely enduring, an arid environment (KC-1.1.I.A).
cards.h: → each society's technique + what it built + the outcome
cards.n: Illustrative examples. Chaco's decline is usually linked to drought and is debated; 'they mysteriously vanished' earns nothing because Pueblo peoples are their descendants.

cards.q: Describe the mixed agricultural and hunter-gatherer economy of the Eastern Woodlands and the settlement pattern it produced.
cards.a: Eastern Woodland peoples farmed maize, beans and squash in cleared fields, then supplemented crops with deer hunting, fishing, shellfish and gathered nuts and berries. Because fields fixed people in place for the growing season while game and fish drew them out seasonally, they built permanent or semi-permanent villages (longhouses, wigwams, palisades) near fields and rivers, moving when soils and firewood were exhausted. Mixed economies favored villages (KC-1.1.I.C).
cards.h: → crops + wild foods → village pattern
cards.n: Listing foods without connecting them to the village pattern is description; the KC asks why mixed economies favored permanent villages.

cards.q: Describe the division of labor by gender in Eastern Woodland farming societies before contact.
cards.a: Women did most of the farming: planting, tending and harvesting maize, beans and squash, gathering wild plants, and controlling fields and household goods; men hunted, fished, cleared land, traded and fought. In matrilineal societies such as the Iroquois, descent passed through mothers and clan mothers chose chiefs. Europeans, who saw farming as men's work, read this as Native men being idle and women overworked, one of the misunderstandings in KC-1.2.III.
cards.h: → who did which work → resulting power → European view
cards.n: Describing Native women as powerless earns nothing; the Woodland pattern gave women control of food production and, among the Iroquois, of political succession.

cards.q: Identify evidence that Native societies before contact were linked by long-distance trade networks.
cards.a: Archaeology shows goods moving hundreds of miles.
