Where one church dominated, dissenters such as Williams and Hutchinson were banished, which founded new havens like Rhode Island.

w.a: Pluralism grew because the colonies had no established churches.
w.why: false; Virginia and Massachusetts had established churches

w.a: Pluralism grew because Britain made all colonists Anglicans.
w.why: contradicts pluralism; Britain did not

w.a: Religious diversity grew because colonists stopped believing in God.
w.why: false; the Great Awakening shows intense belief

cards.q: Explain why a transatlantic print culture tied the colonies more closely both to Britain and to one another.
cards.a: Print moved along the same shipping lanes as goods. Colonial printers reprinted London news and British writers, so colonists read the same debates as Britons; they also exchanged one another's papers, so a Boston reader followed Philadelphia and Charles Town, building shared intercolonial knowledge.
cards.h: → print travels with trade → London news reaches colonists → papers swapped between colonies → a shared public
cards.n: Naming 'newspapers' without both directions of connection, to Britain and among colonies, misses KC-2.2.I.B's point.
o: By the 1740s printers in the major ports, several tied to Franklin's printing partnerships, swapped papers, knitting a colonial print network.
Whitefield was known everywhere because printers in every colony carried his journals and sermons.

w.a: Print culture tied the colonies to Britain because Britain wrote all their newspapers.
w.why: false; colonial printers ran their own papers

w.a: Newspapers mattered little because most colonists could not read.
w.why: false; literacy was high, especially in New England

w.a: Print culture separated the colonies from each other.
w.why: backwards; exchanged papers connected them

cards.q: Explain why Bacon's Rebellion is evidence that the goals of colonial leaders and colonists diverged.
cards.a: Governor Berkeley and his circle wanted peace with Native allies and the profits of the Native trade, while landless freedmen wanted Native land and frontier defense. When Berkeley refused war, Bacon's followers rebelled and burned Jamestown, and the crown's troops and inquiry that followed spread mistrust both ways.
cards.h: → elite want Native trade and peace; freedmen want land and defense → Berkeley refuses war → revolt → crown steps in
cards.n: Treating the rebellion as a fight for democracy misses KC-2.1.III.D's point: colonists split with their leaders over frontier defense and land.
o: The rebels' grievances, heavy taxes, a long-sitting assembly and weak frontier defense, match the issues KC-2.1.III.D lists.
London's response, recalling Berkeley and tightening royal oversight, shows mistrust running from Britain toward colonists too.

w.a: Bacon's Rebellion shows colonists wanted independence from Britain in 1676.
w.why: anachronism; the rebels claimed loyalty to the king

w.a: Bacon's Rebellion was a revolt of enslaved people against planters.
w.why: mostly freedmen and servants, though some Black Virginians joined

w.a: It proves leaders and colonists agreed on Native policy.
w.why: backwards; their disagreement caused the revolt

cards.q: Explain why most people accused of witchcraft at Salem in 1692 were women.
cards.a: Puritan belief held women weaker and more open to the devil, and many accused were women outside expected roles: widows, quarrelsome neighbors, and those holding or due to inherit property beyond male control. In a village strained by land disputes and frontier war, such women became targets.
cards.h: → belief in women's spiritual weakness + women outside male control → suspicion → land and war tensions focus it
cards.n: Illustrative. Carol Karlsen found accused women often stood to inherit property; 'Puritans hated women' alone earns nothing without that mechanism.
o: Most accusers were also young women, whose accusations gave them a public voice rare in Puritan society, so gender shaped both sides of the trials.
Poor, older or marginal women, such as Sarah Good, lacked male protectors who might have shielded them.

w.a: Most accused were women because only women practiced witchcraft.
w.why: accepts the accusation as fact

w.a: Women were accused because Massachusetts barred women from church.
w.why: false; women were church members

w.a: The accused were women because the men were away fighting the Revolution.
w.why: wrong century; the trials were in 1692

cards.q: Contrast New England and the Chesapeake in motive, labor, and demographics.
cards.a: New England was settled by Puritan families seeking a godly community, with mixed farming, fishing, shipbuilding and trade, compact towns, long lives and balanced sex ratios. The Chesapeake was settled mostly by young single men seeking profit, with tobacco on scattered plantations, indentured and then enslaved labor, high death rates and few women. Yet both built elected assemblies and took Native land.
cards.h: → motive, economy, labor, demography for each + a similarity
cards.n: Two parallel lists without a stated difference earn nothing; say what differed and why (environment, migrants' goals). Adding a similarity is the complexity move.

cards.q: Contrast the Middle Colonies with New England in society and religion.
cards.a: New England was ethnically English, religiously Puritan (Congregational), town-centered and intolerant of dissent. The middle colonies were ethnically and religiously plural (Dutch, German, Scots-Irish, Quaker, Jewish), with dispersed commercial farms and larger estates growing wheat for export, and practiced legal toleration. The difference came from their founders: a covenanted Puritan community versus Dutch traders and Quaker proprietors seeking settlers.
cards.h: → ethnicity, religion, settlement, economy for each + why
cards.n: Middle-colony pluralism is a frequent LEQ root of American diversity; a list with no stated difference or reason earns less.

cards.q: Contrast slavery in the Chesapeake with slavery in South Carolina and the West Indies.
cards.a: Chesapeake slavery centered on tobacco, smaller holdings and closer white supervision under the gang system, and by the mid-1700s its enslaved population grew by natural increase. Lowcountry and West Indian slavery rested on rice and sugar, larger plantations and Black majorities, with far higher death rates that required constant imports, but also more cultural autonomy under the task system and among fewer whites.
cards.h: → crop, scale, demography, autonomy for each
cards.n: Treating slavery as one uniform institution loses the point; KC-2.2.II says it reflected each colony's economy, demography and geography.

cards.q: Contrast the Enlightenment and the First Great Awakening as forces in colonial life.
cards.a: The Enlightenment appealed to reason, science and natural law and spread mainly among educated elites through books and learned societies; the Great Awakening appealed to emotion and personal conversion and swept up ordinary people through mass revivals. Yet both taught colonists to trust their own judgment over inherited authority, and so both weakened deference.
cards.h: → how each differed + what they shared
cards.n: The shared effect is the sophistication move: opposite methods, converging consequence. A contrast with no similarity misses it.

cards.q: Compare Spanish and English colonizers' relationships with American Indians in the 1600s.
cards.a: Similarity: both took Native land by force and justified conquest with religion. Difference: Spain sought to incorporate Native peoples into colonial society as converts and laborers, through missions, tribute and intermarriage, so Native people lived inside the Spanish system; the English wanted Native land rather than Native labor, so they pushed Native peoples out and lived apart from them, with few missions and little intermarriage.
cards.h: → one similarity + one difference + the reason
cards.n: 'The Spanish were crueler' (or 'the English were kinder') earns nothing; the difference is incorporation versus separation, driven by labor versus land.

cards.q: Compare French and Spanish approaches to American Indians in North America between 1607 and 1754.
cards.a: Similarity: both sent Catholic missionaries, Jesuits for France and Franciscans for Spain, and relied on Native allies for defense. Difference: France traded for furs as a partner, adapting to Native diplomacy with gifts and intermarriage and settling few colonists; Spain ruled Native peoples as subjects, gathering them into missions and drawing tribute and labor from them, which provoked the Pueblo Revolt.
cards.h: → one similarity + one difference + the reason
cards.n: Listing French and Spanish traits in two paragraphs without naming a similarity or difference earns nothing.

cards.q: Compare the outcomes of the Pueblo Revolt (1680) and King Philip's War (1675-1676) for the Native peoples involved.
cards.a: Similarity: both were coordinated Native uprisings in the same decade against colonial pressure on land, labor and religion. Difference: the Pueblos drove the Spanish out for twelve years and, after the reconquest, won accommodation (no encomienda, some tolerance of their religion), while Metacom's coalition was crushed, its survivors killed, enslaved or scattered, and English settlement spread. Spain needed Pueblo labor and allies; the English needed only the land.
cards.h: → one similarity + the different outcomes + the reason
cards.n: Stopping at 'one succeeded, one failed' misses the reason, what each colonizer needed from Native people, which is the scored comparison.

cards.q: Classify each colony by region (New England, middle, Chesapeake, lower South, British West Indies) and name its main economic base around 1750: Massachusetts · Connecticut · Rhode Island · New Hampshire · New York · New Jersey · Pennsylvania · Delaware · Maryland · Virginia · North Carolina · South Carolina · Georgia · Barbados · Jamaica
cards.a:
Massachusetts → New England; mixed farming, fishing, shipbuilding, Atlantic trade through Boston
Connecticut → New England; family farms, livestock and provisions for the West Indies
Rhode Island → New England; shipping from Newport, including rum and the slave trade
New Hampshire → New England; timber, ship masts and fishing
New York → middle; wheat and flour, the Albany fur trade, the port of New York
New Jersey → middle; grain and livestock farms
Pennsylvania → middle; wheat and flour shipped through Philadelphia
Delaware → middle; grain farms
Maryland → Chesapeake; tobacco (with some wheat), enslaved and servant labor
Virginia → Chesapeake; tobacco on slave plantations
North Carolina → grouped with the Chesapeake by the CED; tobacco, naval stores, small farms
South Carolina → lower South; rice and indigo, Black majority
Georgia → lower South; buffer colony, turning to rice once slavery was allowed (1751)
Barbados → British West Indies; sugar, Black majority
Jamaica → British West Indies; sugar, large Black majority
cards.h: → region; main economic base, each colony
cards.n: The CED pairs North Carolina with the Chesapeake (KC-2.1.II.A); putting Maryland among the middle colonies or Delaware in the South is the usual slip.

cards.q: Support the claim that the Atlantic slave trade shaped every region of British North America, not only the South, with two pieces of specific evidence.
cards.a: Evidence 1: New England's economy depended on the West Indies: merchants sold fish, timber and livestock to sugar plantations, distilled their molasses into rum, and Newport ships carried much of the colonial slave trade. Evidence 2: the middle colonies' port cities held large enslaved minorities, about a fifth of New York City's people around 1740, and the 1741 conspiracy trials show slavery's reach there. Both show slavery at work beyond the plantation South.
cards.h: → two specific pieces, each tied back to the claim
cards.n: Evidence must be specific and connected: 'the North had slaves too' names no evidence and earns nothing. The New York share is an estimate.

cards.q: Write a historically defensible thesis that establishes a line of reasoning for the prompt: 'Evaluate the relative importance of environmental factors in shaping the development of the British colonial regions from 1607 to 1754.'
cards.a: Environmental factors were the most important influence on the regions' economies and labor systems, because long growing seasons and fertile tidewater land made tobacco and rice plantations profitable in the South while thin soil and short seasons pushed New England toward family farms and trade; however, the migrants' own goals, Puritan community versus individual profit, shaped religion, family life and government more than the environment did.
cards.h: → a claim of relative importance + reasons that order it
cards.n: Restating the prompt ('environment was important') earns nothing; the thesis must weigh environment against another factor and preview the reasons.

cards.q: Evaluate whether this thesis earns the thesis point, and revise it if it does not: 'The British colonies developed in many different ways because of many different factors.'
cards.a: It does not earn the point: it makes no defensible claim and sets up no line of reasoning, since 'many ways' and 'many factors' name nothing. Revision: 'The British colonies developed into distinct regions mainly because environment decided which crops could be exported, which in turn decided labor: New England's small farms relied on family workers, while southern tobacco and rice plantations turned to indentured servants and then enslaved Africans.'
cards.h: → verdict + why + a revised thesis
cards.n: Vague 'many factors' claims are the most common thesis failure; a revision must name specific factors and say how they relate.

cards.q: Explain why the British colonies, despite their regional differences, had more in common with one another by 1754 than with New France or New Spain.
cards.a: They shared British institutions and exchanges their rivals lacked: elected assemblies and English law, Protestant churches revived together in the Great Awakening, common print, and British goods. New France and New Spain had no elected assemblies, one established Catholic church and far fewer settlers.
cards.h: → shared British law, assemblies, Protestantism, print and goods → common traits; rivals lack assemblies, settlers
cards.n: A list of regional differences answers the opposite question; the point is a similarity across regions, explained by shared British ties.
o: Every British colony relied increasingly on enslaved African labor, a common thread KC-2.2.II stresses, though its scale differed by region.
Colonists everywhere claimed the rights of Englishmen, which set them apart from the subjects of Catholic, absolutist France and Spain.

w.a: The British colonies were all identical by 1754.
w.why: overstated; the regions stayed distinct

w.a: They had more in common because they all grew tobacco.
w.why: false; only the Chesapeake and North Carolina did

w.a: The British colonies were like New France because both were Catholic.
w.why: false; the British colonies were overwhelmingly Protestant

cards.q: Explain why the Chesapeake and New England, despite different economies, both developed elected assemblies.
cards.a: The same causes worked in both: English charters and law gave colonists a claim to representation, distance and London's lax attention left them to govern themselves, and wide landholding created many voters. So Virginia's Burgesses (1619) and Massachusetts's General Court grew up despite different crops and faiths.
cards.h: → English rights + distance and neglect + wide landholding → assemblies in both despite different economies
cards.n: Citing only differences misses the question; a comparison essay earns analysis credit by explaining a similarity as well as a difference.
o: Elites ran both systems, planters in Virginia and godly town leaders in Massachusetts, so assemblies served local ruling groups in each.
Both resisted royal control, Massachusetts under the Dominion (1686-1689) and Virginia over taxation, showing a shared habit of self-rule.

w.a: Both had assemblies because the king ordered every colony to be a democracy.
w.why: false; the crown tolerated, not ordered, representation

w.a: New England had assemblies but the Chesapeake did not.
w.why: false; Virginia's House of Burgesses dates from 1619

w.a: Both developed assemblies because both grew tobacco.
w.why: false; New England grew no tobacco for export

cards.q: Explain why labor systems differed so sharply between New England and the southern colonies.
cards.a: Crops set the demand for labor. Tobacco, rice and sugar needed large work forces through long seasons for export profit, so southern planters imported servants and then enslaved Africans. New England's small family farms and short seasons needed only family hands, so slavery there stayed small, in households and ports.
cards.h: → staple crops need many workers → servants, then enslaved Africans; family farms need family labor → little slavery
cards.n: Crediting northern morality earns nothing; New Englanders held and traded slaves. Environment and crop explain the contrast.
o: Family migration gave New England a ready labor force of children, while the Chesapeake's skewed, short-lived population could not supply its own workers.
New England profited from slavery indirectly by supplying plantations, so the regions' labor systems were connected even as they differed.

w.a: The South used slaves because southern colonists were lazier.
w.why: a stereotype, not a cause

w.a: New England had no slavery at all.
w.why: false; slavery was legal and present there

w.a: Labor differed because the South had more Native people to enslave.
w.why: misses the main labor source, enslaved Africans

cards.q: Explain why Spanish colonial society incorporated Native peoples while English colonists mostly lived apart from them.
cards.a: Spain built its wealth on Native labor and tribute and saw conversion as the purpose of empire, so it drew Native people into missions, towns and a ranked, mixed casta society. English colonists wanted land to farm with their own families and servants, so they displaced Native peoples and kept apart.
cards.h: → Spain needs Native labor + conversion goal → incorporation; English need land, bring own labor → separation
cards.n: Borrows the casta system from u1. Moral contrasts ('the Spanish were crueler') earn nothing; the difference follows from labor versus land.
o: Spanish migration was mostly male, so Spanish men married or partnered with Native women, while English families often migrated together.
English missions were few (John Eliot's praying towns are the exception) because English colonies had little need of Native converts as workers.

w.a: The Spanish incorporated Native peoples because they saw them as equals.
w.why: false; incorporation was hierarchical

w.a: The English lived apart because no Native people lived near them.
w.why: false; they settled on Native land

w.a: Both empires treated Native peoples exactly the same way.
w.why: ignores the contrast the question asks about

cards.q: Date the boundary years of AP Period 3 and name the event that marks each end.
cards.a: Period 3 runs from 1754 to 1800. It opens with the fighting in the Ohio River valley that began the French and Indian War (the North American part of the Seven Years' War) and closes with the election of 1800, when power passed peacefully from the Federalists to Thomas Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans.
cards.h: → two years + the event that marks each end
cards.n: Starting the period in 1763 or 1776 misses the CED's framing: the imperial war of 1754 is the first cause of the crisis that follows.

cards.q: Place these founding documents in order and give each year: Constitution, Articles of Confederation ratified, Northwest Ordinance, Declaration of Independence, Bill of Rights.
cards.a: Declaration of Independence (1776) → Articles of Confederation ratified (1781) → Northwest Ordinance (July 1787) → Constitution written (September 1787; in effect 1789) → Bill of Rights ratified (1791).
cards.h: → five documents, earliest first, each with its year
cards.n: Dating the Constitution 1776 or placing it before the Northwest Ordinance loses the point; the Confederation Congress passed the Ordinance while the Convention still sat.

cards.q: Describe the three key concepts the CED uses to organize Period 3 (1754-1800).
cards.a: (1) British efforts to tighten imperial control after the Seven Years' War collided with colonial self-government, producing an independence movement and war (KC-3.1). (2) The Revolution's democratic and republican ideals inspired new experiments in government, from state constitutions to the Constitution and the first parties (KC-3.2). (3) Westward migration and competition over land, boundaries and trade intensified conflict among peoples and nations (KC-3.3).
cards.h: → three concepts, one sentence each
cards.n: Listing events (Stamp Act, Constitution, Jay's Treaty) without the process that links them describes nothing; each key concept is a cause-and-effect pattern.

cards.q: Describe the relationship between Britain and its mainland colonies around 1754 that a contextualization paragraph for a Period 3 prompt should establish.
cards.a: Around 1754 the mainland colonies were loyal, prosperous and largely self-governing. Under salutary neglect Britain enforced the Navigation Acts loosely, while elected assemblies controlled taxes and even royal governors' pay. Colonists bought ever more British goods and prized their rights as Englishmen, but felt little unity with one another. Their population, roughly doubling every generation, was pressing west toward French and Native lands.
cards.h: → loyalty + self-rule + trade ties + westward pressure
cards.n: Borrows from u2 (salutary neglect, assemblies, consumer goods). 'The colonies were under British rule' is a phrase, not a described context, and earns nothing.

cards.q: Classify each development under the Period 3 key concept the CED places it in, with a phrase of reasoning: KC-3.1 (imperial crisis and independence), KC-3.2 (new ideals and forms of government), or KC-3.3 (migration and competition over land, boundaries and trade): Stamp Act Congress · Pinckney's Treaty · the Northwest Ordinance's process for admitting states · Common Sense · Treaty of Greenville · Coercive Acts · state constitutions with strong legislatures · Spanish missions in California · Washington's Farewell warning against permanent alliances · The Federalist Papers · Pontiac's Rebellion · republican motherhood
cards.a:
Stamp Act Congress → KC-3.1 (united resistance to taxation without representation)
Pinckney's Treaty → KC-3.3 (Mississippi navigation with Spain)
Northwest Ordinance admission process → KC-3.3 (settlers moving west, new states)
Common Sense → KC-3.2 (republican ideals, attack on monarchy)
Treaty of Greenville → KC-3.3 (Native land ceded to the United States)
Coercive Acts → KC-3.1 (British punishment that united the colonies)
State constitutions → KC-3.2 (new experiments in government)
California missions → KC-3.3 (Spanish expansion, cultural blending)
Farewell Address on alliances → KC-3.3 (safeguarding a neutral nation among European powers)
Federalist Papers → KC-3.2 (debate over ratifying the Constitution)
Pontiac's Rebellion → KC-3.1 (aftermath of the Seven Years' War)
Republican motherhood → KC-3.2 (revolutionary ideals applied to women)
cards.h: → key concept + a reason, for each case
cards.n: Several items touch two concepts; the labels follow the CED's placement, and a label without the reason phrase shows no understanding of the pattern.

cards.q: Explain how a response earns the contextualization point on a Period 3 prompt about the causes of the American Revolution, and what falls short.
cards.a: It must describe, in more than a phrase, a broader development before or during the prompt's years and tie it to the topic. For example: the Seven Years' War roughly doubled Britain's debt and left it a vast territory to garrison, while it removed the French threat that had made colonists value British protection, so Parliament sought colonial revenue just as colonists needed Britain less. Restating the dates or writing 'tensions were rising' earns nothing.
cards.h: → the rule + a model context + what fails
cards.n: Using the Stamp Act itself as the context for the Revolution's causes earns nothing; it is evidence for the argument, not the broader setting.

cards.q: Explain why Period 3 begins in 1754 rather than in 1763 or 1776.
cards.a: The war that began in 1754 set the rest of the period in motion. Britain's victory brought the debt that drove the taxes after 1763, the western lands fought over into the 1790s, and the removal of France that made colonists less dependent on British protection.
cards.h: → 1754 war → debt, western land, France removed → new taxes, frontier conflict, independence movement
cards.n: 'Because the French and Indian War started then' names the event without showing how it caused what follows, and earns nothing.
o: Starting in 1763 would make the imperial crisis look sudden; starting in 1754 shows it grew out of how Britain won and paid for the war.
The contest for western land that opens the period in 1754 is still being settled in 1795 at Greenville and San Lorenzo, so the start date frames a continuity.

w.a: Period 3 begins in 1754 because the colonies declared independence that year.
w.why: false; independence came in 1776

w.a: Period 3 begins in 1754 because the Stamp Act was passed then.
w.why: wrong date; the Stamp Act was 1765

w.a: Historians chose 1754 because it is a round midpoint of the century.
w.why: arbitrary; ignores the war's causal role

cards.q: Explain why the struggle over self-government did not end when the colonies declared independence in 1776.
cards.a: Independence settled who would not rule America, not how Americans would govern themselves. The same fear of distant, unchecked power that drove resistance to Parliament shaped the weak Articles, the fight over ratifying the Constitution, and the 1790s party battles over federal power.
cards.h: → independence removes Britain → how Americans rule themselves stays open → Articles, ratification, 1790s parties
cards.n: 'Americans kept arguing' with no named debate earns nothing; the answer must name later conflicts and the shared fear of concentrated power.
o: Revolutionary ideals set a standard of consent and limited power that every new American government, state or national, then had to meet.
Americans disagreed over who counted as 'the people', so fights over suffrage, representation and slavery continued inside the new governments.

w.a: The Declaration of Independence created a complete national government in 1776.
w.why: it created no government; the Articles took effect in 1781

w.a: The struggle continued only because Britain kept fighting until 1783.
w.why: treats a political question as purely military

w.a: Once the king was gone, Americans agreed on how to govern.
w.why: false; ignores the Articles, ratification and party conflict

cards.q: Explain why competition for land west of the Appalachians links the beginning and the end of Period 3.
cards.a: Western land was the prize that opened and closed the period. Settler expansion into the Ohio valley sparked the 1754 war; British limits on expansion angered colonists after 1763; and in the 1790s the United States fought Native nations and bargained with Britain and Spain over forts and the Mississippi.
cards.h: → Ohio valley war 1754 → Proclamation anger 1763 → 1790s Indian wars and treaties with Britain and Spain
cards.n: Naming 'westward expansion' as a theme without the linked moments shows no continuity; the point is the same contest recurring.
o: American Indian nations sought to limit settlement throughout the period, first allied with France, then with Britain, then in confederacies against the United States.
European empires stayed in the contest to the end: Britain held western forts until Jay's Treaty and Spain controlled the Mississippi until Pinckney's Treaty.

w.a: Western land mattered only at the start of the period, in the French and Indian War.
w.why: ignores the Proclamation and the 1790s conflicts

w.a: The Proclamation of 1763 ended the contest by giving the West to colonists.
w.why: reversed; it barred settlement west of the Appalachians

cards.q: Identify the French and Indian War and give its dates.
cards.a: The French and Indian War (1754-1763) was the North American part of the global Seven Years' War (1756-1763). Britain, its colonists and some Iroquois allies fought France and most Native nations of the Ohio valley and Great Lakes, chiefly for control of the Ohio River valley. Britain won, and the Treaty of Paris of 1763 removed France from mainland North America.
cards.h: → dates + who fought + over what + outcome
cards.n: Giving 1756-1763 supplies the European war's dates; for U.S. history the fighting starts in 1754 in the Ohio valley.

cards.q: Identify the 1754 clash in the Ohio River valley that began the French and Indian War.
cards.a: In 1754 Virginia sent militia under a young George Washington to contest the forks of the Ohio, where the French had just built Fort Duquesne. After his men killed the French officer Jumonville in a skirmish that May, the French forced Washington to surrender at Fort Necessity on July 3, 1754. The clash grew into a war for the continent because both empires, and the valley's Native nations, saw the Ohio as the key to the interior.
cards.h: → place + who + what happened + why it escalated
cards.n: Treating the war as a European quarrel carried to America misses KC-3.1.I.A: it began over British colonial expansion into the interior.

cards.q: Identify the Albany Plan of Union and its author.
cards.a: The Albany Plan of Union was Benjamin Franklin's 1754 proposal, made at the Albany Congress of seven colonies meeting with Iroquois leaders, for a colonial union under a crown-appointed president-general and a grand council chosen by the assemblies, to manage defense and Native relations. Every colonial assembly rejected it, unwilling to give up taxing power, and the Crown never approved it.
cards.h: → author + year + what it proposed + its fate
cards.n: Calling it a step toward independence misreads it: it sought unity under the Crown for war with France, and its rejection shows how weak colonial unity was in 1754.

cards.q: Contrast French and British relations with Native peoples in North America.
cards.a: French relations rested on trade and alliance; British relations rested on land. Relatively few French colonists lived by the fur trade and sealed ties through gift-giving, intermarriage and missions, while far more numerous British colonists wanted farmland and pushed Native peoples off it. That is why most interior nations sided with France in 1754, and why France's defeat left them without their best ally.
cards.h: → one-line contrast + each empire's pattern + consequence
cards.n: 'The French were nicer to the Indians' earns nothing; the difference came from each empire's economic aims and numbers, which the answer must name.

cards.q: State how the Seven Years' War changed Britain's national debt and why that mattered for the colonies.
cards.a: The war roughly doubled Britain's national debt, to about £130 million by 1763, and Britain decided to keep about 10,000 troops in North America. Because Britons at home were already heavily taxed and the war had been fought partly to defend the colonies, ministers such as George Grenville concluded that colonists should help pay, which led to the Sugar Act (1764) and the Stamp Act (1765).
cards.h: → scale of the debt + the policy conclusion drawn from it
cards.n: Debt and troop figures are approximate and vary by source. 'Britain was in debt so it taxed them' earns little without the garrison cost and the argument that colonists benefited.

cards.q: Identify the terms of the Treaty of Paris of 1763.
cards.a: France gave up mainland North America: Canada and its lands east of the Mississippi went to Britain, and Louisiana west of the river, with New Orleans, had already passed to Spain in a secret 1762 agreement. Spain ceded Florida to Britain in exchange for the return of Havana. Britain now claimed everything east of the Mississippi.
cards.h: → who gained what, empire by empire
cards.n: Confusing it with the 1783 Treaty of Paris is the classic slip: 1763 ends France's mainland empire, 1783 recognizes the United States.

cards.q: Identify Pontiac's Rebellion.
cards.a: Pontiac's Rebellion (1763-1766) was a pan-Indian war in the Great Lakes and Ohio valley, led in part by the Ottawa leader Pontiac and inspired by the Delaware prophet Neolin's call to reject European ways. Angered by settlers crossing the mountains and by General Jeffery Amherst's end to customary gifts of goods and ammunition, warriors took most of the smaller British forts in the region, though not Detroit or Fort Pitt.
cards.h: → years + leaders + causes + what it achieved
cards.n: Explaining it only as loyalty to France misses KC-3.1.I.C: Native nations wanted continued trade with Europeans and protection of their land from settlers.

cards.q: Define the Proclamation of 1763.
cards.a: The Proclamation of 1763 was a royal order of October 1763 that drew a line along the crest of the Appalachians, closed the land beyond it to colonial settlement and to private land purchases from Native nations, and reserved it for Native peoples. Britain issued it to avoid another costly frontier war like Pontiac's Rebellion.
cards.h: → date + what it forbade + why Britain issued it
cards.n: Calling it a defense of Native rights misreads the motive: Britain wanted to cut military costs, and it later moved the line west by treaty (Fort Stanwix, 1768).

cards.q: Name the three developments of 1763 and put them in order.
cards.a: Treaty of Paris ending the French and Indian War (February 1763) → Pontiac's Rebellion (from May 1763) → Proclamation of 1763 (October 1763). The order carries the causation: peace removed France, Native nations rose against British rule and advancing settlers, and Britain answered with a settlement line.
cards.h: → three events of one year, earliest first
cards.n: Putting the Proclamation before Pontiac's Rebellion reverses cause and effect; the line was Britain's response to the uprising.

cards.q: Explain the consequences of the French and Indian War for Britain and its colonies.
cards.a: Victory left Britain with huge debts and a vast territory to defend, so it ended salutary neglect and began taxing the colonies. Colonists, freed from the French threat, needed British protection less and resented the new taxes and the limits on westward settlement, setting up the imperial crisis.
cards.h: → victory → debt and new land → taxes, troops, Proclamation → colonists less dependent, more resentful
cards.n: Listing effects ('debt, taxes, land') without linking Britain's needs to the colonists' reactions misses the causal chain the point requires.
o: The war gave colonists military experience and confidence, while British officers' contempt for colonial troops bred mutual distrust.
With France gone, American Indian nations could no longer play empires against each other, which provoked Pontiac's Rebellion and the Proclamation Line.

w.a: The war made the colonies independent because Britain lost.
w.why: false; Britain won

w.a: After the war, grateful colonists were closer to Britain than ever.
w.why: ignores the resentment the taxes and the line produced

w.a: The war's main consequence was that France took over Canada.
w.why: reversed; Britain took Canada from France

cards.q: Explain why the Ohio River valley became the flashpoint for war between Britain and France in 1754.
cards.a: The valley linked France's Canadian and Louisiana settlements, and its fur trade there depended on Native allies. Britain's fast-growing colonies, with Virginia land companies claiming the region, were pushing traders and settlers into it, so each empire saw the forks of the Ohio as the key to the interior.
cards.h: → French corridor and fur trade + British settlers and land claims push west → collision at the forks of the Ohio
cards.n: 'Both sides wanted land' earns little; name the French trade corridor and the British settler and speculator push that collided there.
o: Native nations of the valley, such as the Shawnee and Delaware, tried to keep their autonomy between the two empires, and both built forts to win them over.
The Ohio Company of Virginia's land grant gave colonial elites, Washington's patrons among them, a direct stake in pushing the French out.

w.a: The valley mattered because it held gold mines both empires wanted.
w.why: invented; the stakes were land, trade and routes

w.a: The war began there when the Iroquois attacked the French.
w.why: wrong trigger; Virginia militia under Washington clashed with the French

cards.q: Explain why colonists resented the Proclamation of 1763.
cards.a: Colonists had fought partly to open the Ohio valley, so a royal line closing it seemed to rob them of their victory. Speculators, including wealthy Virginians, held western claims, settlers were already crossing the mountains, and the order came from a distant government that was also adding troops and taxes.
cards.h: → fought to win western land → line closes it → speculators and settlers lose out → seen as imperial overreach
cards.n: 'They wanted more land' earns little unless tied to the war's aims and to the new, heavier British control after 1763.
o: The line treated colonists as subjects to be managed rather than as partners in the empire, feeding the constitutional grievances of the 1760s.
Keeping troops to police the line looked like a peacetime standing army, a classic threat to liberty in colonial eyes.

w.a: Colonists resented it because it forced them to move to Canada.
w.why: invented; it barred westward settlement and moved no one

w.a: Colonists resented it because it raised the tax on sugar.
w.why: confuses it with the Sugar Act of 1764

w.a: Colonists resented it because it handed the western land back to France.
w.why: France had just lost that land; the line reserved it for Native nations

cards.q: Explain why the end of French power in North America provoked Pontiac's Rebellion.
cards.a: With France gone, Native nations lost the rival empire they had used to win gifts and fair trade and to check settlement. Britain, under Amherst, cut gifts, restricted ammunition and let settlers cross the mountains, so Native peoples faced one empire bent on their land and struck back in 1763.
cards.h: → France removed → no rival empire to play off → Amherst cuts gifts, settlers advance → uprising
cards.n: 'They were loyal to France' earns nothing; the point is Native strategy, which relied on rivalry between empires to protect trade and land.
o: Neolin's religious call to reject European goods and ways gave the rising a unifying message across many nations.
British forts that stayed garrisoned after the peace looked like occupation rather than the trading posts Native allies expected.

w.a: Pontiac rebelled because Britain passed the Stamp Act.
w.why: wrong cause; the Stamp Act came in 1765 and taxed colonists

w.a: Native nations rebelled because France paid them to keep fighting after the war.
w.why: unsupported; the rising pursued Native aims

cards.q: Identify the Sugar Act of 1764.
cards.a: The Sugar Act (1764) was George Grenville's law that cut the duty on foreign molasses from sixpence to threepence a gallon but enforced it strictly, sending accused smugglers to vice-admiralty courts that sat without juries. Its stated purpose was to raise revenue from the colonies, not only to regulate trade, which is what colonial critics such as James Otis attacked.
cards.h: → year + what it changed + why colonists objected
cards.n: Saying it raised the tax is the trap: it lowered the rate. The grievances were strict enforcement, jury-less courts and the revenue purpose.

cards.q: Identify the Stamp Act of 1765.
cards.a: The Stamp Act (1765) required colonists to buy stamps for newspapers, pamphlets, legal documents, licenses, playing cards and other paper goods. It was Parliament's first direct internal tax on the colonies, meant to help pay for troops stationed in America, and it hit printers, lawyers and merchants hardest. Colonial resistance forced its repeal in 1766.
cards.h: → year + what it taxed + why it was new + outcome
cards.n: Calling it a tax on imports misses what made it explosive: it taxed everyday colonial paper inside the colonies, so it could not pass as trade regulation.

cards.q: Define virtual representation and state the colonial counterargument.
cards.a: Virtual representation was the British claim that every member of Parliament represented the whole empire, so colonists were represented even though they elected no members, like the many Britons who could not vote. Colonists answered that only actual representation counted: only a legislature they elected could tax them, which is why their own assemblies, not Parliament, held that power.
cards.h: → British claim + colonial reply
cards.n: Saying colonists mainly wanted seats in Parliament misstates their case; most argued that only their own elected assemblies could tax them.

cards.q: Identify the Stamp Act Congress and its central claim.
cards.a: The Stamp Act Congress met in New York in October 1765 with delegates from nine colonies. Its Declaration of Rights and Grievances professed loyalty to the king and accepted Parliament's general authority, but insisted that colonists, as British subjects, could be taxed only by their own elected assemblies: no taxation without representation.
cards.h: → year + who met + the claim + its limits
cards.n: Treating it as a call for independence misreads 1765; the claim was loyal and rested on the rights of British subjects.

cards.q: Identify the Sons of Liberty.
cards.a: The Sons of Liberty were groups of artisans, shopkeepers, laborers and some merchants and lawyers, formed in 1765 to resist the Stamp Act. They organized boycotts, printed propaganda, led crowd actions and pressured stamp distributors, such as Boston's Andrew Oliver, to resign, so the tax could never be collected.
cards.h: → who they were + when + tactics + result
cards.n: Describing them as elite Founders misses KC-3.1.II.C: their force came from laborers and artisans acting in the streets.

cards.q: Identify the Quartering Act of 1765.
cards.a: The Quartering Act (1765) required colonial assemblies to house and supply British troops stationed in their colonies. New York's assembly refused full compliance, and Parliament's Restraining Act of 1767 threatened to suspend it until it obeyed. Colonists saw both a tax imposed without their consent and a standing army kept among them in peacetime.
cards.h: → year + requirement + colonial response + why it was feared
cards.n: Saying it forced soldiers into private homes overstates the 1765 law, which used barracks, inns and empty buildings.

cards.q: Identify the Declaratory Act of 1766.
cards.a: Passed alongside the repeal of the Stamp Act in March 1766, the Declaratory Act asserted Parliament's full power to make laws binding the colonies 'in all cases whatsoever.' Britain retreated in practice but conceded nothing in principle, so the constitutional dispute over taxation stayed unresolved.
cards.h: → year + what it asserted + why it mattered
cards.n: Treating the repeal as a British surrender misses this act: celebrating colonists largely ignored it, and Parliament used the claimed power again in 1767.

cards.q: Identify the Townshend Acts of 1767.
cards.a: The Townshend Acts (1767) put duties on imported glass, lead, paint, paper and tea, created a customs board in Boston, and used the revenue to pay royal governors and judges, freeing them from colonial assemblies. Colonists answered with renewed boycotts and John Dickinson's argument that any duty meant to raise revenue was unconstitutional. Parliament repealed all but the tea duty in 1770.
cards.h: → year + what was taxed + use of revenue + response
cards.n: Stopping at the list of taxed goods misses the deeper grievance: paying officials from Crown revenue attacked the assemblies' power of the purse.

cards.q: Identify the Boston Massacre and give its date.
cards.a: On March 5, 1770, British soldiers stationed in Boston fired into a crowd that was taunting and pelting them outside the Custom House, killing five colonists, among them Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Native descent. John Adams defended the soldiers at trial: Captain Preston and six soldiers were acquitted and two were convicted of manslaughter.
cards.h: → date + what happened + the trials
cards.n: Taking the Patriot label 'massacre' at face value earns nothing on a sourcing task; the crowd's role and the acquittals complicate the propaganda.

cards.q: Identify the point of view and purpose of Paul Revere's engraving of the Boston Massacre (1770).
cards.a: Revere, a Boston silversmith and Son of Liberty, made the print weeks after the shooting to rouse colonists against the troops. It shows redcoats firing a volley on an officer's command into a calm, defenseless crowd beside a Custom House labeled 'Butcher's Hall', and omits the taunting and thrown objects described at the trials. As propaganda it is weak evidence of what happened but strong evidence of Patriot efforts to shape opinion.
cards.h: → maker's view + audience + purpose + effect on the image
cards.n: Reading the engraving as an accurate record earns nothing; sourcing credit needs the maker's purpose and how it shaped what the image shows and leaves out.

cards.q: Identify the Committees of Correspondence.
cards.a: Committees of Correspondence were networks of local Patriot committees that exchanged letters to share news and coordinate resistance. Samuel Adams launched Boston's committee in 1772, and in 1773 Virginia's House of Burgesses proposed committees linking the colonial legislatures. They built the communication system that made united action, including the First Continental Congress, possible.
cards.h: → what they were + who began them + when + result
cards.n: Confusing them with the Continental Congress misses their role: they were the network that came first and made a congress possible.

cards.q: Identify the Tea Act of 1773 and explain the colonial objection.
cards.a: The Tea Act (1773) let the struggling East India Company sell tea directly in the colonies through its own agents, making legal tea cheaper than smuggled Dutch tea while keeping the Townshend tea duty. Colonists objected that buying cheap taxed tea meant accepting Parliament's right to tax them, and merchants feared a monopoly that cut them out.
cards.h: → year + what it did + the two objections
cards.n: Saying colonists protested higher tea prices is the trap: the tea got cheaper. The objection was the principle of taxation plus monopoly.

cards.q: Identify the Boston Tea Party and give its date.
cards.a: On December 16, 1773, Sons of Liberty, some disguised as Mohawks, boarded East India Company ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of tea, worth roughly £10,000, after Governor Thomas Hutchinson refused to let the ships leave without unloading. Destroying private property divided colonial opinion and provoked Parliament's Coercive Acts.
cards.h: → date + what happened + why + consequence
cards.n: Presenting it as universally applauded misses the division it caused: Franklin and others urged paying for the tea, and Britain answered with the Coercive Acts.

cards.q: Identify the Coercive (Intolerable) Acts of 1774.
cards.a: The Coercive Acts (1774) punished Massachusetts for the Tea Party. The Boston Port Act closed the harbor until the tea was paid for; the Massachusetts Government Act curtailed the charter, made the council royally appointed and limited town meetings; the Administration of Justice Act let accused royal officials be tried outside the colony; and a new Quartering Act eased the housing of troops. General Thomas Gage became governor.
cards.h: → year + purpose + each component act
cards.n: Listing the Quebec Act as one of the four is a common slip; colonists grouped it with them, but Parliament passed it separately for other reasons.

cards.q: Identify the Quebec Act of 1774 and why colonists grouped it with the Intolerable Acts.
cards.a: The Quebec Act (1774) gave Quebec a government with no elected assembly, recognized the Catholic Church's position there, kept French civil law, and extended Quebec's boundary south to the Ohio River. Protestant colonists saw an unrepresentative, Catholic-tolerating regime planted on western lands they claimed, and, since it came the same year as the Coercive Acts, read it as part of a design against their liberties.
cards.h: → year + provisions + colonial reading
cards.n: Calling it a punishment for the Tea Party is wrong; Britain meant it to govern conquered French Canada, and colonists linked it to the Coercive Acts.

cards.q: Identify the First Continental Congress and its actions.
cards.a: The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in September and October 1774, with 56 delegates from twelve colonies (Georgia sent none). It endorsed the Suffolk Resolves, rejected Joseph Galloway's plan of union within the empire, adopted a Declaration and Resolves asserting colonial rights, created the Continental Association to enforce a boycott of British goods, and agreed to meet again in 1775.
cards.h: → when + who + what it did + what it did not do
cards.n: Saying it declared independence confuses it with the Second Congress; in 1774 it still sought redress within the empire.

cards.q: Date the First Continental Congress, the Second Continental Congress, and the Declaration of Independence.
cards.a: First Continental Congress: September-October 1774. Second Continental Congress: convened May 1775, weeks after Lexington and Concord. Declaration of Independence: adopted July 4, 1776, two days after Congress voted for independence on July 2.
cards.h: → three dates in order
cards.n: Collapsing these into one moment misses the point: nearly two years separate the first Congress from independence, and fighting began more than a year before the Declaration.

cards.q: Place these British measures in chronological order: Townshend Acts, Sugar Act, Coercive Acts, Stamp Act, Tea Act, Declaratory Act.
cards.a: Sugar Act (1764) → Stamp Act (1765) → Declaratory Act (1766) → Townshend Acts (1767) → Tea Act (1773) → Coercive Acts (1774). Each colonial protest was met by a new assertion of Parliament's authority, the action-and-reaction pattern that explains the escalation.
cards.h: → six measures, earliest first, with years
cards.n: Putting the Declaratory Act before the Stamp Act reverses the logic: it accompanied the Stamp Act's repeal in 1766.

cards.q: Contrast the colonial constitutional argument in 1765 with the argument by 1774.
cards.a: In 1765 colonists accepted Parliament's right to regulate imperial trade and objected only to taxes levied without their consent. By 1774 leading writers, such as Jefferson in A Summary View and John Adams as 'Novanglus', denied Parliament any authority over the colonies, claimed allegiance to the king alone, and rested their case increasingly on natural rights as well as the rights of Englishmen.
cards.h: → 1765 position + 1774 position + what changed
cards.n: Describing each year's protests without naming the shift in who could legislate for the colonies earns nothing on a change-over-time task.

cards.q: Explain why the Stamp Act provoked far broader colonial resistance than the Sugar Act.
cards.a: The Stamp Act was a direct internal tax that touched nearly every colonist and fell hardest on the most vocal groups, printers, lawyers and merchants, while the Sugar Act mainly affected merchants in the molasses trade. That breadth spread resistance from petitions to boycotts, crowds and an intercolonial congress.
cards.h: → internal tax on everyday paper → hits printers, lawyers, merchants → boycotts, crowds, Stamp Act Congress
cards.n: 'The Stamp Act cost more' misses the point; its breadth, its internal character and the groups it targeted explain the scale of resistance.
o: No one could defend a tax on colonial legal papers as trade regulation, so the Stamp Act made the constitutional issue of taxation without representation unmistakable.
Printers had to buy the stamps, so the newspapers that spread news of resistance had a direct stake in fighting the act.

w.a: Colonists ignored the Sugar Act because it raised molasses prices only slightly.
w.why: misstates it; the act cut the duty but enforced it strictly

w.a: The Stamp Act was the first tax Britain had ever placed on the colonies.
w.why: false; trade duties such as the Molasses Act of 1733 already existed

cards.q: Explain how nonimportation agreements and the Daughters of Liberty worked as resistance.
cards.a: Boycotts turned colonial buying power into political pressure. Merchants pledged not to import British goods, and women's spinning bees and homespun cloth replaced imports, so British merchants lost sales and lobbied Parliament, which repealed the Stamp Act and most Townshend duties.
cards.h: → refuse British goods, make homespun → British merchants lose sales → they lobby Parliament → repeal
cards.n: Describing spinning bees without the pressure on British merchants and Parliament shows no mechanism; the link to repeal is the point.
o: Boycotts drew women and ordinary households into public politics, since what a family bought or made became a patriotic act.
The committees that enforced nonimportation built local networks later used by the Continental Association of 1774.

w.a: The Daughters of Liberty fought as soldiers in the Continental Army.
w.why: wrong; they organized boycotts and homespun production

w.a: Nonimportation worked because the colonies stopped trading with every country.
w.why: overstated; the boycotts targeted British goods

w.a: Boycotts failed because Parliament never repealed any tax.
w.why: false; the Stamp Act and most Townshend duties were repealed

cards.q: Explain why the Coercive Acts united the colonies instead of isolating Massachusetts.
cards.a: Britain meant to make an example of Boston, but closing its port, rewriting a colonial charter and curbing town meetings showed every colony that Parliament could strip away its self-government at will. Other colonies sent food to Boston, and twelve sent delegates to the First Continental Congress in 1774.
cards.h: → punish Boston → any charter can be revoked → shared threat → aid to Boston and the First Continental Congress
cards.n: 'The colonies felt sorry for Boston' earns nothing; the threat to every colony's charter and assembly is the mechanism.
o: The Quebec Act of the same year seemed to confirm a plan to govern colonies without assemblies, so colonists read the laws together as a design against liberty.
Committees of correspondence already linked the colonies, so news of the acts spread fast and sympathy became coordinated action.

w.a: The Coercive Acts united the colonies because they taxed all thirteen equally.
w.why: wrong; they punished Massachusetts and levied no general tax

w.a: The colonies united because the acts declared war on America.
w.why: no war was declared; fighting began in 1775

cards.q: Explain how the Revolutionary War expanded colonial women's economic responsibilities.
cards.a: With husbands and sons in the army or militia, many women ran farms, shops and household finances themselves, bargained with buyers, and coped with shortages and occupying armies. Necessity gave them economic authority, but under coverture property and legal rights stayed with men after the war.
cards.h: → men leave to fight → women run farms, shops, money → wartime authority → no lasting legal change under coverture
cards.n: Claiming women won legal or voting rights from this work earns nothing; wartime authority rarely outlasted the war.
o: Women also supplied the army, raising money through groups such as the Ladies Association of Philadelphia (1780) and sewing shirts, so household labor became part of the war effort.
Shortages and inflation made managing a household a daily fight over prices, and some women led crowd actions against merchants accused of hoarding.

w.a: The war gave women the right to vote in every state.
w.why: false; only New Jersey briefly let property-owning women vote

w.a: Women's lives did not change in the war because they stayed at home.
w.why: ignores their running of farms, shops and supply

cards.q: Define republicanism as Americans of the Revolutionary era understood it.
cards.a: Republicanism was the belief that legitimate government rests on the people rather than on a hereditary monarch or aristocracy, with power exercised by elected representatives. A republic was thought to survive only through civic virtue: citizens who put the public good above private interest and were independent enough, usually through owning property, to judge freely.
cards.h: → source of power + form of rule + what it needs to survive
cards.n: Equating it with the later Republican Party or with direct democracy earns nothing; it meant representative rule by virtuous citizens without a king.

cards.q: Identify the thinker or text behind each idea that shaped revolutionary thought: natural rights to life, liberty and property · government by consent, with a right to alter or abolish it · separating legislative, executive and judicial power · standing armies and ministerial corruption as threats to liberty · an island should not rule a continent · hereditary rule is absurd since a wise king may leave a foolish heir · all men are created equal, with unalienable rights · no taxation without consent and trial by jury as English rights · no one may be compelled to support a church · resisting tyranny as a Christian duty
cards.a:
Natural rights to life, liberty and property → John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1690)
Consent and the right to alter or abolish → Locke, applied in the Declaration of Independence (1776)
Separation of powers → Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748)
Standing armies and corruption → English radical Whig writers, such as Trenchard and Gordon's Cato's Letters (1720s)
Island should not rule a continent → Thomas Paine, Common Sense (1776)
Hereditary rule is absurd → Paine, Common Sense
All men created equal → Jefferson, Declaration of Independence
English rights → Magna Carta (1215) and the English Bill of Rights (1689)
No compelled support of a church → Jefferson, Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom (1786)
Resisting tyranny as a duty → dissenting Protestant ministers, such as Jonathan Mayhew (1750 sermon)
cards.h: → thinker or text for each idea
cards.n: Names beyond Locke, Paine and the Declaration are illustrative; the exam tests the idea-to-source match, and crediting Locke with separation of powers is the classic miss.

cards.q: Explain how religion strengthened colonists' view of themselves as a people blessed with liberty.
cards.a: Protestant tradition taught colonists to see themselves as a covenanted people whose liberty came from God, and the First Great Awakening had accustomed many to questioning established authority and choosing their own ministers. Many Congregational and Presbyterian clergy preached resistance to tyranny as a religious duty and cast British measures as corruption, so defending liberty became a sacred cause.
cards.h: → covenant tradition + Awakening + sermons → sacred cause
cards.n: Borrows from u2 (First Great Awakening). 'Religion was important to colonists' is a phrase; the point needs the mechanism that linked faith to resistance.

cards.q: Identify Common Sense and its author.
cards.a: Common Sense was Thomas Paine's pamphlet of January 1776. Written in plain language for ordinary readers, it attacked monarchy and hereditary rule as absurd and contrary to scripture, argued that an island should not rule a continent, and urged immediate independence and a republic. It spread through many reprints and public readings; sales estimates range from tens of thousands to over 100,000.
cards.h: → author + date + argument + reach
cards.n: Saying Paine attacked Parliament's taxes misses his target: he attacked the king and monarchy itself, the last tie colonists still honored.

cards.q: Identify the Declaration of Independence and give its date and principal author.
cards.a: The Declaration of Independence, drafted chiefly by Thomas Jefferson for a committee of five, was adopted by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, two days after Congress voted for independence. It declared the united colonies free and independent states, justified separation by natural rights and government by consent, and listed grievances against George III.
cards.h: → date + author + what it declared + how it justified it
cards.n: Confusing it with the Constitution (1787) is the classic slip; the Declaration created no government.

cards.q: State roughly how many specific grievances the Declaration of Independence levels against George III, and give two examples.
cards.a: The Declaration lists about 27 grievances against George III. For example, he 'dissolved Representative Houses repeatedly' for opposing him, kept 'Standing Armies' among the colonists in peacetime without their legislatures' consent, and joined others in 'imposing Taxes on us without our Consent.' The list is the evidence that the king broke the contract, justifying separation.
cards.h: → approximate number + two examples + what the list proves
cards.n: The count varies slightly with how clauses are split. Citing Jefferson's attack on the slave trade as part of the final text is an error; Congress cut it.

cards.q: Identify Jefferson's Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom (1786).
cards.a: Drafted by Jefferson in 1777 and carried through the Virginia legislature by James Madison in 1786, the statute ended state support for the Anglican (Episcopal) Church, declared that no one could be compelled to attend or support any church, and protected freedom of belief. Jefferson counted it among his three proudest achievements, and it shaped the First Amendment's religion clauses.
cards.h: → author + year + what it did + later influence
cards.n: An illustrative example of Enlightenment ideas applied to religion. Saying it banned religion from public life misreads it: it ended compulsory support, not faith.

cards.q: Identify two later movements that used the language of the Declaration of Independence to press their claims.
cards.a: The women's rights movement: the Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments (1848) rewrote it to say 'all men and women are created equal.' The abolitionist movement: Frederick Douglass's 1852 Fourth of July address used its promise of equality to condemn slavery. Lincoln at Gettysburg (1863) and Martin Luther King Jr. (1963) invoked it too, showing how its ideals resonated through American history.
cards.h: → two movements + how each used the text
cards.n: Borrows from u4 and later periods. Naming a movement without showing how it used the Declaration's language of equality earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain why Common Sense was so influential.
cards.a: Paine moved the target from Parliament to the king and monarchy itself, breaking the last loyalty that held colonists back. He wrote in plain, biblical language that ordinary readers and tavern listeners could follow, and he published in January 1776, when months of war had made reconciliation look hopeless.
cards.h: → attacks monarchy itself + plain style for a mass audience + timing after fighting began → independence
cards.n: 'It convinced people to be independent' restates the effect; the point needs the argument, the audience and the timing.
o: By arguing that America could trade freely with the world, Paine made independence seem practical as well as right, answering fears that the colonies could not survive alone.
Reprinted across the colonies and read aloud, it reached people who never read legal pamphlets, widening the independence movement beyond elites.

w.a: Common Sense mattered because Congress required every colonist to read it.
w.why: invented; its reach came from reprints and readings

w.a: Common Sense was the first pamphlet to criticize British taxes.
w.why: false; tax protests began in 1764-1765

w.a: It was influential because Paine was a famous Virginia planter.
w.why: wrong; Paine was a recent English immigrant

cards.q: Explain the political theory underlying the Declaration of Independence.
cards.a: The Declaration applies Locke's social contract: people hold unalienable natural rights, governments exist by consent to secure them, and when a government becomes destructive of them the people may alter or abolish it. The grievances are the evidence that George III broke the contract, justifying separation.
cards.h: → natural rights → government by consent to secure them → right to abolish it → grievances prove the breach
cards.n: Naming 'Enlightenment ideas' or 'Locke' without the chain from rights to consent to revolution earns nothing; the reasoning is the point.
o: The document is built as a syllogism: the right of revolution is the major premise, the king's abuses the minor premise, and independence the conclusion.
By grounding rights in nature rather than in English charters, it claimed rights for all people, a universal promise later groups would use.

w.a: The Declaration argues that Parliament, not the king, should rule the colonies.
w.why: reversed; it rejected the authority of both

w.a: Its theory is that kings rule by divine right.
w.why: the opposite; it grounds power in consent

w.a: It rests on the Constitution's separation of powers.
w.why: anachronism; the Constitution came in 1787

cards.q: Explain why colonists' loyalty to the king weakened between 1763 and 1776.
cards.a: At first colonists blamed Parliament and ministers and appealed to George III as their protector. When he backed the Coercive Acts, rejected the Olive Branch Petition, proclaimed the colonies in rebellion and hired German troops, many decided the king himself was the tyrant; Paine's Common Sense finished the shift.
cards.h: → king seen as protector → he backs Parliament, rejects petitions, hires Hessians → king seen as tyrant → Common Sense
cards.n: Saying colonists 'always hated the king' ignores the change the question asks about; loyalty to the Crown was strong in the 1760s.
o: Once colonists denied Parliament's authority, their only link to Britain was the king, so his choices decided their loyalty.
Enlightenment ideas of government by consent gave colonists a standard for judging a monarch by whether he protected their rights.

w.a: Loyalty weakened because George III personally wrote the Stamp Act.
w.why: wrong; Grenville's ministry and Parliament passed it

w.a: Colonists turned on the king because he gave the Ohio valley to France.
w.why: invented; France lost that land in 1763

cards.q: Explain why the Declaration of Independence blamed George III rather than Parliament for the colonists' grievances.
cards.a: By 1776 Patriots held that Parliament had never had authority over the colonies, so their only tie to Britain ran through the king. Breaking that tie meant showing the king himself had violated the contract, and one named tyrant also made a clearer case to a 'candid world', including hoped-for allies such as France.
cards.h: → Parliament's authority already denied → king is the only tie → prove his tyranny → break it, win foreign support
cards.n: 'Because the king controlled Parliament' misreads the constitution; the point is that colonists had rejected Parliament, leaving only the king to renounce.
o: Common Sense had already turned opinion against monarchy itself, so the Declaration could build on that attack rather than on arguments about Parliament.
Foreign powers were likelier to aid a people rejecting a tyrant than subjects disputing tax law, so the framing served the aim of winning alliances.

w.a: The Declaration blamed the king because Parliament had voted for independence.
w.why: invented; Parliament never supported independence

w.a: It blamed the king because Parliament did not meet in 1776.
w.why: false; Parliament was passing laws against the colonies

cards.q: Identify the battles of Lexington and Concord and give the date.
cards.a: On April 19, 1775, British regulars marched from Boston to seize militia arms stored at Concord. They exchanged fire with militia on Lexington green, reached Concord, and were harried by thousands of militiamen firing from cover all the way back to Boston. These were the first battles of the Revolutionary War, fought more than a year before independence was declared.
cards.h: → date + what happened + significance
cards.n: Dating them after the Declaration reverses the order; the war began in April 1775 while Congress still hoped for reconciliation.

cards.q: Identify the Second Continental Congress and its major decisions.
cards.a: The Second Continental Congress convened in Philadelphia in May 1775. It created the Continental Army with George Washington as commander, printed paper money, sent the Olive Branch Petition to George III, opened diplomacy with foreign powers, declared independence in July 1776, and drafted the Articles of Confederation, acting as the national government without a written constitution until 1781.
cards.h: → when + key decisions + its unusual status
cards.n: Treating it as legally empowered from the start misses the point: it governed by the states' consent until the Articles took effect in 1781.

cards.q: Contrast Patriots and Loyalists in numbers and motivation.
cards.a: Historians estimate that roughly 40 to 45 percent of white colonists were active Patriots and 15 to 20 percent Loyalists, with the rest neutral or shifting. Patriots acted on constitutional rights, republican ideals and local grievances; Loyalists on allegiance to the Crown, office or trade ties, Anglican faith, fear of disorder, or distrust of Patriot elites. Many enslaved people and Native nations sided with Britain.
cards.h: → estimated shares + each side's motives
cards.n: The shares are estimates. Treating Loyalists as a handful of officials earns nothing; the Revolution was also a civil war that split communities and families.

cards.q: Identify Dunmore's Proclamation.
cards.a: In November 1775 Virginia's royal governor, Lord Dunmore, promised freedom to enslaved people and servants of rebels who escaped and fought for Britain. Hundreds joined his 'Ethiopian Regiment', and thousands more fled to British lines during the war. The offer terrified planters and pushed many wavering white Virginians into the Patriot camp.
cards.h: → who + when + the offer + effects
cards.n: Calling Dunmore an abolitionist misreads it: he freed only rebels' slaves to weaken the rebellion. The irony is Britain offering a liberty Patriots denied.

cards.q: Identify the Battle of Saratoga and give its year.
cards.a: In October 1777 American forces under Horatio Gates, with Benedict Arnold prominent in the fighting, defeated General John Burgoyne and forced his army to surrender at Saratoga in upstate New York. The victory wrecked Britain's plan to cut off New England along the Hudson and persuaded France to ally with the United States in 1778.
cards.h: → year + commanders + outcome + consequence
cards.n: Stopping at 'an American victory' misses why it matters; the point graders want is the French alliance it produced.

cards.q: Identify the European allies and volunteers who aided the Patriot cause and what each contributed.
cards.a: France, allied from 1778, sent money, arms, an army under Rochambeau and the fleet that trapped Cornwallis at Yorktown. Spain (at war with Britain from 1779 as France's ally) and the Dutch Republic (from 1780) stretched British forces worldwide, and Dutch bankers lent money. Volunteers included the Marquis de Lafayette, a trusted general; Baron von Steuben, who drilled the army at Valley Forge; and Thaddeus Kosciuszko, an engineer.
cards.h: → each ally or volunteer + what they gave
cards.n: Calling Spain a formal ally of the United States overstates it; Spain fought Britain as France's ally. Volunteers' names are illustrative.

cards.q: Support the claim that George Washington's leadership was essential to the Patriot victory with two pieces of specific evidence.
cards.a: Washington kept the army alive, which was the Patriots' path to victory. First, after losing New York in 1776, he recrossed the Delaware to win at Trenton (December 26, 1776) and Princeton, saving the army and its morale. Second, he held the army together through the Valley Forge winter of 1777-1778, where von Steuben's drilling made it a more professional force. His coordination with the French then produced the victory at Yorktown in 1781.
cards.h: → claim + two specific pieces, each tied to the claim
cards.n: Praising his character ('he was a great leader') is not evidence; each example must be specific and explain how it helped win the war.

cards.q: Identify the Battle of Yorktown and give its year.
cards.a: In 1781 Washington's Continental Army and Rochambeau's French troops besieged General Charles Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, while Admiral de Grasse's French fleet blocked rescue by sea. Cornwallis surrendered about 8,000 men on October 19, 1781, ending major fighting and leading Parliament to seek peace.
cards.h: → year + who + why the British were trapped + result
cards.n: Crediting the Americans alone misses the French army and fleet, without which the trap could not have closed.

cards.q: Identify the terms of the Treaty of Paris of 1783.
cards.a: Britain recognized American independence and set generous boundaries: the Mississippi River in the west, roughly the Great Lakes and Canada in the north, and the 31st parallel, bordering Spanish Florida, in the south. Americans kept fishing rights off Newfoundland, and Congress agreed that British creditors could collect prewar debts and to recommend that states restore Loyalist property. American Indian nations were not consulted.
cards.h: → recognition + boundaries + other terms + who was left out
cards.n: Missing the unmet debt and Loyalist clauses misses their sequel: Britain used them to justify keeping its western forts until Jay's Treaty (1794).

cards.q: Place these Revolutionary events in order: Yorktown, Lexington and Concord, Declaration of Independence, Saratoga, Treaty of Paris.
cards.a: Lexington and Concord (April 1775) → Declaration of Independence (July 1776) → Saratoga (October 1777) → Yorktown (October 1781) → Treaty of Paris (September 1783).
cards.h: → five events, earliest first, with dates
cards.n: Treating Yorktown as the end of the war is only half right: major fighting stopped in 1781, but peace was not signed until 1783.

cards.q: Explain why Saratoga was the turning point of the Revolutionary War.
cards.a: Saratoga convinced France that the Americans could win, so France signed an alliance in 1778 that brought money, troops and a navy. Spain and the Dutch Republic then joined the war against Britain, turning a colonial rebellion into a global war that stretched British resources and made Yorktown possible.
cards.h: → Saratoga victory → France convinced → 1778 alliance → money, troops, navy + wider war → Britain overstretched
cards.n: 'It was a big American win' earns nothing; the turning point is the causal link to the French alliance.
o: The surrender of a whole British army ended Britain's plan to isolate New England and pushed it to shift the war south.
News of Saratoga led Britain to offer the colonists everything short of independence in 1778, a sign that London itself saw the war turning.

w.a: Saratoga was the turning point because it was the last battle of the war.
w.why: false; Yorktown came four years later

w.a: Saratoga mattered because Washington captured Cornwallis there.
w.why: confuses Saratoga with Yorktown

w.a: Saratoga made Britain recognize independence at once.
w.why: wrong; recognition came in 1783

cards.q: Explain how the Americans won the Revolutionary War despite British advantages.
cards.a: Americans only had to survive, while Britain had to conquer and hold a vast territory 3,000 miles from home. Washington kept the Continental Army intact, militias and Patriot commitment controlled the countryside, and French money, troops and ships, with Spain and the Dutch also at war, tipped the balance.
cards.h: → Britain must conquer, Americans must survive → army preserved + militias hold countryside + French aid → victory
cards.n: Crediting one cause alone, French help or American virtue, earns less than a balanced answer that ties several causes to Britain's problems.
o: Britain's strategy relied on Loyalist support that proved weaker and less dependable than it expected, especially in the South.
Once it became a global war, the conflict grew costly and unpopular in Britain, so Parliament chose peace after Yorktown.

w.a: The Americans won because their army was larger and better trained than Britain's.
w.why: false; Britain had the stronger regular forces

w.a: The Americans won because Britain never sent soldiers to America.
w.why: false; Britain sent tens of thousands of troops

w.a: The Americans won because every colonist supported independence.
w.why: false; many were Loyalists or neutral

cards.q: Explain why Britain's southern strategy failed after 1780.
cards.a: Britain moved south expecting Loyalists to rise and hold what it won, and it took Savannah and Charleston. But raids and reprisals drove neutrals toward the Patriots, militia won at Kings Mountain, and Greene and Morgan wore Cornwallis down at Cowpens and Guilford Courthouse until he marched into the Yorktown trap.
cards.h: → counts on Loyalists → early wins → backcountry turns → militia and Greene wear Cornwallis down → Yorktown
cards.n: Naming Kings Mountain or Cowpens without explaining why Loyalist support failed shows no causation.
o: Britain could take southern ports but not hold the countryside, because militias and partisans such as Francis Marion kept rising behind its lines.
British reliance on escaped enslaved people and on Native allies in the South hardened white southern opposition.

w.a: The southern strategy failed because the South had no Loyalists at all.
w.why: false; Loyalists were numerous but less reliable than hoped

w.a: Britain lost in the South because the French captured Charleston.
w.why: invented; Britain held Charleston until late 1782

cards.q: Explain what happened to Loyalists after the Revolutionary War.
cards.a: Many Loyalists lost property to state confiscation laws and faced harassment, so an estimated 60,000 or more left, mostly for Nova Scotia and Quebec, others for Britain and the Caribbean. The treaty only 'recommended' restoring their property, though most who stayed were gradually reabsorbed.
cards.h: → Patriot victory → confiscation and harassment → emigration → weak treaty protection → most who stayed reabsorbed
cards.n: Emigration figures are estimates. Saying all Loyalists were executed or expelled earns nothing; most who stayed quietly rejoined their communities.
o: Black Loyalists who had escaped slavery were evacuated by the British, some to Nova Scotia and later Sierra Leone, while others were re-enslaved.
The Loyalist exodus helped shape English-speaking Canada, including the creation of New Brunswick in 1784.
