w.a: All Loyalists were executed for treason after the war.
w.why: false; confiscation and exile, not mass execution

w.a: Loyalists kept their property because the Treaty of Paris guaranteed it.
w.why: the treaty only recommended restoration

cards.q: Define republican motherhood.
cards.a: Republican motherhood was the post-Revolutionary ideal that women served the republic by teaching republican values, virtue and patriotism, to their children, especially sons, within the family. It gave women a new importance in political culture and justified better schooling for girls, such as the Young Ladies' Academy of Philadelphia (1787), while still keeping women out of voting and office.
cards.h: → what it asked of women + what it gave + its limit
cards.n: Calling it a step toward women's suffrage misreads it: it gave women a civic role through the family, not the ballot.

cards.q: Identify Abigail Adams's 'Remember the Ladies' letter to John Adams.
cards.a: In a March 1776 letter, Abigail Adams asked her husband John, then in the Continental Congress, to 'remember the ladies' in the new code of laws and not to put 'unlimited power' into the hands of husbands. Turning the Revolution's own language on him, she warned that women would not be bound by laws in which they had 'no voice, or representation.' John Adams dismissed the request.
cards.h: → date + audience + what she asked + how it was received
cards.n: Saying she demanded the vote overstates the letter; she asked for legal limits on husbands' power, and it is an illustrative example of women's appeals.

cards.q: Identify Judith Sargent Murray and her argument in 'On the Equality of the Sexes.'
cards.a: Judith Sargent Murray was a Massachusetts writer whose essay 'On the Equality of the Sexes' (written in 1779, published in 1790) argued that women's apparent intellectual inferiority came from unequal education, not from nature, and that girls should be educated like boys. She applied Enlightenment ideas of reason and equality to women, an early example of women's appeals for expanded roles.
cards.h: → who + work and date + argument + significance
cards.n: An illustrative example. Saying she demanded political rights misstates her focus: she argued for equal education and intellectual equality.
x: On the Equality of the Sexes

cards.q: Identify the 'Molly Pitcher' legend and the broader role of women who followed the Continental Army as camp followers.
cards.a: 'Molly Pitcher' is largely a legend, a composite often linked to Mary Ludwig Hays, said to have carried water to soldiers and served a cannon at the Battle of Monmouth (1778). It stands for thousands of real women who followed the Continental Army as camp followers, cooking, washing, nursing and hauling water in return for rations, and a few, such as Margaret Corbin, who fought.
cards.h: → legend vs. history + what camp followers did
cards.n: Treating Molly Pitcher as one documented person earns nothing; the point is the real support work of the women whose service prompted republican motherhood.

cards.q: Identify gradual emancipation in the northern states.
cards.a: Between 1777 and 1804 every state from Pennsylvania north acted against slavery, most by gradual emancipation: laws that freed only children born after the law, and only after they had served their mothers' owners into adulthood, often into their twenties. Vermont's 1777 constitution barred adult slavery, Pennsylvania passed the first gradual act (1780), Massachusetts courts ended slavery in the 1780s, New York acted in 1799 and New Jersey in 1804.
cards.h: → time span + how the laws worked + key states
cards.n: Saying the North freed all enslaved people at once is wrong: gradual laws freed only the future-born, so some Northerners were still enslaved decades later.

cards.q: Identify the claim in this excerpt and the revolutionary idea it uses. Labelled paraphrase of a January 1777 petition to the Massachusetts legislature from Prince Hall and other Black Bostonians: 'We have, in common with all other men, a natural and unalienable right to the freedom that the Creator gave equally to all people. Every principle on which America has acted in its dispute with Great Britain pleads more strongly for us than a thousand arguments. We ask you to restore us to freedom, and that our children be free at twenty-one.'
cards.a: The petitioners claim that slavery violates their natural rights and should end in Massachusetts. They use the Revolution's own argument: if unalienable natural rights justified the colonies' break with Britain, those rights apply even more strongly to enslaved people. Asking that children be freed at 21 shows them shaping the claim to what a legislature might accept. It illustrates how revolutionary ideals exposed inequality and prompted calls for abolition.
cards.h: → the claim + the revolutionary principle it borrows
cards.n: Summarizing ('they want freedom') misses half the task; the point is the claim plus the revolutionary reasoning it turns against slavery.

cards.q: Identify two ways revolutionary ideals made state politics more democratic after 1776, and one limit of that change.
cards.a: First, some states widened the vote: Pennsylvania's 1776 constitution let free adult male taxpayers vote for a one-house legislature elected every year, and New Jersey's let propertied 'inhabitants', including some women and free Black men, vote until 1807. Second, states gave more seats to western districts and moved capitals inland, as Virginia did to Richmond in 1780. The limit: most states kept property qualifications, and women and enslaved people were excluded.
cards.h: → two specific changes + one specific limit
cards.n: 'The Revolution made America a democracy' is too sweeping to earn credit; name specific state changes and the exclusions that remained.

cards.q: Identify how the American Revolution influenced the French Revolution and the independence movements of Spanish America.
cards.a: France: officers such as Lafayette brought republican ideas home, the cost of aiding the Americans deepened the royal debt crisis that led to 1789, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man (1789) echoed the Declaration of Independence's natural rights. Spanish America: creole leaders such as Francisco de Miranda, who toured the United States in 1783-1784, and later Simon Bolivar cited the American example in the independence wars of the 1810s-1820s.
cards.h: → France: people, debt, ideas + Spanish America: example
cards.n: Claiming the American Revolution alone caused these revolutions overstates it; it inspired and helped fund conditions for them, alongside local causes.

cards.q: Identify Toussaint Louverture and the Haitian Revolution's effect on U.S. politics.
cards.a: Toussaint Louverture, a formerly enslaved man, became the leading general of the revolution that began in the French colony of Saint-Domingue in 1791, ended slavery there and made him its governor, before Napoleon's forces captured him in 1802; he died in a French prison in 1803, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared Haiti independent in 1804. In the United States it inspired enslaved people, terrified slaveholders, and blocked U.S. recognition of Haiti until 1862.
cards.h: → who + what the revolution did + U.S. reactions
cards.n: Presenting Haiti only as a copy of 1776 misses the point: it was a revolution of enslaved people, which is why white Americans reacted so differently to it.

cards.q: Explain why the Haitian Revolution alarmed many white Americans who celebrated their own revolution.
cards.a: Both revolutions invoked liberty, but Haiti's was made by enslaved people who destroyed slavery and drove out their masters. Slaveholders saw a model for revolt by the people they held in bondage, so ideals they honored at home looked like a threat when claimed by Black people.
cards.h: → same language of liberty → claimed by enslaved people who ended slavery → slaveholders fear revolt at home
cards.n: 'They were racist' names an attitude without the mechanism; tie the fear to slaveholding and the example of a successful slave revolt.
o: Refugees reaching Charleston, Norfolk and Philadelphia from Saint-Domingue in the 1790s brought vivid accounts of the fighting, sharpening fears in slaveholding communities.
Leaders split along the lines of slavery: John Adams's government traded with Toussaint's forces in 1799, while the slaveholder Jefferson was hostile.

w.a: White Americans feared the Haitian Revolution because Haiti planned to invade the United States.
w.why: invented; the fear was of slave revolt at home

w.a: Americans opposed it because it was a revolt against Spanish rule.
w.why: wrong empire; Saint-Domingue was French

cards.q: Explain why republican motherhood raised women's political importance without giving them political rights.
cards.a: A republic was thought to need virtuous citizens, and mothers shaped children's character, so women's work at home became a civic duty that justified educating girls. But the ideal placed that duty inside the family, which reinforced the view that voting and office belonged to men.
cards.h: → republic needs virtue → mothers teach it → civic role and schooling → role stays in the home, not the polls
cards.n: Describing the ideal without both the gain and the limit misses the comparison the question asks for.
o: It answered women's wartime service and appeals like Abigail Adams's with praise and schooling rather than legal change, leaving coverture in place.
Measured against colonial ideas it was a change in how women's work was valued; measured against men's new rights it continued women's exclusion.

w.a: Republican motherhood gave women the right to vote in the new republic.
w.why: false; it confined their civic role to the family

w.a: Republican motherhood meant women should join the Republican Party.
w.why: anachronism; that party formed in the 1850s

cards.q: Explain why revolutionary ideals led to gradual rather than immediate emancipation in the northern states.
cards.a: Natural-rights ideals made slavery hard to defend where it was not central to the economy, so northern legislatures acted. But lawmakers also held property rights sacred, so most laws freed only children born later, after years of unpaid service that compensated owners.
cards.h: → natural rights condemn slavery → property rights also sacred → free only the future-born after service → slow end
cards.n: 'The North did not need slaves' with no reference to revolutionary ideals or to property rights explains only half the outcome.
o: Slaveholders in New York and New Jersey had enough political weight to delay abolition there until 1799 and 1804 and to keep it gradual.
Gradual laws let legislators honor revolutionary principle while avoiding the cost of compensating owners in cash.

w.a: Northern states freed all enslaved people immediately in 1776.
w.why: false; the laws came from 1777 to 1804 and were mostly gradual

w.a: The North abolished slavery because it had never had enslaved people.
w.why: false; New York and New Jersey held thousands

cards.q: Identify the Articles of Confederation and give the year of ratification.
cards.a: The Articles of Confederation, drafted by the Second Continental Congress in 1777 and ratified in 1781 (Maryland held out until states with western land claims agreed to cede them), were the first national constitution. They created a 'firm league of friendship': a one-house Congress in which each state had one vote, with no separate executive or national courts, while each state kept its 'sovereignty, freedom, and independence.'
cards.h: → drafted + ratified + structure + where sovereignty lay
cards.n: Dating the Articles to 1787 or 1776 confuses them with the Constitution or the Declaration: drafted 1777, in force 1781.

cards.q: State the major weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation.
cards.a: Congress could not tax, only request money from the states; it could not regulate interstate or foreign commerce; it had no executive to enforce laws and no national courts; major laws needed nine of thirteen states and amendments all thirteen; and it could only ask states for troops. So it could not pay its debts, answer British trade restrictions or put down unrest such as Shays' Rebellion.
cards.h: → each weakness + the crisis it caused
cards.n: A bare list of weaknesses is description; the point is tying at least one weakness to a crisis it caused (debt, trade, unrest).

cards.q: State the genuine achievements of the Articles of Confederation government.
cards.a: The Confederation government won the war and the Treaty of Paris of 1783, which recognized independence and set the western boundary at the Mississippi. It settled the western land question by persuading states to cede their claims, then set up an orderly system to survey and sell that land (Land Ordinance, 1785) and to turn territories into equal states (Northwest Ordinance, 1787).
cards.h: → war and peace + western land policy
cards.n: Calling the Articles a total failure misses these lasting achievements; the first Congress under the Constitution re-enacted the Northwest Ordinance in 1789.

cards.q: Identify the Land Ordinance of 1785.
cards.a: The Land Ordinance of 1785 set up a rectangular survey of the western territory into townships six miles square, each divided into 36 sections of 640 acres, to be sold at auction to raise revenue for Congress. One section in every township was reserved to support public schools. The grid still shapes the map of the Midwest.
cards.h: → what it surveyed + how + why + the school section
cards.n: Confusing it with the Northwest Ordinance is common: the 1785 law surveyed and sold land; the 1787 law set up government and statehood.

cards.q: Identify the Northwest Ordinance of 1787.
cards.a: The Northwest Ordinance (1787) organized the territory north of the Ohio River and set a path to statehood: first a governor and judges appointed by Congress, then an elected assembly once there were 5,000 free adult men, then admission as a state equal to the original thirteen at 60,000 inhabitants. It protected property, religious freedom and jury trial, declared that schools 'shall forever be encouraged', and banned slavery in the territory.
cards.h: → territory + stages to statehood + rights + slavery
cards.n: Saying it abolished slavery in the United States overstates it: the ban covered only the Northwest Territory, and it also provided for returning fugitive slaves.

cards.q: Identify Shays' Rebellion and give its dates.
cards.a: Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787) was an uprising of indebted farmers in western Massachusetts, led in part by the Revolutionary veteran Daniel Shays, who closed county courts to stop foreclosures and debt suits driven by heavy state taxes payable in hard money. Their attack on the federal arsenal at Springfield in January 1787 was repulsed by a state militia paid for by Boston merchants, because Congress had no army to send.
cards.h: → dates + who + grievance + how it was put down
cards.n: Calling the rebels simple anti-tax radicals misses their demand, relief from debt suits; the lesson nationalists drew was Congress's helplessness.

cards.q: Identify the Newburgh Conspiracy of 1783.
cards.a: In March 1783, unpaid Continental Army officers camped at Newburgh, New York, circulated anonymous addresses hinting that the army would defy Congress unless it received back pay and promised pensions; some nationalists in Congress seem to have hoped the pressure would win a national tax. Washington met the officers on March 15, appealed to their honor, and ended the threat, preserving civilian control of the military.
cards.h: → when + who + what they threatened + how it ended
cards.n: An illustrative example. For KC-3.2.II.B, the point is the finances: a Congress that could not tax could not pay its own army.

cards.q: Identify the features most of the first state constitutions shared.
cards.a: Most state constitutions written from 1776 on were written documents that placed power in the legislature, often elected every year, and kept governors weak, with short terms, usually no veto, and in many states selection by the legislature. Many began with a declaration of rights, such as Virginia's (1776). Most kept property or taxpaying qualifications for voting and higher ones for holding office.
cards.h: → where power sat + the executive + rights + who voted
cards.n: Stopping at 'they limited government' misses the pattern: power flowed to legislatures, and property qualifications survived the Revolution.

cards.q: Identify the problems in trade, foreign relations and finance that the Confederation government could not solve in the 1780s.
cards.a: Trade: Britain closed its West Indies to American ships and flooded American markets with goods, while states set rival tariffs, deepening a postwar depression; Congress could not retaliate because it could not regulate commerce. Foreign relations: Britain kept its forts on U.S. soil in the Northwest, Spain closed the lower Mississippi to Americans in 1784, and Barbary states seized American ships. Finance: without taxing power, Congress could not pay its war debts.
cards.h: → one problem each for trade, diplomacy, money + why stuck
cards.n: Listing problems without why Congress could not act (no tax, no commerce power, no army) loses the causal point graders look for.

cards.q: Identify the evidence the author uses to support his argument. Labelled paraphrase of a letter George Washington wrote to James Madison in November 1786: 'We are fast verging on anarchy. Thirteen sovereign states pulling against one another, all tugging at the federal head, will soon bring ruin on the whole. Look at the disorders in Massachusetts, where men are closing the courts by force. Congress asks the states for money, and they ignore the request. A government that can only recommend, and cannot compel, is hardly a government at all.'
cards.a: Washington argues that the Confederation is failing and needs a stronger central government. His evidence is, first, the uprising in Massachusetts, where armed men closed the courts (Shays' Rebellion), showing Congress could not keep order; and second, the states' refusal to pay Congress's requests for money, showing that a government that can only ask cannot function. 'Thirteen sovereign states' pulling apart is his summary of both.
cards.h: → the argument, then each piece of evidence named
cards.n: Restating the claim ('he says the government is weak') is not identifying evidence; name the specific examples the author offers.

cards.q: Explain the long-term significance of the Northwest Ordinance.
cards.a: By making territories future states equal to the original thirteen, it rejected a colonial model for the West, and by banning slavery north of the Ohio it drew the first federal line between free and slave territory, a precedent cited in later fights over slavery in the territories.
cards.h: → territories become equal states → no internal colonies; slavery barred north of the Ohio → free-soil precedent
cards.n: 'It helped the West grow' earns little; the point is the equal-statehood model and the free-soil precedent.
o: Its promises to encourage schools and to protect property and religious liberty set the pattern for organizing later western states.
Its pledge of 'utmost good faith' toward Native nations was soon broken, so it also set the stage for the wars over the Ohio country in the 1790s.

w.a: The Northwest Ordinance mattered because it abolished slavery everywhere in the United States.
w.why: overstated; the ban covered only the Northwest Territory

w.a: Its main significance was organizing the Louisiana Territory.
w.why: wrong; Louisiana was bought in 1803

cards.q: Explain why Shays' Rebellion led to the Constitutional Convention.
cards.a: Shays' Rebellion convinced nationalists such as Washington and Madison that the Confederation could neither keep order nor protect property, since Congress had no army and no revenue. The alarm gave the Annapolis meeting's call for a convention broad support, and twelve states sent delegates to Philadelphia in 1787.
cards.h: → debt crisis → farmers close courts → Congress cannot respond → elites alarmed → Philadelphia 1787
cards.n: Describing the rebellion without linking it to what nationalists concluded about the Articles shows no causation.
o: The rebellion suggested that state legislatures might bow to debtor majorities, so nationalists wanted a central government that could check the states.
The Annapolis Convention of 1786 had drawn delegates from only five states; the rebellion gave its call for a new convention the urgency it lacked.

w.a: Shays' Rebellion led to the Convention because the rebels demanded a new constitution.
w.why: the rebels sought debt relief, not a constitution

w.a: Shays' Rebellion broke out after the Constitution was ratified.
w.why: wrong order; 1786-1787, before ratification

cards.q: Explain why the first state constitutions gave most power to the legislature.
cards.a: Colonists had come to see royal governors as agents of tyranny and their elected assemblies as defenders of liberty. After independence they weakened executives, with short terms and little or no veto, and trusted the branch closest to the voters.
cards.h: → royal governors seen as tyrants, assemblies as defenders → weak governors, strong legislatures
cards.n: 'They were afraid of tyranny' names a feeling without the colonial experience with governors that shaped the design.
o: Republican theory held that power belonged as close to the people as possible, and the legislature was the most directly elected branch.
Legislative dominance soon worried leaders like Madison, whose critique of state legislatures fed the push for checks and balances in 1787.

w.a: State legislatures got most of the power because the Articles of Confederation required it.
w.why: states wrote their constitutions on their own authority

w.a: States made their governors weak so they could copy the British monarchy.
w.why: reversed; they reacted against royal power

cards.q: Explain why the Articles of Confederation created a central government with such limited power.
cards.a: Having just fought a distant government that taxed them without consent, Americans would not create another that could. States guarded their own sovereignty, so the Articles gave Congress no power to tax or regulate trade and required unanimous consent to amend.
cards.h: → war against a distant taxing power → fear of central authority + state loyalty → Congress with no tax or trade power
cards.n: Listing the weaknesses answers a different question; the point is the experience that made Americans want a weak center.
o: The Articles were drafted in wartime, when cooperation among states seemed enough and loyalty to one's state ran deeper than any national identity.
Small states insisted on equal votes and every state on unanimity for amendments, which locked the weaknesses in place.

w.a: The Articles were weak because Britain wrote them to keep America dependent.
w.why: invented; Congress drafted them

w.a: The Articles were weak because the states wanted a king to hold real power.
w.why: reversed; they feared executive power

cards.q: Identify the Constitutional Convention of 1787.
cards.a: The Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia from May to September 1787, with 55 delegates from twelve states (Rhode Island stayed away) and Washington presiding. Called to revise the Articles, it met in secret and instead drafted a new Constitution through a series of compromises, which 39 delegates signed on September 17, 1787.
cards.h: → where + when + who + mandate vs. what it did
cards.n: Saying it was called to write a new constitution misstates its mandate: it was called to revise the Articles, and the delegates went further.

cards.q: Identify the Virginia Plan.
cards.a: The Virginia Plan, drafted chiefly by James Madison and presented by Edmund Randolph in May 1787, proposed a strong national government: a two-house legislature with representation in both houses based on population or wealth, a national executive and judiciary chosen by the legislature, and a congressional veto over state laws. It favored the large states.
cards.h: → author + structure + basis of representation + who gained
cards.n: Mixing it up with the New Jersey Plan is the classic slip: Virginia = population in both houses; New Jersey = one vote per state.

cards.q: Identify the New Jersey Plan.
cards.a: The New Jersey Plan, presented by William Paterson in June 1787, kept a one-house Congress with one vote per state, as under the Articles, but gave Congress power to raise revenue through import duties and stamp taxes and to regulate trade, with a plural executive chosen by Congress. It protected the small states.
cards.h: → author + structure + basis of representation + who gained
cards.n: Calling it a defense of the Articles unchanged misses that it too strengthened Congress; the real dispute was representation.

cards.q: Define the Great (Connecticut) Compromise.
cards.a: The Great (Connecticut) Compromise, proposed by Connecticut's Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth and adopted in July 1787, created a two-house Congress: a House of Representatives apportioned by population and elected by the people, where revenue bills must begin, and a Senate with two members per state chosen by the state legislatures. It broke the deadlock between large and small states.
cards.h: → proposers + the two houses + the conflict it settled
cards.n: Confusing it with the Three-Fifths Compromise is common; the Great Compromise settled large vs. small states, not free vs. slave states.

cards.q: Define the Three-Fifths Compromise.
cards.a: The Three-Fifths Compromise counted three-fifths of a state's enslaved population ('all other persons') when apportioning seats in the House and direct taxes among the states. It gave slaveholding states extra seats in Congress and extra electoral votes, strengthening southern power for decades, while granting enslaved people no rights.
cards.h: → what was counted + for what + who gained
cards.n: Saying it made enslaved people three-fifths of a citizen or gave them partial votes is the trap; it counted them only to boost slaveholders' power.

cards.q: Define the Commerce Compromise and the slave trade clause.
cards.a: Congress received power to regulate interstate and foreign commerce by simple majority but was barred from taxing exports, protecting southern staple crops. In a related bargain it could not ban the importation of enslaved people before 1808 (and could tax each one brought in at no more than ten dollars). Congress banned the international slave trade from January 1, 1808.
cards.h: → commerce power + export ban + slave trade clause
cards.n: Saying the Constitution ended the slave trade in 1787 is wrong: it protected the trade for twenty years, and the 1808 ban left slavery and the domestic trade intact.

cards.q: Identify the Federalists and their main arguments.
cards.a: The Federalists, led by Madison, Hamilton and John Jay and backed by Washington's prestige, supported ratification. They argued that the Articles had failed, that a stronger union was needed for defense, commerce and order, that separation of powers and checks and balances would prevent tyranny, and that a large republic would control factions. Their strength lay in merchants, towns and coastal areas.
cards.h: → leaders + main arguments + base of support
cards.n: Confusing them with the Federalist Party of the 1790s is a trap: in 1787-1788 the word meant supporters of ratification, and Madison later led the opposition.

cards.q: Identify the Anti-Federalists and their main objections.
cards.a: The Anti-Federalists, such as Patrick Henry, George Mason and the essayist 'Brutus', opposed ratification. They warned that a distant national government with taxing power and a standing army would swallow the states and threaten liberty, that the Constitution lacked a bill of rights, that a republic could not survive across a large territory, and that the presidency and Senate could become a monarchy and an aristocracy. Many were small farmers and backcountry people.
cards.h: → leaders + main objections + base of support
cards.n: Calling them opponents of union or of the Revolution misreads them; they carried the Revolution's fear of distant power, and they won the Bill of Rights.

cards.q: Contrast Federalist and Anti-Federalist views of a large republic.
cards.a: Anti-Federalists, following Montesquieu, held that a republic survives only in a small territory where citizens share interests and can watch their representatives, so a vast national republic would slide into tyranny. Madison, in Federalist No. 10, reversed this: a large republic is safer, because it holds so many competing factions that no single majority faction can easily form and oppress others.
cards.h: → one view + the other + the reversal between them
cards.n: Stating each view separately lists rather than contrasts; name the reversal, Madison turning size from a danger into a safeguard.

cards.q: Identify the argument of Federalist No. 10.
cards.a: In Federalist No. 10 (1787), Madison argues that factions arise from human nature, above all from the unequal distribution of property, so they cannot be removed without destroying liberty; their effects must be controlled instead. A large republic does this: representatives filter popular passions, and the great number of interests makes it hard for any majority faction to combine and oppress others.
cards.h: → the problem + why it cannot be removed + the remedy
cards.n: Saying Madison wanted to abolish factions or parties reverses him; he aimed to control their effects, not remove their causes.

cards.q: Identify the argument of Federalist No. 51.
cards.a: In Federalist No. 51 (1788), Madison argues that because 'men are not angels', government must be built so that 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition.' Separation of powers and checks and balances give each branch the means and the motive to resist the others, and dividing power between nation and states adds a 'double security' for the people's rights.
cards.h: → premise about human nature + the structural remedy
cards.n: Mixing up No. 10 and No. 51 is the classic slip: No. 10 is faction and the large republic; No. 51 is checks within the government.

cards.q: Identify the Bill of Rights and give the year of ratification.
cards.a: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments, drafted chiefly by James Madison in the first Congress (1789) and ratified in 1791. It protects freedoms of religion, speech, press, assembly and petition, the right to bear arms and the rights of the accused, and the Tenth Amendment reserves powers not delegated to the national government to the states or the people. It kept the Federalists' ratification promise.
cards.h: → what + who + year + contents + why it was added
cards.n: Saying the Bill of Rights was part of the original Constitution is wrong; its absence was the Anti-Federalists' strongest objection.

cards.q: Explain the 'Massachusetts Compromise' that helped secure ratification of the Constitution.
cards.a: In February 1788, facing likely defeat in the Massachusetts ratifying convention, Federalists won over John Hancock and Samuel Adams by agreeing that the state would ratify while recommending amendments, including protections of rights, for the first Congress to consider. Massachusetts ratified 187 to 168, and Virginia and New York later followed the same pattern of ratifying with recommended amendments.
cards.h: → the problem + the deal + the vote + what it set in motion
cards.n: Saying Massachusetts ratified on condition that amendments come first is wrong; ratification was unconditional, with amendments only recommended.

cards.q: Identify Charles Beard's 'An Economic Interpretation of the Constitution' (1913).
cards.a: In An Economic Interpretation of the Constitution (1913), the Progressive historian Charles Beard argued that the framers were men of property, especially holders of public securities, who wrote a Constitution that protected their economic interests against debtor majorities in the states. Historians such as Robert E. Brown and Forrest McDonald in the 1950s challenged his evidence, but he made economic interest a lasting question about the founding.
cards.h: → historian + date + claim + how it was received
cards.n: An illustrative historiography example. Treating Beard as a primary source is the trap: it is a 1913 interpretation shaped by Progressive-era concerns.

cards.q: Explain how the Constitution addressed slavery without naming it.
cards.a: The framers protected slavery in euphemism: the three-fifths clause counted 'other persons' to add southern seats, the slave trade was shielded until 1808, and a fugitive clause returned any 'person held to service or labour.' Avoiding the word kept the South in while sparing delegates open endorsement.
cards.h: → South demands protection, many Northerners uneasy → veiled clauses → union kept, slavery protected
cards.n: Naming the clauses without why the framers used euphemism (southern demands, northern discomfort, union) earns only part.
o: Leaving the word out let antislavery delegates hope slavery would fade while still giving slaveholders the guarantees they demanded.
The silence later let both sides read the Constitution their own way, some abolitionists as antislavery and southerners as a proslavery bargain.

w.a: The Constitution did not deal with slavery at all.
w.why: false; three clauses protected it in veiled language

w.a: The Constitution abolished slavery but let states wait until 1808.
w.why: confuses the slave trade clause with abolition

cards.q: Explain why the Federalists won ratification despite widespread Anti-Federalist opposition.
cards.a: Federalists were better organized, strong in the towns and ports that controlled most newspapers, and offered a concrete plan while opponents mainly objected. Their promise to add a bill of rights won wavering delegates in closely divided states such as Massachusetts, Virginia and New York.
cards.h: → organized, urban, press + a plan vs. objections + bill-of-rights promise → close states ratify
cards.n: Crediting the Federalist Papers alone overstates their reach; name the organization, the bill-of-rights promise or the nine-state pressure.
o: The Articles' failures, such as Shays' Rebellion, made the status quo hard to defend, so undecided delegates saw ratification as the lesser risk.
Once nine states ratified in June 1788, the holdouts faced being left outside the new union, which pressured Virginia and New York.

w.a: The Federalists won because most Americans wanted a king.
w.why: false; both sides rejected monarchy

w.a: All thirteen states ratified the Constitution unanimously in 1787.
w.why: false; votes were close and Rhode Island waited until 1790

cards.q: Explain why the Great Compromise was needed to keep the Constitutional Convention together.
cards.a: Large states wanted representation by population, as in the Virginia Plan; small states wanted equal votes, as in the New Jersey Plan, fearing domination. With delegates deadlocked by July, a House by population and a Senate with equal state votes gave each side a chamber it trusted.
cards.h: → large states want population, small states equality → deadlock → each side gets one house
cards.n: Describing the two plans without the deadlock and what each side gained shows no reasoning.
o: Small-state delegates such as Delaware's threatened to leave, so the compromise preserved the union as well as the Convention.
The compromise mixed a national principle, representing people, with a federal one, representing states, which is why Congress embodies federalism.

w.a: The Great Compromise was needed to settle how enslaved people would be counted.
w.why: that was the Three-Fifths Compromise

w.a: Small states wanted representation based on population.
w.why: reversed; they wanted equal votes

cards.q: Define federalism, separation of powers, and checks and balances.
cards.a: Federalism divides power between the national government and the states, each supreme in its own sphere. Separation of powers assigns making, enforcing and judging the law to three distinct branches: Congress, the president and the courts. Checks and balances give each branch ways to restrain the others, such as the veto, the veto override, impeachment, and the Senate's approval of appointments and treaties.
cards.h: → three definitions, each with its dividing line
cards.n: Treating the three as synonyms earns nothing: federalism divides power between levels, separation of powers among branches, and checks let branches restrain one another.

cards.q: Contrast the Articles of Confederation with the Constitution on taxation, commerce, executive power, and amendment.
cards.a: Taxation: under the Articles Congress could only request money; under the Constitution it levies taxes directly. Commerce: the Articles gave no power to regulate interstate or foreign trade; the Constitution gives Congress both. Executive: the Articles had none; the Constitution creates a president to enforce the laws, plus federal courts. Amendment: the Articles needed all thirteen states; the Constitution needs two-thirds of Congress and three-fourths of the states.
cards.h: → four paired points, Articles vs. Constitution
cards.n: Describing the Constitution alone is not a contrast; each point must pair the Articles' rule with the Constitution's.

cards.q: Define the Necessary and Proper (elastic) Clause.
cards.a: The necessary and proper clause (Article I, Section 8) lets Congress make all laws 'necessary and proper' for carrying out its enumerated powers. It is the basis of implied powers: in 1791 Hamilton used it to defend a national bank as a means to Congress's taxing and borrowing powers, while Jefferson argued 'necessary' meant indispensable. It helps make the government limited to listed powers yet able to stretch them.
cards.h: → where + what it says + the implied-powers dispute
cards.n: Saying it lets Congress pass any law it wants overstates it: a law must carry out an enumerated power, which is exactly what the Bank debate was about.

cards.q: Identify Federalist No. 78 and its argument.
cards.a: In Federalist No. 78 (1788), Hamilton argues that the judiciary is the 'least dangerous' branch because it has neither 'force nor will', neither the sword nor the purse, but only judgment. Judges need tenure during good behavior to stay independent, and courts must treat the Constitution as fundamental law and declare void any act contrary to it, an argument for judicial review.
cards.h: → author + claim about the judiciary + two consequences
cards.n: Saying Federalist No. 78 created judicial review overstates it: it argued for the power, which the Supreme Court asserted in Marbury v. Madison (1803).

cards.q: Date the writing of the Constitution, its taking effect, and the Bill of Rights.
cards.a: Written at the Philadelphia Convention and signed on September 17, 1787 → ratified when New Hampshire became the ninth state in June 1788 → in operation from March 1789, with Washington inaugurated in April 1789 → Bill of Rights ratified in December 1791.
cards.h: → three or four dates in order
cards.n: Treating 1787 as the year the Constitution took effect is the slip: written 1787, ratified 1788, in operation 1789.

cards.q: Identify which branch holds each constitutional power and which branch it checks: presidential veto · override of a veto by two-thirds of each house · impeachment by the House and trial by the Senate · Senate confirmation of appointments · Senate approval of treaties by two-thirds · presidential nomination of federal judges · Congress's power to create the lower federal courts · Congress's control of spending (the power of the purse) · judges serving during good behavior · Congress declaring war while the president is commander in chief
cards.a:
Presidential veto → executive checks the legislature
Veto override → legislature checks the executive
Impeachment and trial → legislature checks the executive and the judges
Senate confirmation → legislature checks the executive's appointments
Treaty approval → legislature (Senate) checks the executive's diplomacy
Nomination of judges → executive shapes the judiciary
Creating lower courts → legislature shapes the judiciary (as in the Judiciary Act of 1789)
Power of the purse → legislature checks the executive
Good-behavior tenure → shields the judiciary from both other branches
War powers split → legislature and executive check each other
cards.h: → holder → branch checked, for each power
cards.n: Naming the branch without the one it checks misses the idea: each check lets one branch restrain another, which is what separation of powers depends on.

cards.q: Identify how the original Constitution limited direct popular influence on the national government.
cards.a: Only the House was elected directly by voters. Senators were chosen by state legislatures for six-year terms, the president by electors appointed as each state legislature directed, and federal judges by presidential nomination and Senate confirmation, to serve during good behavior. States also set voting qualifications, which usually required property.
cards.h: → which offices were filtered + how, one by one
cards.n: Calling the 1787 Constitution fully democratic misses its design: the framers deliberately filtered popular majorities while resting power on the people.

cards.q: Identify how the original Constitution provided for choosing the president and vice president.
cards.a: Each state chose electors, equal to its number of representatives plus senators, in whatever way its legislature directed. Each elector cast two votes for president; the candidate with the most votes, if a majority of electors, became president and the runner-up vice president. With no majority or a tie, the House chose, each state delegation casting one vote. The Twelfth Amendment (1804) later required separate votes for the two offices.
cards.h: → electors + two votes + runner-up rule + House backup
cards.n: Assuming voters chose the president directly misreads 1787; the runner-up rule is what produced the split result of 1796 and the tie of 1800.

cards.q: Identify two features of the national government that continued from the Articles of Confederation into the Constitution, and the main change.
cards.a: Continuities: the national government kept the powers Congress had held under the Articles to make war and peace, coin and borrow money, run the post office and govern western territory, and the Northwest Ordinance was re-enacted in 1789; the states kept broad control of their internal affairs, such as property law and voting qualifications. The main change was new national power to tax, regulate commerce and enforce laws through a president and courts.
cards.h: → two continuities + the change
cards.n: Treating 1787 as a total break misses the question: name powers the Articles already granted that carried over, then the change.

cards.q: Explain why the Constitution created a central government that was both limited and dynamic.
cards.a: The framers wanted enough power to fix the Articles' failures but feared tyranny. So they listed Congress's powers and divided and checked authority, making it limited, yet granted taxing and commerce powers and a necessary and proper clause that let it stretch to new needs, making it dynamic.
cards.h: → Articles too weak + fear of tyranny → listed, divided, checked powers + tax, commerce, elastic clause
cards.n: Defining 'limited' and 'dynamic' without naming the provisions that make the government each earns little.
o: An amendment process easier than the Articles' unanimity let the Constitution change over time without a new convention.
Federalism left states strong in their own sphere while making national law supreme where it applied, a balance later generations kept renegotiating.

w.a: The Constitution was dynamic because the president could change it by decree.
w.why: false; amendment needs Congress and the states

w.a: The Constitution was limited because Congress still could not tax, as under the Articles.
w.why: reversed; the Constitution gave Congress taxing power

cards.q: Explain why the framers divided power between the national government and the states instead of abolishing the states.
cards.a: The states were existing political communities with their own constitutions and citizens' loyalty, and ratification needed their consent. Federalism gave the nation power over common concerns such as taxes, trade and defense, left local affairs to the states, and added another check on tyranny.
cards.h: → states already sovereign, needed to ratify → divide power → nation for common matters, states local, extra check
cards.n: 'To balance power' is a phrase; the answer needs the states' existing sovereignty and what each level controlled.
o: Madison argued in Federalist No. 51 that dividing power between two levels gave a 'double security' to the rights of the people.
Small states and slaveholding states would not accept a union that erased state power, so federalism was also a condition of agreement.

w.a: The framers kept the states because the Articles had already made them weak and harmless.
w.why: reversed; the Articles left the states powerful

w.a: Federalism means the national government is always subordinate to the states.
w.why: wrong; national law is supreme within its sphere

cards.q: Explain why the Constitution changed the national government's relationship with individual citizens compared with the Articles.
cards.a: Under the Articles, Congress acted only on the states, requesting money and troops they could refuse. The Constitution let the national government tax, make laws for and try individuals directly, through its own officers and courts, so its laws no longer depended on state cooperation.
cards.h: → Articles act on states, which refuse → Constitution acts on individuals → enforceable national law
cards.n: Saying the new government was 'stronger' without showing that it now reached individuals directly misses the change.
o: The supremacy clause made the Constitution, federal laws and treaties the supreme law, binding on state judges, which the Articles never achieved.
Because voters elected the House directly, the national government drew authority from the people, not only from the states.

w.a: Nothing changed, because the Constitution kept the Articles' system of requisitions.
w.why: false; it gave Congress direct taxing power

w.a: The Constitution let citizens vote directly for senators and the president.
w.why: false in 1787; legislatures chose senators and electors

cards.q: Identify the precedents set by Washington as president.
cards.a: Washington set precedents the Constitution did not spell out: he formed a cabinet of department heads (Jefferson at State, Hamilton at the Treasury, Knox at War, Randolph as attorney general) to advise him; accepted the plain title 'Mr. President'; took the lead in foreign policy with the 1793 neutrality proclamation; used federal force to uphold federal law in the Whiskey Rebellion; and stepped down after two terms, a custom kept until 1940.
cards.h: → four or five precedents, each specific
cards.n: Listing precedents without saying the Constitution did not require them misses why they matter: Washington turned a text into working institutions.

cards.q: Identify the Judiciary Act of 1789.
cards.a: The Judiciary Act of 1789 created the federal court system the Constitution only outlined: a Supreme Court of six justices, thirteen district courts and three circuit courts, plus the office of attorney general. Its Section 25 let the Supreme Court review state court decisions involving federal law, a key step in making national law supreme.
cards.h: → what it created + why it was needed
cards.n: An illustrative example. Confusing it with the Constitution is a slip: Article III left the lower courts and the Court's size to Congress, and this act filled them in.

cards.q: Identify the Whiskey Rebellion and give its year.
cards.a: In 1794 farmers in western Pennsylvania rose against the 1791 federal excise tax on whiskey, which fell hardest on grain farmers who distilled their crops to transport and sell them. Washington called up about 13,000 militiamen from four states and rode with them part of the way; the rebels scattered without a battle. It showed that the new government could enforce federal law.
cards.h: → year + who + grievance + federal response + meaning
cards.n: Treating it as a replay of Shays' Rebellion misses the contrast: this time the national government raised an army and enforced its own law.

cards.q: Identify the election of 1796 and the flaw in the electoral system it exposed.
cards.a: In 1796, the first contested presidential election, Federalist John Adams won 71 electoral votes to Democratic-Republican Thomas Jefferson's 68. Under the original rule that the runner-up became vice president, Jefferson took that office, so the president and vice president came from rival parties, a flaw the Twelfth Amendment (1804) corrected.
cards.h: → candidates + result + the flaw it exposed
cards.n: Saying Jefferson was Adams's running mate is wrong; there were no tickets in the Constitution, and the runner-up rule paired rivals.

cards.q: Identify the four main parts of Hamilton's financial plan.
cards.a: Hamilton proposed (1) funding the national debt at full face value, (2) federal assumption of the states' war debts, (3) a Bank of the United States (chartered 1791) to hold federal money, lend and issue a sound currency, and (4) revenue from import tariffs and a new excise tax on whiskey (1791). Together they aimed to establish the nation's credit and tie wealthy creditors to the new government.
cards.h: → four parts + the shared aim
cards.n: Calling the tariff purely protective is a slip: Congress set it mainly for revenue and rejected most of Hamilton's Report on Manufactures.

cards.q: Differentiate the funding of the national debt from the assumption of state debts in Hamilton's financial plan.
cards.a: Funding meant paying the national government's Revolutionary debt at full face value, by exchanging old certificates for new interest-bearing bonds, to establish the nation's credit; it was controversial because speculators had bought many certificates cheaply from veterans. Assumption meant the federal government also taking over the states' war debts (up to 21.5 million dollars), a separate step that angered states that had already paid theirs.
cards.h: → each term defined + its own controversy
cards.n: Merging the two into one 'debt plan' misses their separate objections: funding rewarded speculators; assumption burdened states that had paid.

cards.q: Identify the Compromise of 1790 (the 'dinner table bargain').
cards.a: The Compromise of 1790 was a bargain that, by Jefferson's later account, was struck at a dinner he hosted in June 1790: Madison agreed to let federal assumption of state debts pass Congress, and in exchange the permanent national capital would be built on the Potomac River, in the South, with Philadelphia as the temporary capital for ten years.
cards.h: → who + what each side gave + what each got
cards.n: Treating it as the Bank bargain is a slip: it traded assumption, not the Bank, for the capital's location.

cards.q: Contrast loose and strict construction of the Constitution using the Bank debate.
cards.a: Hamilton argued for loose construction: the necessary and proper clause implies power to use any reasonable means toward an enumerated end, so a bank that helps collect taxes and borrow money is constitutional. Jefferson argued for strict construction: powers not delegated are reserved to the states, and 'necessary' means indispensable, so a merely convenient bank is unconstitutional. Washington accepted Hamilton's view and signed the bill in 1791.
cards.h: → Hamilton's reading vs. Jefferson's + the outcome
cards.n: Stating each position without tying it to the clause and the Bank lists instead of contrasting; the dispute was the meaning of 'necessary'.

cards.q: Identify Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (1791) and its central argument.
cards.a: In his Report on Manufactures (December 1791), Hamilton argued that the government should actively promote manufacturing with protective tariffs, bounties (subsidies) and improved transportation, to diversify the economy, put more people to work and end dependence on British goods. Congress rejected most of it, but it became a blueprint for later protectionist policies.
cards.h: → date + proposals + purpose + fate
cards.n: Saying Congress adopted it is wrong; its subsidies were rejected in the 1790s, and its influence came later.

cards.q: Contrast Hamilton's and Jefferson's visions of the ideal American economy.
cards.a: Hamilton wanted a diversified commercial economy of trade, finance and manufacturing, built on national credit, a national bank and tariffs, with wealthy investors tied to the government's success. Jefferson wanted an agrarian republic of independent farmers, whose landownership he believed secured the virtue and independence a republic needed; he distrusted banks, public debt and cities as sources of corruption and dependence.
cards.h: → each man's economy + the reason behind it
cards.n: Saying Jefferson opposed all trade misreads him: he wanted farmers to export surpluses; he objected to finance, factory cities and dependence.

cards.q: Contrast Hamiltonian Federalists and Jeffersonian Democratic-Republicans.
cards.a: Federalists wanted a strong national government, loose construction, Hamilton's credit and banking system, closer ties to Britain, and leadership by men of wealth and education; their base was New England and the commercial Northeast. Democratic-Republicans wanted limited federal power, strict construction, a farmers' republic, sympathy for revolutionary France, and more trust in ordinary white men; their base was the South and the West.
cards.h: → paired points: power, Constitution, economy, abroad, base
cards.n: A list of each party's traits is not a contrast; pair each point side by side and name the dividing issue.

cards.q: Identify the rival partisan newspapers of the 1790s.
cards.a: John Fenno's Gazette of the United States (from 1789) championed Hamilton and the Federalists, while Philip Freneau's National Gazette (from 1791), whose editor Jefferson had given a State Department clerkship, attacked Hamilton's program; Benjamin Franklin Bache's Philadelphia Aurora later took up the Republican cause. The papers spread party loyalties beyond Congress and made the opposition press a target of the Sedition Act.
cards.h: → each paper + its side + what the press war did
cards.n: An illustrative example. Calling these papers neutral reporting misses their purpose: each was a party organ that built partisan loyalty.

cards.q: Identify the Democratic-Republican societies of the 1790s.
cards.a: The Democratic-Republican societies were several dozen local political clubs formed from 1793, many inspired by the French Revolution and by the French envoy Edmond Genet's visit, that criticized Federalist policies such as Hamilton's finances, neutrality and Jay's Treaty. Washington blamed 'self-created societies' for encouraging the Whiskey Rebellion, and Federalists saw organized popular opposition as illegitimate.
cards.h: → what they were + when + what they opposed + reaction
cards.n: Treating them as the Democratic-Republican Party itself overstates them; they were local clubs that fed the opposition's growth.

cards.q: Identify the Proclamation of Neutrality of 1793.
cards.a: In April 1793, after revolutionary France and Britain went to war, Washington proclaimed that the United States would be impartial toward the warring powers, despite the 1778 alliance with France. It kept the weak nation out of a European war and asserted the president's lead in foreign policy, but Democratic-Republicans charged that it betrayed an ally and a sister republic.
cards.h: → date + context + what it declared + reaction
cards.n: Saying it ended the French alliance overstates it; the 1778 treaty stayed in force until 1800, and the proclamation did not mention it.

cards.q: Identify Jay's Treaty and give its year.
cards.a: Jay's Treaty (signed 1794, approved by the Senate in 1795) with Britain secured British withdrawal from its forts in the Northwest by 1796 and sent prewar debts and boundary disputes to arbitration, but won nothing on impressment or neutral shipping rights. It averted war with Britain amid ship seizures, yet Democratic-Republicans denounced it, and the fight over it hardened the parties.
cards.h: → year + gains + failures + political effect
cards.n: Calling it a triumph or a pure surrender both miss the point: it bought peace and the forts at the price of neutral rights, and it split the parties.

cards.q: Identify Pinckney's Treaty and give its year.
cards.a: Pinckney's Treaty (the Treaty of San Lorenzo, 1795) with Spain gave Americans free navigation of the Mississippi River and the right of deposit at New Orleans to store goods for export, and set Spanish Florida's northern border at the 31st parallel. Spain, fearing a British-American alliance after Jay's Treaty, conceded what western farmers most needed.
cards.h: → year + terms + why Spain agreed
cards.n: Confusing it with Jay's Treaty is the classic slip: Jay dealt with Britain and the forts; Pinckney with Spain and the Mississippi.

cards.q: State the main advice of Washington's Farewell Address.
cards.a: In his Farewell Address (1796), Washington urged Americans to value national unity above loyalty to section, warned against the 'baneful effects of the spirit of party', and advised the nation to 'steer clear of permanent alliances' while trading with all nations. He also urged support for public credit, religion and morality.
cards.h: → unity + parties + alliances
cards.n: Saying Washington urged isolation from all foreign contact misreads it: he warned against permanent alliances while favoring commerce with every nation.

cards.q: Identify the historical situation and the purpose of Washington's Farewell Address (1796).
cards.a: Situation: Washington published it in September 1796 as he declined a third term, amid bitter party conflict over Hamilton's program and Jay's Treaty, while Britain and France were at war and French diplomats openly courted the Democratic-Republicans. Purpose: to urge Americans to put national unity above party and section and to avoid permanent alliances, a warning aimed at pro-French partisans as well as at future generations. Hamilton helped draft it.
cards.h: → situation (when, amid what) + purpose (aimed at whom)
cards.n: Treating it as timeless neutral advice ignores its situation; its warnings against faction and foreign influence had partisan targets in 1796.

cards.q: Identify the XYZ Affair.
cards.a: In 1797 French agents, named in published dispatches only as X, Y and Z, told three American envoys sent by President Adams that talks would require a bribe for Foreign Minister Talleyrand and a loan to France. Made public in 1798, the insult set off a wave of anti-French feeling, a Federalist surge, the undeclared Quasi-War at sea and the Alien and Sedition Acts.
cards.h: → year + what happened + consequences
cards.n: Treating the affair as a French declaration of war is wrong; it produced an undeclared naval war and a domestic crackdown on dissent.

cards.q: Identify the Quasi-War with France.
cards.a: The Quasi-War (1798-1800) was an undeclared naval war with France, which had been seizing American merchant ships after Jay's Treaty. Congress created a Navy Department, built warships and ended the 1778 treaties, and American ships fought French privateers in the Caribbean. Adams, defying his party's war faction, sent a new peace mission, and the Convention of 1800 ended the conflict and the alliance.
cards.h: → dates + cause + fighting + how it ended
cards.n: Calling it a declared war is wrong; Adams resisted Federalist pressure for full war, which split his party before the election of 1800.

cards.q: Identify the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798.
cards.a: The Alien and Sedition Acts (1798), passed by the Federalist Congress during the Quasi-War, were four laws: the Naturalization Act raised the residency requirement for citizenship from 5 to 14 years; the Alien Friends and Alien Enemies Acts let the president deport or detain dangerous foreigners; and the Sedition Act made it a crime to publish 'false, scandalous and malicious' writing against the government. It was used against Republican editors and Congressman Matthew Lyon.
cards.h: → year + context + the four laws + how they were used
cards.n: Treating them only as wartime security measures misses their partisan use: prosecutions fell almost entirely on Democratic-Republican critics.

cards.q: State what the Naturalization Act of 1798 changed and why the Federalists wanted it.
cards.a: The Naturalization Act of 1798 raised the residency requirement for U.S. citizenship from 5 to 14 years. Federalists wanted it because recent immigrants, especially Irish and French arrivals, tended to support the Democratic-Republicans, so a longer wait delayed their votes. Jefferson's Congress restored the five-year requirement in 1802.
cards.h: → the change + the partisan motive + its fate
cards.n: Treating it as a security law only misses its partisan aim: delaying citizenship delayed opposition votes.

cards.q: Identify the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions.
cards.a: The Kentucky (1798, 1799) and Virginia (1798) Resolutions, secretly written by Jefferson and Madison, declared the Alien and Sedition Acts unconstitutional. They argued that states could judge when Congress exceeded its powers; Virginia's called on states to 'interpose', and Kentucky's 1799 resolution named 'nullification' as the rightful remedy. No other state endorsed them, but they became a founding text of states' rights.
cards.h: → authors + year + what they claimed + response
cards.n: Saying they nullified the acts in practice overstates them: no other state joined, and most of the laws expired or were repealed by 1802.

cards.q: Define the compact theory of the Union laid out in the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions.
cards.a: The compact theory held that the states created the Constitution as a compact among themselves, so the federal government had only the powers the states had delegated, and each state could judge for itself when Congress exceeded them. Jefferson and Madison used it in 1798 to declare the Alien and Sedition Acts void; later defenders of nullification and secession built on it.
cards.h: → who made the Constitution + what states may do
cards.n: Taking the theory as settled law is a trap: Federalists answered that the people, not the states, made the Constitution, and the federal courts decide.

cards.q: Place these events of the 1790s in chronological order: Jay's Treaty, Whiskey Rebellion, Alien and Sedition Acts, Farewell Address, Pinckney's Treaty, XYZ Affair.
cards.a: Whiskey Rebellion (summer 1794) → Jay's Treaty (signed November 1794) → Pinckney's Treaty (1795) → Farewell Address (September 1796) → XYZ Affair (1797, made public 1798) → Alien and Sedition Acts (1798).
cards.h: → six events, earliest first, with years
cards.n: Placing the Alien and Sedition Acts before the XYZ Affair reverses cause and effect: the war scare after XYZ produced the acts.

cards.q: Identify the Spanish mission system in California and its effects.
cards.a: From San Diego in 1769, Franciscans led by Junipero Serra, backed by soldiers in presidios, built a chain of missions along the California coast (21 by 1823) to convert Native peoples and hold the region against Russian and British rivals. Missions ran on the bonded labor of converted Native people, who could not leave freely and died in large numbers of disease. Soldiers and settlers found chances to gain land and status, and Spanish, Catholic and Native cultures blended.
cards.h: → when + who + purpose + labor + social and cultural effects
cards.n: Describing the missions as purely religious misses the key concept's points: Native bonded labor, soldiers' social mobility and cultural blending.

cards.q: Explain why political parties emerged in the 1790s despite the Founders' hostility to them.
cards.a: Hamilton's program and the war between Britain and revolutionary France forced lasting choices about federal power, the economy and foreign policy. Each side came to see the other as a threat to the republic, so leaders built newspapers, clubs and voter networks, turning factions into parties.
cards.h: → Hamilton's program + French Revolution divide leaders → each sees a threat → press and voter networks → parties
cards.n: Naming the two parties is not a cause; the answer needs the specific disputes that divided leaders.
o: Regional economies pulled apart: commercial New England favored Hamilton's credit system, while southern and western farmers opposed it.
Jay's Treaty forced every member of Congress to take a side on Britain, hardening loose alignments into party voting.

w.a: Parties emerged because the Constitution required a two-party system.
w.why: false; the Constitution never mentions parties

w.a: Parties formed because Washington founded the Federalist Party to win the presidency.
w.why: wrong; Washington deplored parties and ran unopposed

cards.q: Explain why Virginia and other states without large war debts opposed Hamilton's assumption plan.
cards.a: Virginia and some other states had already paid off much of their war debt, so assumption would tax their citizens to pay debts owed mainly by states such as Massachusetts and South Carolina. Critics also saw it enriching speculators and strengthening federal power over the states.
cards.h: → Virginia had paid its debts → assumption taxes Virginians for others' debts + enriches speculators → opposition
cards.n: 'It was unfair' is a verdict, not an explanation; the point is who would pay whose debts, and the fear of federal and speculator power.
o: Critics feared that making creditors dependent on the federal treasury would build a moneyed interest loyal to Hamilton's government.
The dispute was settled only by the Compromise of 1790, which traded assumption for a southern capital on the Potomac.

w.a: Virginia opposed assumption because it wanted to keep paying its own large debts.
w.why: reversed; Virginia had already paid much of its debt

w.a: Virginia opposed assumption because it would move the capital to New York.
w.why: the deal put the capital on the Potomac

cards.q: Explain why the war between Britain and revolutionary France deepened party conflict in the United States.
cards.a: Federalists, tied to British trade and alarmed by the French Revolution's violence, leaned toward Britain; Democratic-Republicans saw France as a sister republic and resented British ship seizures. Each crisis, from neutrality to Jay's Treaty and the XYZ Affair, forced a choice that sharpened the divide.
cards.h: → Britain-France war → Federalists lean British, Republicans French → Jay, XYZ force choices → parties harden
cards.n: 'People disagreed about Europe' earns nothing; tie each party's position to interests or ideals and to a specific crisis.
o: Foreign policy became a test of loyalty, so each party accused the other of serving a foreign power, which Federalists used to justify the Sedition Act.
Seizures of American ships by both powers made neutral trading rights a practical economic issue for merchants and farmers.

w.a: The United States joined France's war against Britain in 1793.
w.why: false; Washington proclaimed neutrality

w.a: Both parties agreed on foreign policy and differed only over taxes.
w.why: ignores their split over Britain and France

cards.q: Explain why the uncertain legal relationship between the federal government and American Indian nations led to conflict over land in the 1790s.
cards.a: The federal government treated Native nations as sovereign enough to sign treaties, yet claimed ultimate power over their land, while settlers and states ignored treaty lines. Nations of the Ohio country resisted by war, and their defeat forced cessions such as the 1795 Treaty of Greenville.
cards.h: → nations are treaty partners, but U.S. claims their land → settlers ignore treaties → war → forced cessions
cards.n: Naming battles without the legal ambiguity, treaty partners whose land the U.S. claimed, misses the cause the key concept names.
o: The 1790 Intercourse Act required federal approval for buying Native land, but the government could not stop settlers or states from ignoring it.
Federal officials hoped to 'civilize' Native peoples through farming and assimilation, a policy that assumed their land would pass to settlers.

w.a: The federal government treated Native nations as foreign countries and never took their land.
w.why: false; treaties often forced cessions

w.a: The United States signed no treaties with Native nations in the 1790s.
w.why: false; Greenville and others were treaties

cards.q: Explain why the election of 1800 is called the 'Revolution of 1800.'
cards.a: For the first time, power passed from one party to its rival peacefully: defeated Federalists handed the presidency and Congress to Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans without violence. It showed the Constitution could survive partisanship, though a tie with Burr, broken by the House, led to the Twelfth Amendment.
cards.h: → bitter party contest → Federalists lose and step aside → first peaceful transfer → Constitution survives
cards.n: Describing the tie and the House vote without the peaceful transfer between rival parties misses why the name fits.
o: Jefferson himself called it a revolution in principle, a return to limited government and strict construction after Federalist rule.
The result ended Federalist control of the national government for good; the party never again won the presidency.

w.a: It was called a revolution because Jefferson took power by force.
w.why: false; the transfer was peaceful

w.a: It was a revolution because women and enslaved people gained the vote.
w.why: false; suffrage did not change

cards.q: Identify how painters of the Revolutionary era expressed a new national identity.
cards.a: Painters turned the Revolution and its leaders into shared national images. John Trumbull painted heroic Revolutionary scenes such as The Death of General Warren at the Battle of Bunker's Hill (1786) and The Declaration of Independence (begun 1786); Gilbert Stuart's 1796 portraits of Washington became the standard image of the first president; and Charles Willson Peale painted Revolutionary leaders and opened a Philadelphia museum of portraits and natural history (1786).
cards.h: → artist + work + what it made national
cards.n: Illustrative examples; the CED names no artists. Listing painters without saying how their work built a shared national story earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify how Noah Webster tried to create a distinctly American language and education.
cards.a: Noah Webster argued that 'as an independent nation, our honor requires us to have a system of our own, in language as well as government' (1789). His 'blue-backed' American Spelling Book (1783) taught generations of American children, and he promoted American spellings such as 'color' and 'center', later fixed in his American Dictionary (1828). He believed a common American speech and schooling would unite the states.
cards.h: → his aim + the speller + the spellings + why it mattered
cards.n: Illustrative example. Citing only the 1828 dictionary puts him in the wrong period; his Period 3 work was the 1783 speller and the call for an American standard.

cards.q: Identify how neoclassical architecture expressed the ideals of the new republic.
cards.a: Americans borrowed Greek and Roman forms, columns, domes and temple fronts, to link their republic with ancient self-government and Roman republican virtue. Jefferson modeled the Virginia State Capitol (designed 1785) on a Roman temple, the Maison Carree at Nimes, and Pierre L'Enfant's 1791 plan for Washington, D.C. set the Capitol and the President's House on a monumental scale fit for a new republic.
cards.h: → the style + the ideal it signaled + two examples
cards.n: Illustrative examples. Saying Americans copied British fashion misses the point: classical forms claimed the heritage of ancient republics, not of monarchy.

cards.q: Identify how writers of the Revolutionary era and early republic promoted a distinct American identity.
cards.a: Writers set out to show that the new nation had its own character. J. Hector St. John de Crevecoeur's Letters from an American Farmer (1782) asked 'What then is the American, this new man?' and described a people blended from many European nations; Royall Tyler's play The Contrast (1787) set a plain, honest American against a foppish imitator of British manners; and Mercy Otis Warren's satirical plays of the 1770s mocked royal officials.
cards.h: → writer + work + the idea of Americanness it offered
cards.n: Illustrative examples. Crevecoeur's 'new man' blended Europeans only; noting whom it left out, African and Native Americans, is what shows complexity.

cards.q: Identify two national symbols or rituals the United States created in its first decades.
cards.a: The Great Seal (adopted 1782), with its eagle and the motto 'E pluribus unum' ('out of many, one'), expressed a union made from many states. Fourth of July celebrations, held from 1777 with parades, toasts and readings of the Declaration, gave Americans a shared founding story. The cult of Washington, in portraits, birthday celebrations and nationwide mourning at his death in 1799, gave the nation a unifying hero.
cards.h: → two symbols or rituals + what each expressed
cards.n: Illustrative examples. Naming a symbol without what it expressed (unity of many states, a shared founding story) earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify regional differences that persisted alongside the new national culture in the 1790s.
cards.a: New England kept its town meetings, established Congregational churches and commercial, seafaring economy. The Middle States remained the most ethnically and religiously mixed, with Quakers, Germans and Scots-Irish. The South stayed rural and slaveholding, led by a planter gentry. The backcountry and trans-Appalachian West grew a frontier culture of small farms, evangelical religion and distrust of eastern elites. These regions shaped the parties' bases.
cards.h: → one trait per region + why it mattered
cards.n: Assuming national culture erased regional differences misses the key concept: it grew alongside them, and they resurfaced in party and sectional conflict.

cards.q: Explain why Americans after independence worked to create a national culture distinct from Britain's.
cards.a: Independence ended political ties but not cultural dependence: Americans still read British books and followed British tastes. Leaders believed a republic needed citizens loyal to something beyond their own states, so they promoted American schoolbooks, art, symbols and holidays to build a common identity.
cards.h: → political break but cultural dependence → republic needs shared loyalty → American books, art, symbols, holidays
cards.n: 'To be different from Britain' restates the question; name the dependence that remained and the civic need for unity.
o: The states shared little besides the Revolution, so celebrating its battles, heroes and Declaration became the common story that bound them.
European writers doubted that a republic could produce refined culture, and Americans set out to prove them wrong.

w.a: Americans built a national culture because Britain banned its books in the United States.
w.why: invented; British books kept circulating widely

w.a: By 1800 the new national culture had replaced all regional differences.
w.why: false; regional cultures persisted

cards.q: Explain why artists and architects of the early republic drew on classical Greek and Roman models.
cards.a: Americans saw their republic as the heir of ancient Athens and republican Rome, whose citizen virtue their political writers praised. Classical columns, temple fronts and heroic poses cast American leaders and buildings as embodiments of those republican ideals rather than of monarchy.
cards.h: → republic sees itself as heir of Athens and Rome → classical forms signal virtue and self-rule → buildings, art
cards.n: Describing columns and domes without the link to republican ideals shows no reasoning about identity.
o: An education steeped in Latin and ancient history made Roman figures natural models; Washington was praised as a modern Cincinnatus for giving up power.
Neoclassicism was fashionable across the Atlantic world in the 1780s, so Americans joined a wider style while giving it a republican meaning.

w.a: They used classical models because Greek and Roman builders designed the new Capitol.
w.why: anachronism; the architects were modern

w.a: Classical styles showed Americans' continuing loyalty to the British king.
w.why: reversed; they symbolized republics, not monarchy

cards.q: Explain why the national culture of the 1790s still carried strong continuities with colonial culture.
cards.a: Americans kept the English language, English common law, Protestant faith and many British tastes, and colonial regional patterns, New England towns, southern plantations and backcountry farms, persisted. The new national symbols and republican themes were layered on these older foundations rather than replacing them.
cards.h: → language, law, religion, tastes persist + colonial regions persist → new symbols layered on old foundations
cards.n: A continuity-and-change answer needs both sides; describing only the new symbols or only the continuities earns half at best.
o: Slavery and the exclusion of women from politics continued from colonial society, limiting whom the new culture treated as full Americans.
Even symbols of independence used familiar forms, such as sermons, printed pamphlets and toasts, to carry new republican meanings.

w.a: American culture broke completely with Britain after 1776.
w.why: overstated; language, law and religion continued

w.a: Americans stopped speaking English after independence to show their break with Britain.
w.why: false; Webster sought American spellings, not a new language

cards.q: Identify the Paxton Boys and their 1763 uprising.
cards.a: The Paxton Boys were Scots-Irish frontiersmen from around Paxton, Pennsylvania, who in December 1763, during Pontiac's War, murdered twenty peaceful Conestoga people, including those sheltered in the Lancaster workhouse. In early 1764 several hundred marched on Philadelphia to demand frontier defense and fairer representation; Benjamin Franklin persuaded them to turn back. It exposed the gulf between frontier settlers and an eastern, Quaker-influenced government.
cards.h: → who + when + what they did + what it revealed
cards.n: An illustrative example. Casting them as frontier defenders ignores that they killed peaceful Conestogas; the point is anti-Native violence and frontier-east tension.

cards.q: Identify the Regulator movement in the North and South Carolina backcountry.
cards.a: The Regulators were backcountry farmers in the Carolinas in the late 1760s and early 1770s.
