cards.h: → push factors + resources + where they settled + work
cards.n: Treating both groups as poor Catholic city laborers erases the contrast; Germans were more often farmers and artisans in the Midwest.

cards.q: State the approximate volume of Irish and German immigration in the 1840s-1850s.
cards.a: Official U.S. arrival counts record roughly 780,000 immigrants from Ireland and 430,000 from the German states in the 1840s, and about 1.7 million Irish and 1.4 million Germans across 1841-1860. Together they made up about seven in ten of the roughly 4.3 million immigrants of those two decades, the largest foreign-born streams before the Civil War.
cards.h: → approximate numbers for each group + share of the total
cards.n: Rounded official counts; the 1850s surge belongs to Period 5. Answers in the tens of millions confuse this wave with 1880-1920.

cards.q: Define nativism and name its main political expression in the 1850s.
cards.a: Nativism was hostility to immigrants, especially Catholics, and a demand to favor native-born Protestants. In the 1830s and 1840s it produced anti-Catholic writings and violence, such as the burning of the Ursuline convent in Charlestown, Massachusetts (1834) and the Philadelphia riots of 1844. Its main political expression in the 1850s was the American (Know-Nothing) Party, which sought a 21-year wait for citizenship and bars on immigrant officeholding.
cards.h: → definition + Period 4 examples + the 1850s party
cards.n: Borrows the 1850s Know-Nothings from u5. Treating nativism as only about jobs misses its anti-Catholic core.

cards.q: Explain why most famine Irish immigrants stayed in Northeastern cities while many German immigrants moved inland.
cards.a: Most famine Irish arrived penniless, without money for land and tools, so they took unskilled work in the port cities where they landed and on nearby canals and railroads. Germans more often had savings and farm or craft skills, so they could travel to the Midwest and buy land or open shops among other Germans.
cards.h: → Irish: no money, unskilled → jobs near the port; Germans: savings, skills → travel inland → farms and shops
cards.n: 'They liked different places' earns nothing; the point needs the difference in resources and skills that shaped each group's choices.
o: Some historians argue that bitter experience of tenant farming and famine made many Irish wary of farming.
Catholic parishes and, later, city party organizations in the Northeast gave Irish newcomers support networks.

w.a: The Irish stayed in cities because the Homestead Act excluded them.
w.why: anachronism; the Homestead Act came in 1862

w.a: Germans moved inland because they were banned from Eastern cities.
w.why: invented; many Germans lived in Eastern cities too

cards.q: Describe the patterns of migration west of the Appalachians from 1800 to 1848.
cards.a: Northerners and European immigrants moved into the Old Northwest (Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan), often along the Ohio River, the National Road and the Erie Canal, building family farms and river and lake towns such as Cincinnati, St. Louis and Chicago. Southern planters and yeomen, taking enslaved people, moved into the Old Southwest (Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas) to grow cotton. Ohio grew from about 45,000 people in 1800 to nearly 2 million in 1850.
cards.h: → two streams: who, which routes, where, what they built
cards.n: 'People moved west' without the two streams (free-labor North, slave-labor South) misses the pattern the CED names.

cards.q: Contrast the early Lowell workforce with the mill workforce by the 1840s-1850s.
cards.a: In the 1820s and 1830s the Lowell mills hired mostly young, unmarried, native-born New England farm women who worked a few years under paternalistic rules, lived in company boardinghouses, and sent money home or saved for marriage. After wage cuts and speedups in the 1830s and 1840s provoked protests and many left, owners turned to Irish immigrants, including whole families and children, who accepted lower pay and had fewer choices.
cards.h: → who worked there early + what changed + why
cards.n: Saying the mills always used immigrant labor misses the change; the cause was falling pay and harder work, not machines replacing workers.

cards.q: Identify the protests of Lowell mill workers in the 1830s and 1840s.
cards.a: Mill women 'turned out' (struck) against a wage cut in 1834 and against higher boardinghouse charges in 1836. In 1845 Sarah Bagley and others formed the Lowell Female Labor Reform Association, which petitioned the Massachusetts legislature for a ten-hour day; a legislative committee declined to act, but the protests showed women claiming a public voice as wage earners.
cards.h: → two early strikes + 1840s organization + demand + result
cards.n: Saying the protests won a ten-hour law earns nothing: the 1845 petition failed; the significance lies in women organizing as workers.

cards.q: Identify Commonwealth v. Hunt (1842).
cards.a: In Commonwealth v. Hunt (1842), the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court under Chief Justice Lemuel Shaw ruled that a labor union was not in itself an illegal conspiracy and that workers could organize and refuse to work for employers who hired nonmembers, as long as they used lawful means. The ruling protected unions in the state, though unions stayed small and weak for decades.
cards.h: → court + holding + significance
cards.n: It was a state court ruling, not a U.S. Supreme Court case; don't claim it created a strong labor movement.

cards.q: Explain why the market revolution produced both a larger middle class and a growing population of laboring poor.
cards.a: Commerce and factories multiplied jobs for clerks, managers, merchants and professionals, who gained from rising incomes and cheaper goods. Meanwhile machines and bigger workshops eroded artisans' skills and independence, turning many into wage workers exposed to low pay and downturns such as the Panic of 1837.
cards.h: → commerce needs managers, clerks → middle class grows; machines de-skill artisans → wage dependence → laboring poor
cards.n: Naming the two groups without the mechanism that produced each (new white-collar work; de-skilled wage labor) earns nothing.
o: A small business elite of merchants and mill owners grew very rich, widening the gap between top and bottom.
Immigrants arriving without capital filled the lowest-paid jobs, swelling the urban poor.

w.a: Everyone became middle class because factories paid high wages.
w.why: false; many workers stayed poor

w.a: The laboring poor grew because the market revolution ended wage work.
w.why: reversed; it spread wage work

cards.q: Define the cult of domesticity.
cards.a: The cult of domesticity ('true womanhood') was the middle-class ideal, spread from the 1820s and 1830s by magazines, advice books and sermons, that a woman's proper sphere was the home, where piety, purity, submissiveness and domestic skill made her the family's moral guardian, while men competed in the public sphere of work and politics. It grew as the market revolution moved paid work out of the household.
cards.h: → the ideal + who held it + its link to the economy
cards.n: Presenting it as how all women lived misses the point: it was a middle-class ideal that mill women, enslaved women and poor women could not follow.

cards.q: Explain why the separation of home and workplace changed ideas about women's roles in middle-class families.
cards.a: As paid work moved from farm and shop to offices and factories, middle-class men earned the income away from home, and the household no longer looked like a place of production. Writers recast it as a moral refuge run by women, the separate-spheres ideal, which honored women's influence but confined it to the home.
cards.h: → paid work leaves the home → men earn outside it → home redefined as a moral refuge → women's sphere is the home
cards.n: 'Women stayed home' describes the result; the point needs the economic change that made the separate-spheres ideal possible.
o: Middle-class families could afford for wives not to earn wages, so domesticity became a marker of class status.
Falling birth rates and more schooling put new weight on mothers' moral training of their children.

w.a: Women's roles changed because a federal law barred them from factories.
w.why: invented; many women worked in mills

w.a: Separating home and work gave women equal political rights.
w.why: false; it confined them to a private sphere

cards.q: Contrast the cult of domesticity with the women's rights movement of the 1840s.
cards.a: The cult of domesticity confined women to a private, moral sphere and kept them out of politics; the women's rights movement demanded public and legal equality, including the vote, property rights and access to education and professions, as at Seneca Falls (1848). Yet many reformers turned domesticity's claim of female moral superiority into a reason to act in public, in temperance, antislavery and charity work.
cards.h: → the difference + the link between them
cards.n: A contrast that stops at 'one kept women home, the other didn't' misses how domestic ideals were used to justify women's public activism.

cards.q: Contrast republican motherhood with the cult of domesticity.
cards.a: Republican motherhood (1780s-1790s) gave women's domestic role a civic purpose: raising virtuous sons for the new republic, which justified better schooling for girls. The cult of domesticity (from the 1820s) cast the home as a private refuge from the competitive market economy, stressing piety and purity rather than civic duty, and grew as paid work separated from the household.
cards.h: → era + purpose of each ideal + what drove the change
cards.n: Borrows republican motherhood from u3. Treating them as the same ideal misses the shift from civic duty to private moral refuge.

cards.q: Identify how states changed voting qualifications for white men between 1800 and 1840.
cards.a: State by state, legislatures and constitutional conventions replaced property qualifications with taxpaying or residence requirements and then dropped most of those, so by about 1840 nearly all adult white men could vote (Rhode Island held out until 1842). New Western states such as Indiana (1816) and Illinois (1818) entered with broad white male suffrage, older states such as New York (1821) followed, and voters, not legislatures, came to choose electors.
cards.h: → what replaced property tests + timing + who led the way
cards.n: Crediting a constitutional amendment or Jackson himself earns nothing: states changed their own rules, much of it before Jackson's election.

cards.q: Explain why property qualifications for white male voters disappeared in most states between 1800 and 1840.
cards.a: The Revolution's language of equality made property tests hard to defend; new Western states, eager for settlers, offered broad white male suffrage, pressing Eastern states to match them; and the market economy created many wage earners and renters who paid taxes and served in militias yet could not vote.
cards.h: → revolutionary ideals + Western states compete for settlers + propertyless taxpayers → states drop property tests
cards.n: 'People wanted democracy' earns nothing; the point needs specific pressures, such as Western states and taxpaying men without property.
o: Rhode Island's Dorr Rebellion (1841-1842) showed the pressure: men shut out by a property rule formed a rival government, and the state widened suffrage in 1842.
Party competition gave politicians a reason to court new voters by widening the franchise.

w.a: Property qualifications ended when the Fifteenth Amendment passed.
w.why: anachronism; that amendment came in 1870

w.a: Jackson abolished property rules by executive order.
w.why: invented; states set voting rules

cards.q: Identify the groups whose voting rights narrowed or stayed closed as white male suffrage expanded from 1800 to 1848.
cards.a: Free Black men lost ground: New Jersey limited voting to white men in 1807 (ending voting there by propertied women and Black men), New York's 1821 constitution kept a 250-dollar property requirement only for Black men, and Pennsylvania disfranchised Black men in 1838; most new states barred them from the start. Women could vote nowhere after New Jersey's change, and American Indians were not treated as citizens.
cards.h: → each group + a specific restriction
cards.n: Saying democracy expanded for 'all men' misses the pattern: the conventions that freed white men from property tests often wrote race into the rules.

cards.q: Explain why the expansion of voting rights for white men coincided with new restrictions on free Black voters.
cards.a: Once voting rested on manhood rather than property, race and sex became the lines of citizenship; conventions that dropped property tests for whites often wrote 'white' into suffrage clauses. Rising racial hostility in Northern cities, and Democrats' fear that Black men voted for rivals, pushed the same way.
cards.h: → property test gone → race and sex become the line → 'white' written into constitutions → hostility, party fear add
cards.n: Treating the restrictions as leftovers from colonial times misses the change: several states took the vote from Black men who had held it.
o: New York's 1821 convention shows the link directly: it dropped property rules for white men while raising them for Black men.
White workers competing with free Black workers for jobs backed exclusion, tying economic anxiety to disfranchisement.

w.a: Free Black men were never allowed to vote anywhere before the Civil War.
w.why: false; several states allowed it, then withdrew it

w.a: The Constitution was amended in 1821 to bar Black voters.
w.why: invented; states made these changes

cards.q: Identify the 'Corrupt Bargain' of 1824.
cards.a: In 1824 no candidate won an electoral majority: Andrew Jackson led with 99 electoral votes and the most popular votes, followed by John Quincy Adams (84), William Crawford (41) and Henry Clay (37). The House, choosing among the top three, elected Adams after Clay backed him, and Adams then named Clay secretary of state; Jacksonians charged a 'corrupt bargain' and organized to win in 1828.
cards.h: → the result + the House vote + the appointment + the charge
cards.n: Saying Clay was a finalist in the House vote is wrong: he finished fourth and was out, which is why his support was decisive for Adams.

cards.q: Explain why the election of 1828 is considered a turning point toward mass democracy.
cards.a: By 1828 most states had dropped property requirements for white men and let voters, not legislatures, choose presidential electors, so the number of votes cast roughly tripled, from about 365,000 in 1824 to about 1.15 million. Jackson's supporters built a national party, the Democrats, with rallies, barbecues, hickory-pole raisings, partisan newspapers and personal attacks, the mass-politics style of the Second Party System.
cards.h: → wider electorate + campaign methods + resulting party
cards.n: Saying turnout rose because women or Black men gained the vote is false; the growth came from white men and from popular choice of electors.

cards.q: Explain why national nominating conventions replaced the congressional caucus in choosing presidential candidates.
cards.a: The caucus, where a party's congressmen picked its nominee, was attacked as undemocratic 'King Caucus' after its choice, Crawford, ran third in 1824. Conventions of delegates chosen by local party members gave ordinary voters a voice; the Anti-Masons held the first in 1831, and the major parties followed.
cards.h: → caucus seen as elite → discredited in 1824 → conventions of local delegates → Anti-Masons first, major parties follow
cards.n: 'Conventions were more exciting' earns nothing; the point needs the charge that the caucus was undemocratic and the shift to locally chosen delegates.
o: Conventions also built national party organizations by bringing local leaders together and adopting platforms.
The breakup of one-party Republican rule after 1824 left no single caucus able to speak for the whole party.

w.a: The Constitution required nominating conventions starting in 1824.
w.why: invented; conventions are party practice, not law

w.a: Jackson was the congressional caucus's nominee in 1824.
w.why: false; he ran against the caucus choice

cards.q: Define Jacksonian democracy.
cards.a: Jacksonian democracy was the political culture of the 1820s and 1830s that celebrated the 'common man' against privileged elites: nearly universal white male suffrage, popular choice of presidential electors, party nominating conventions, rotation in office, and hostility to monopolies such as the national bank. It was democracy for white men: women, most free Black men and American Indians were excluded, and Indian removal advanced alongside it.
cards.h: → its ideal + its practices + its limits
cards.n: Omitting the limits loses the point on most prompts: its expansion of democracy came alongside Black disfranchisement and Indian removal.

cards.q: Define the spoils system.
cards.a: The spoils system was the practice of rewarding party supporters with government jobs. Jackson defended it as 'rotation in office' that kept officials from becoming an entrenched elite and let ordinary citizens serve; the name comes from Senator William Marcy's 1832 remark that 'to the victor belong the spoils.' Jackson replaced only a minority of federal officeholders, but the practice became standard for both parties.
cards.h: → the practice + Jackson's defense + the name's origin
cards.n: Saying Jackson invented patronage overstates it (Jefferson also removed Federalists); what was new was defending rotation as democratic.

cards.q: Explain the criticism leveled against Jackson's spoils system.
cards.a: Critics, mostly Whigs, charged that handing out jobs for party loyalty rather than skill made government incompetent and corrupt, turned officeholders into party workers who owed campaign money and labor, and let the president build a personal machine. The complaint grew after the Civil War and produced the civil service reform movement and the Pendleton Act (1883), which introduced merit exams.
cards.h: → who objected + what they charged + what it led to
cards.n: Borrows the Pendleton Act from u6. Saying the spoils system ended in the 1830s is wrong: merit reform began only in 1883.

cards.q: Differentiate the First Party System from the Second Party System.
cards.a: The First Party System (1790s to about 1815) pitted Federalists against Jeffersonian Republicans in a politics of limited suffrage, deference to elites and candidates chosen by congressional caucus. The Second Party System (about 1828 to the early 1850s) pitted Jacksonian Democrats against Whigs with nearly universal white male suffrage, national nominating conventions, mass rallies and partisan newspapers, and turnout near 80 percent in 1840.
cards.h: → era + parties + how politics worked, for each
cards.n: Borrows the First Party System from u3. Naming the parties without contrasting how politics worked (elite versus mass) misses the difference.

cards.q: Identify the 'Log Cabin and Hard Cider' campaign of 1840 and its significance.
cards.a: The Whigs ran William Henry Harrison, a wealthy general from a Virginia planter family, as a hard-cider-drinking frontiersman from a log cabin, with slogans ('Tippecanoe and Tyler too'), songs, parades and rallies, while casting President Van Buren as a luxury-loving aristocrat blamed for the depression after 1837. Turnout reached about 80 percent of eligible voters and Harrison won, showing the Whigs had mastered the Democrats' mass politics.
cards.h: → candidate and image + methods + turnout + significance
cards.n: Taking the log-cabin image at face value misses the point: it was manufactured, and the significance is the mass-campaign style both parties now used.

cards.q: Define the Tariff of Abominations of 1828.
cards.a: The Tariff of 1828, which Southern opponents called the Tariff of Abominations, raised duties on imported manufactured goods and some raw materials to the highest levels yet. Southerners saw it as enriching Northern manufacturers at the expense of cotton planters, who sold abroad and bought imports, and it prompted Calhoun's South Carolina Exposition and Protest.
cards.h: → what it did + who named it and why + what it set off
cards.n: The name was its opponents' label; Jacksonians in Congress had loaded it with high duties partly to embarrass Adams, a maneuver that backfired.

cards.q: Define Calhoun's theory of nullification as laid out in the South Carolina Exposition and Protest.
cards.a: Calhoun, then vice president, argued anonymously in the South Carolina Exposition and Protest (1828) that the states had created the Union by compact and remained sovereign, so a state convention could declare a federal law unconstitutional and void within its borders; the law could be enforced there only if three-fourths of the states then approved an amendment granting the disputed power. South Carolina applied the theory to the tariffs of 1828 and 1832.
cards.h: → the premise + the power claimed + the check on it
cards.n: Nullification is not secession: Calhoun offered it as a way to stay in the Union while blocking a law. It built on the 1798 Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions.

cards.q: Identify the nullification crisis.
cards.a: In November 1832 a South Carolina convention, applying Calhoun's theory, declared the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 null and void in the state and threatened secession if the federal government used force. Jackson called nullification treason, and Congress passed the Force Bill (1833) authorizing military enforcement alongside Clay's Compromise Tariff (1833), which lowered rates over ten years. South Carolina then withdrew its ordinance but nullified the Force Bill.
cards.h: → what South Carolina did + the federal response + outcome
cards.n: Saying Jackson sided with South Carolina because he was a Southerner is the classic miss: he defended the Union against nullification.

cards.q: Explain how the Compromise Tariff of 1833 modifies the argument that Jackson defeated nullification by force.
cards.a: It shows the crisis ended through compromise, not force alone: the Force Bill was never used, and South Carolina rescinded its ordinance only after Clay's bill promised lower rates. Both sides claimed victory, and the constitutional question of nullification was left unsettled.
cards.h: → Force Bill threatened, unused → Clay's tariff cuts rates → SC withdraws ordinance → both claim victory, question open
cards.n: Restating that Jackson threatened force supports rather than modifies the argument; the point needs the concession that ended the crisis.
o: South Carolina's symbolic nullification of the Force Bill shows it never accepted Jackson's view of federal supremacy.
No other Southern state joined South Carolina, so isolation, not only force or compromise, pushed it to back down.

w.a: It proves Jackson won by force because the army occupied Charleston.
w.why: false; no troops were used against the state

w.a: The Compromise Tariff raised rates, forcing South Carolina to yield.
w.why: reversed; it lowered rates over ten years

cards.q: Explain the long-term significance of the nullification crisis.
cards.a: The crisis rehearsed the constitutional argument that later led to secession: whether the Union was a compact of sovereign states that could void federal laws or leave, or a perpetual nation whose laws bound every state. The compromise averted force but settled nothing, and South Carolina, having found that defiance could win concessions, would lead secession in 1860.
cards.h: → question raised + why it stayed open + later link
cards.n: Saying it caused the Civil War overstates it; its significance is as a rehearsal of the states' rights argument, left unresolved.

cards.q: Identify the Bank War.
cards.a: The Bank War was Jackson's fight against the Second Bank of the United States. When Clay and Webster pushed an early recharter bill in 1832, Jackson vetoed it as an unconstitutional monopoly that served the wealthy and foreign investors at ordinary people's expense, won reelection on the issue, and from 1833 moved federal deposits into selected state 'pet' banks, crippling the bank before its charter expired in 1836.
cards.h: → the fight + the veto and its argument + the aftermath
cards.n: Mixing the Bank War up with the tariff fight confuses two crises; the bank was attacked as a privileged monopoly, and its fall helped set up the Panic of 1837.
x: Second Bank of the United States

cards.q: Explain why Andrew Jackson's presidency changed the power of the presidency.
cards.a: Claiming to be the one official elected by all the people, Jackson vetoed more bills than all his predecessors combined, often on policy rather than constitutional grounds, removed the deposits over Congress's objections, and faced down South Carolina, making the president a party and policy leader.
cards.h: → claims popular mandate → vetoes on policy, removes deposits, faces nullifiers → president leads party and policy
cards.n: 'Jackson was a strong president' earns nothing; the change was using the veto and a popular mandate to lead policy, which Whigs attacked as tyranny.
o: Whigs took their name from the English opponents of royal power, casting Jackson as 'King Andrew.'
The Senate censured Jackson in 1834 for removing the deposits, showing how far he had stretched presidential power; the censure was expunged in 1837.

w.a: Jackson changed the presidency by serving three terms.
w.why: false; he served two

w.a: His power grew because Congress took the veto away from later presidents.
w.why: invented

cards.q: Explain how Jackson's financial policies contributed to the Panic of 1837.
cards.a: Federal deposits in pet banks, heavy British investment and high cotton prices fed easy credit and speculation in Western land. Jackson's Specie Circular (1836) then required gold or silver for public land, draining coin from banks, while the Bank of England tightened credit and cotton prices fell; banks suspended payments in May 1837, and a depression lasted into the early 1840s.
cards.h: → causes of the boom + triggers of the bust
cards.n: Blaming Jackson alone misses the international causes (British credit, falling cotton prices) that historians now stress.

cards.q: Explain the human and economic toll of the Panic of 1837.
cards.a: The panic began a depression that lasted, with a second crash in 1839, until about 1843: hundreds of banks failed or suspended payments, businesses closed, farm and cotton prices fell, and unemployment and wage cuts hit city workers hard. Several states defaulted on canal and bank debts, and the hard times doomed Van Buren's reelection in 1840.
cards.h: → length + economic damage + political result
cards.n: Precise unemployment rates for 1837 are not known, so avoid inventing figures; the point is the depth and length of the depression and its political fallout.

cards.q: Contrast the Whigs and the Jacksonian Democrats.
cards.a: Whigs, led by Clay and Daniel Webster, wanted an active federal government promoting growth through the American System (a national bank, protective tariffs, internal improvements), favored moral reform, and distrusted strong presidents; they drew merchants, manufacturers and evangelical Protestants. Democrats wanted limited federal power, no national bank, low tariffs, expansion and a strong president; they drew small farmers, many urban workers and Catholic immigrants.
cards.h: → view of government + key policies + voters, for each party
cards.n: A contrast that lists policies without naming the underlying split over the federal government's role in the economy misses the point.

cards.q: Explain how federal Indian policy changed between the 1790s and the 1830s.
cards.a: In the 1790s the government acquired land by treaty while urging Native nations to adopt farming and Christianity in place. By the 1830s, as cotton planters and settlers demanded Southeastern land, it forced removal west even of nations like the Cherokee that had adopted farming, a written constitution and a newspaper.
cards.h: → 1790s: treaties + 'civilization' in place → cotton, settler demand → 1830s: forced removal even of assimilated nations
cards.n: Describing only removal ignores the change; the point needs the earlier policy of assimilation in place and why it was abandoned.
o: Continuity: throughout, the U.S. used treaties, often signed under pressure or by unrepresentative leaders, to take Native land.
The Cherokee constitution (1827) and the Cherokee Phoenix (1828) show that assimilation no longer protected Native land.

w.a: In the 1790s the government removed all Native nations west of the Mississippi.
w.why: anachronism; removal came in the 1830s

w.a: Policy changed because Native nations asked to move west.
w.why: false; most resisted

cards.q: Identify the Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears.
cards.a: The Indian Removal Act (1830) authorized the president to negotiate treaties exchanging Native lands east of the Mississippi for lands in the West, in present-day Oklahoma. Under it the Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, Cherokee and Seminole nations were forced west in the 1830s; the Cherokee removal of 1838-1839 under U.S. troops, in which an estimated 4,000 of about 16,000 people died, is called the Trail of Tears.
cards.h: → what the act allowed + who was removed + Trail of Tears
cards.n: On its face the act authorized negotiated exchanges; the coercion came through the treaties and their enforcement. Death tolls are estimates.

cards.q: Date the Indian Removal Act, Worcester v. Georgia, and the Cherokee Trail of Tears.
cards.a: Indian Removal Act 1830; Worcester v. Georgia 1832; Treaty of New Echota 1835; the Cherokee Trail of Tears 1838-1839.
cards.h: → three dates in order
cards.n: Placing the Trail of Tears in 1830 confuses the law with its enforcement: the Cherokees were removed eight years later.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Worcester v. Georgia (1832) and what followed.
cards.a: Worcester v. Georgia (1832): the Marshall Court ruled that the Cherokee Nation was a distinct political community under federal, not state, authority, so Georgia's laws had no force in Cherokee territory and its conviction of the missionary Samuel Worcester was void. Jackson did nothing to enforce the ruling, and Georgia and the federal government pressed removal anyway.
cards.h: → holding + what followed
cards.n: Confusing it with Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831), which called the Cherokees a 'domestic dependent nation' and dismissed their suit, is the common slip.

cards.q: Explain how Jackson's Indian removal policy defied the Supreme Court's ruling in Worcester v. Georgia.
cards.a: The ruling denied Georgia authority in Cherokee territory, but Jackson, who supported removal, refused to use federal power to protect the Cherokees from Georgia. The line 'John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it' is probably apocryphal, but his inaction let Georgia keep seizing Cherokee land and pushed the Cherokees toward the removal treaty of 1835.
cards.h: → what the Court said + what Jackson did not do + result
cards.n: Quoting the famous line as fact overstates the evidence; the point is that federal inaction left the ruling unenforced.

cards.q: Identify the Treaty of New Echota (1835) and why it was considered fraudulent.
cards.a: The Treaty of New Echota (1835) ceded all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi for 5 million dollars and land in Indian Territory. It was signed by a small 'Treaty Party' led by Major Ridge, John Ridge and Elias Boudinot, not by the Cherokee government under Principal Chief John Ross, and most Cherokees protested it; the Senate ratified it by a single vote in 1836, and it became the legal basis for the 1838 removal.
cards.h: → terms + who signed + why it was fraudulent + result
cards.n: Saying the Cherokee Nation as a whole agreed to move misses the fraud: an unauthorized minority signed over the elected government's protests.

cards.q: Explain why the Cherokee strategy of resisting removal through the courts failed.
cards.a: The Cherokees used American law and won in Worcester v. Georgia (1832), but the Court could not enforce its ruling without the president, and Jackson and Georgia ignored it. The Treaty of New Echota, signed by a minority faction and ratified by the Senate, then gave removal a legal basis the Court would not undo.
cards.h: → win in court → no enforcement without the president → Jackson, Georgia ignore it → minority treaty gives legal cover
cards.n: 'The Cherokees lost the case' is false; the point is that winning did not help because enforcement depended on hostile officials.
o: Cherokee petitions, the Cherokee Phoenix and their constitution won Northern sympathy, but the Removal Act had already passed Congress, narrowly, in 1830.
Division between Ross's government and the Treaty Party weakened unified Cherokee resistance.

w.a: It failed because the Supreme Court ruled for Georgia in Worcester.
w.why: reversed; the Court ruled against Georgia

w.a: It failed because the Cherokees refused to use American courts.
w.why: false; they sued twice

cards.q: Identify the Black Hawk War (1832) and the Second Seminole War (1835-1842).
cards.a: In the Black Hawk War, the Sauk leader Black Hawk led about a thousand Sauk and Meskwaki (Fox) people back across the Mississippi into Illinois to reclaim their lands; militia and army troops pursued them and killed many at the Bad Axe River, and the Sauk ceded more land. In the Second Seminole War, Seminoles led by Osceola, joined by Black Seminoles, fought removal from Florida in a long, costly guerrilla war; some were never removed.
cards.h: → who resisted, where, how + outcome, for each
cards.n: Treating removal as unresisted misses these wars; the CED's point is that Native resistance led to a sequence of wars and federal efforts at control.

cards.q: Define Romanticism as it shaped American culture in the early 1800s.
cards.a: Romanticism was a European-born movement that, reacting against Enlightenment rationalism, prized emotion, intuition, imagination, nature and the individual, and believed in human perfectibility. In America it shaped transcendentalist philosophy, Hudson River School painting, Cooper's frontier novels, and reformers' faith that people and society could be perfected.
cards.h: → what it valued + what it reacted against + American forms
cards.n: Defining it as love stories earns nothing; the CED ties Romantic belief in human perfectibility to literature, art, philosophy and reform.

cards.q: Explain why Americans after the War of 1812 set out to create a distinctly national culture.
cards.a: Postwar nationalism made cultural dependence on Britain feel like unfinished independence, so writers, painters and educators set out to prove the republic could produce its own art and learning, using American landscapes, frontier stories and language while borrowing European forms such as Romanticism.
cards.h: → postwar nationalism → dependence on Britain feels unfinished → artists use American subjects in European forms
cards.n: 'Americans were proud' earns nothing; the point needs the link from postwar nationalism to the drive for cultural independence.
o: British sneers, such as the 1820 question 'who reads an American book?', spurred writers like Irving and Cooper to prove critics wrong.
Rising literacy, cheap printing and common schools created a national audience for American books and papers.

w.a: Americans built a national culture because Congress banned British books.
w.why: invented; there was no such ban

w.a: The new culture rejected every European influence.
w.why: false; it adapted Romanticism and Greek Revival

cards.q: Identify the creator of each work and what it shows about the new national culture: The Sketch Book, with 'Rip Van Winkle' (1819-1820) · The Last of the Mohicans (1826) · An American Dictionary of the English Language (1828) · 'The American Scholar' (1837) · The Oxbow (1836) · the Second Bank of the United States building in Philadelphia (completed 1824) · McGuffey's Eclectic Readers (from 1836) · 'The Raven' (1845)
cards.a:
The Sketch Book → Washington Irving: among the first American books praised in Europe; gave the Hudson Valley a folklore of its own
The Last of the Mohicans → James Fenimore Cooper: frontier romance making the wilderness and Native Americans distinctly American subjects
American Dictionary → Noah Webster: American spellings and words (color, center), a declaration of cultural independence in language
'The American Scholar' → Ralph Waldo Emerson: urged Americans to stop imitating Europe and think for themselves
The Oxbow → Thomas Cole (Hudson River School): the American landscape as sublime, with unease about civilization's advance
Second Bank building → William Strickland: Greek Revival architecture linking the republic to ancient Athens
McGuffey Readers → William Holmes McGuffey: schoolbooks spreading shared Protestant morals and patriotism
'The Raven' → Edgar Allan Poe: dark Romanticism, emotion and the uncanny over reason
cards.h: → creator + what it shows, for each work
cards.n: The works are illustrative (the CED names none); matching creators without saying what each shows about American, European or regional influences earns little.

cards.q: Define transcendentalism.
cards.a: Transcendentalism was a New England philosophical and literary movement of the 1830s and 1840s, led by Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau, holding that each person could reach spiritual truth directly through intuition and communion with nature, beyond reason and church authority. It prized self-reliance and conscience, which led some into reform, as when Thoreau went to jail (1846) rather than pay a tax to a government that upheld slavery and fought Mexico.
cards.h: → who + core belief + what it led to
cards.n: Calling it a religious revival confuses it with the Second Great Awakening; it was an intellectual movement that distrusted churches and doctrines.

cards.q: Identify Margaret Fuller and her contribution to transcendentalism and early feminist thought.
cards.a: Margaret Fuller edited the transcendentalist journal The Dial (1840-1842) and wrote Woman in the Nineteenth Century (1845), which applied the transcendentalist ideal of self-culture to women, arguing that they deserved the same freedom as men to develop their minds and choose their work. She later became a foreign correspondent for Horace Greeley's New York Tribune.
cards.h: → role in the movement + main work + its argument
cards.n: Fuller was not at Seneca Falls (she was in Europe); link her to transcendentalism and to the ideas the women's movement drew on.

cards.q: Identify George Ripley and Brook Farm.
cards.a: George Ripley, a Unitarian minister turned transcendentalist, founded Brook Farm (1841) in West Roxbury, Massachusetts, as a cooperative community where members shared manual and intellectual labor to free time for learning and self-culture. It later reorganized on Charles Fourier's socialist plan and dissolved in 1847 after a costly fire; Nathaniel Hawthorne, an early member, satirized it in The Blithedale Romance (1852).
cards.h: → founder + aims + fate
cards.n: Confusing Brook Farm with Oneida or the Shakers misses its character: a secular, intellectual experiment, not a religious sect.

cards.q: Identify the Hudson River School and explain what its landscape paintings expressed.
cards.a: The Hudson River School was a group of landscape painters, led by Thomas Cole from the 1820s and later including Asher Durand and Frederic Church, who painted the Hudson Valley, the Catskills and other American wilderness on a grand, Romantic scale. Their work expressed national pride in a landscape unlike Europe's, awe at nature as a sign of the divine, and, in works such as Cole's The Oxbow (1836), unease about civilization's advance.
cards.h: → who + subjects + what the paintings expressed
cards.n: Describing the paintings as realistic records of the landscape misses their Romantic, nationalist message.

cards.q: Define minstrelsy and its role in antebellum popular culture.
cards.a: Blackface minstrelsy was stage entertainment in which white performers darkened their faces to present songs, dances and skits caricaturing enslaved and free Black Americans. It began with acts such as Thomas D. Rice's 'Jim Crow' character (around 1830) and became, with full troupes from the 1840s, the most popular entertainment of Northern working-class audiences, spreading racist stereotypes nationwide.
cards.h: → what it was + origins + audience + effect
cards.n: Treating it as harmless comedy misses its role in spreading racist stereotypes; the name 'Jim Crow' later labeled segregation laws.

cards.q: Identify the penny press and Benjamin Day's New York Sun.
cards.a: Beginning with Benjamin Day's New York Sun (1833), penny papers sold for one cent instead of six, relied on advertising and street sales rather than subscriptions, and covered crime, local news and human-interest stories alongside politics. Cheap steam-powered presses and rising literacy let them reach the first mass readership, spreading a shared popular culture.
cards.h: → who started it + what was new + effect
cards.n: Calling the penny press a party newspaper misses what was new: cheap, advertising-funded papers aimed at ordinary readers, not party subscribers.

cards.q: Explain why American culture from 1800 to 1848 combined national, European and regional elements.
cards.a: Writers and artists filled European forms, Romanticism and Greek Revival, with American subjects such as the frontier and the wilderness. Meanwhile regions and groups kept their own voices, from New England transcendentalists to frontier humorists and enslaved people's spirituals, so the culture was a blend.
cards.h: → European forms + American subjects → regions and groups keep their own voices → a blended national culture
cards.n: Listing examples without explaining why the mix occurred (borrowed forms, American subjects, regional ways of life) earns nothing.
o: Minstrel shows mixed African American music and dance with white caricature, showing how group cultures were absorbed and distorted.
Immigrant communities, such as German Americans with their newspapers and societies, added their own traditions.

w.a: American culture was purely national because the country cut all ties with Europe.
w.why: false; European forms shaped it

w.a: Regional cultures disappeared once the Erie Canal opened.
w.why: overstated; regional identities grew stronger

cards.q: Define the Second Great Awakening.
cards.a: The Second Great Awakening was a wave of Protestant revivals from about 1800 to the 1840s, spreading from frontier camp meetings to the towns of upstate New York and beyond. Preachers such as Charles Grandison Finney rejected strict predestination and taught that individuals could choose salvation through emotional conversion and then work to perfect themselves and society; Methodists and Baptists grew fastest.
cards.h: → when and where + what preachers taught + who grew
cards.n: Confusing it with the First Great Awakening (1730s-1740s), or omitting free will and perfectionism, loses the point.

cards.q: Identify the Cane Ridge camp meeting (1801) and the role of camp meetings in the Second Great Awakening.
cards.a: At Cane Ridge, Kentucky, in August 1801, Presbyterian, Methodist and Baptist preachers addressed a crowd estimated at 10,000 to 20,000 for about a week, with emotional conversions marked by weeping, shouting and fainting. Camp meetings brought scattered frontier families together, spread evangelical religion across the West and South, and made emotional, individual conversion the Awakening's hallmark.
cards.h: → where, when + what happened + why camp meetings mattered
cards.n: Crowd sizes are contemporary estimates. Placing Cane Ridge in New England misses that the Awakening's early fire was on the frontier.

cards.q: Identify the churches that grew fastest in the Second Great Awakening and the methods they used.
cards.a: Methodists and Baptists: by 1850 they were the two largest Protestant denominations. Methodist circuit riders on horseback carried preaching to scattered frontier settlements, Baptist congregations chose lay preachers from among themselves, and both preached free will and emotional conversion in plain language, welcoming poor whites, women and African Americans.
cards.h: → which churches + how they reached people + whom they drew
cards.n: Naming the Congregational or Episcopal churches reverses the pattern: established, seminary-trained clergy lost ground to lay and traveling preachers.

cards.q: Identify Charles Grandison Finney and the 'burned-over district.'
cards.a: Charles Grandison Finney, a lawyer turned revivalist, led dramatic revivals in upstate New York in the 1820s and 1830s, notably at Rochester (1830-1831), using 'new measures' such as the anxious bench for sinners near conversion, protracted meetings and women praying in public. Western New York along the Erie Canal was called the burned-over district because revivals swept it so often; it also produced new movements such as Mormonism and Millerism.
cards.h: → who Finney was + his methods + what the district was
cards.n: Placing the burned-over district in the South or on the far frontier misses its link to the canal-boom towns of western New York.

cards.q: Explain how the market revolution contributed to the Second Great Awakening.
cards.a: Canals, factories and commerce uprooted families, loosened old community ties and brought drinking and disorder to boom towns such as Rochester. Revivals offered stability, purpose and self-discipline, and middle-class converts embraced a faith of self-control and hard work that suited the new economy.
cards.h: → market revolution uproots people, loosens ties → anxiety, disorder in boom towns → revivals offer order, discipline
cards.n: 'People were stressed by change' earns little; name the specific changes (mobility, wage work, disorder) and how revivals answered them.
o: Historian Paul Johnson argued that Rochester's employers embraced revivalism partly to discipline workers who no longer lived in their households.
The Erie Canal corridor, the heart of the burned-over district, was also the region most transformed by the market.

w.a: Factories caused the Awakening by requiring church attendance.
w.why: invented mechanism

w.a: The Awakening came before any market changes, so the two are unrelated.
w.why: ignores the link the CED names

cards.q: Explain why the Second Great Awakening's message fit the democratic spirit of the early 1800s.
cards.a: Revivalists rejected Calvinist predestination and taught that anyone could choose salvation, just as states dropped property tests and trusted ordinary men's choices. Untrained preachers spoke plainly to mass audiences, so religious authority, like political power, shifted from educated elites toward the people.
cards.h: → free will replaces predestination → salvation open to all → plain lay preachers → authority shifts to the people
cards.n: 'Religion and democracy were both popular' is a parallel, not a link; the point needs how the message and methods mirrored democratic change.
o: The explosive growth of Methodists and Baptists, who let ordinary men preach, shows the democratizing of American religion.
Revival culture, with mass meetings and emotional appeals, used techniques like those of the new mass political campaigns.

w.a: The Awakening taught that only the elect chosen by God could be saved.
w.why: reversed; that is the predestination it rejected

w.a: Revivals fit democracy because ministers were elected to Congress.
w.why: invented link

cards.q: Explain why the Second Great Awakening was partly a response to Enlightenment rationalism.
cards.a: Deists and Unitarians treated religion as a matter of reason and pictured a distant God, which revivalists saw as cold and dangerous to morality in a republic. They answered with emotional, personal experience of sin and grace and warned that reason alone could not save souls.
cards.h: → deism, Unitarianism stress reason, a distant God → revivalists fear moral decay → emotional conversion as the answer
cards.n: Saying the Awakening rejected science misreads it; the response was to rationalist religion (deism, Unitarianism), not to learning itself.
o: Timothy Dwight led revivals at Yale around 1802 partly to counter deism's popularity among students.
Paine's The Age of Reason (1794-1795) became a symbol of the 'infidelity' revivalists preached against.

w.a: The Awakening was a rationalist movement that rejected emotion.
w.why: reversed; it stressed emotion

w.a: Revivalists answered rationalism by founding the Enlightenment.
w.why: garbled; the Enlightenment came earlier

cards.q: Identify Joseph Smith and the founding of Mormonism.
cards.a: Joseph Smith, raised in the burned-over district of western New York, published the Book of Mormon and founded the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in 1830. Persecution drove the Mormons from New York to Ohio, Missouri and Nauvoo, Illinois; a mob killed Smith at nearby Carthage in 1844, and Brigham Young then led most followers west to the Great Salt Lake valley (1846-1847).
cards.h: → founder, place, date + persecution + the trek west
cards.n: Mormonism grew out of the Awakening's religious ferment but was a new faith, not a Protestant revival; the Utah trek leads into Period 5 settlement.

cards.q: Classify each piece of evidence under the cause of the Second Great Awakening it best illustrates, as the CED lists them: (1) democratic and individualistic beliefs, (2) a response to rationalism, (3) changes to society caused by the market revolution, (4) social and geographic mobility: preachers teaching that anyone could choose salvation · revivalists attacking Unitarian and deist reliance on reason · camp meetings for scattered frontier families · Rochester employers converted after the Erie Canal boom who pledged to reform their workers · Methodist circuit riders following settlers west · lay preachers without seminary training · artisans anxious as wage work replaced household workshops · Thomas Paine's The Age of Reason denounced from pulpits
cards.a:
Anyone could choose salvation → (1): salvation opened to individual choice, like the widening vote
Attacks on Unitarian and deist reason → (2): emotion and faith answering cold rationalism
Camp meetings for scattered families → (4): settlers moving west beyond the reach of churches
Rochester employers reforming workers → (3): new commercial wealth and disorder in canal towns
Circuit riders following settlers → (4): churches chasing a population on the move
Lay preachers without seminary training → (1): religious authority opened to ordinary men
Anxious artisans → (3): wage work and markets unsettling old ways of life
The Age of Reason denounced → (2): revivalists fighting deism
cards.h: → cause number + a reason, for each case
cards.n: Several items fit two causes (mobility and the market revolution overlap); a label without its reason shows no grasp of the cause.

cards.q: Explain the link between the Second Great Awakening and antebellum reform movements.
cards.a: Revivalists taught that people could choose to stop sinning and that converted Christians should perfect society to prepare for Christ's return, so converts, many of them middle-class women, formed voluntary societies to fight sins such as drunkenness and slavery and to rescue the poor, the insane and the imprisoned. Finney's converts, such as the abolitionist Theodore Weld, filled the ranks of temperance and antislavery societies.
cards.h: → what revivalists taught + how converts acted + an example
cards.n: 'Religion inspired reform' is a phrase; the point needs the mechanism: free will and perfectionism made reforming society a Christian duty.

cards.q: Contrast the moral and the economic arguments for temperance.
cards.a: The moral argument, pressed by evangelical groups such as the American Temperance Society (1826), held that drink was a sin that destroyed souls, families and women's safety, so drinkers must pledge total abstinence. The economic argument, pressed by employers and middle-class reformers, held that sober workers were punctual, productive and safe around machines, and that drink bred the poverty and crime taxpayers paid for.
cards.h: → each argument: who made it + what it claimed
cards.n: Merging the two into 'alcohol was bad' misses the contrast between sin and productivity that the question asks for.

cards.q: Identify the Maine Law of 1851.
cards.a: Maine's 1851 law, championed by Portland's mayor Neal Dow, was the first statewide ban on making and selling alcohol, except for medicinal, mechanical and manufacturing uses. About a dozen states and territories passed similar laws by 1855, but courts and voters struck down or weakened most of them before the Civil War.
cards.h: → what, where, when + who pushed it + what followed
cards.n: Borrows 1851 from u5, just past Period 4. Confusing it with national Prohibition (Eighteenth Amendment, 1919) misses that it was a state law.

cards.q: Identify Dorothea Dix and her reform campaign.
cards.a: Dorothea Dix, a Massachusetts teacher, investigated jails and almshouses where mentally ill people were caged and neglected, and presented her findings in a memorial to the Massachusetts legislature (1843). Her campaigns persuaded many states to build public asylums offering treatment rather than punishment; a federal land-grant bill she championed was vetoed by President Pierce in 1854.
cards.h: → who + what she found + what she achieved
cards.n: Saying Dix reformed prisons for criminals misses her focus: mentally ill people held in jails and almshouses.

cards.q: Identify Horace Mann and the common school movement.
cards.a: As first secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education (1837-1848), Horace Mann championed common schools: free, tax-supported public schools, officially nonsectarian but Protestant in tone, with a longer school year, graded classes and teachers trained in state normal schools (the first opened in 1839). He argued that education would form good citizens and act as 'the great equalizer' of social conditions.
cards.h: → his post + what common schools were + his argument
cards.n: Saying he created federal schools or free colleges misreads it; common-school reform was state-level elementary education.

cards.q: Explain why reformers such as Horace Mann and Dorothea Dix turned to state governments when most reformers worked through voluntary societies.
cards.a: Moral suasion could change individual behavior, but building schools, asylums and penitentiaries took taxes and laws, so these reformers lobbied legislatures. They shared the evangelical faith that people could be improved, but relied on public institutions to shape character rather than on conversion alone.
cards.h: → goals need buildings, taxes, laws → voluntary means fall short → lobby legislatures → institutions shape character
cards.n: 'They wanted government to help' earns nothing; the point is the comparison: building institutions needed public money, unlike persuasion campaigns.
o: Temperance shows the same shift over time: from pledges and persuasion in the 1820s to state prohibition laws such as Maine's in 1851.
Penitentiary reformers built prisons such as Auburn and Eastern State to reform inmates through discipline and solitude.

w.a: They turned to government because voluntary societies were illegal.
w.why: false; voluntary societies flourished

w.a: Mann and Dix got Congress to fund schools and asylums nationwide.
w.why: false; their gains came in the states

cards.q: Define utopian communities and name several examples.
cards.a: Utopian communities were experimental settlements that withdrew from ordinary society to model a perfected way of life, many in reaction to the competitive market economy and conventional family life. Examples: the Shakers (celibacy, communal property, shared leadership of men and women), Robert Owen's secular socialist New Harmony, Indiana (1825), transcendentalist Brook Farm (1841), and John Humphrey Noyes's Oneida (1848, complex marriage).
cards.h: → what they were + why they formed + examples
cards.n: Treating them as mass movements overstates them: most were small and short-lived; their significance is the belief that society could be perfected.

cards.q: Identify Mother Ann Lee and the Shaker practice of celibacy.
cards.a: Ann Lee, an English visionary whom followers called Mother Ann, brought the Shakers (the United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing) to America in 1774. Shakers lived in celibate, communal villages with men and women sharing leadership, known for ecstatic dance in worship and plain craftsmanship; since they bore no children, they grew only by conversion and by taking in orphans, reaching several thousand members around the 1840s.
cards.h: → founder + beliefs and practices + how they grew
cards.n: Saying the Shakers began in the Second Great Awakening misdates them: they arrived in 1774, though revivals later helped them grow.

cards.q: Identify John Humphrey Noyes and the Oneida Community's practice of 'complex marriage.'
cards.a: John Humphrey Noyes, a perfectionist preacher, taught that Christ's Second Coming had already occurred, so believers could live free of sin. He founded the Oneida Community in New York (1848), where members held property in common and practiced 'complex marriage,' in which all adults were considered married to one another and sexual relations and childbearing were regulated by the community.
cards.h: → founder + belief + community practices
cards.n: Confusing complex marriage with Mormon plural marriage is a common slip: Oneida rejected exclusive marriage of any kind.

cards.q: Identify how gradual emancipation changed the free African American population of the North by 1848, and the limits states placed on free Black people.
cards.a: Northern states ended slavery through gradual emancipation laws (Pennsylvania 1780, New York 1799 with final freedom in 1827, New Jersey 1804), so free Black communities grew, especially in cities such as Philadelphia, New York and Boston. Yet states restricted them: Ohio's Black Laws required bonds and barred testimony against whites, several states took away Black men's votes, and schools, churches and public places were segregated.
cards.h: → how slavery ended + growth + restrictions
cards.n: Borrows the 1780-1804 laws from u3. Saying slavery ended in the North at independence is wrong: gradual laws freed people slowly, some in New Jersey only after 1848.

cards.q: Identify the American Colonization Society.
cards.a: The American Colonization Society (founded 1816) sought to end slavery gradually by freeing enslaved people and resettling them, with free Black Americans, in Africa, founding Liberia (1822) for that purpose. Its members included slaveholders such as Henry Clay who wanted to remove free Black people from the country; most free African Americans rejected it, and by the 1830s Garrison's immediatists attacked it as racist.
cards.h: → goal + method + who backed it and who rejected it
cards.n: Calling it abolitionist like Garrison misses the contrast: it was gradualist, aimed partly at removing free Black people, and rejected by most Black Americans.

cards.q: Identify William Lloyd Garrison and The Liberator.
cards.a: William Lloyd Garrison began publishing The Liberator in Boston in January 1831, demanding immediate, uncompensated emancipation and equal rights for Black Americans and rejecting colonization; he helped found the American Anti-Slavery Society (1833). He relied on moral suasion rather than electoral politics and later denounced the Constitution as a proslavery 'covenant with death.'
cards.h: → newspaper and date + demands + methods
cards.n: Saying Garrison favored gradual, compensated emancipation or colonization reverses his position: immediatism was his defining demand.

cards.q: Contrast Garrison's and Douglass's strategies for ending slavery.
cards.a: Garrison held the Constitution proslavery, refused to vote or join parties, relied on moral suasion to change consciences, and called for Northern disunion from slaveholders. Douglass, at first a Garrisonian, broke with him around 1851, arguing that the Constitution could be read as antislavery and that abolitionists should use voting, antislavery parties and his own newspaper to end slavery.
cards.h: → each man's view of the Constitution + his method
cards.n: The break came in 1851, just past Period 4; saying both rejected politics erases the key difference.

cards.q: Explain why abolitionists divided over strategy by 1840.
cards.a: Garrisonians relied on moral suasion, called the Constitution proslavery and welcomed women as equal leaders, while others wanted political action through the new Liberty Party and objected to women's public role. The American Anti-Slavery Society split in 1840 over these questions.
cards.h: → disputes over politics, the Constitution, women's role → Garrisonians vs political abolitionists → 1840 split
cards.n: 'They disagreed' restates the question; name the issues (political action, the Constitution, women's leadership) that divided them.
o: Black abolitionists such as Henry Highland Garnet (1843) urged enslaved people to resist, a more militant path than moral suasion.
Political abolitionists ran James G. Birney for president in 1840 and 1844 on the Liberty Party ticket.

w.a: Abolitionists split because some wanted slavery in Texas.
w.why: false; no abolitionist favored that

w.a: The movement divided because Garrison joined the Liberty Party.
w.why: reversed; Garrison rejected party politics

cards.q: Identify Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott.
cards.a: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, a Quaker minister, were abolitionists who met in London in 1840, when the World Anti-Slavery Convention refused to seat women delegates. That exclusion helped convince them to organize for women's rights; they called the Seneca Falls Convention (1848), and Stanton drafted its Declaration of Sentiments.
cards.h: → who they were + the 1840 spark + what they organized
cards.n: Saying they met at Seneca Falls reverses the story: the 1840 London exclusion led them to call the convention.

cards.q: Explain why many women moved from antislavery work to demanding rights for women.
cards.a: In antislavery societies women learned to organize, petition and speak in public, yet were attacked for doing so, as when ministers condemned the Grimké sisters for addressing mixed audiences and a London convention refused women delegates (1840). The parallel with slavery inspired Seneca Falls.
cards.h: → antislavery work teaches organizing, speaking → women attacked for public roles → parallel with slavery → Seneca Falls
cards.n: 'Women wanted rights too' earns nothing; the point needs the experience in abolition and the backlash that pushed women toward their own cause.
o: Sarah Grimké's Letters on the Equality of the Sexes (1838) answered ministers who told women to keep silent.
Temperance work taught similar lessons, since the law left the wives of drunkards without control of property or children.

w.a: Women left abolition because they supported slavery.
w.why: false; most stayed abolitionists

w.a: An 1840 amendment let women speak in public, so they formed new groups.
w.why: invented

cards.q: Identify the Seneca Falls Convention.
cards.a: The Seneca Falls Convention (July 1848, Seneca Falls, New York), organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott and others, was the first women's rights convention in the United States. About 300 attended, and 100 women and men, including Frederick Douglass, signed its Declaration of Sentiments, which demanded equal legal, economic, educational and religious rights; the resolution for woman suffrage passed only narrowly, after Douglass spoke for it.
cards.h: → when, where, who + what it demanded + the suffrage vote
cards.n: Saying Seneca Falls won women the vote is the classic miss: it launched the demand, and suffrage was its most controversial resolution.

cards.q: State what the Declaration of Sentiments argued and what document it imitated.
cards.a: It was modeled on the Declaration of Independence, declaring that 'all men and women are created equal' and listing a history of 'repeated injuries and usurpations on the part of man toward woman': denial of the vote, of married women's property and wages, of fair divorce and custody laws, of higher education and most professions, and of an equal role in the church.
cards.h: → the model document + its core claim + the grievances
cards.n: Naming the Constitution as its model is the common slip; imitating the Declaration of Independence was the rhetorical point.

cards.q: Date the Seneca Falls Convention and the founding of the American Anti-Slavery Society and its female auxiliaries.
cards.a: American Anti-Slavery Society founded December 1833; women formed female antislavery societies from 1833 (in Philadelphia and Boston) and held the Anti-Slavery Convention of American Women in 1837; the Seneca Falls Convention met in July 1848.
cards.h: → dates in order
cards.n: Placing Seneca Falls before the antislavery societies reverses the causation: women's abolition work came first and fed the women's movement.

cards.q: Explain why arguments arose within the women's rights movement over whether to narrow its goals to white women.
cards.a: The movement grew out of abolitionism and included Black women such as Sojourner Truth, but many white leaders feared that linking women's rights to Black rights would cost support. The rift opened after the Civil War, when the Fifteenth Amendment enfranchised Black men but not women.
cards.h: → roots in abolition, Black women's voices → white leaders fear lost support → Fifteenth Amendment splits the movement
cards.n: Borrows the post-1865 split from u5. Saying the movement always embraced all women equally ignores the CED's point that arguments over narrowing emerged.
o: Some accounts of Sojourner Truth's 1851 Akron speech describe white participants objecting to a Black woman speaking.
Black women such as Frances Ellen Watkins Harper insisted that race and sex discrimination had to be fought together.

w.a: The movement narrowed because Black women opposed suffrage.
w.why: false; Black women were active suffragists

w.a: Seneca Falls voted to exclude Black women from membership.
w.why: invented

cards.q: Identify Gabriel's conspiracy (1800) and Denmark Vesey's conspiracy (1822).
cards.a: In 1800 Gabriel, an enslaved blacksmith, planned an armed march of enslaved men on Richmond, Virginia, to demand freedom; a storm and informers stopped it, and he and about 25 others were hanged. In 1822 Denmark Vesey, a free Black carpenter in Charleston, South Carolina, was accused of planning a large uprising; authorities hanged him and 34 others, and some historians question how far the plot really went.
cards.h: → who, where, when + what happened, for each
cards.n: Calling these rebellions that freed people misreads them: both were betrayed before they began, which is why the CED calls Southern efforts unsuccessful.

cards.q: Identify Nat Turner's Rebellion and give its year.
cards.a: Nat Turner, an enslaved preacher who believed God had called him to strike against slavery, led an uprising in Southampton County, Virginia, in August 1831 in which about 55 to 60 white people were killed. Militia and troops crushed it within days; Turner and dozens of enslaved and free Black people were executed, and white mobs killed many more, most of them uninvolved.
cards.h: → who + where and when + scale + aftermath
cards.n: Dating it to the 1850s or linking it to John Brown confuses two events; Turner's 1831 revolt came the same year as The Liberator.

cards.q: Explain how Nat Turner's Rebellion changed the South's approach to slavery.
cards.a: The revolt ended open debate about gradual emancipation in the South: the Virginia legislature debated and rejected it in 1831-1832, and Southern states tightened slave codes, banning teaching enslaved people to read, restricting Black preachers and gatherings, and policing free Black people more closely. Coming the same year as The Liberator, it pushed Southern leaders to defend slavery as a 'positive good' and to suppress abolitionist speech.
cards.h: → legislative response + restrictions + new defense
cards.n: Saying the revolt weakened slavery reverses its effect: it hardened slavery and closed the South to antislavery debate.

cards.q: Explain why antislavery efforts in the South were largely limited to unsuccessful rebellions by enslaved people.
cards.a: White Southerners silenced antislavery speech, banned abolitionist mail and outlawed teaching enslaved people to read, so no open movement could grow. Enslaved people, facing patrols, militias and informers, could resist openly only through rare armed plots, such as Gabriel's, Vesey's and Turner's, which were crushed.
cards.h: → antislavery speech suppressed → no Southern movement → patrols, informers → rare plots, crushed
cards.n: Saying enslaved people accepted slavery is false; the point is that repression kept resistance mostly hidden and made rebellion rare and doomed.
o: Each failed plot brought harsher codes, which made the next rebellion even harder.
Most resistance was everyday and hidden: slowdowns, sabotage, running away and keeping family and faith alive.

w.a: Southern antislavery efforts failed because slavery ended there in 1808.
w.why: false; 1808 ended only imports

w.a: Rebellions failed because the Union Army put them down.
w.why: wrong; militias and local whites did

cards.q: Identify Richard Allen and the African Methodist Episcopal Church.
cards.a: Richard Allen, a formerly enslaved Methodist preacher in Philadelphia, led Black worshipers out of St. George's Methodist Church after they were forced into segregated seating, founded Bethel Church (1794), and in 1816 organized the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church, the first independent Black denomination, becoming its first bishop. Black churches became centers of community life, education, mutual aid and antislavery activity.
cards.h: → who + why he left + what he founded + its role
cards.n: The walkout's date is uncertain (sources say 1787 to 1793). Calling the AME a white-led mission misses that it was Black-founded and Black-governed.

cards.q: Identify David Walker's Appeal.
cards.a: David Walker, a free Black clothing dealer in Boston, published his Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World (1829), condemning slavery and white Christians' hypocrisy, rejecting colonization, and urging enslaved people to resist, by force if necessary. Southern states banned it and punished those who circulated it, a bounty was reportedly offered for Walker, and sailors smuggled copies into Southern ports.
cards.h: → author + date + argument + reaction
cards.n: Treating Walker as a white abolitionist or a gradualist misreads him: he was a free Black militant who called for resistance.

cards.q: Identify Frederick Douglass and his contribution to abolition.
cards.a: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the abolition movement's most powerful speaker. His Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845) exposed slavery from the inside and answered doubters who could not believe so eloquent a speaker had been enslaved; in 1847 he founded the North Star in Rochester, and at Seneca Falls (1848) he spoke for woman suffrage.
cards.h: → background + writings + newspaper + wider causes
cards.n: Placing his escape or Narrative after the Civil War misdates him; his work shows free African Americans joining political efforts to change their status.

cards.q: Identify Sojourner Truth.
cards.a: Born Isabella Baumfree and enslaved in New York until she escaped with her infant daughter in 1826, Sojourner Truth took her new name in 1843 and became a traveling preacher and speaker for abolition and women's rights. At an 1851 women's convention in Akron, Ohio, she challenged the idea that women were too frail for equal rights; the famous 'Ain't I a Woman?' wording comes from a version published in 1863.
cards.h: → background + causes she spoke for + her famous speech
cards.n: Quoting 'Ain't I a Woman?' as her exact words overstates the record; the report published in 1851 uses different wording.

cards.q: Explain how life for free African Americans in the North changed and stayed the same from 1800 to 1848.
cards.a: Change: gradual emancipation enlarged free Black communities, which built churches, schools, aid societies, newspapers such as Freedom's Journal (1827) and conventions. Continuity: they still faced segregation, exclusion from many trades, mob violence and, in several states, loss of the vote, so freedom stayed partial.
cards.h: → change: larger communities build institutions → continuity: segregation, violence, lost votes → partial freedom
cards.n: Giving only change or only continuity loses the point; the task needs both, each with evidence.
o: The national Black convention movement, begun in 1830, gave free African Americans a political voice when most could not vote.
Race riots in Cincinnati (1829) and Philadelphia (1834) show hostility continuing even as communities grew.

w.a: Free African Americans in the North won full equality once slavery ended there.
w.why: false; segregation and disfranchisement continued

w.a: Nothing changed, because Northern Black people stayed enslaved.
w.why: false; they were free, if unequal

cards.q: Identify Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad.
cards.a: The Underground Railroad was a loose, secret network of free Black and white helpers, many of them Quakers, who sheltered freedom seekers and guided them to free states and Canada. Harriet Tubman escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and returned about thirteen times in the 1850s to lead roughly seventy people to freedom; in the Civil War she served the Union Army as a scout and spy.
cards.h: → what the network was + who Tubman was + her missions
cards.n: Borrows Tubman's 1850s missions from u5. Crediting her with hundreds of rescues repeats a myth; about seventy is the current estimate.

cards.q: Explain how the growth of the domestic slave trade modifies the claim that enslaved people successfully protected their family structures.
cards.a: It qualifies the claim: enslaved people did build families and kin networks, but sales from the Upper South to the cotton frontier broke up many marriages and separated children from parents. Families survived by stretching kinship across distance and adopting fictive kin, so protection was real but never secure.
cards.h: → families formed → domestic trade separates them → kinship stretched and rebuilt → protection real but insecure
cards.n: Saying the trade proves no families existed refutes rather than modifies; the point is to qualify the claim with the trade's effect.
o: Owners' debts and deaths triggered estate sales that split families, so slavery's legal basis, not only the trade, threatened kinship.
Naming children after relatives kept family memory alive across separation.

w.a: The trade could not affect families because it was banned in 1808.
w.why: only the foreign trade was banned

w.a: The domestic trade shows enslaved people formed no families at all.
w.why: overstated; it refutes rather than modifies

cards.q: Explain how the cotton gin expanded slavery.
cards.a: Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) removed seeds from short-staple cotton quickly, making it profitable to grow across the Deep South's interior. As British and Northern mills demanded ever more cotton, planters spread cultivation onto new lands and bought more enslaved workers to plant and pick it, so slavery, which some had expected to decline, expanded: the enslaved population grew from about 0.9 million in 1800 to about 3.2 million in 1850.
cards.h: → what the gin did + demand + how slavery grew, with numbers
cards.n: Borrows the 1793 gin from u3. Saying the gin reduced the need for enslaved labor reverses its effect: it cleaned cotton faster, so planters grew far more.

cards.q: Explain how the cotton gin's success reshaped the geography of American slavery.
cards.a: Because the gin made short-staple cotton profitable across the Deep South, planters moved from the worn-out soils of the Upper South and the seaboard into the fertile Black Belt of Alabama and Mississippi, the lower Mississippi valley and later Texas. The domestic slave trade forcibly moved hundreds of thousands of enslaved people from Virginia and Maryland to the new cotton lands, shifting slavery's center southwest.
cards.h: → where planters went + how enslaved people moved + result
cards.n: Saying slavery spread north into the Old Northwest confuses the regions; the shift was southwest, into the Old Southwest and Texas.

cards.q: Identify why planters moved west from the Southeast in the early 1800s, and the region they moved to.
cards.a: Decades of tobacco and cotton planting without rotation or fertilizer had exhausted soils in Virginia, the Carolinas and Georgia, while the defeat and removal of Native nations opened fertile lands to the west. Planters and many yeoman families moved in waves, the 'Alabama fever' after 1815, into Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and Arkansas and later Texas, taking or buying enslaved people, so slavery grew west of the Appalachians.
cards.h: → push (soil) + pull (new land) + where they went + effect
cards.n: Naming only the new land misses the push the CED stresses: overcultivation had depleted the Southeast's soil.

cards.q: Differentiate the international slave trade from the domestic slave trade after 1808.
cards.a: The international slave trade, bringing captives from Africa, was banned by Congress from January 1, 1808, the earliest date the Constitution allowed. The domestic slave trade stayed legal and grew: traders and migrating owners moved roughly a million enslaved people from the Upper South to the Deep South between 1790 and 1860 (estimates vary), separating families and making the sale of people a major Southern business.
cards.h: → legal status of each trade + scale + effect
cards.n: Saying slavery or all slave trading ended in 1808 is the classic miss: only imports stopped, and the domestic trade boomed.

cards.q: Explain why reliance on staple-crop exports gave the South a distinctive regional identity.
cards.a: Southern wealth came from exporting cotton, rice, sugar and tobacco grown by enslaved people, so planters put capital into land and slaves, not factories, and politics centered on slavery and low tariffs. With few cities or immigrants, the rural, planter-led South developed its own culture of hierarchy and honor.
cards.h: → staple exports, enslaved labor → capital into land, slaves → few cities, factories → planter culture, sectionalism
cards.n: Listing crops earns nothing; the point needs how the export economy shaped investment, society and politics into a separate identity.
o: Southern planters relied on Northern and British merchants to finance and ship their crops, which bred resentment of 'Yankee' commercial power.
Richmond's Tredegar Iron Works (1837) and a few textile mills were exceptions that show how little industry the South developed.

w.a: The South was distinctive because it had more factories than the North.
w.why: reversed; the North industrialized
