w.a: Southern identity came from its large immigrant population.
w.why: false; few immigrants settled there

cards.q: Identify how slaveholding was distributed among white Southern families by the mid-1800s.
cards.a: Most white Southern families owned no enslaved people: by the 1860 census about one in four did, a share that had been higher in earlier decades and was near half in Mississippi and South Carolina. Nearly half of slaveholders held fewer than five people, while planters with twenty or more, roughly one slaveholder in eight, held about half of all enslaved people and dominated Southern politics.
cards.h: → share of families + spread among holders + planter elite
cards.n: Figures are approximate and from the 1860 census, just past Period 4. Picturing every white Southerner as a planter is the misconception the CED targets.

cards.q: Explain why most white Southerners who owned no enslaved people still supported slavery.
cards.a: Slavery gave every white man, however poor, a status above all Black people; many hoped to own enslaved workers someday; yeomen depended on planters for markets, credit and cotton ginning and were tied to them by kinship and church; and leaders cast defending slavery as defending Southern liberty.
cards.h: → racial status + hope of ownership + economic ties to planters + planter politics → yeomen defend slavery
cards.n: Saying non-slaveholders profited directly from slavery misses the point; the key reasons were racial status, aspiration and ties to planters.
o: Fear that emancipation would bring job competition and social equality with freed Black people bound poor whites to the system.
Planters' dominance of churches, courts and newspapers spread the positive-good argument to all classes.

w.a: Non-slaveholders backed slavery because the law required them to own slaves.
w.why: invented

w.a: Most white Southerners owned many enslaved people, so all profited.
w.why: false; most owned none

cards.q: Contrast the 'necessary evil' and 'positive good' defenses of slavery.
cards.a: Many Revolutionary-era Southern leaders, such as Jefferson, called slavery a necessary evil: an inherited wrong they could not yet safely end and hoped would fade. From the 1830s, facing abolitionist attacks and Nat Turner's revolt, leaders such as John C. Calhoun (Senate speech, 1837) called it a positive good that civilized and cared for enslaved people better than Northern employers cared for wage workers, and a permanent basis of Southern society.
cards.h: → each view: who held it, when, what it claimed
cards.n: Crediting the 'positive good' view to Jefferson's generation reverses the chronology; the shift came in the 1830s under abolitionist pressure.

cards.q: Explain why Southern leaders shifted from calling slavery a necessary evil to calling it a positive good in the 1830s.
cards.a: Cotton made slavery more profitable than ever, and in the early 1830s Garrison's immediatism, Nat Turner's revolt and Britain's abolition of slavery in its colonies (1833) put slaveholders on the defensive. Rather than concede slavery was wrong, leaders such as Calhoun argued it benefited enslaved people and society.
cards.h: → cotton profits raise stakes → abolitionists, Turner, British emancipation → South on the defensive → 'positive good'
cards.n: 'They changed their minds' earns nothing; the point needs the profits that raised the stakes and the attacks that forced a defense.
o: The positive-good argument drew on racial theories, biblical passages and comparisons with Northern 'wage slavery.'
Virginia's 1831-1832 debate, the last serious Southern debate on emancipation, ended in rejection and marked the turn.

w.a: The shift happened because slavery had become unprofitable.
w.why: reversed; cotton made it more profitable

w.a: Southerners changed views after the Emancipation Proclamation.
w.why: anachronism; that came in 1863

cards.q: Identify George Fitzhugh's paternalist defense of slavery.
cards.a: George Fitzhugh, a Virginia writer, argued in Sociology for the South (1854) and Cannibals All! (1857) that free-labor capitalism was a war of all against all that left Northern 'wage slaves' worse off than enslaved people, whom masters supposedly cared for from birth to old age. He pushed the positive-good defense into an attack on free society itself.
cards.h: → who + works + argument + significance
cards.n: Borrows the 1850s from u5. Presenting Fitzhugh's claims about enslaved people's welfare as fact repeats proslavery propaganda; treat them as a source's argument.

cards.q: Write a thesis for the prompt: Evaluate the extent to which politics, economics and foreign policy promoted the development of an American national identity from 1800 to 1848.
cards.a: From 1800 to 1848 economic growth and foreign policy did the most to build an American identity: the market revolution's canals and railroads tied regions into one market, and the War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine bred confidence in an independent nation. Yet that same growth sharpened sectional identities, as cotton, tariffs and new western lands made slavery a dividing line, so national identity grew alongside rival regional loyalties.
cards.h: → a ranked claim + categories of reasoning + a limit
cards.n: A thesis that says all three 'contributed' without ranking them or naming a limit sets up no line of reasoning.

cards.q: Explain how the War of 1812 contributed to the development of American national identity.
cards.a: Surviving a second war with Britain, capped by Jackson's victory at New Orleans, bred pride in a truly independent nation; heroes and symbols, like 'The Star-Spangled Banner' (1814), and the Federalists' disgrace made national loyalty a political test, and nationalism produced the Second Bank and the 1816 tariff.
cards.h: → survival, New Orleans → pride, symbols, Federalists discredited → nationalist policies → shared identity
cards.n: 'People felt patriotic' earns nothing; name the mechanisms (symbols, discredited dissent, nationalist policies) that turned the war into identity.
o: Wartime shortages spurred domestic manufacturing, giving economic nationalism a practical base in the American System.
A counterpoint: New England's opposition at Hartford shows the war also exposed sectional divisions.

w.a: The war built identity because the U.S. conquered Canada.
w.why: false; the invasions failed

w.a: National identity came from the war ending slavery.
w.why: false; the war did not touch slavery

cards.q: Classify each cause of rising sectional tension from 1800 to 1848 as economic, political or territorial, and as a long-term cause or a short-term trigger, with a phrase of reasoning: the spread of cotton after the gin · the Tallmadge Amendment · the Tariff of 1828 · the Hartford Convention · the gag rule · east-west canals and railroads · the annexation of Texas (1845) · the Wilmot Proviso (1846)
cards.a:
Spread of cotton → economic, long-term: tied the South to slavery and staple exports for decades
Tallmadge Amendment → political, trigger: set off the Missouri crisis in 1819
Tariff of 1828 → economic, trigger: sparked the nullification crisis within a long tariff dispute
Hartford Convention → political, trigger: New England's wartime protest against Southern and Western power
Gag rule → political, long-running (1836-1844): made slavery a question of Northern whites' rights
East-west canals and railroads → economic, long-term: bound the Northwest to the Northeast rather than the South
Texas annexation → territorial, trigger: led to war with Mexico and reopened slavery's expansion
Wilmot Proviso → territorial, trigger: split Congress by section over slavery in the Mexican Cession
cards.h: → category + time scale + a reason, for each case
cards.n: Many labels are arguable (a tariff is also politics); credit goes to the reasoning, and labels without it show nothing. Texas and the Proviso lead into Period 5.

cards.q: Support the claim that the market revolution strengthened national unity from 1800 to 1848, using two pieces of specific evidence.
cards.a: The Erie Canal (1825) and the canals and railroads that followed tied Midwestern farms to Eastern cities and ports, so Old Northwest grain and pork fed Northeastern workers who in turn sold the West cloth and tools. Southern cotton supplied Northern and British mills and was financed, insured and shipped by New York merchants, knitting North and South into one commercial economy.
cards.h: → claim + two pieces of evidence, each tied to unity
cards.n: Evidence that shows only growth ('factories spread') does not support unity; each piece must show regions tied together.

cards.q: Explain the difference between a long-term cause and a short-term trigger, using the nullification crisis as the example.
cards.a: A long-term cause builds over years and makes an event likely; a trigger sets it off at a particular moment. The nullification crisis's long-term causes were the South's dependence on cotton exports, fear that federal power could someday reach slavery, and the compact theory dating to 1798; its trigger was the Tariff of 1828, and then the 1832 tariff's failure to cut rates enough.
cards.h: → define each + apply both to the example
cards.n: Defining the terms without applying them, or calling the tariff the only cause, misses the task.

cards.q: Identify a primary and a secondary cause of Indian removal in the 1830s, and explain your ranking.
cards.a: Primary: the demand of cotton planters and settlers, and after 1829 Georgia gold seekers, for the fertile Native lands of the Southeast, which gave states and Jackson political reasons to act. Secondary: the belief, shared by Jackson and many whites, that Native nations could not survive beside white settlement, which shaped the policy's justification. Land demand ranks first because removal targeted even nations that had adopted farming and constitutions.
cards.h: → primary cause + secondary cause + why that order
cards.n: Ranking without a reason earns nothing; the ranking must rest on evidence, such as the removal of nations that had already adopted American ways.

cards.q: Describe one way regional and group identities limited the growth of a single American national identity from 1800 to 1848.
cards.a: Many Americans identified first with their section or group: New England Federalists at Hartford (1814) and South Carolina's nullifiers (1832) put regional interests above national authority, and slaveholders defended a Southern way of life. African Americans, American Indian nations and Catholic immigrants built separate communities and institutions partly because the nation excluded them from its idea of citizenship.
cards.h: → regional identities + group identities, with evidence
cards.n: Asserting that 'not everyone felt American' earns nothing; name the specific regional or group identity and the evidence for it.

cards.q: Explain why economic development from 1800 to 1848 both unified the nation and deepened regional differences.
cards.a: Canals, railroads and trade tied regions into one market of Western food, Southern cotton and Northern goods. But specialization gave each region its own interests: the industrial North wanted tariffs and free labor, the cotton South free trade and slavery's expansion, so interdependence came with sectional conflict.
cards.h: → transport, trade link regions → specialization → different interests on tariffs, labor, slavery → unity plus conflict
cards.n: Arguing only unity or only division misses the complexity the question asks for; the point is that the same process did both.
o: The CED's KC-4.2.III says this directly: economic development helped unify the nation while encouraging the growth of different regions.
Transportation networks linked the North and Midwest more tightly than either to the South, so even unity took a sectional shape.

w.a: Economic growth only unified the nation, ending all sectional disputes.
w.why: false; tariff and slavery disputes grew

w.a: The economy divided the nation because the regions stopped trading.
w.why: false; trade among them grew

cards.q: Date the boundary years of AP Period 5 and the development that marks each end.
cards.a: Period 5 runs from 1844 to 1877. It opens with the election of 1844, when James K. Polk won on a promise to annex Texas and claim Oregon, launching the expansion that reopened the slavery question. It closes with the Compromise of 1877, when federal troops stopped propping up the last Republican governments in the South, ending Reconstruction.
cards.h: → two years + the event that marks each end
cards.n: Starting in 1850 or 1861 misses the CED framing: the expansion of the mid-1840s set off the chain. The period overlaps Period 4 (to 1848) and Period 6 (from 1865).

cards.q: Describe the three key concepts the CED uses to organize Period 5 (1844-1877).
cards.a: (1) Popular enthusiasm for expansion, backed by economic and security interests, added western lands, drew migrants from Europe and Asia, and sharpened debates over rights and citizenship (KC-5.1). (2) Expansion and deepening regional divisions made slavery the central political question and led to secession and war (KC-5.2). (3) Union victory and a contested Reconstruction ended slavery and secession but left federal power and citizenship rights unsettled (KC-5.3).
cards.h: → three concepts, one sentence each
cards.n: Listing events (Texas, Dred Scott, Appomattox) without the process that links them describes nothing; each key concept is a cause-and-effect pattern.

cards.q: Identify three ways the United States became more connected with the world between 1844 and 1877.
cards.a: Migration: millions of immigrants arrived, mainly from Ireland and Germany, and Chinese migrants came to California after the gold rush. Trade: cotton exports to British mills tied the South to a global economy, and treaties with China (1844) and Japan (1854) opened Asian ports to American ships. War and diplomacy: the war with Mexico, the Oregon settlement with Britain, and Union efforts to keep Britain and France from recognizing the Confederacy.
cards.h: → three categories, one specific example each
cards.n: Naming 'immigration' or 'trade' alone earns little; tie each connection to a specific people, place or treaty from the period.

cards.q: Classify each development under the Period 5 key concept the CED places it in, with a phrase of reasoning: KC-5.1 (expansion, migration, and debates over rights), KC-5.2 (slavery debates leading to civil war), or KC-5.3 (Union victory and Reconstruction): Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo · anti-Catholic nativist movement · Dred Scott decision · black codes · Perry's expedition to Japan · Freeport Doctrine · Homestead Act · Uncle Tom's Cabin · Emancipation Proclamation · Irish famine migration · 15th Amendment · sharecropping
cards.a:
Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo → KC-5.1 (new western territory won from Mexico)
Nativist movement → KC-5.1 (debate over immigrants' rights and influence)
Dred Scott decision → KC-5.2 (a failed attempt to settle slavery in the territories)
Black codes → KC-5.3 (southern resistance that shaped Reconstruction)
Perry's expedition → KC-5.1 (new ties with Asia)
Freeport Doctrine → KC-5.2 (slavery debate splitting the Democrats)
Homestead Act → KC-5.1 (legislation promoting western settlement)
Uncle Tom's Cabin → KC-5.2 (abolitionists' moral case against slavery)
Emancipation Proclamation → KC-5.3 (policy that helped win the war)
Irish famine migration → KC-5.1 (migrants settling in ethnic communities)
15th Amendment → KC-5.3 (new definition of citizenship and voting rights)
Sharecropping → KC-5.3 (why Reconstruction fell short of economic freedom)
cards.h: → key concept + a reason, for each case
cards.n: Some items touch two concepts (the nativists also helped break the parties, KC-5.2); the labels follow the CED, and a label without its reason shows no grasp of the pattern.

cards.q: Date these Period 5 events and put them in chronological order: Dred Scott decision · Wilmot Proviso · Emancipation Proclamation takes effect · Kansas-Nebraska Act · annexation of Texas · Compromise of 1877 · Fort Sumter · Compromise of 1850 · 15th Amendment ratified · John Brown's raid · Reconstruction Acts · Lincoln's election
cards.a:
Annexation of Texas → 1845
Wilmot Proviso → 1846
Compromise of 1850 → 1850
Kansas-Nebraska Act → 1854
Dred Scott decision → 1857
John Brown's raid → 1859
Lincoln's election → 1860
Fort Sumter → 1861
Emancipation Proclamation takes effect → 1863 (January 1)
Reconstruction Acts → 1867
15th Amendment ratified → 1870
Compromise of 1877 → 1877
cards.h: → twelve events, earliest first, each with its year
cards.n: Swapping Kansas-Nebraska (1854) and Dred Scott (1857) is the classic slip: Congress repealed the Missouri line first, then the Court called it unconstitutional.

cards.q: Write a two-sentence contextualization for an essay on the causes of the Civil War.
cards.a: Model: In the decades before 1844, the market revolution bound the North and the Old Northwest into a free-labor economy of farms, factories and cities, while the cotton boom made the South ever more dependent on enslaved labor and on expansion. The Missouri Compromise of 1820 and two national parties with members in both sections kept slavery out of national politics, but westward expansion in the 1840s threatened to put slavery in the territories back at the center.
cards.h: → earlier development + its link to the prompt
cards.n: Borrows from u4. A phrase ('there was tension over slavery') or a list of 1850s events is not context; describe what came before and show why it bears on the war.

cards.q: Explain why territorial expansion, more than slavery in the existing states, became the center of the sectional conflict after 1844.
cards.a: Nearly all white northerners accepted that the Constitution left slavery in the states alone, so the fight turned on the territories, where Congress had power. Each new acquisition, from Texas to the Mexican Cession, would decide whether future states and Senate seats were slave or free.
cards.h: → slavery in states off limits → Congress rules territories → new land decides slave or free states → clash
cards.n: 'Because of slavery' is too vague to earn the point; name the territories as the arena and explain why the balance of future states made them so contested.
o: Free-soil northerners who did not object to slavery on principle still opposed its spread, because they wanted the West for free white labor, so expansion united far more northerners than abolition did.
Southern leaders believed slavery had to expand to survive, since worn-out soils and a growing enslaved population pushed planters west and new slave states protected southern power in the Senate.

w.a: Expansion mattered because the North wanted to abolish slavery everywhere in 1844.
w.why: false; most northerners then opposed only its spread

w.a: Expansion was central because southerners wanted cotton land in Oregon.
w.why: Oregon was unsuited to cotton and organized as free

w.a: Expansion mattered because every new territory automatically allowed slavery.
w.why: no; the rule for each territory was the fight

cards.q: Explain how the Civil War and Reconstruction settled some of Period 5's central questions but left others unresolved.
cards.a: They settled slavery and secession: the 13th Amendment abolished slavery, and Union victory ended any claim of a right to leave the Union. They left open how far federal power would protect citizens' rights, as the 14th and 15th amendments' guarantees were soon undercut by violence, court rulings and northern retreat.
cards.h: → Union victory + 13th Amendment → slavery, secession settled → federal enforcement fades → rights unresolved
cards.n: Saying Reconstruction simply 'solved' or 'failed' earns nothing; the point needs what was settled and what was not, with evidence for each.
o: The question of women's citizenship was reopened and then deferred when the 15th Amendment barred racial but not sex discrimination in voting.
Power shifted permanently toward the national government, yet the Slaughterhouse Cases (1873) left most civil rights under state control.

w.a: The war settled everything, since after 1865 African Americans had full equality.
w.why: ignores black codes, Klan terror and Redemption

w.a: The war settled nothing because slavery legally continued after 1865.
w.why: the 13th Amendment ended legal slavery

cards.q: Explain how the market revolution and the cotton boom before 1844 set the stage for the sectional conflict of Period 5.
cards.a: They pulled the sections apart: canals and railroads tied the Northwest to northeastern cities and a free-labor economy, while cotton made southern wealth depend on enslaved labor and new land. Each section came to see the other's labor system as a threat to its own future in the West.
cards.h: → canals, factories tie North and West → cotton ties South to slavery and new land → rival systems clash over the West
cards.n: Borrows from u4. Calling the North 'industrial' and the South 'agricultural' without linking the economies to rival claims on the West misses the point.
o: The Missouri crisis of 1819-1821 had already shown that each new state would be counted as slave or free, a pattern expansion in the 1840s revived with higher stakes.

w.a: The market revolution caused the war because the South had no railroads.
w.why: false; the South had fewer, not none

w.a: Cotton set the stage because northern mills refused southern cotton.
w.why: northern mills bought large amounts of it

cards.q: Define manifest destiny.
cards.a: Manifest destiny was the belief, popular in the 1840s, that Providence destined the United States to expand across North America to the Pacific, spreading its democratic institutions and Protestant civilization. The journalist John L. O'Sullivan named it in 1845, and expansionists used it to justify annexing Texas, claiming Oregon and taking the Mexican Cession.
cards.h: → the belief + who named it + what it justified
cards.n: Leaving out its racial side misses what graders reward: it assumed Anglo-American superiority over Mexicans and American Indians and excused taking their lands.

cards.q: Identify the Homestead Act, the Pacific Railway Act, and the Morrill Land Grant Act.
cards.a: All three passed in 1862, when the seceded states had no members in Congress. The Homestead Act gave 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and farmed it for five years; the Pacific Railway Act gave land grants and federal bonds to build a transcontinental railroad; the Morrill Act granted public land to the states to fund agricultural and mechanical colleges.
cards.h: → year + one sentence per law
cards.n: Calling homesteads 'free land for anyone' misses the five-year residence rule; the laws passed because secession removed the southern votes that had blocked them.

cards.q: Identify the Ostend Manifesto of 1854.
cards.a: The Ostend Manifesto (1854) was a confidential dispatch from three U.S. ministers in Europe, including James Buchanan, urging the United States to buy Cuba from Spain and, if Spain refused and Cuba endangered American interests, to take it by force. Its publication in 1855 convinced many northerners that a Slave Power wanted another slave state, and the Pierce administration dropped the plan.
cards.h: → who wrote it + what it proposed + the reaction
cards.n: It was a diplomats' proposal, never U.S. policy; saying the U.S. invaded Cuba is the trap. It shows manifest destiny turning south to serve slavery.

cards.q: Identify the election of 1844 and why expansionists treated it as a mandate.
cards.a: Democrat James K. Polk, a dark-horse candidate and ally of Andrew Jackson, defeated the Whig Henry Clay on a platform calling for the 'reannexation' of Texas and the 'reoccupation' of all of Oregon. Clay's hedging on Texas and the antislavery Liberty Party's votes in New York cost him the election, and outgoing president John Tyler treated the result as approval for annexing Texas by joint resolution in 1845.
cards.h: → winner + platform + why the loser lost + result
cards.n: Calling it a landslide overstates it: Polk won the popular vote by under two points. The 'mandate' was what expansionists made of the result.

cards.q: Identify the California Gold Rush and its effect on migration to the West.
cards.a: After gold was found at Sutter's Mill in January 1848, migrants poured into California from the eastern states, Latin America, Europe and China. The non-Native population jumped from roughly 14,000 in 1848 to about 100,000 by the end of 1849, so California applied for statehood as a free state, reopening the fight over slavery that the Compromise of 1850 addressed.
cards.h: → trigger + who came + population change + political effect
cards.n: Population figures are estimates. Stopping at 'people got rich' misses the link graders reward: the rush made California a free-state applicant.

cards.q: Identify the Mormon migration to Utah and what drove it.
cards.a: After a mob killed the church's founder Joseph Smith in Illinois in 1844, Brigham Young led members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints west, reaching the Great Salt Lake valley in 1847, then Mexican territory. Seeking refuge from persecution over their beliefs, bloc voting and rumored polygamy, they built irrigated farming towns; the land passed to the United States in 1848 and became Utah Territory in 1850.
cards.h: → push factor + leader + destination + result
cards.n: Religious refuge is one of the three motives the CED names; saying the Mormons went west for gold confuses them with the forty-niners.

cards.q: Identify the Oregon Trail and the migrants who used it.
cards.a: The Oregon Trail ran about 2,000 miles from Missouri River towns such as Independence to Oregon's Willamette Valley. From the early 1840s families traveled it in wagon trains, mostly Midwestern farmers seeking fertile land, on a journey of four to six months. With the California and Mormon trails that shared its route, it carried an estimated 400,000 emigrants before the transcontinental railroad.
cards.h: → route + who traveled + why + scale
cards.n: The totals are estimates. 'Oregon fever' was about farmland; treating trail families as gold seekers misses that most sought land for family farms.

cards.q: Identify Commodore Matthew Perry's expedition to Japan (1853-1854).
cards.a: Commodore Matthew Perry led U.S. warships into Edo (Tokyo) Bay in 1853 and returned with a larger fleet in 1854, pressing the Tokugawa shogunate to sign the Treaty of Kanagawa. It opened two ports to American ships for supplies and allowed a U.S. consul, ending Japan's two-century policy of limiting contact with Western nations and advancing American trade ambitions in Asia.
cards.h: → who + when + how + treaty result
cards.n: The show of naval force is the point; saying Perry colonized Japan is wrong: he won port access and a consul, not territory.

cards.q: Identify the Treaty of Wanghia (1844) and the Burlingame Treaty (1868) with China.
cards.a: The Treaty of Wanghia, negotiated by Caleb Cushing after Britain's victory in the First Opium War, gave the United States trading rights in five Chinese ports, most-favored-nation status and extraterritoriality for Americans in China. The Burlingame Treaty of 1868 recognized free migration between the two countries, encouraging the Chinese immigration that supplied labor for western railroads.
cards.h: → two treaties: terms and purpose of each
cards.n: Say what each did for trade or migration. Making the United States the victor of the Opium War is the common slip: Britain fought it.

cards.q: Contrast Democratic and Whig attitudes toward territorial expansion in the 1840s.
cards.a: Democrats, led by Polk, championed rapid expansion into Texas, Oregon and California as land for independent farmers and a fulfillment of manifest destiny. Whigs preferred developing the existing nation through Henry Clay's program of tariffs, a national bank and internal improvements; they feared new territory would reopen the slavery question and bring war with Mexico, and many condemned that war as executive aggression.
cards.h: → each party's goal and reason, point by point
cards.n: Borrows from u4 (the Whig program). 'Whigs opposed the West' overstates it: they wanted slower, developed growth, and most voted war supplies once fighting began.

cards.q: Date the Oregon Treaty, the Mormons' arrival in the Great Salt Lake valley, the discovery of gold in California, and California's admission as a state.
cards.a: Oregon Treaty with Britain, 1846; Mormon pioneers reach the Great Salt Lake valley, 1847; gold found at Sutter's Mill, January 1848; California admitted as a free state, September 1850.
cards.h: → four events, four years, in order
cards.n: Placing the gold discovery after the war's end misses the irony graders like: gold was found nine days before the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo was signed.

cards.q: Explain why Texas annexation was delayed nine years after independence.
cards.a: Annexing Texas meant adding a large slave state, so antislavery northerners and Whigs opposed it, and Jackson and Van Buren held back to avoid a sectional fight and war with Mexico. A treaty failed in the Senate in 1844; only after Polk's victory did Congress annex Texas by joint resolution in 1845.
cards.h: → new slave state → northern, Whig opposition + fear of war → treaty fails 1844 → Polk wins → joint resolution
cards.n: 'Mexico refused' or 'Congress was busy' misses the cause graders want: slavery made annexation a sectional question.
o: A joint resolution needed only simple majorities in both houses, so it bypassed the two-thirds Senate vote that had defeated the 1844 treaty.
Fear that Britain would gain influence over an independent Texas helped Tyler and Calhoun press annexation in 1844.

w.a: Texas waited nine years because Texans did not want to join the United States.
w.why: Texans voted for annexation in 1836

w.a: Annexation was delayed because Texas had abolished slavery.
w.why: false; the Texas republic protected slavery

w.a: Annexation was delayed by the Civil War.
w.why: wrong era; annexation came in 1845

cards.q: Explain how and why the Oregon boundary dispute was settled short of war.
cards.a: Polk compromised with Britain on the 49th parallel in 1846 because war with Mexico had begun and he would not fight two wars, while Britain, its fur trade declining, accepted a line that kept Vancouver Island. The United States gained Puget Sound's harbors, which mattered for Pacific trade.
cards.h: → war with Mexico under way + British fur trade fading → both accept 49th parallel → U.S. gains Puget Sound
cards.n: 'Fifty-four forty or fight' was an expansionist cry, not the outcome; saying the U.S. won all of Oregon is the trap.
o: Britain and the United States had shared Oregon under joint occupation since 1818, and thousands of American settlers in the Willamette Valley strengthened the U.S. claim south of the Columbia.
Northern expansionists felt betrayed that Polk fought Mexico for southern land but compromised on northern land, which deepened sectional suspicion.

w.a: The U.S. won all of Oregon up to 54°40' after a short war with Britain.
w.why: no war; the line was the 49th parallel

w.a: Oregon was divided by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.
w.why: that treaty ended the war with Mexico

cards.q: Explain why the Homestead Act passed in 1862 after similar bills failed in the 1850s.
cards.a: Southern members had blocked homestead bills because free western farms would fill the territories with free-soil settlers, and Buchanan vetoed one in 1860. Secession removed those votes, so the Republican Congress passed the Homestead Act in 1862 as part of its free-labor program.
cards.h: → free homesteads = free-soil West → southern votes and Buchanan's veto block it → secession removes them → 1862
cards.n: 'Congress wanted settlers' misses the cause: what changed was political, the departure of southern opponents, not a new idea.
o: The Republican platform of 1860 promised a homestead law, so passage fulfilled a pledge that had won votes in the Northwest.
Some eastern employers had feared free western land would drain their workers, but wartime Republican control made settling the West a national priority.

w.a: The Homestead Act passed because the Civil War ended in 1862.
w.why: the war lasted until 1865

w.a: Southern planters demanded it to spread slavery west.
w.why: they opposed it for the opposite reason

cards.q: Explain why migration to the West increased in the 1840s and 1850s.
cards.a: Economic hopes drew most migrants: fertile farmland in Oregon and California after the hard times following the Panic of 1837, then gold after 1848. Others sought religious refuge, as the Mormons did in Utah, and victories over Britain and Mexico brought these lands under U.S. rule.
cards.h: → farmland + gold + religious refuge + new U.S. territory → wagon trains to Oregon, California, Utah
cards.n: Listing 'land, gold, religion' without tying each to a specific migration earns less than explaining one cause fully.
o: Guidebooks and John C. Frémont's expedition reports spread images of a fertile, reachable West that pulled families onto the trails.
Manifest destiny gave migration a patriotic meaning, so settling Oregon was framed as securing the continent against Britain.

w.a: People moved west mainly because the transcontinental railroad made the trip easy.
w.why: it was finished in 1869, after this wave

w.a: Settlers went west because the Homestead Act gave them land in the 1840s.
w.why: that act passed in 1862

cards.q: Identify the terms of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.
cards.a: Signed in February 1848, the treaty ended the war, fixed the Texas border at the Rio Grande, and transferred California, New Mexico and the rest of the Mexican Cession to the United States for 15 million dollars plus U.S. assumption of about 3.25 million dollars in American claims against Mexico. Mexicans in the ceded lands could become U.S. citizens, and their property was to be 'inviolably respected.'
cards.h: → date + border + land + price + promises to residents
cards.n: Saying Mexicans kept their land stops at the promise; courts, taxes and fraud stripped many Californios and Tejanos of property despite it.

cards.q: Date the annexation of Texas, the Mexican-American War, and the Gadsden Purchase.
cards.a: Texas annexed 1845 (joint resolution in March, statehood in December); Mexican-American War 1846-1848, ended by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848; Gadsden Purchase 1853, a strip of southern Arizona and New Mexico bought for 10 million dollars for a southern railroad route.
cards.h: → events in sequence, each with its year
cards.n: Dating the war to 1848 alone confuses it with the treaty; the Wilmot Proviso (1846) was offered when the fighting had barely begun.

cards.q: State how much territory the United States gained from Mexico in 1848 and which future states it included.
cards.a: The Mexican Cession covered roughly 525,000 square miles, about half of Mexico's prewar territory once Texas is counted. It included all of California, Nevada and Utah and parts of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Wyoming.
cards.h: → size + share of Mexico + future states
cards.n: Figures are rounded. Adding Texas or Oregon to the Cession is the common slip: Texas was annexed in 1845 and Oregon came by treaty with Britain.

cards.q: Identify Lincoln's Spot Resolutions (1847).
cards.a: As a first-term Whig congressman in December 1847, Abraham Lincoln introduced resolutions demanding that President Polk identify the exact 'spot' where American blood had been shed, implying the first clash had taken place on Mexican soil. They voiced the Whig charge that Polk had provoked the war; Congress never acted on them, and they hurt Lincoln at home, where the war was popular.
cards.h: → who + when + the demand + the point being made
cards.n: Calling the resolutions pacifist misses their purpose: a partisan Whig attack on Polk's account of how the war began.

cards.q: Compare the main ideas of these two sources. Source 1 (paraphrase of President Polk's war message to Congress, May 1846): Mexico has crossed the boundary of the United States, invaded our territory and shed American blood on American soil; war exists by Mexico's own act. Source 2 (composite paraphrase of antiwar resolutions by northern Whig legislators, 1847): the president began this war without the consent of Congress, to extend slavery and strengthen the slave states; it is a war of conquest against the interests of the free states, and it should be ended.
cards.a: Both sources treat the question of who started the war as decisive, but they answer it oppositely. Source 1 says Mexico began it by invading U.S. soil, so the war is defensive and just. Source 2 says the president began it without Congress, for a sectional purpose, the spread of slavery, so it is a war of conquest that northerners should oppose.
cards.h: → one similarity + the key difference, each explained
cards.n: Summarizing each source in turn is not a comparison; name the shared question (who began the war) and the opposed answers.

cards.q: Identify the California Land Act of 1851 and its effect on Californios.
cards.a: The act created a Board of Land Commissioners and required holders of Spanish and Mexican land grants to prove their titles, in English-language hearings and appeals that often dragged on for many years. Legal fees, squatters, taxes and debts forced many Californios to sell or lose their ranchos, so much of their land passed to Anglo Americans despite the treaty's guarantees.
cards.h: → what it required + how the process worked + result
cards.n: Most claims were eventually confirmed; saying the courts voided all grants is the trap. Delay and legal cost, not rejection, stripped many owners.

cards.q: Identify California's Foreign Miners' Tax of 1850.
cards.a: The 1850 law charged foreign miners 20 dollars a month to work claims, a prohibitive sum aimed at Mexican, Chilean and other Latin American miners. It drove many Spanish-speaking miners from the goldfields, including some Californios who were U.S. citizens under the treaty, before it was repealed in 1851; a lower tax passed in 1852 fell mainly on Chinese miners.
cards.h: → amount + targets + effect + what followed
cards.n: The tax shows citizenship promises failing in practice: who counted as 'foreign' was judged by language and race, not by the treaty's terms.

cards.q: Identify the Dakota War of 1862 in Minnesota.
cards.a: In August 1862 Dakota warriors, facing starvation after federal treaty payments were delayed and traders refused credit, attacked settlers and soldiers in southern Minnesota; hundreds of settlers and many Dakota died. Military commissions then sentenced 303 Dakota men to death; Lincoln approved 39 sentences, one was later reprieved, and 38 men were hanged at Mankato in December 1862, the largest mass execution in U.S. history.
cards.h: → causes + events + punishment + scale
cards.n: The count of sentences is a detail; graders want the cause (broken treaty payments) and the result, the Dakota's expulsion from Minnesota in 1863.

cards.q: Identify the Sand Creek Massacre of 1864.
cards.a: In November 1864 Colorado volunteer cavalry under Colonel John Chivington attacked Black Kettle's Cheyenne and Arapaho camp at Sand Creek, which flew an American flag and had been told it was under army protection. The troops killed at least 150 people, mostly women, children and the elderly, and mutilated the dead; congressional and army inquiries condemned the attack, but no one was punished.
cards.h: → who attacked whom + circumstances + toll + aftermath
cards.n: The toll is an estimate (some put it near 200). The inquiries' condemnation without punishment is the evidence graders reward for how western violence escalated.

cards.q: Identify the Long Walk of the Navajo.
cards.a: In 1863-1864 the army, with Kit Carson leading a scorched-earth campaign, forced about 8,000 to 9,000 Navajo (Diné) to walk some 300 miles to Bosque Redondo near Fort Sumner, New Mexico. Hundreds died on the march and many more from disease and failed crops there, until the Treaty of 1868 let the Navajo return to a reservation on part of their homeland.
cards.h: → who + when + route + conditions + outcome
cards.n: Numbers are estimates. It happened during the Civil War: federal conquest of Native lands in the new Southwest did not pause for it.

cards.q: Identify Red Cloud's War and the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868.
cards.a: From 1866 to 1868 the Oglala Lakota leader Red Cloud and allied Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho fought the army over forts guarding the Bozeman Trail to the Montana goldfields. The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie closed the forts and recognized the Great Sioux Reservation, including the Black Hills, one of the few Plains wars that ended on Native terms.
cards.h: → leader + cause + outcome + treaty terms
cards.n: The promise collapsed after gold was found in the Black Hills in 1874, the pattern graders reward: treaty rights ignored once resources were at stake.

cards.q: Explain how Polk brought on the Mexican-American War.
cards.a: Polk wanted California, and when Mexico refused to sell it or accept the Rio Grande border, he sent Zachary Taylor's army into the land disputed between the Nueces and the Rio Grande. After Mexican troops attacked a patrol there in April 1846, Polk told Congress Mexico had shed American blood on American soil.
cards.h: → wants California + offer refused → troops into Nueces-Rio Grande strip → clash → 'American blood on American soil'
cards.n: 'Mexico attacked first' repeats Polk's claim without the disputed border; graders want the troop movement and Polk's goals.
o: Mexico had never accepted Texas independence or annexation, so it saw the army's advance as an invasion, and a clash was the predictable result.
Polk's envoy John Slidell, sent in 1845 to buy California and the Rio Grande line, was refused a hearing, which shows Polk aimed at territory as well as the border.

w.a: Polk brought on the war by annexing California before it began.
w.why: California was taken in the war, in 1848

w.a: The war began when Mexico invaded Louisiana.
w.why: invented; fighting began near the Rio Grande

cards.q: Explain why some Americans opposed the Mexican-American War.
cards.a: Whigs charged that Polk had provoked an unconstitutional war of conquest, and antislavery northerners saw a Slave Power plan to add slave territory; Thoreau went to jail rather than pay a tax he tied to the war. Others, such as Calhoun, opposed taking all of Mexico because it would absorb millions of Mexicans.
cards.h: → executive aggression (Whigs) + slavery's spread (antislavery) + racial fears of 'All Mexico' → opposition
cards.n: 'Some people thought war was bad' earns nothing; name the group and its reason, since opponents disagreed with one another.
o: Most of the war's opponents in Congress still voted to supply the troops, so opposition centered on the war's origins and aims rather than on stopping it.

w.a: Most Americans opposed the war because the United States lost it.
w.why: the U.S. won decisively

w.a: Southerners opposed the war because it would add only free states.
w.why: most southern Democrats backed it

cards.q: Explain how the U.S. victory over Mexico affected Mexicans living in the ceded territory.
cards.a: The treaty offered them U.S. citizenship and promised to protect their property, but many became second-class residents: title lawsuits, taxes and squatters stripped Californios and Tejanos of land, and laws like the Foreign Miners' Tax and mob violence pushed them from mines and politics.
cards.h: → treaty promises citizenship and property → costly title fights, taxes, violence → land and status lost
cards.n: 'They became Americans' stops at the promise; the point needs how the promise was broken in practice.
o: In New Mexico, where Hispanos stayed the majority, many kept land and political influence longer than in California, where the gold rush quickly made them a small minority.
Many Mexican Americans became a low-wage workforce on ranches and later railroads, a pattern that continued into Period 6.

w.a: All Mexicans in the Cession were deported after the war.
w.why: most stayed, as the treaty allowed

w.a: Mexicans in the Cession got full voting rights and kept their land.
w.why: ignores land losses and exclusion

cards.q: Explain how the gold rush affected California's American Indian peoples.
cards.a: Miners and settlers who flooded in after 1848 seized Native land and streams and destroyed food sources, while state-funded militias and vigilantes killed thousands. An 1850 state law let whites hold Native people as indentured laborers; the Native population fell from about 150,000 to 30,000 by 1870 (estimates).
cards.h: → mass migration → land and food destroyed + militia killings + indenture law → population collapse
cards.n: The figures are estimates. Blaming disease alone misses what historians stress: violence and forced labor sanctioned and paid for by the state.
o: Governor Peter Burnett's 1851 call for a 'war of extermination' and state payments to volunteer companies show government sponsorship of the killing.

w.a: The gold rush helped Native Californians by giving them mining jobs.
w.why: ignores violence, dispossession and forced labor

w.a: Native Californians were moved to Oklahoma under the Indian Removal Act.
w.why: wrong policy and era

cards.q: Identify the Wilmot Proviso and its fate.
cards.a: The Wilmot Proviso, offered in 1846 by Pennsylvania Democrat David Wilmot as an amendment to a war appropriations bill, would have banned slavery from any territory acquired from Mexico. It passed the House, where the free states held a majority, but failed in the Senate, where the sections were evenly balanced, and never became law.
cards.h: → who + when + what it proposed + where it died
cards.n: The votes split by section rather than party, the point graders reward; saying it became law or banned slavery in Texas is wrong.

cards.q: Define popular sovereignty as applied to slavery in the territories.
cards.a: Popular sovereignty was the doctrine, advanced by Lewis Cass in 1848 and championed by Stephen Douglas, that the settlers of a territory, through their territorial legislature or constitution, should decide whether to allow slavery, rather than Congress. It was applied to Utah and New Mexico in 1850 and to Kansas and Nebraska in 1854.
cards.h: → who decides + who proposed it + where it was applied
cards.n: It sounded democratic but never said when settlers could decide, which invited both sides to rush settlers into Kansas; that vagueness is the point to name.

cards.q: Identify the five provisions of the Compromise of 1850.
cards.a: (1) California admitted as a free state; (2) the rest of the Mexican Cession organized as the Utah and New Mexico territories, with slavery left to popular sovereignty; (3) the Texas-New Mexico boundary settled against Texas's larger claim, with the federal government paying 10 million dollars toward Texas's debts; (4) the slave trade, but not slavery, banned in Washington, D.C.; (5) a stringent new Fugitive Slave Act.
cards.h: → five provisions: which favored the North, which the South
cards.n: Saying it abolished slavery in D.C. is the classic error: only the slave trade was banned there. Douglas passed it as separate bills after Clay's omnibus failed.

cards.q: Date the Wilmot Proviso, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act.
cards.a: Wilmot Proviso, 1846; Compromise of 1850, passed in September 1850; Kansas-Nebraska Act, 1854.
cards.h: → three events, three years, in order
cards.n: The four years from 1850 to 1854 were the Compromise's whole life; saying it held until the war overstates how long the truce lasted.

cards.q: Identify the provisions of the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850.
cards.a: The act created federal commissioners to hear claims to escaped enslaved people without a jury, barred the accused from testifying, and paid commissioners 10 dollars for ruling for the claimant but 5 dollars for freeing the accused. It ordered federal marshals to enforce it, let them call on bystanders for help, and punished anyone aiding a fugitive with up to 1,000 dollars in fines and six months in jail.
cards.h: → procedure + fees + obligations + penalties
cards.n: The 10-dollar versus 5-dollar fee and the missing jury are the details graders reward; saying it applied only in the South misses that it reached into every free state.

cards.q: Compare the four positions on slavery in the territories debated from 1846 to 1850.
cards.a: Wilmot Proviso (free soil): Congress bans slavery from all land taken from Mexico. Extending the Missouri line: carry 36°30' to the Pacific, allowing slavery south of it, a plan Polk favored. Popular sovereignty (Cass, Douglas): territorial settlers decide, keeping the issue out of Congress. Calhoun: the territories belong to all the states, so neither Congress nor settlers may exclude slaveholders.
cards.h: → four positions: who held each + what it would do
cards.n: Listing names is not a comparison; the key differences are who decides (Congress or settlers) and whether anyone may exclude slavery at all.

cards.q: Identify the position each leader took in the debate over the Compromise of 1850: Henry Clay · John C. Calhoun · Daniel Webster · William H. Seward · Stephen A. Douglas · President Zachary Taylor · President Millard Fillmore
cards.a:
Henry Clay → drafted the compromise as one omnibus bill, trading concessions to each section to save the Union
John C. Calhoun → rejected it; demanded equal access for slaveholders to the territories, strict return of fugitives and a guarantee of southern power, or else separation (speech read for him, March 4, 1850)
Daniel Webster → backed it in his Seventh of March speech, accepting a tougher fugitive slave law to save the Union, which outraged antislavery New England
William H. Seward → opposed any concession to slavery, appealing to 'a higher law than the Constitution'
Stephen A. Douglas → split the package into separate bills and passed each with shifting majorities
Zachary Taylor → wanted California admitted at once and resisted the omnibus; died in July 1850
Millard Fillmore → Taylor's successor; backed the measures and signed them in September 1850
cards.h: → each leader's stance, one line each
cards.n: Clay and Webster backed the deal while Calhoun and Seward opposed it from opposite sides; lumping the old Senate giants together is the usual miss.

cards.q: State the balance of free and slave states in 1850 and how California's admission changed it.
cards.a: In 1850 there were 15 free states and 15 slave states, giving each section 30 senators. Admitting California as a free state made it 16 to 15, ending the Senate balance the South had relied on since the Missouri Compromise, which is why southern leaders demanded concessions in return.
cards.h: → count before + count after + why it mattered
cards.n: Saying the South lost its House majority confuses the chambers: the North already controlled the House, so the Senate balance was the South's shield.

cards.q: Identify the Nashville Convention of 1850.
cards.a: In June 1850 delegates from nine slave states met in Nashville to plan a common southern response if Congress barred slavery from the Mexican Cession. Moderates outnumbered secessionists, and the convention called for extending the Missouri Compromise line to the Pacific; a second session after the compromise passed drew fewer delegates and little support.
cards.h: → when + who met + why + outcome
cards.n: Calling it a secession convention overstates it: moderates controlled the first session, one reason the Compromise could win southern acceptance.

cards.q: Identify northern personal liberty laws and their purpose.
cards.a: Personal liberty laws were northern state statutes, several passed or strengthened after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, that hindered its enforcement: they gave accused fugitives jury trials or counsel, barred state officials and jails from helping captors, and punished the kidnapping of free Black people. Southerners cited them as proof that the North would not honor the Constitution's fugitive slave clause.
cards.h: → who passed them + what they did + southern response
cards.n: They withheld state help rather than voiding the federal law; missing their place in South Carolina's 1860 case for secession loses the link graders want.

cards.q: Identify the Anthony Burns case of 1854.
cards.a: Anthony Burns, who had escaped slavery in Virginia, was arrested in Boston in May 1854 under the Fugitive Slave Act. An abolitionist attack on the courthouse failed to free him, and President Pierce sent federal troops and marines to march him to a ship past crowds of angry Bostonians, at great public expense. The spectacle turned many conservative New Englanders against the law.
cards.h: → who + where + what the government did + effect
cards.n: Stopping at the arrest misses the effect graders want: a federal show of force in Boston, in the same month as Kansas-Nebraska, pushed moderates toward antislavery politics.

cards.q: Contrast how the Missouri Compromise and the Compromise of 1850 handled slavery in the territories.
cards.a: The Missouri Compromise (1820) drew a fixed line, 36°30', banning slavery north of it in the Louisiana Purchase, so Congress decided the question in advance. The Compromise of 1850 drew no line in the Mexican Cession outside California: it left slavery in the Utah and New Mexico territories to popular sovereignty, shifting the decision from Congress to settlers and leaving it open to future contest.
cards.h: → method of each + who decides + what it left open
cards.n: Borrows from u4. The key difference is a fixed line versus local choice; the 1850 principle then undid the 1820 line in the Kansas-Nebraska Act.

cards.q: Explain why the Mexican Cession reopened the slavery question.
cards.a: The Missouri Compromise line covered only the Louisiana Purchase, so the vast new Southwest had no rule on slavery. Every proposal, from the Wilmot Proviso to extending the line, forced a sectional vote, and the two parties, which held together by avoiding slavery, could no longer dodge it.
cards.h: → Missouri line covers only Louisiana Purchase → Cession has no rule → every plan forces a sectional vote
cards.n: 'Because of slavery' repeats the prompt; the point needs why the old settlement did not apply and how that forced the issue into Congress.
o: California's rapid settlement during the gold rush turned an abstract question into an urgent one by 1849, when it applied for statehood as a free state.
Ralph Waldo Emerson predicted in 1846 that conquering Mexico would 'poison us,' anticipating how new land would inflame the sectional quarrel.

w.a: The Cession reopened slavery because Mexico was a slave country.
w.why: Mexico had abolished slavery in 1829

w.a: It reopened the question because the Missouri Compromise was repealed in 1848.
w.why: it was repealed in 1854

cards.q: Explain why the Fugitive Slave Act radicalized northern opinion.
cards.a: It turned slavery from a distant southern institution into a northern one: marshals could compel bystanders to help, accused fugitives had no jury, and free Black people risked kidnapping. Public captures, like Anthony Burns's in Boston, bred outrage, rescues and personal liberty laws.
cards.h: → northerners made to help + no jury + free Black people seized → visible captures → outrage, rescues, state laws
cards.n: 'Northerners disliked it' earns nothing; name the provision that implicated them and the concrete reaction it produced.
o: Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852), written in response to the law, carried that outrage to hundreds of thousands of readers.
Seeing northern states obstruct enforcement, southerners concluded the North would not keep its side of the Compromise of 1850.

w.a: It radicalized the North because it abolished slavery in the territories.
w.why: it did nothing of the kind

w.a: Northerners were radicalized because it legalized slavery in their states.
w.why: it enforced capture, not slavery, in the North

cards.q: Explain one difference between northern and southern attitudes toward the Compromise of 1850.
cards.a: The sections valued opposite parts of it: southerners prized the Fugitive Slave Act as the test of northern good faith and accepted California's free admission reluctantly, while many northerners accepted the territorial terms but resisted that act. Each side's grudging compliance looked like betrayal to the other.
cards.h: → South prizes Fugitive Slave Act, North resists it → each sees the other breaking the deal → trust erodes
cards.n: Saying one section liked it and the other did not is too simple: both accepted it grudgingly, but for opposite provisions.
o: Georgia's 1850 platform accepted the Compromise but warned that failure to enforce the Fugitive Slave Act would justify disunion, so southern acceptance was conditional.
The North itself was divided: Webster backed the deal to save the Union and business ties, while antislavery Whigs like Seward rejected it on moral grounds.

w.a: Northerners opposed the Compromise because it made California a slave state.
w.why: California entered as a free state

w.a: Southerners opposed it because it strengthened the fugitive slave law.
w.why: that was the part the South most wanted

cards.q: Explain one similarity in how northern and southern moderates approached the Compromise of 1850.
cards.a: Moderates in both sections treated it as a bargain to preserve the Union, not a settlement of slavery's morality: each side accepted terms it disliked, California's free admission or the Fugitive Slave Act, to secure terms it wanted.
cards.h: → both trade disliked terms for wanted ones → both aim to save the Union → a truce, not a settlement
cards.n: A similarity must be shared and explained; 'both sides wanted peace' is too thin without the trade of concessions behind it.
o: Northern and southern Democrats both backed popular sovereignty for Utah and New Mexico because it moved the decision out of Congress, where slavery split the party by section.

w.a: Both sections agreed slavery should be banned in all new territories.
w.why: the South rejected any ban

w.a: Both saw the Compromise as a permanent end to the slavery issue.
w.why: many on both sides saw a truce

cards.q: Identify the ethnic communities Irish and German immigrants built in the 1840s and 1850s.
cards.a: Irish immigrants, mostly poor Catholic refugees from the famine of 1845-1852, clustered in eastern port cities such as Boston and New York, building parish churches, Catholic schools, mutual-aid societies and ties to the Democratic Party. Germans, more often skilled workers or farmers with some savings, settled in Midwestern cities and farm districts around Milwaukee, Cincinnati and St. Louis, keeping German-language newspapers, churches, schools and clubs.
cards.h: → each group: where it settled + institutions it built
cards.n: The CED stresses preserving language and customs; describing quick assimilation misses why nativists saw immigrants as a cultural threat.

cards.q: Identify Chinese immigration to California in the 1850s and the reception it met.
cards.a: Drawn by the gold rush and pushed by hardship in southern China, tens of thousands of Chinese men came to California in the 1850s, working claims, running businesses and later building the Central Pacific Railroad. They met special taxes such as the foreign miners' tax, mob violence and legal exclusion: in People v. Hall (1854) California's supreme court barred Chinese testimony against white people.
cards.h: → why they came + what they did + how they were treated
cards.n: The CED names migrants from Asia as well as Europe; treating anti-Chinese policy as starting in 1882 misses the state-level discrimination of the 1850s.

cards.q: Differentiate free soil from abolition.
cards.a: Abolitionists demanded an end to slavery everywhere, usually immediately, as a moral sin. Free-soilers only opposed slavery's expansion into the western territories, mainly to keep the West for free white farmers and workers, and accepted slavery where it already existed under the Constitution.
cards.h: → goal of each + scope + motive
cards.n: Calling the Republican or Free Soil parties abolitionist is the classic trap: both aimed to contain slavery, not end it where it existed.

cards.q: Identify the Free Soil Party and its founding year.
cards.a: Founded in 1848 after the Wilmot Proviso's defeat, the Free Soil Party united antislavery Whigs, Democrats and Liberty Party men under the slogan 'free soil, free speech, free labor, and free men.' It nominated former president Martin Van Buren, who won about 10 percent of the popular vote, and many of its members later became Republicans.
cards.h: → year + who joined + slogan + candidate + legacy
cards.n: Most Free Soilers opposed slavery's spread to protect white labor, not out of concern for enslaved people; that motive is the distinction graders reward.

cards.q: Define the free labor ideology of the antebellum North.
cards.a: Free labor ideology held that the North's economy rested on free men who worked for wages only until they saved enough to own a farm or shop, so any hard-working man could rise to independence. Its supporters argued that slavery degraded all labor and blocked that mobility, so it had to be kept out of the West, where free men's future lay.
cards.h: → core belief + view of wage work + view of slavery
cards.n: Free labor was not abolitionism: many who held it wanted the West for white men and cared little about enslaved people; that distinction earns the point.

cards.q: Contrast the northern and southern economies on the eve of the Civil War.
cards.a: The North had most of the nation's manufacturing, railroad mileage and banking, fast-growing cities, commercial family farms, and a free wage-labor force swelled by immigrants. The South's wealth rested on staple crops, above all cotton, grown by nearly four million enslaved people; it had fewer cities, factories and immigrants, and much of its capital was invested in enslaved people and land.
cards.h: → side by side: industry, labor, cities, capital
cards.n: Calling the South 'poor' is wrong: planters were among the richest Americans. The contrast is the labor system and where capital was invested.

cards.q: Date the Panic of 1857 and explain why it deepened sectional tension.
cards.a: The Panic of 1857 began in August 1857, when the Ohio Life Insurance and Trust Company failed amid overinvestment in railroads and land and falling grain prices. It hit northern banks, factories and workers hard while cotton prices held up, so southern leaders claimed slavery's economy was superior, and northerners blamed the low Tariff of 1857, boosting Republican calls for protection and homesteads.
cards.h: → date + cause + regional impact + political effect
cards.n: Stopping at the crash earns half at best; the point is how each section read the uneven damage as proof about its own labor system.

cards.q: Identify Uncle Tom's Cabin and its impact.
cards.a: Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel, serialized in 1851 and published as a book in 1852 in response to the Fugitive Slave Act, dramatized slavery's cruelty through the sale and separation of families and the suffering of the Christian Uncle Tom. It became the best-selling American novel of the century, made slavery a personal moral question for many northern readers, and was denounced and suppressed across much of the South.
cards.h: → author + trigger + method + effect in each section
cards.n: Say how it worked on readers (family separation, Christian suffering); 'it started the Civil War' overstates its role and earns nothing.

cards.q: State the sales impact of Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852).
cards.a: About 300,000 copies sold in the United States in the first year and more than a million in Britain soon after, an unprecedented figure for the time, and stage versions reached still larger audiences. That reach turned an antislavery novel into a mass political event.
cards.h: → U.S. figure + British figure + wider reach
cards.n: Sales figures are estimates. Southern writers answered with 'anti-Tom' novels of contented slaves, a good example of rival sectional print cultures.

cards.q: Identify John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry.
cards.a: In October 1859 John Brown led about twenty men, Black and white, in seizing the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, hoping to arm enslaved people for a rising. None came; U.S. Marines under Robert E. Lee captured Brown, and Virginia tried him for treason and hanged him in December. Northern writers such as Emerson and Thoreau praised him as a martyr, which southerners took as proof the North endorsed slave insurrection.
cards.h: → when + target + goal + outcome + reactions
cards.n: The reaction matters more than the raid: northern praise convinced many southerners that a Republican victory in 1860 meant danger, a key link to secession.

cards.q: Identify James Henry Hammond's 'mudsill' speech (1858).
cards.a: In a March 1858 Senate speech, South Carolina's James Henry Hammond declared that 'Cotton is king,' so no power dared make war on the South, and claimed every society needed a 'mudsill' class to do its menial work. The South used enslaved Black people for it, he said, while the North's white wage workers were slaves in all but name.
cards.h: → who + when + two claims + the comparison drawn
cards.n: It is both a positive-good defense and an attack on free labor; missing the jab at northern wage workers loses the point.

cards.q: Identify Alexander Stephens's 'Cornerstone Speech' (1861).
cards.a: In March 1861 the Confederacy's new vice president, Alexander Stephens, told a Savannah audience that the Confederate government's 'cornerstone' was the 'great truth' that Black people were not equal to white people and that slavery was their natural condition. He rejected the founders' view of slavery as a wrong, making racial doctrine the open basis of the new nation.
cards.h: → speaker + office + date + central claim
cards.n: It refutes the later Lost Cause claim that the Confederacy fought only for states' rights; Stephens softened it after the war, itself a sourcing point.

cards.q: Explain one similarity and one difference between the northern free-labor critique of slavery and Hammond's proslavery critique of wage labor.
cards.a: Similarity: both judged a society by how it treated its laborers, and each called the other's system a form of slavery. Difference: free-labor advocates saw wage work as a temporary step to independence that slavery blocked, while Hammond said every society needed a permanent laboring class, better enslaved than free.
cards.h: → both judge societies by their labor, each calls the other slavery → differ: mobility vs a permanent lower class
cards.n: Describing each view separately earns nothing; the comparison must name what they share and what divides them.
o: Both sides reached for economic evidence: Hinton Helper's census figures on southern white poverty (1857) answered southern boasts, after the Panic of 1857, that cotton made the South more stable.

w.a: Both sides agreed that wage labor was better than slavery.
w.why: Hammond argued the reverse

w.a: Both wanted slavery abolished in the South.
w.why: neither did; Hammond defended it

cards.q: Explain why most northerners who opposed the spread of slavery were not abolitionists.
cards.a: Most opposed slavery's expansion out of self-interest: they wanted western land for free white farmers and feared competition from enslaved labor. Many shared the era's racism, as Black exclusion laws in Illinois, Indiana and Oregon show, and saw immediate abolition as radical and unconstitutional.
cards.h: → West for free whites + fear of slave competition + racism + abolition seen as radical → contain, not end
cards.n: Treating the Republican Party as abolitionist is the classic trap; most free-soilers wanted slavery contained, often with Black people kept out too.
o: Northern merchants and textile manufacturers depended on southern cotton, which gave them reasons to avoid attacking slavery where it existed.
Garrison's public burning of the Constitution in 1854 made abolitionists look dangerous to many northerners who still disliked slavery.

w.a: Most northerners were abolitionists by 1850 because of Uncle Tom's Cabin.
w.why: abolitionists remained a minority

w.a: They were not abolitionists because slavery was still legal in the North.
w.why: northern states had abolished it

cards.q: Explain how abolitionists' methods differed by the 1850s.
cards.a: Garrisonians relied on moral suasion and refused to vote under what they called a proslavery Constitution; political abolitionists such as Frederick Douglass worked through parties and elections; Black and white vigilance committees helped fugitives escape; and a few, like John Brown, turned to violence.
cards.h: → moral suasion vs politics vs aiding escapes vs violence → one goal, rival methods
cards.n: Lumping abolitionists together misses the CED's list (moral arguments, aiding escapes, sometimes violence); contrast at least two methods.
o: The Fugitive Slave Act and Bleeding Kansas pushed some once-peaceful abolitionists, such as the 'Secret Six' who funded John Brown, toward accepting force.

w.a: All abolitionists used violence like John Brown.
w.why: most rejected violence

w.a: Abolitionists differed mainly over whether slavery was wrong.
w.why: all agreed it was; they split over methods

cards.q: Explain why a strongly anti-Catholic nativist movement arose in the 1840s and 1850s.
cards.a: Famine-era immigration made Irish Catholics a large, poor, urban population; nativists feared their loyalty to the pope, blamed them for crime and low wages, and resented their votes for Democratic machines. Fights over Bibles in public schools and over temperance sharpened the clash.
cards.h: → mass Irish Catholic arrival → fears of papal loyalty, crime, low wages, machine votes → nativism
cards.n: 'People did not like immigrants' is too vague; the CED stresses the anti-Catholic core and the aim of limiting immigrants' political power.
o: Nativists proposed a 21-year wait for naturalization, aimed directly at immigrants' voting power.
Philadelphia's 1844 riots, sparked by a dispute over Catholic children's use of their own Bible in public schools, showed the religious core of the conflict.

w.a: Nativism arose because most immigrants of the 1850s came from China.
w.why: most came from Ireland and Germany

w.a: Nativists opposed immigrants because they were mostly Protestant.
w.why: reversed; the target was Catholics

cards.q: Identify the Kansas-Nebraska Act and what it repealed.
cards.a: Stephen Douglas's Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) organized the Kansas and Nebraska territories and left slavery there to popular sovereignty, which repealed the Missouri Compromise's ban on slavery north of 36°30' in the Louisiana Purchase. Douglas wanted the territories organized for a central transcontinental railroad route and needed southern votes to pass the bill.
cards.h: → author + year + mechanism + what it voided + motive
cards.n: Repealing a 34-year-old sectional settlement is what made it explosive; saying it created slave states misses that it only opened the question to settlers.

cards.q: Identify Bleeding Kansas.
cards.a: Bleeding Kansas was the violence of 1855-1859 in Kansas Territory as proslavery settlers and Missouri 'border ruffians' fought free-state settlers. Rival governments formed after fraud-ridden elections, and the incidents included the sack of Lawrence and John Brown's killing of five proslavery settlers at Pottawatomie Creek, both in 1856; roughly 50 to 60 people died in political violence.
cards.h: → when + who fought + rival governments + named incidents
cards.n: The toll is an estimate. The point graders want: popular sovereignty in practice produced fraud and violence rather than a peaceful vote.

cards.q: Identify the caning of Charles Sumner (1856).
cards.a: In May 1856, two days after Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts finished his 'Crime Against Kansas' speech insulting South Carolina's Senator Andrew Butler, Butler's kinsman, Representative Preston Brooks, beat Sumner unconscious with a cane at his Senate desk. Northerners saw proof of southern brutality; many southerners praised Brooks and sent him new canes, and Sumner was absent from the Senate for about three years.
cards.h: → who + when + why + reaction in each section
cards.n: The point is the opposite reactions in each section, showing the violence over Kansas had reached Congress; describing only the beating earns little.

cards.q: Identify the American (Know-Nothing) Party's rise and collapse in the 1850s.
cards.a: Growing out of secret nativist lodges whose members were said to answer questions with 'I know nothing,' the American Party won control of Massachusetts and strong showings elsewhere in 1854-1855, promising to curb Catholic and immigrant political power. It split over slavery in 1855-1856; its 1856 candidate, Millard Fillmore, carried only Maryland, and most northern members moved to the Republicans.
cards.h: → origin + program + peak + split + where members went
cards.n: The CED ties nativism and slavery together as the forces that ended the Second Party System; covering only the anti-immigrant side misses why the party died.

cards.q: Identify the outcome of the election of 1856 and what it revealed.
cards.a: Democrat James Buchanan won with 174 electoral votes, carrying every slave state except Maryland plus five free states. Republican John C. Frémont, in the party's first presidential race, carried 11 free states, and the American Party's Millard Fillmore carried Maryland. A party with no southern support had come within reach of the presidency.
cards.h: → three candidates + who carried what + what it showed
cards.n: The lesson graders want: adding Pennsylvania and one or two more free states would give Republicans the presidency with northern votes alone, as happened in 1860.

cards.q: Identify the three holdings of Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857).
cards.a: Chief Justice Roger Taney's majority held (1) that Black people, free or enslaved, were not and could not be U.S. citizens, so Scott could not sue in federal court; (2) that Scott's residence in free territory had not made him free; and (3) that Congress could not bar slavery from any territory, because the Fifth Amendment protected slaveholders' property, so the Missouri Compromise ban had been unconstitutional.
cards.h: → three holdings: citizenship, residence, Congress's power
cards.n: The third holding voided the Republican plan to ban slavery in the territories; leaving it out misses why the ruling inflamed the North.

cards.q: Identify the Lecompton Constitution and why it split the Democrats.
cards.a: Drafted in 1857 by a proslavery convention at Lecompton, Kansas, chosen in an election free-state settlers boycotted, it protected slavery, and voters were offered only a choice that left slaves already in Kansas enslaved either way. President Buchanan urged Congress to admit Kansas under it, but Stephen Douglas denounced it as a mockery of popular sovereignty, splitting the party; Kansans rejected it overwhelmingly in 1858.
cards.h: → who wrote it + how + who backed and opposed it + outcome
cards.n: The Buchanan-Douglas break over Lecompton, not only the Freeport Doctrine, is what divided the Democrats before 1860.

cards.q: Define the 'Slave Power' as northern Republicans used the term.
cards.a: The Slave Power was the Republican charge that a small class of wealthy slaveholders controlled the federal government, including the presidency, Congress and the Supreme Court, and used it to spread slavery and trample northern rights. Republicans cited the gag rule, the Fugitive Slave Act, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, the Ostend Manifesto and the Dred Scott decision as evidence.
cards.h: → who allegedly held power + what they sought + evidence
cards.n: It was a political argument, not a proven plot; treating it as an actual organization misreads the source. Its force lay in uniting anti-southern northerners.

cards.q: Identify Lincoln's 'House Divided' speech (1858).
cards.a: Accepting the Illinois Republican nomination for the Senate in June 1858, Lincoln declared that 'a house divided against itself cannot stand' and that the nation could not endure permanently half slave and half free; it would become all one thing or all the other. He charged that Douglas, Pierce, Taney and Buchanan were working, knowingly or not, to spread slavery nationwide.
cards.h: → occasion + central claim + accusation
cards.n: Lincoln was not calling for abolition in the states; he argued that containment would put slavery on a course of 'ultimate extinction,' the distinction graders reward.

cards.q: Identify the Lincoln-Douglas debates and the Freeport Doctrine.
cards.a: The Lincoln-Douglas debates were seven 1858 debates across Illinois in the race for Douglas's Senate seat, centered on slavery in the territories. At Freeport, Douglas argued that despite Dred Scott, settlers could keep slavery out by refusing to pass the local police laws, or slave codes, it needed. The answer satisfied Illinois voters but angered southern Democrats.
cards.h: → year + office + topic + Douglas's answer + effect
cards.n: Douglas kept his seat (the legislature chose senators), but the Freeport answer cost him the South and made Lincoln a national figure; missing that loses the point.

cards.q: Compare the positions of Lincoln and Douglas on slavery in the territories in 1858.
cards.a: Douglas held that territorial settlers should decide under popular sovereignty and said he did not care whether slavery was voted up or down; after Dred Scott he argued settlers could still exclude it by refusing to pass slave codes. Lincoln called slavery a moral wrong that Congress should bar from every territory, though he disclaimed any power to touch it in the states and rejected full racial equality.
cards.h: → who decides + moral view + limits of each position
cards.n: Presenting Lincoln as an abolitionist or racial egalitarian in 1858 is wrong; the real divide was whether slavery was a moral wrong to be contained.

cards.q: Explain how the Kansas-Nebraska Act reshaped the party system.
cards.a: By repealing the Missouri line, it split the Whigs, whose northern and southern wings could not agree, and cost northern Democrats heavily in 1854. Antislavery Whigs, Free Soilers and anti-Nebraska Democrats formed the Republican Party, a sectional party pledged to stop slavery's spread.
cards.h: → Missouri line repealed → Whigs split, northern Democrats beaten → Republicans form as a northern party
cards.n: 'It caused the Civil War' skips the mechanism; name the party that died, the party that was born and why it was sectional.
o: Nativism drew many former Whigs to the Know-Nothings first, so the Republicans had to absorb that movement before becoming the North's main party by 1856.
Once the Know-Nothings split in 1856, only the Democrats remained a national party, and that party split in 1860.

w.a: The Kansas-Nebraska Act created the Whig Party.
w.why: the Whigs formed in the 1830s and now collapsed

w.a: It united the Democrats behind popular sovereignty for good.
w.why: northern Democrats lost heavily in 1854
