cards.q: Explain why Dred Scott intensified rather than settled the sectional crisis.
cards.a: By declaring that Congress could not bar slavery from any territory, the Court made the Republican platform unconstitutional and seemed to open the whole West to slavery. Republicans refused to accept it, calling it proof of a Slave Power conspiracy, and it deepened the Democrats' split over popular sovereignty.
cards.h: → Congress can't ban slavery in territories → Republican platform voided → Slave Power charge → Democrats split
cards.n: 'It angered the North' is too thin; name the holding that closed off containment and the political reaction it produced.
o: Lincoln warned in 1858 that the next ruling might bar free states from excluding slavery, since property rights in slaves now seemed to follow owners anywhere.
The ruling forced Douglas to square popular sovereignty with it, and his Freeport answer alienated southern Democrats.

w.a: Dred Scott settled the crisis by freeing Scott and banning slavery in the West.
w.why: reversed; Scott lost and the ban was voided

w.a: It intensified conflict because it struck down the Fugitive Slave Act.
w.why: it did nothing of the kind

cards.q: Explain why popular sovereignty failed in Kansas.
cards.a: Popular sovereignty set no time or rules for deciding, so both sides rushed settlers in: Missourians crossed over to vote illegally for a proslavery legislature, free-staters formed a rival government, and fraud turned into violence. Instead of a peaceful local vote, Kansas produced rival governments and bloodshed.
cards.h: → no timing or rules → both sides race settlers in → illegal voting, rival governments → violence
cards.n: 'People disagreed' earns nothing; the point needs the flaw in the doctrine and how it produced fraud and rival governments.
o: Outside groups such as the New England Emigrant Aid Company sent free-state settlers, making Kansas a national contest rather than a local decision.
Buchanan's backing of the Lecompton Constitution showed Washington siding with a proslavery minority, undermining the claim that settlers ruled.

w.a: It failed because Kansas settlers voted to become a slave state.
w.why: Kansas entered as a free state in 1861

w.a: Popular sovereignty failed because Congress banned slavery in Kansas.
w.why: Congress left it to the settlers

cards.q: Explain how slavery and nativism together ended the Second Party System in the 1850s.
cards.a: The Whigs, already split into Cotton and Conscience wings, collapsed after Kansas-Nebraska, and anti-immigrant fears drew many of their voters to the Know-Nothings. When the Know-Nothings in turn split over slavery, most northern members joined the Republicans, leaving parties organized by section.
cards.h: → slavery splits Whigs + nativism draws off voters → Know-Nothings split over slavery → sectional parties
cards.n: Naming only slavery misses the CED: nativism also broke old loyalties, and the Know-Nothings were a bridge to the Republicans.
o: The deaths of Henry Clay and Daniel Webster in 1852 removed the Whigs' leading compromisers just before the Kansas-Nebraska crisis.

w.a: The Second Party System ended because the Democrats dissolved in 1854.
w.why: the Whigs dissolved; the Democrats survived

w.a: Nativism ended it because immigrants founded the Republican Party.
w.why: most immigrants voted Democratic

cards.q: Identify the Republican platform of 1860.
cards.a: Meeting in Chicago, the Republicans nominated Lincoln on a platform that opposed any extension of slavery into the territories while denying any intent to interfere with it in the states, and that condemned John Brown's raid. It added economic planks: a protective tariff, a homestead law and federal aid for a Pacific railroad, broadening the party's appeal to northern farmers, workers and manufacturers.
cards.h: → core slavery plank + its limits + economic planks + effect
cards.n: Saying Republicans promised abolition is the trap; the platform promised containment, plus economic planks that helped win Pennsylvania and the Northwest.

cards.q: Identify how the Democratic Party split in 1860.
cards.a: At the Charleston convention in April 1860, Lower South delegates walked out when northern Democrats refused a platform demanding a federal slave code to protect slavery in all territories. After a second convention at Baltimore, northern Democrats nominated Stephen Douglas on popular sovereignty, and southern Democrats nominated Vice President John C. Breckinridge on federal protection for slavery in the territories.
cards.h: → where + the dispute + the walkout + the two nominees
cards.n: The split was over a federal slave code, not over secession itself; linking it to Douglas's Freeport answer earns the causal point.

cards.q: Identify the four candidates in the election of 1860 and the outcome.
cards.a: Abraham Lincoln (Republican), Stephen Douglas (northern Democrat), John C. Breckinridge (southern Democrat) and John Bell (Constitutional Union). Lincoln won 180 electoral votes, a clear majority, with about 40 percent of the popular vote, carrying every free state (sharing New Jersey with Douglas) and no slave state; Breckinridge took most of the Deep South and Bell took Virginia, Kentucky and Tennessee.
cards.h: → four names and parties + result + regional pattern
cards.n: Lincoln was not on the ballot in ten southern states; saying he won only because the Democrats split ignores his outright majorities in enough free states.

cards.q: Identify the debate between immediate secessionists and cooperationists in the Lower South in 1860-1861.
cards.a: After Lincoln's election, immediate secessionists urged each state to leave at once, while cooperationists wanted to wait for joint southern action, for demands on the North, or for an overt act by Lincoln. Conventions in all seven Lower South states voted to secede between December 1860 and February 1861, though cooperationist candidates won a substantial share of the vote in states such as Georgia, Alabama and Louisiana.
cards.h: → two positions + what each wanted + outcome
cards.n: The CED's 'contested debates about secession' means it was not unanimous; claiming the white South agreed at once ignores the cooperationists.

cards.q: Identify South Carolina's Declaration of the Immediate Causes of secession (December 1860).
cards.a: Issued by South Carolina's secession convention days after the state left the Union, the declaration argued that northern states had broken the constitutional compact by refusing to enforce the Fugitive Slave Act, tolerating abolitionist societies, and electing a president whose party was hostile to slavery. It based secession on the defense of slavery, framed as protecting the states' constitutional rights.
cards.h: → who issued it + when + grievances + what it defended
cards.n: Reading it as a pure states' rights argument misses its content: every grievance concerns slavery, and it attacks northern states for using their own rights.

cards.q: Date South Carolina's secession, the formation of the Confederacy, and Fort Sumter.
cards.a: South Carolina seceded on December 20, 1860; the Confederate States of America was formed at Montgomery, Alabama, in February 1861; Confederate batteries fired on Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861, and the fort surrendered the next day.
cards.h: → three dates across two years
cards.n: Only seven states had left before Sumter; Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee and North Carolina went after Lincoln's call for 75,000 volunteers.

cards.q: Identify Lincoln's first inaugural address (March 1861).
cards.a: Lincoln declared the Union perpetual and secession legally void, promised not to interfere with slavery in the states where it existed, and pledged to hold federal property and collect duties without invading anyone. He put the choice of war on the seceded states and closed with an appeal to 'the better angels of our nature.'
cards.h: → view of secession + promises + firm line + tone
cards.n: Saying Lincoln promised to end slavery is wrong; the address was conciliatory on slavery and firm only on the Union and federal property.

cards.q: Classify each of the 15 slave states of 1860 as seceding before Fort Sumter, seceding after Lincoln's call for troops, or staying in the Union: Alabama · Arkansas · Delaware · Florida · Georgia · Kentucky · Louisiana · Maryland · Mississippi · Missouri · North Carolina · South Carolina · Tennessee · Texas · Virginia
cards.a:
Alabama → before Sumter (January 1861)
Arkansas → after the call for troops (May 1861)
Delaware → stayed in the Union
Florida → before Sumter (January 1861)
Georgia → before Sumter (January 1861)
Kentucky → stayed (declared neutrality, then sided with the Union)
Louisiana → before Sumter (January 1861)
Maryland → stayed (under heavy federal military pressure)
Mississippi → before Sumter (January 1861)
Missouri → stayed (despite a rival pro-Confederate government)
North Carolina → after the call for troops (May 1861)
South Carolina → before Sumter (December 20, 1860)
Tennessee → after the call for troops (May-June 1861)
Texas → before Sumter (February 1861)
Virginia → after the call for troops (April 1861, ratified by voters in May)
cards.h: → one of three categories for each state
cards.n: The seven-then-four pattern is the point: the Upper South left only when forced to choose sides, and West Virginia later split off to stay in the Union.

cards.q: Identify Jefferson Davis and the Confederate Constitution.
cards.a: Jefferson Davis, a former Mississippi senator and U.S. secretary of war, was chosen president of the Confederacy in February 1861, its only president. The Confederate Constitution closely copied the U.S. Constitution but explicitly protected slavery, including in any territory the Confederacy might acquire, banned protective tariffs, and limited the president to a single six-year term.
cards.h: → Davis's background + the constitution: copied vs changed
cards.n: Its explicit guarantees of slavery are the evidence graders want against the claim that secession was only about states' rights; it also banned the foreign slave trade.

cards.q: Identify the Union border states and explain why Lincoln handled them carefully.
cards.a: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky and Missouri were slave states that stayed in the Union (West Virginia joined them in 1863). Lincoln avoided early moves against slavery partly to keep them loyal: Maryland surrounded Washington, D.C., on three sides, and Kentucky and Missouri commanded the Ohio and Mississippi river routes and held men and supplies the Confederacy wanted.
cards.h: → four states + why each mattered + effect on policy
cards.n: Lincoln wrote in 1861 that to lose Kentucky was nearly to lose the whole game; the Emancipation Proclamation exempted these states for the same reason.

cards.q: Explain why Lincoln's election triggered secession even though he promised not to touch slavery where it existed.
cards.a: Winning without a single southern electoral vote showed the North could now hold the presidency alone, ending the South's power to protect slavery in national politics. Secessionists expected Republicans to block slavery's expansion, build southern support through patronage, and doom slavery over time.
cards.h: → northern-only victory → South loses its national veto → containment, patronage → slavery doomed over time → secede
cards.n: Saying Lincoln planned immediate abolition earns nothing; the cause was the loss of long-term political security, as the secession declarations said.
o: South Carolina's Declaration of Causes named the election of a president hostile to slavery and northern refusal to enforce the Fugitive Slave Act as its reasons.
After John Brown's raid, many white southerners believed a Republican administration would tolerate or encourage slave insurrection.

w.a: The South seceded because Lincoln abolished slavery when he took office.
w.why: he promised not to touch it in the states

w.a: Secession came because Lincoln lost the popular vote to Douglas.
w.why: Lincoln led the popular vote

cards.q: Explain why the Crittenden Compromise of 1860-61 failed to prevent secession.
cards.a: Crittenden proposed amendments extending the 36°30' line to the Pacific and permanently guaranteeing slavery where it existed. Lincoln and most Republicans refused any extension of slavery into territories, the core of their platform, so the plan died in committee and the Senate as the Lower South left.
cards.h: → extend 36°30' + permanent guarantees → Republicans refuse expansion → plan dies → secession goes on
cards.n: 'Congress could not agree' is too vague; name the provision Republicans could not accept and why it contradicted their platform.
o: Lincoln feared that a line covering territories 'hereafter acquired' would encourage slaveholders to seek conquests in Mexico, Cuba and Central America.

w.a: The Crittenden Compromise failed because it would have abolished slavery.
w.why: it would have protected slavery

w.a: It failed because southerners found the Missouri line too generous to slavery.
w.why: Republicans, not the South, blocked it

cards.q: Explain Lincoln's strategy at Fort Sumter and why it worked politically.
cards.a: Lincoln told South Carolina he would resupply Sumter's garrison with food only, not troops or arms, forcing the Confederacy either to accept a federal fort in Charleston harbor or to fire the first shot. When it fired, the North united behind the war as a defense of the Union.
cards.h: → send food only → Confederacy must accept fort or attack → it attacks → North unites against aggression
cards.n: The gain had a cost graders reward: his call for 75,000 volunteers then drove four Upper South states out of the Union.
o: By letting the Confederacy strike first, Lincoln kept northern Democrats and border-state Unionists from blaming him for starting the war.

w.a: Lincoln attacked Fort Sumter to start the war on his own terms.
w.why: Confederate batteries fired on the fort

w.a: Lincoln abandoned Sumter to avoid war, which united the North.
w.why: he chose to resupply it

cards.q: Explain why the Upper South seceded only after the attack on Fort Sumter.
cards.a: The Upper South had fewer enslaved people, less dependence on cotton, closer ties to the North and strong Unionist parties, so it waited on compromise. Lincoln's April 1861 call for 75,000 volunteers forced a choice between fighting fellow slave states and leaving; Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee and North Carolina left.
cards.h: → fewer enslaved, more Unionism → wait → call for troops forces a side → four states secede
cards.n: Saying these states left because Lincoln won the election misses the timing; their trigger was the call for troops, not the vote.
o: Their decision roughly doubled the Confederacy's white population and added industry such as Richmond's Tredegar Iron Works.

w.a: The Upper South seceded first, in December 1860.
w.why: South Carolina led; the Upper South left in spring 1861

w.a: They seceded because Lincoln freed their slaves in April 1861.
w.why: emancipation came in 1863

cards.q: Contrast Union and Confederate advantages at the start of the Civil War.
cards.a: The Union had about 22 million people to the Confederacy's 9 million (about 3.5 million of them enslaved), roughly 90 percent of the nation's manufacturing, about two-thirds of its railroad mileage, a navy, and an established government and treasury. The Confederacy had able officers, interior lines, the need only to defend rather than conquer, and hopes that Britain's need for cotton would bring recognition.
cards.h: → side by side: people, industry, transport vs strategy
cards.n: Figures are rounded estimates. A list of northern strengths is not a contrast; pair each with what the South had instead, and note resources did not decide the early war.

cards.q: Identify the Anaconda Plan.
cards.a: General Winfield Scott's 1861 strategy was to squeeze the Confederacy: blockade the southern coast, take control of the Mississippi River to split the South in two, and apply steady pressure rather than seek one decisive battle. Mocked at first as too slow, its main elements, the blockade and the fall of Vicksburg in 1863, became central to Union victory.
cards.h: → author + three elements + early reaction + outcome
cards.n: Northern opinion in 1861 demanded a quick march on Richmond and got Bull Run; recognizing that the slow plan largely won the war is the point.

cards.q: Identify the Trent Affair of 1861.
cards.a: In November 1861 Captain Charles Wilkes of the USS San Jacinto stopped the British mail ship Trent and seized two Confederate envoys, James Mason and John Slidell, bound for Britain and France. Britain demanded their release and sent troops to Canada; Lincoln released them, reportedly saying 'one war at a time,' and avoided British intervention.
cards.h: → who seized whom + British reaction + Lincoln's decision
cards.n: It shows Union diplomacy keeping Britain neutral, the world side of this topic; saying Britain went to war over it is wrong.

cards.q: State the casualty toll of the Battle of Antietam (September 17, 1862).
cards.a: About 23,000 soldiers on both sides were killed, wounded or missing in a single day, the bloodiest single day in American military history. Because Lee then withdrew to Virginia, Lincoln treated the battle as the victory he needed and issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation five days later.
cards.h: → figure + what it ranks as + consequence
cards.n: The figure is an estimate and counts killed, wounded and missing together; saying 23,000 men died is the common slip.

cards.q: Identify Grant's appointment as general-in-chief in 1864 and his strategic shift.
cards.a: In March 1864 Lincoln promoted Ulysses S. Grant, victor at Vicksburg and Chattanooga, to lieutenant general and general-in-chief of all Union armies. Grant dropped the search for one decisive battle and coordinated simultaneous offensives, pressing Lee in Virginia himself while Sherman drove on Atlanta, using the Union's greater manpower to wear down Confederate armies.
cards.h: → when + who + new approach + how it used Union strengths
cards.n: The CED credits 'improvements in leadership and strategy'; Grant is the example, and saying he won with one decisive battle misses the strategy of attrition.

cards.q: Identify Sherman's March to the Sea and total war.
cards.a: After capturing Atlanta in September 1864, William T. Sherman marched about 60,000 men through Georgia to Savannah (November-December 1864) and then north through the Carolinas, destroying railroads, crops, factories and property to break the South's ability and will to fight. It is the standard American example of total war, aimed at the enemy's economy and civilians' morale as well as its armies.
cards.h: → route + dates + method + label
cards.n: The fall of Atlanta also rescued Lincoln's reelection against McClellan in 1864, a political effect graders reward alongside the military one.

cards.q: Date Appomattox, Lincoln's assassination, and the 13th Amendment's ratification.
cards.a: Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865; Lincoln was shot on April 14, 1865, and died the next morning; the 13th Amendment was ratified in December 1865.
cards.h: → three events in one year, in order
cards.n: Congress passed the 13th Amendment in January 1865 but ratification came in December; mixing the two dates is the common slip.

cards.q: State the approximate death toll of the Civil War.
cards.a: Roughly 620,000 soldiers died by the traditional count, and a 2011 demographic estimate by J. David Hacker puts the figure nearer 750,000. About two-thirds of the deaths came from disease rather than battle, making it the deadliest war in U.S. history.
cards.h: → traditional figure + revised estimate + main cause
cards.n: Both figures are estimates; saying most soldiers died in battle is the common error, since disease killed about twice as many.

cards.q: Identify the New York City draft riots of 1863.
cards.a: In July 1863, days after Gettysburg, mostly Irish working-class mobs in New York City attacked draft offices, Republican targets and Black residents for four days, lynching Black men and burning the Colored Orphan Asylum. They were enraged by the first federal draft, which let wealthier men pay a 300-dollar commutation fee or hire a substitute; troops sent from Gettysburg restored order after roughly 120 deaths.
cards.h: → when + who + targets + grievance + outcome
cards.n: The death toll is an estimate. Missing the racial violence misses the point: rioters blamed Black New Yorkers for the war and feared job competition.

cards.q: Identify the Copperheads.
cards.a: Copperheads, or Peace Democrats, were northern Democrats who opposed the war, emancipation and the draft and called for a negotiated peace with the Confederacy, with strength in the lower Midwest and among immigrant workers. Their leader, Ohio's Clement Vallandigham, was arrested by the army in 1863 and banished to the Confederacy, and their 'war is a failure' plank entered the 1864 Democratic platform.
cards.h: → who + positions + base + key figure + influence
cards.n: They are the CED's 'home front opposition' in the North, but not every Democrat was one: War Democrats backed the fighting.

cards.q: Identify Lincoln's suspension of habeas corpus and the controversy it caused.
cards.a: Beginning in Maryland in 1861, Lincoln suspended the writ of habeas corpus, letting the military arrest and hold suspected Confederate sympathizers without trial. Chief Justice Taney ruled in Ex parte Merryman (1861) that only Congress could suspend it, but Lincoln ignored him; Congress authorized suspension in 1863, and after the war Ex parte Milligan (1866) barred military trials of civilians where civil courts were open.
cards.h: → what was suspended + where + judicial challenge + outcome
cards.n: It was the Union's answer to home-front opposition; dating Milligan to the war is the trap, since the Court ruled only in 1866.

cards.q: Identify the Confederacy's 'Twenty Negro Law' of 1862.
cards.a: Part of the Confederacy's second conscription act (October 1862), it exempted one white man from the draft for every plantation with twenty or more enslaved people, to keep an owner or overseer at home to control them. Poor whites resented it as proof of 'a rich man's war and a poor man's fight,' which fed desertion.
cards.h: → when + provision + purpose + reaction
cards.n: The Confederacy began conscription in April 1862, almost a year before the Union; that a states' rights government drafted first is the irony graders note.

cards.q: Identify the National Banking Acts of 1863-1864 and their purpose.
cards.a: The acts created federally chartered national banks that bought U.S. bonds and issued a uniform national currency backed by them, helping finance the war and replacing the confusing mix of state bank notes. A 10 percent federal tax on state bank notes, passed in 1865, drove those notes out of circulation.
cards.h: → what they created + how it worked + two purposes
cards.n: The system lasted until the Federal Reserve (1913); calling it a central bank like the Second Bank of the United States is the common error.

cards.q: Define greenbacks and explain the constitutional fight over paper currency resolved in the Legal Tender Cases.
cards.a: Greenbacks were paper dollars the Union issued from 1862 under the Legal Tender Act, backed by the government's credit rather than gold or silver and made legal tender for debts. In Hepburn v. Griswold (1870) the Supreme Court held they could not be forced on creditors for debts made before 1862, but in the Legal Tender Cases (1871) a reshaped Court reversed itself and upheld them.
cards.h: → definition + law + first ruling + reversal
cards.n: Chief Justice Chase, who had issued greenbacks as Treasury secretary, wrote the 1870 ruling against them; Grant's two new justices flipped it the next year.

cards.q: Identify Clara Barton and the U.S. Sanitary Commission's role in the Civil War.
cards.a: Clara Barton brought supplies and nursing care to Union soldiers near the front, earning the name 'angel of the battlefield,' and later founded the American Red Cross (1881). The U.S. Sanitary Commission, a private relief agency created in 1861 and run largely by women volunteers, raised money through sanitary fairs, inspected camps and hospitals, and supplied medicine and food to the Union army.
cards.h: → Barton's role + the commission's origin, staff and work
cards.n: Their work mattered because disease killed about twice as many soldiers as combat; it is an example of the Union mobilizing society, not just armies.

cards.q: Explain the significance of the Battle of Antietam.
cards.a: By stopping Lee's first invasion of the North in September 1862, Antietam ended the Confederacy's best chance that autumn to win British and French recognition. It also gave Lincoln the victory he wanted before issuing the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, which turned the war against slavery.
cards.h: → Lee's invasion stopped → European recognition stalls → preliminary Emancipation Proclamation
cards.n: Tactically a draw, it counts as a strategic Union victory because Lee withdrew; calling it a crushing Union win overstates it.
o: McClellan's failure to pursue Lee's battered army led Lincoln to remove him in November 1862, part of the search for effective leadership the CED credits.

w.a: Antietam mattered because it ended the war in 1862.
w.why: the war lasted until 1865

w.a: Antietam was a Confederate victory that brought Britain into the war.
w.why: Lee withdrew and Britain stayed out

cards.q: Explain why July 1863 is called the turning point of the Civil War.
cards.a: At Gettysburg (July 1-3) the Union army under Meade turned back Lee's second invasion of the North, and Lee never again invaded in force. On July 4 Vicksburg surrendered to Grant, and with Port Hudson's fall days later the Union controlled the Mississippi, splitting the Confederacy.
cards.h: → Gettysburg ends Lee's invasions + Vicksburg gives the Union the Mississippi → Confederacy split, on the defensive
cards.n: Naming only Gettysburg misses half the answer; Vicksburg completed a key goal of the Anaconda Plan and made Grant's reputation.
o: The twin defeats further dimmed Confederate hopes of European recognition and hurt southern morale, though the war lasted almost two more years.

w.a: July 1863 was the turning point because Lee surrendered at Gettysburg.
w.why: Lee surrendered at Appomattox in 1865

w.a: It was the turning point because Sherman took Atlanta that month.
w.why: Atlanta fell in September 1864

cards.q: Explain how Civil War legislation transformed the federal government's role in the economy.
cards.a: With southern members gone, Congress created national banks and a uniform currency, issued greenbacks, levied the first federal income tax, raised protective tariffs, and subsidized railroads, homesteads and colleges. Washington now shaped currency, credit, land and transportation directly.
cards.h: → southern opposition gone → banks, currency, income tax, tariffs, subsidies → lasting federal economic power
cards.n: Listing the laws is description; the point needs the change: federal power over money, land and infrastructure expanded and stayed.
o: These measures laid groundwork for Period 6 industrial growth, as railroad land grants and high tariffs continued after 1865.

w.a: The war shrank the federal government because the Constitution banned new taxes.
w.why: Congress levied new taxes, including an income tax

w.a: The legislation mainly helped the South rebuild its plantations.
w.why: it passed without the South, for northern aims

cards.q: Explain how the Civil War expanded northern women's paid employment outside the home.
cards.a: With men at the front, women took paid jobs as government clerks, arsenal and factory workers, teachers and nurses in unprecedented numbers, as the war's demand for labor and supplies made their work part of Union mobilization. Many lost these jobs when the men returned.
cards.h: → men leave → labor shortage + war demand → women as clerks, factory hands, nurses → many jobs lost after
cards.n: Stopping at 'women helped' earns little; name the kinds of paid work and note that the change was partly temporary.
o: Women's wartime service became an argument for suffrage, which is why many felt betrayed when the 15th Amendment left them out.
In the South, women ran farms and plantations, and women led the 1863 Richmond bread riot against wartime shortages.

w.a: The war let women vote for the first time in 1863.
w.why: women won national suffrage in 1920

w.a: Women served as regular soldiers in both armies.
w.why: only a few served, in disguise

cards.q: Explain one similarity and one difference in how the Union and the Confederacy financed the war.
cards.a: Both printed paper money and borrowed, but the Union also taxed heavily, including the first income tax, sold bonds widely and built national banks, so its greenbacks kept much of their value. The Confederacy taxed little and printed money, and its prices rose roughly 9,000 percent.
cards.h: → both print and borrow → Union also taxes, sells bonds, builds banks → Confederacy mostly prints → runaway inflation
cards.n: The inflation figure is an estimate. 'The North had more money' is description; the answer must name the shared method and the decisive difference.
o: The blockade cut Confederate cotton exports, the South's main source of foreign credit, so its finances worsened as the war went on.

w.a: The Confederacy paid for the war mainly with an income tax on planters.
w.why: it relied on printed money

w.a: The Union paid for the war entirely with California gold.
w.why: it used taxes, bonds and greenbacks

cards.q: Identify the 'contraband' policy begun at Fort Monroe in 1861.
cards.a: In May 1861 General Benjamin Butler, commanding Fort Monroe in Virginia, refused to return three men who had escaped slavery, calling them 'contraband of war' because their owners were using enslaved labor for the Confederate war effort. Thousands of enslaved people then fled to Union lines, and the policy spread, pushing the Union toward the Confiscation Acts and emancipation.
cards.h: → who + where + reasoning + what followed
cards.n: The term treated people as enemy property, not as free persons; the CED's point is that enslaved people's own flight forced the policy.

cards.q: Identify the Confiscation Acts of 1861-1862.
cards.a: The First Confiscation Act (August 1861) let the Union seize property used to support the rebellion, including enslaved people forced to work for Confederate forces. The Second (July 1862) declared free the enslaved people of anyone supporting the rebellion who escaped to Union lines or came under Union control. Together they moved Union policy toward emancipation before the Emancipation Proclamation.
cards.h: → two acts: date + what each allowed
cards.n: They show emancipation developing step by step under congressional pressure, not appearing overnight in 1863; enforcement was limited.

cards.q: Identify the District of Columbia Compensated Emancipation Act of 1862.
cards.a: Signed in April 1862, it freed about 3,000 enslaved people in Washington, D.C., paying loyal owners up to 300 dollars per person and offering money to freedpeople who chose to emigrate. Two months later Congress banned slavery in all federal territories, defying the Dred Scott decision.
cards.h: → date + terms + who was paid + what followed
cards.n: Compensation and colonization mark Lincoln's early, gradual approach; the contrast with the uncompensated Emancipation Proclamation is the change graders reward.

cards.q: Identify Lincoln's August 1862 letter to Horace Greeley and why its timing matters.
cards.a: Answering the New York Tribune editor's demand for emancipation, Lincoln wrote that his 'paramount object' was to save the Union: if he could do so without freeing any slave, or by freeing all, or some, he would. He had already drafted the Emancipation Proclamation and was waiting for a victory, so the letter prepared northern opinion to accept emancipation as a war measure.
cards.h: → context + stated aim + three options + hidden timing
cards.n: Reading the letter as proof Lincoln did not care about slavery ignores its purpose: public reassurance while the proclamation waited in his desk.

cards.q: Differentiate what the Emancipation Proclamation did from what it did not do.
cards.a: Effective January 1, 1863, it declared enslaved people free in areas still in rebellion, committed the army and navy to maintain their freedom, and authorized enlisting Black men in Union forces. It did not apply to the loyal border states, Tennessee, or Union-held parts of Louisiana and Virginia, and as a war measure it could not abolish slavery as an institution; that took the 13th Amendment.
cards.h: → what it declared and authorized vs its limits
cards.n: 'It freed no one' overstates the limit: it freed people wherever Union armies went, starting in occupied places like the Sea Islands, but it exempted border-state slavery.

cards.q: Identify the 54th Massachusetts Regiment and its significance for Black soldiers in the Civil War.
cards.a: The 54th Massachusetts, one of the first Black regiments raised in the North (1863), was led by white Colonel Robert Gould Shaw and won fame for its assault on Fort Wagner, South Carolina, in July 1863, where Shaw and many of his men died. Its courage helped change northern opinion about Black soldiers, about 180,000 of whom served in the Union army, most in the United States Colored Troops.
cards.h: → when + leader + key battle + wider significance
cards.n: Black soldiers were paid less than white soldiers until 1864, and the 54th refused its pay in protest; leaving that out tells only half the story.

cards.q: Identify Harriet Tubman's role as a Union Army scout during the Civil War.
cards.a: Tubman served the Union in South Carolina as a nurse, spy and scout, and in June 1863 guided Colonel James Montgomery's raid up the Combahee River, which freed more than 700 enslaved people. The raid is often described as the first armed U.S. military operation planned or led in part by a woman.
cards.h: → roles + key raid + date + result
cards.n: She is the CED's kind of evidence that African Americans helped undermine the Confederacy; she never got a soldier's pension, only a widow's, later raised.

cards.q: Identify the Gettysburg Address and how it redefined the war's purpose.
cards.a: At the dedication of the soldiers' cemetery at Gettysburg in November 1863, Lincoln spoke for about two minutes, tracing the nation to 1776 ('four score and seven years ago') and its proposition that all men are created equal. He cast the war as a test of whether such a nation could endure and called for 'a new birth of freedom,' tying the Union cause to equality.
cards.h: → occasion + date + founding reference + redefined purpose
cards.n: Dating the nation from 1776 put the Declaration, not the Constitution that protected slavery, at its center; that choice is the CED's point.

cards.q: Identify Lincoln's second inaugural address (March 1865).
cards.a: Delivered weeks before the war ended, it named slavery as 'somehow the cause of the war' and suggested that the war's suffering was God's judgment on North and South alike for the sin of slavery. Lincoln closed by calling for peace 'with malice toward none, with charity for all' and for binding up the nation's wounds.
cards.h: → date + cause named + interpretation + call to action
cards.n: It shows Lincoln's view of the war's meaning changed after 1861: slavery, not union alone, now stood at the center.

cards.q: Date Juneteenth and explain what it commemorates.
cards.a: Juneteenth marks June 19, 1865, when Union General Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston, Texas, and announced that enslaved people there were free under the Emancipation Proclamation, two and a half years after it took effect. It commemorates the end of slavery in the United States and became a federal holiday in 2021.
cards.h: → date + place + event + what it marks
cards.n: Slavery ended legally only with the 13th Amendment (December 1865), which freed those in the border states; Galveston shows freedom arriving where the army did.

cards.q: Explain the strategic significance of the Emancipation Proclamation.
cards.a: Making the war a fight against slavery made it politically impossible for Britain and France, whose publics opposed slavery, to recognize the Confederacy. It also encouraged enslaved people to flee, draining Confederate labor, and opened the Union army to Black men, about 180,000 of whom served.
cards.h: → war against slavery → Europe can't back the Confederacy + enslaved flee + Black enlistment → Union stronger
cards.n: Black enlistment is the effect students most often omit and graders reward; 'it freed the slaves' alone misses the strategic effects.
o: It committed the Union to emancipation as a war aim, so a negotiated peace that restored slavery became much harder.

w.a: The Proclamation brought Britain into the war on the Union side.
w.why: Britain stayed neutral

w.a: It mattered because it freed all slaves in the border states.
w.why: it exempted the border states

cards.q: Explain how Lincoln's war aims changed from 1861 to 1865.
cards.a: In 1861 Lincoln fought only to restore the Union and disclaimed any aim against slavery in the states. By 1863 military need, enslaved people's flight and Radical pressure led him to make emancipation a war aim, and by 1865 he backed the 13th Amendment, calling for a new birth of freedom.
cards.h: → 1861 Union only → flight to Union lines, war needs, Radical pressure → 1863 emancipation → 1865 13th Amendment
cards.n: A CCOT answer needs both the continuity (saving the Union stayed his first aim) and the change (abolition became means and goal).
o: Continuity ran alongside change: Lincoln still promoted colonizing freedpeople abroad in 1862-1863 before abandoning the idea.

w.a: Lincoln intended to abolish slavery everywhere from the day the war began.
w.why: he disclaimed that aim in 1861

w.a: Lincoln's aims never changed; he fought only for the Union to the end.
w.why: ignores emancipation and the 13th Amendment

cards.q: Explain how enslaved people's own actions pushed the Union toward emancipation.
cards.a: By fleeing to Union lines by the thousands from 1861, enslaved people forced commanders and Congress to decide their status; 'contraband' camps and the Confiscation Acts followed. Their labor and later military service made freedom useful to the Union, helping turn emancipation into policy.
cards.h: → mass flight to Union lines → army must decide their status → contraband, Confiscation Acts → emancipation policy
cards.n: Saying Lincoln alone freed the slaves ignores what the CED stresses: African Americans fled and enlisted, undermining the Confederacy themselves.
o: By one common estimate, about half a million enslaved people reached Union lines during the war, a heavy drain on Confederate labor.

w.a: Enslaved people stayed on plantations until 1865 because they knew nothing of the war.
w.why: many fled from 1861 on

w.a: They pushed emancipation by forming their own Confederate regiments.
w.why: invented; they joined Union forces

cards.q: Explain how the Gettysburg Address linked the Civil War to the nation's founding ideals.
cards.a: Lincoln dated the nation from the Declaration of 1776 and its creed that all men are created equal, casting the war as a test of whether a nation built on it could survive. Continuity with the founding became a call for change: a 'new birth of freedom' that included the end of slavery.
cards.h: → nation dated from 1776 and equality → war tests that idea → 'new birth of freedom' → founding ideals widened
cards.n: Calling it a victory speech misses its purpose; the CED's point is that it portrayed the fight against slavery as fulfilling founding ideals.
o: By naming neither slavery nor the South nor the battle itself, Lincoln made the soldiers' sacrifice universal, which helped the speech outlast its occasion.

w.a: The Gettysburg Address announced the end of the war in 1863.
w.why: the war went on until 1865

w.a: Lincoln based the address on the Constitution's protection of slavery.
w.why: he grounded it in the Declaration's equality

cards.q: Contrast Lincoln's Ten Percent Plan with the Wade-Davis Bill.
cards.a: Lincoln's 1863 plan let a state form a new government once 10 percent of its 1860 voters swore future loyalty and accepted emancipation, with pardons for most Confederates. The 1864 Wade-Davis Bill required a majority of white men to swear loyalty and let only men who took an 'ironclad oath' that they had never supported the Confederacy form the new government; Lincoln pocket-vetoed it.
cards.h: → threshold + oath + who controls, for each
cards.n: The clash began the fight between president and Congress over who controlled Reconstruction; describing each plan without the contrast earns little.

cards.q: Identify the black codes.
cards.a: The black codes were laws passed by southern states in 1865-1866, under Presidential Reconstruction, to control freedpeople's labor and movement. Vagrancy laws let unemployed Black men be fined and hired out, labor contracts bound workers for a year, apprenticeship laws took Black children from their families, and other laws barred Black people from renting farmland, serving on juries or owning guns.
cards.h: → when + purpose + specific restrictions
cards.n: They rebuilt slavery's labor control without legal ownership, which is why Congress answered with the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the 14th Amendment.

cards.q: Contrast Presidential Reconstruction under Johnson with Radical Reconstruction under Congress.
cards.a: Johnson (1865-1866) required southern states only to abolish slavery, ratify the 13th Amendment, void secession and repudiate Confederate debts; he pardoned planters freely and left freedpeople's rights to all-white state governments, which passed black codes. Congress, from 1867, put the South under military rule, required new constitutions with Black male suffrage and ratification of the 14th Amendment, and used federal power to protect freedpeople.
cards.h: → requirements + who protected freedpeople, for each
cards.n: The black codes and Johnson's vetoes are what provoked the congressional takeover; presenting the two plans without that cause misses the link.

cards.q: Identify the Radical Republicans and their Reconstruction goals.
cards.a: The Radical Republicans, led by Thaddeus Stevens in the House and Charles Sumner in the Senate, wanted to remake the South: punish Confederate leaders, protect freedpeople's civil and voting rights with federal power, and, in Stevens's case, confiscate plantations to give land to freedpeople. They led Congress's break with Johnson from 1866.
cards.h: → leaders + goals + clash with Johnson
cards.n: Radicals were a faction, not a majority; moderate Republicans wrote most Reconstruction law, and Stevens's land confiscation plan never passed.

cards.q: Identify the Freedmen's Bureau.
cards.a: The Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, created by Congress in March 1865 and led by General O. O. Howard, gave formerly enslaved people and white refugees food, medical care and legal help, supervised labor contracts, and above all supported schools, helping found Black colleges such as Howard and Fisk. Congress ended most of its work by 1869 and closed it in 1872.
cards.h: → date + leader + services + greatest legacy + end
cards.n: It was the first large federal social welfare agency; Johnson's 1866 veto of its extension was a key step in his break with Congress.

cards.q: Identify the Civil Rights Act of 1866.
cards.a: Passed over Andrew Johnson's veto in April 1866, it declared all persons born in the United States (except untaxed American Indians) to be citizens and guaranteed them equal rights to make contracts, sue, own property and enjoy the full benefit of the laws, aiming directly at the black codes. Congress then wrote its guarantees into the 14th Amendment so that a later Congress or court could not undo them.
cards.h: → when + how passed + what it guaranteed + what followed
cards.n: It was the first major law enacted over a presidential veto, marking Johnson's break with moderate Republicans, not just the Radicals.

cards.q: State what the 13th Amendment did.
cards.a: Ratified in December 1865, the 13th Amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States, 'except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted,' and gave Congress power to enforce it. It freed the enslaved people the Emancipation Proclamation had not reached, including those still held in Kentucky and Delaware.
cards.h: → year + what it abolished + the exception + enforcement
cards.n: The punishment exception later enabled convict leasing in the South; missing it loses the detail graders reward.

cards.q: State what the 14th Amendment did.
cards.a: Ratified in 1868, it made all persons born or naturalized in the United States citizens of the nation and of their state, and barred states from abridging citizens' privileges or immunities or denying any person due process or the equal protection of the laws. It also cut representation for states that denied adult men the vote, barred many former Confederate officials from office, and repudiated the Confederate debt.
cards.h: → year + citizenship + three guarantees + other sections
cards.n: It overturned Dred Scott's citizenship holding and became the basis of 20th-century civil rights law; saying it gave Black men the vote confuses it with the 15th.

cards.q: State what the 15th Amendment did and what it left out.
cards.a: Ratified in 1870, it barred the federal and state governments from denying the vote 'on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.' It did not guarantee the vote outright, so literacy tests, poll taxes and property requirements stayed possible, and it did not bar denial on account of sex.
cards.h: → year + what it banned + what it left open
cards.n: Its silence on sex split the woman suffrage movement in 1869, and its loopholes let southern states disfranchise Black voters after 1890.

cards.q: Date the ratification of the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments.
cards.a: 13th Amendment, 1865; 14th Amendment, 1868; 15th Amendment, 1870.
cards.h: → three years in order
cards.n: The order follows the logic: freedom (1865), then citizenship and equal protection (1868), then voting (1870); swapping the 14th and 15th is the usual slip.

cards.q: Identify the Reconstruction Acts of 1867.
cards.a: Passed over Johnson's vetoes, they divided the ten unreconstructed southern states into five military districts under army commanders, required new state constitutions written by conventions elected with Black male voters, and made readmission depend on ratifying the 14th Amendment and guaranteeing Black male suffrage. Former Confederate leaders barred by the amendment could not vote for the conventions.
cards.h: → how passed + structure + conditions for readmission
cards.n: Tennessee, readmitted in 1866, was left out; these acts begin Radical (Congressional) Reconstruction proper.

cards.q: Identify the impeachment of Andrew Johnson.
cards.a: In February 1868 the House impeached Johnson, chiefly for removing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act, the climax of his fight with Congress over Reconstruction. In May the Senate voted 35 to 19 to convict, one vote short of the two-thirds required, so he was acquitted and served out his term with little power.
cards.h: → when + charge + context + margin + outcome
cards.n: Moderate senators who voted to acquit feared that removing a president over policy would unbalance the branches; saying he was removed is wrong.

cards.q: Identify the extent of Black political participation during Reconstruction.
cards.a: Some 2,000 Black men held public office, from local posts to Congress; sixteen served in Congress, including Senators Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce of Mississippi, and P. B. S. Pinchback briefly served as governor of Louisiana. Black delegates helped write state constitutions that created the South's first public school systems and expanded voting rights.
cards.h: → how many + highest offices + what they achieved
cards.n: Numbers are estimates (Foner counts about 2,000). Black men never controlled a state government, so talk of 'Black rule' repeats a hostile myth.

cards.q: Identify Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce.
cards.a: Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black U.S. senator in 1870, filling one of the seats left empty when Mississippi seceded, and Blanche K. Bruce, also of Mississippi, became the first Black senator to serve a full term (1875-1881). Both were chosen by Reconstruction legislatures before white Redeemer governments shut Black southerners out of power.
cards.h: → who + state + firsts + when
cards.n: No Black American sat in the Senate again until Edward Brooke of Massachusetts in 1967, a measure of how completely Redemption closed the door.

cards.q: Differentiate carpetbaggers from scalawags.
cards.a: Both were insults that white southern Democrats used for Republicans. 'Carpetbaggers' were northerners who moved south after the war, cast as greedy adventurers, though many were Union veterans, teachers, missionaries and investors. 'Scalawags' were white southerners who joined the Republicans, often upcountry yeoman farmers and former Whigs who had opposed secession.
cards.h: → origin of each group + who they really were
cards.n: Both terms come from hostile propaganda, so a sourcing question will ask about point of view; taking them as neutral labels is the trap.

cards.q: Identify the growth of independent Black churches during Reconstruction.
cards.a: Freedpeople left white-controlled congregations to build their own churches, especially African Methodist Episcopal and Black Baptist congregations, which grew rapidly after 1865. They became the most durable Black-led institutions of the era, housing schools, mutual-aid societies and political meetings, and training ministers who became officeholders.
cards.h: → what freedpeople did + denominations + roles
cards.n: Eric Foner counts independent Black churches among Reconstruction's lasting achievements; they are evidence of the 'other leadership roles' the CED names.

cards.q: Identify how Reconstruction-era citizenship law treated American Indians and Chinese immigrants.
cards.a: The 14th Amendment excluded 'Indians not taxed' from the population count, and Congress and the courts treated most American Indians as members of their own nations rather than U.S. citizens until 1924. The Naturalization Act of 1870 opened naturalization to people of African descent but, over Charles Sumner's objections, not to Asian immigrants, so Chinese immigrants stayed ineligible, though their U.S.-born children won citizenship under the 14th Amendment in 1898.
cards.h: → Indians' status + Chinese status + later rulings
cards.n: Borrows later dates from u6 and beyond. The CED's 'other minorities' means the new citizenship had limits; saying everyone born here became a citizen ignores Indians.

cards.q: Explain how evidence about Reconstruction's biracial state governments refutes the Dunning School's claim that they were corrupt failures.
cards.a: The evidence refutes it. Biracial governments wrote constitutions that created the South's first public school systems, expanded voting rights, rebuilt railroads and founded hospitals, and many Black officeholders were educated ministers, teachers and Union veterans. Corruption existed but matched that of northern and later Redeemer governments. W. E. B. Du Bois (Black Reconstruction, 1935) and later Eric Foner (1988) used such evidence to overturn the Dunning view.
cards.h: → claim + evidence that contradicts it + who made the case
cards.n: Simply calling the Dunning School racist is not an explanation; the point needs specific evidence (schools, constitutions, officeholders) that contradicts its claim.

cards.q: Explain why Congress took control of Reconstruction from Andrew Johnson in 1866-1867.
cards.a: Johnson's lenient terms let former Confederates return to power and pass black codes, and he vetoed the Freedmen's Bureau and Civil Rights bills. Northern voters, alarmed by the codes and by the Memphis and New Orleans massacres, gave Republicans veto-proof majorities in 1866, and Congress imposed its own plan in 1867.
cards.h: → lenient terms → ex-Confederates, black codes + Johnson's vetoes → 1866 Republican sweep → Reconstruction Acts
cards.n: Blaming only the Radicals misses that moderate Republicans broke with Johnson over his vetoes; the point needs the causal chain.
o: Southern voters and legislatures sent prominent former Confederates to Congress in 1865-1866, including the Confederacy's vice president, Alexander Stephens, which Republicans read as defiance.

w.a: Congress took over because Johnson wanted to punish the South too harshly.
w.why: reversed; he was lenient

w.a: Congress took control after Johnson was removed by impeachment.
w.why: he was acquitted and stayed in office

cards.q: Explain how the 1866 Memphis and New Orleans riots affected Congressional Reconstruction.
cards.a: White mobs, often joined by police, killed dozens of Black residents in Memphis in May and New Orleans in July 1866. The massacres convinced many northern voters that Johnson's lenient policy endangered freedpeople and Unionists, so Republicans swept the 1866 midterms and passed the Reconstruction Acts of 1867.
cards.h: → mob violence → northern outrage at Johnson's policy → Republican sweep in 1866 → Reconstruction Acts 1867
cards.n: The link to the 1866 elections is the mechanism graders want; describing the riots alone earns nothing on causation.
o: Johnson's 1866 'Swing Around the Circle' speaking tour, in which he traded insults with hecklers, also hurt his allies at the polls.

w.a: The riots ended Reconstruction because Congress withdrew the troops.
w.why: they led to more federal intervention

w.a: The riots helped Johnson win a Democratic Congress in 1866.
w.why: Republicans won big in 1866

cards.q: Explain the accomplishments and limits of the Freedmen's Bureau.
cards.a: It distributed food and medical care, helped reunite families, helped found schools and colleges such as Howard and Fisk, and oversaw labor contracts. But it was underfunded and understaffed, often pushed freedpeople back to work for planters, could not deliver the land they wanted, and Congress let it expire by 1872.
cards.h: → relief, schools, contracts achieved → underfunded, pro-contract, no land → limited, then ended
cards.n: The answer needs both sides; listing achievements only, or calling it a failure only, misses the balance graders reward.
o: Its labor contracts, meant to protect freedpeople, often hardened into the sharecropping arrangements that later trapped them.

w.a: The Freedmen's Bureau gave every freed family forty acres and a mule.
w.why: that promise was never kept

w.a: The Bureau lasted into the 1900s and ended segregation.
w.why: it closed in 1872

cards.q: Explain how Reconstruction altered the relationship between the states and the federal government.
cards.a: The 14th Amendment made national citizenship primary and forbade states to deny due process or equal protection, and each Reconstruction amendment let Congress enforce it. Federal troops, courts and the Freedmen's Bureau acted inside states, reversing the prewar assumption that states alone defined citizens' rights.
cards.h: → national citizenship + enforcement clauses + federal troops, courts → states' power over rights curbed
cards.n: 'The federal government got stronger' is too vague; name the constitutional mechanism (citizenship, equal protection, enforcement) and a concrete use.
o: The change proved partial: by the 1870s the Supreme Court's narrow readings, as in the Slaughterhouse Cases, returned much of rights enforcement to the states.

w.a: Reconstruction gave the states more power over citizenship than before.
w.why: reversed; national citizenship came first

w.a: Nothing changed because the Constitution was never amended.
w.why: three amendments were ratified

cards.q: Explain why the woman suffrage movement split into two rival organizations in 1869.
cards.a: The 15th Amendment barred racial but not sex discrimination in voting. Stanton and Anthony's National Woman Suffrage Association opposed it and sought a federal suffrage amendment; Lucy Stone's American Woman Suffrage Association backed it, accepting that Black men's suffrage came first, and worked state by state.
cards.h: → 15th Amendment omits sex → NWSA opposes it, seeks federal amendment → AWSA backs it, works state by state
cards.n: The CED's point is 'emboldened and divided': name the amendment's omission as the cause and each organization's strategy.
o: The movement was also emboldened: in the 'New Departure' women argued the 14th Amendment already made them voters, and Anthony voted in 1872, until Minor v. Happersett (1875) rejected the claim.
The 14th Amendment's second section wrote the word 'male' into the Constitution for the first time, which reformers saw as a step backward.

w.a: The movement split because the 15th Amendment gave women the vote but not Black men.
w.why: reversed; it covered race, not sex

w.a: Women split over whether women should vote at all.
w.why: both groups sought suffrage

cards.q: Identify the Port Royal Experiment.
cards.a: After Union forces took the South Carolina Sea Islands in November 1861 and planters fled, northern reformers and freedpeople ran the abandoned plantations as a test of free Black labor, with wages, schools and some land sales to freedpeople. Most of the land sold for taxes went to northern investors, and after the war much was returned to former owners.
cards.h: → where + when + what was tried + outcome
cards.n: An early test of free labor and land ownership; it foreshadowed both Special Field Order No. 15 and the land question Reconstruction never settled.

cards.q: Identify Special Field Order No. 15 and its reversal.
cards.a: Issued by General William T. Sherman in January 1865, it set aside coastal land from South Carolina to northern Florida, including the Sea Islands, for freed families in plots of up to forty acres; some also received army mules, the origin of '40 acres and a mule.' Within the year President Andrew Johnson ordered most of the land returned to its former owners, whom he had pardoned.
cards.h: → who + when + what land + plot size + reversal
cards.n: Its reversal is central evidence for the CED's point that freedpeople sought land but fell short of self-sufficiency; Congress never confiscated plantations.

cards.q: Define sharecropping.
cards.a: Sharecropping was the postwar southern labor system in which a landowner provided land, a cabin and often tools, seed and a mule, and a family farmed a plot and paid a share of the crop, commonly half, as rent. It replaced slavery's gang labor with family tenancy but left most freedpeople without land of their own.
cards.h: → who supplied what + how rent was paid + what it replaced
cards.n: It was a compromise: planters wanted wage gangs and freedpeople wanted their own land, and neither got it; calling it wage labor is the common slip.

cards.q: Identify the Freedman's Savings Bank and its 1874 collapse.
cards.a: Chartered by Congress in 1865 to encourage thrift among formerly enslaved people, the Freedman's Savings and Trust Company attracted tens of thousands of Black depositors. Mismanagement, risky loans and fraud by its white trustees, worsened by the Panic of 1873, caused it to fail in 1874, wiping out much of its depositors' savings.
cards.h: → when + purpose + who deposited + why it failed + effect
cards.n: Despite the name it was not part of the Freedmen's Bureau; its failure is evidence for why freedpeople fell short of economic self-sufficiency.

cards.q: Identify the Ku Klux Klan and the federal response.
cards.a: Founded in Pulaski, Tennessee, in 1866 by Confederate veterans, the Klan became a terrorist arm of white Democrats, using whipping, arson and murder against Black voters, officeholders and teachers and against white Republicans. Congress answered with the Enforcement Acts of 1870-1871, including the Ku Klux Klan Act, which let federal courts and troops prosecute conspiracies against civil and voting rights.
cards.h: → origin + targets + methods + federal answer
cards.n: The Enforcement Acts largely broke the first Klan by 1872, which shows Reconstruction failed from lost will more than from lack of legal tools.

cards.q: Identify the Ku Klux Klan Act (Enforcement Act) of 1871.
cards.a: The April 1871 law made conspiracies to deprive citizens of their civil rights or equal protection federal crimes and let the president use the army and suspend habeas corpus against them. Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties that fall, and federal prosecutions broke much of the Klan.
cards.h: → when + what it made a crime + powers + how it was used
cards.n: It worked for a time; the Court's narrow reading in United States v. Cruikshank (1876) and fading northern will are what undid federal enforcement.

cards.q: Identify the holding of the Slaughterhouse Cases (1873).
cards.a: Ruling on a Louisiana law that gave one company control of New Orleans slaughtering, the Court held 5 to 4 that the 14th Amendment's privileges or immunities clause protected only a narrow set of rights of national citizenship, such as access to ports and federal protection abroad, leaving most civil rights under state control. It sharply limited federal protection of individual rights.
cards.h: → case facts + which clause + narrow reading + effect
cards.n: The case involved white butchers, not freedpeople, which is the trap; its narrow reading of the clause still gutted federal protection for Black citizens.

cards.q: Identify the Colfax Massacre of 1873 and the Supreme Court case that followed it.
cards.a: On Easter Sunday 1873, after a disputed Louisiana election, a white paramilitary force attacked Black militiamen holding the courthouse in Colfax, Louisiana, killing dozens and perhaps as many as 150, many after they surrendered. In United States v. Cruikshank (1876) the Supreme Court overturned the few convictions, ruling that the 14th Amendment restrained only states, not private individuals, which crippled federal prosecution of such violence.
cards.h: → when + where + what happened + the Court's ruling + effect
cards.n: The toll is an estimate. Cruikshank's 'state action' reasoning left Klan-style violence to hostile state courts, the link graders want.

cards.q: Define the Redeemers and their political goal.
cards.a: Redeemers were white southern Democrats who set out to 'redeem' their states from Republican, biracial government, using fraud, economic pressure and paramilitary violence to regain control; by 1877 they held every former Confederate state. In power they cut taxes and spending, including on the public schools Reconstruction had built, and restored planter and business power.
cards.h: → who + goal + methods + what they did in power
cards.n: Mississippi's 1875 campaign of terror and fraud (the 'Mississippi Plan') is the model example; 'redeem' is their own loaded word, a sourcing point.

cards.q: Identify the Compromise of 1877.
cards.a: The disputed 1876 election between Republican Rutherford B. Hayes and Democrat Samuel Tilden, who led the popular vote, turned mainly on contested returns from South Carolina, Florida and Louisiana. An electoral commission gave all the disputed votes to Hayes, and in an informal bargain Democrats accepted his victory while Hayes withdrew federal troops from the southern statehouses, ending Reconstruction.
cards.h: → election dispute + who decided + the bargain + result
cards.n: Troops did not leave the South entirely; they stopped propping up the last Republican governments in South Carolina and Louisiana, which then fell to Democrats.

cards.q: Identify the holding of the Civil Rights Cases (1883).
cards.a: The Court struck down the public accommodations sections of the Civil Rights Act of 1875, ruling 8 to 1 that the 14th Amendment reached only state action, not discrimination by private businesses such as inns, theaters and railroads. Justice John Marshall Harlan was the lone dissenter.
cards.h: → law struck down + doctrine + dissenter
cards.n: 1883 falls in Period 6 (borrowed from u6), but the CED places such rulings in Reconstruction's failure; private segregation stood until the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

cards.q: Identify the 'Lost Cause' myth of Confederate memory.
cards.a: The Lost Cause was a postwar interpretation, spread through memoirs, textbooks, monuments and groups such as the United Daughters of the Confederacy, that cast the Confederacy as a noble fight for states' rights rather than slavery, romanticized the Old South and 'loyal slaves,' and portrayed Reconstruction as a corrupt imposition on an honorable, defeated people.
cards.h: → its claims about the war, Old South, Reconstruction
cards.n: It is a source to analyze, not history to repeat; secession documents that name slavery refute its central claim. It shaped white southern identity for decades.

cards.q: Differentiate what Reconstruction achieved from what it failed to achieve.
cards.a: Achieved: the 13th, 14th and 15th amendments, Black voting and officeholding, independent Black churches and reunited families, and the South's first public school systems. Failed: land redistribution and economic independence for freedpeople, lasting protection of voting and civil rights, and security from terror once federal enforcement ended; many gains were lost by 1900, though the amendments survived to be revived in the 20th century.
cards.h: → two columns: achieved and failed
cards.n: Foner's 'unfinished revolution' is the standard framing; a one-sided list earns nothing, and 'Reconstruction did nothing' is simply false.

cards.q: Compare the main ideas of these two sources. Source 1 (composite paraphrase of Black southerners' testimony to the congressional Klan inquiry, 1871): Disguised men came at night and whipped my husband for voting Republican; they said any Black man who voted again would be killed, and the sheriff did nothing. Source 2 (composite paraphrase of editorials in white southern Democratic newspapers, 1874): This state has been plundered by corrupt carpetbag rulers and ignorant voters; honest white men must unite to redeem it and restore good government by any means necessary.
cards.a: Both describe southern politics in the early 1870s as a struggle over who would govern, but they disagree about who the wrongdoers were. Source 1 presents disguised white night riders as terrorists using violence to keep Black citizens from voting, with local officials complicit. Source 2 presents Republican government as the wrong, corrupt and illegitimate, and justifies white unity 'by any means' to redeem the state.
cards.h: → shared subject + opposed view of who is to blame
cards.n: Summarizing each source in turn is not a comparison; note too that Source 2's 'any means necessary' implicitly excuses the violence Source 1 describes.

cards.q: Identify how the 14th and 15th amendments later became the basis for 20th-century civil rights rulings and laws.
cards.a: The 14th Amendment's equal protection clause was the basis for Brown v. Board of Education (1954), which struck down segregated public schools, and its due process clause was later used to apply most of the Bill of Rights to the states. The 15th Amendment's enforcement clause supported the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which the Court upheld in South Carolina v. Katzenbach (1966).
cards.h: → amendment + clause + landmark ruling or law, for each
cards.n: Borrows from u8. The CED's point is continuity: amendments stripped of force after 1877 revived decades later; naming only Brown misses the 15th.

cards.q: Explain how sharecropping and the crop-lien system trapped families in debt.
cards.a: Sharecroppers bought seed, food and tools on credit from merchants or landlords at high prices and interest, pledging the coming crop as security. Falling cotton prices meant the harvest rarely covered the debt, so it carried over, and laws and contracts bound families to the land year after year.
cards.h: → supplies on credit + crop as collateral → high interest, falling cotton prices → debt carries over → families bound
cards.n: 'They were poor' misses the mechanism graders want: credit secured by the crop, and debt that rolled over every year.
o: Merchants often demanded cotton as the collateral crop, which kept families from growing food and deepened both dependence and soil exhaustion.

w.a: Sharecroppers fell into debt because they paid federal income tax on their crops.
w.why: invented; the trap was local credit

w.a: The crop-lien system gave freedpeople full ownership of their land.
w.why: it bound tenants who owned no land

cards.q: Explain why most freedpeople were unable to obtain land of their own after the Civil War.
cards.a: Congress never confiscated and redistributed plantations, and Johnson returned lands seized during the war to pardoned owners, reversing Sherman's field order. Without land, capital or credit, and facing planters who refused to sell to Black buyers, most freedpeople became sharecroppers.
cards.h: → no confiscation + Johnson restores land → no capital or credit + planters won't sell → sharecropping
cards.n: The CED's claim is continuity: planters kept most of the land. 'Freedpeople did not want land' is false; they sought it eagerly.
o: The Southern Homestead Act of 1866 opened public land, but most of it was poor, remote and hard to claim without tools or money, so few freedpeople benefited.

w.a: Freedpeople got no land because they preferred factory work in the North.
w.why: most stayed in the rural South seeking land

w.a: The Homestead Act gave every freed family 160 acres in the South.
w.why: it never reached freedpeople on that scale

cards.q: Explain one continuity and one change in the lives of Black southern farmworkers from slavery to sharecropping.
cards.a: Continuity: planters still owned most of the land, cotton still dominated, and debt and law kept workers tied to plantations. Change: freedpeople were legally free, worked as families rather than in gangs under overseers, could move when a contract ended, and built their own churches and schools.
cards.h: → same land, same crop, new debt ties → but legal freedom, family labor, mobility, own institutions
cards.n: A CCOT answer needs both halves explained; 'nothing changed' or 'everything changed' each earns nothing.
o: Moving from gang labor to family plots let many women withdraw partly from field work, which planters resented as lost labor.

w.a: Nothing changed because sharecroppers were still legally owned by planters.
w.why: slavery was abolished

w.a: Sharecropping ended cotton farming in the South.
w.why: cotton remained dominant

cards.q: Explain why Reconstruction ended.
cards.a: Northern voters tired of intervention amid the Panic of 1873 and Grant-era scandals; Supreme Court rulings narrowed the amendments; white Democrats retook southern states through violence and fraud; and the Compromise of 1877 withdrew the last federal support for Republican governments.
cards.h: → northern fatigue + depression + court rulings + southern violence → Compromise of 1877 → federal retreat
cards.n: Blaming the Compromise of 1877 alone misses that most southern states had already been 'redeemed'; weigh several causes.
o: Liberal Republicans broke with Grant in 1872, putting civil service reform and sectional reconciliation ahead of protecting freedpeople.
Racism in the North left many white voters unwilling to keep defending Black rights in the South.

w.a: Reconstruction ended because all its goals had been achieved by 1877.
w.why: Black rights were being stripped away

w.a: Reconstruction ended when the South won the Civil War.
w.why: the Union won

cards.q: Compare the effects of the Civil War on the power of the federal government and on the meaning of citizenship.
cards.a: Both expanded, but unevenly. Federal power grew lastingly: a national currency and banks, an income tax, conscription, land grants, and the settled denial of any right to secede. Citizenship was redefined by the 14th and 15th amendments as national and color-blind in law, but by 1877 federal enforcement had faded, so the change in citizenship proved far less secure in practice than the growth of federal power.
cards.h: → one similarity + a difference in how lasting each was
cards.n: Listing effects in two columns is not a comparison; the point is a judgment about which change proved more durable and why.

cards.q: Write a thesis for this prompt: Evaluate the relative significance of the effects of the Civil War on American values from 1861 to 1877.
cards.a: Model: The Civil War's most significant effect on American values was to redefine freedom and citizenship as national, ending slavery and writing equal protection into the Constitution; its strengthening of federal authority over the states was nearly as lasting, while its promise of racial equality proved least durable, as violence, court rulings and northern retreat hollowed out Black rights by 1877.
cards.h: → one or two sentences: ranked effects + reasons
cards.n: Restating the prompt or saying the war 'had many effects' earns nothing; the thesis must rank the effects and preview why.

cards.q: Compare the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act as attempts to settle slavery in the territories.
cards.a: All three tried to manage slavery's expansion by national legislation, but the method shifted. 1820 drew a fixed line, 36°30', decided by Congress; 1850 admitted California free and left Utah and New Mexico to popular sovereignty; 1854 applied popular sovereignty north of the old line, repealing it. Each settled less than the last: the first held for 34 years, the second about four, and the third set off Bleeding Kansas at once.
cards.h: → shared aim + method of each + how long each held
cards.n: Borrows from u4. Describing each law in turn is not a comparison; name the shared aim and the shift from a congressional line to local choice.

cards.q: Compare the status of African Americans in 1844 and in 1877.
cards.a: Change: slavery, which held roughly three million people in the mid-1840s, had been abolished, and Black men had become citizens with constitutional rights to equal protection and the vote, had held office, and had built independent churches and schools. Continuity: most Black southerners still worked land owned by white planters, now as indebted sharecroppers, and by 1877 violence and Redeemer governments were stripping away their political rights.
cards.h: → what changed + what continued, with evidence for each
cards.n: The population figure is a census-based estimate. 'African Americans were free after 1865' alone ignores the continuity in land and labor.

cards.q: Compare the effects of the American Revolution and the Civil War on slavery.
cards.a: Both wars were fought partly in the name of liberty, and in both enslaved people sought freedom by fleeing to armies that promised it. The Revolution's effects were limited and regional: northern states adopted gradual emancipation, while slavery expanded in the South and the Constitution protected it. The Civil War abolished slavery nationally through the 13th Amendment and made freedpeople citizens, a far more sweeping change.
cards.h: → one similarity + the key difference in scope
cards.n: Borrows from u3. Saying the Revolution freed northern slaves at once is wrong; gradual emancipation took decades, which sharpens the contrast.

cards.q: Classify each effect of the Civil War and Reconstruction as mainly a change in federal power, in citizenship and rights, or in the economy, with a phrase of reasoning: 13th Amendment · national banking system · 14th Amendment's equal protection clause · military districts of the Reconstruction Acts · Homestead Act · end of any claimed right of secession · 15th Amendment · Pacific Railway Act · first federal income tax · sharecropping
cards.a:
13th Amendment → citizenship and rights (slavery ended nationwide)
National banking system → economy (a uniform currency under federal charters)
Equal protection clause → citizenship and rights (states barred from unequal treatment)
Military districts → federal power (the army governed states until readmission)
Homestead Act → economy (federal land for settlers)
End of secession → federal power (the Union made perpetual by war, affirmed in Texas v. White, 1869)
15th Amendment → citizenship and rights (race barred as a voting test)
Pacific Railway Act → economy (federal subsidies for a transcontinental railroad)
Income tax → federal power (a new national reach into citizens' incomes)
Sharecropping → economy (a new labor system replacing slavery)
cards.h: → category + a reason, for each effect
cards.n: Several items fit two categories (the income tax is both federal power and economy); the reasoning phrase, not the label, shows understanding.

cards.q: Explain which effect of the Civil War on American values was most significant.
cards.a: The redefinition of freedom and citizenship mattered most: the 13th and 14th amendments ended slavery and made equal protection a national guarantee. Even when Reconstruction's enforcement failed, these amendments survived to become the basis of the 20th-century civil rights movement.
cards.h: → pick one effect → show its reach → weigh it against a rival effect → explain why it lasted
cards.n: Relative significance needs a comparison; praising one effect without weighing it against another (federal power, economic change) earns nothing.
o: One can argue that the growth of federal authority mattered most, since the war ended any right to secede and gave Washington lasting power over money, taxes and land.
One can argue that the triumph of the free-labor economy mattered most, because Republican wartime laws set the course for rapid industrialization after 1865.

w.a: The most significant effect was that the war made the South richer than the North.
w.why: the South was devastated

w.a: The main effect was full racial equality, which lasted into the 1900s.
w.why: Black rights were stripped by the 1890s

cards.q: Explain one similarity and one difference between how the United States treated Mexicans in the lands ceded in 1848 and how it treated freedpeople after 1865.
cards.a: Similarity: both were promised citizenship and protection, yet many lost land and rights to courts, taxes, fraud and violence. Difference: freedpeople's rights were written into the Constitution and backed for a time by troops and federal laws; the treaty's promises to Mexican Americans had almost no enforcement.
cards.h: → both promised citizenship and rights → both lose land, rights in practice → only freedpeople get amendments, troops
cards.n: 'Both faced racism' is too thin; a comparison must explain both halves with the specific promises and what became of them.
o: A further difference: many Californios began as landowners who lost property, while most freedpeople began with no land and never gained it.

w.a: Mexicans and freedpeople were both enslaved before gaining citizenship.
