w.why: Mexicans in the Cession were not enslaved

w.a: Both groups kept their land thanks to strong federal protection.
w.why: both suffered heavy losses

cards.q: Explain how the meaning of American freedom changed between 1844 and 1877.
cards.a: In 1844 freedom was widely defined as white men's independence, compatible with slavery and protected mainly by the states. By 1877 the 13th, 14th and 15th amendments had made freedom national and color-blind in law, though Redemption was already showing how far practice lagged behind.
cards.h: → 1844: white men's liberty, state-defined, beside slavery → war, amendments → 1877: national in law, weak in practice
cards.n: A CCOT answer needs the starting point, the turning point and the limits; 'freedom expanded' with no evidence earns nothing.
o: Free-labor ideology tied freedom to owning one's own labor, which Republicans used first against slavery's spread and then to define emancipation.

w.a: Freedom did not change because slavery was still legal in 1877.
w.why: the 13th Amendment ended it in 1865

w.a: By 1877 women and Black men had equal voting rights nationwide.
w.why: women were left out; Black voting was under attack

cards.q: Define the Gilded Age.
cards.a: The Gilded Age is the label, taken from Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner's 1873 novel The Gilded Age, for roughly 1870 to 1900. Gilded means a thin coat of gold over cheaper metal: spectacular industrial growth and fortunes covering political corruption, labor conflict, and a widening gap between rich and poor. Historians use it for the era of KC-6.1 to KC-6.3: industrial capitalism, mass migration, and fierce debate over how to govern both.
cards.h: → origin of the term + what the metaphor claims
cards.n: 'A golden age of prosperity' reverses the meaning: gilded is a thin gold surface over something cheaper, which is the whole point of the label.

cards.q: Date the beginning and end of Period 6 and state the development that marks each boundary.
cards.a: 1865 to 1898. The period opens with the end of the Civil War in 1865, when a reunited nation with a Republican, pro-growth federal government turned to railroads, industry and western settlement (it overlaps Period 5's Reconstruction, which ran to 1877). It closes in 1898 with the Spanish-American War, when the United States took an overseas empire and entered Period 7's debates over its world role and Progressive reform.
cards.h: → two years, each tied to one development
cards.n: Period 6 overlaps Periods 5 and 7 on purpose; '1877 to 1900' confuses the looser Gilded Age label with the CED's period dates.

cards.q: Identify the three broad developments that the key concepts of Period 6 are organized around.
cards.a: (1) The rise of industrial capitalism (KC-6.1): technology, mass production and new markets brought rapid growth and consolidation, and workers and farmers organized in response. (2) Migration (KC-6.2): international and internal migrants built cities and a new urban culture, while settlement of the West provoked violent conflict. (3) Ideas and politics (KC-6.3): movements that defended or challenged the new order, and fights over citizenship, corruption and business power.
cards.h: → three developments, one clause each
cards.n: A list of events (Haymarket, Plessy, Dawes) is not a development; name the broad process each event belongs to.

cards.q: Describe the Civil War-era federal economic policies that set the stage for industrial growth after 1865.
cards.a: With southern opposition gone, Republican Congresses passed a pro-growth program: the Pacific Railway Acts (1862, 1864) gave land grants and loans for a transcontinental railroad; the Homestead Act (1862) offered western land to settlers; protective tariffs, starting with the Morrill Tariff of 1861, sheltered manufacturers; and the National Banking Acts (1863, 1864) created a national currency. These subsidies and protections framed Gilded Age growth.
cards.h: → the laws, then what each did for growth
cards.n: Borrows from u5. Naming the laws without what each did for business earns nothing; the context point is that secession removed the South's long opposition.

cards.q: Explain how global developments of the late nineteenth century formed a broader context for American industrialization.
cards.a: American industrialization was part of a worldwide transformation. Britain and Germany were industrializing too, and European investors financed American railroads and bought American grain and cotton. Poverty and upheaval in southern and eastern Europe and in China pushed millions of migrants toward American jobs; steamships and the transatlantic cable (1866) tied markets together; and European imperial rivalry pushed Americans to seek markets abroad by the 1890s.
cards.h: → global process → how it shaped the United States
cards.n: Context must describe a process beyond the prompt that shaped it; 'the world was changing too' is a phrase and earns nothing.

cards.q: Classify each feature of American life in 1898, compared with 1865, as mainly a CHANGE or a CONTINUITY, with a phrase of reasoning: size of the largest businesses · the South's dependence on cotton · share of Americans living in cities · American Indian land and sovereignty · main sources of immigration · Black southerners' voting rights · federal regulation of business · the two-party system · women's right to vote in federal elections · U.S. rank in world manufacturing · the monetary standard · federal subsidies and tariffs for business
cards.a:
Largest businesses → change (national corporations and trusts such as Standard Oil replace local firms)
South and cotton → continuity (sharecropping and tenancy keep cotton king despite New South mills)
Urban share → change (about 20% in 1860 to about 40% in 1900)
Indian land and sovereignty → change (treaty-making ends 1871, reservations, Dawes allotment 1887)
Immigration sources → change (southern and eastern Europe dominate after about 1880; Chinese excluded 1882)
Black voting → change, a reversal (voting and office-holding in the 1870s, disfranchisement by the 1890s)
Federal regulation → mostly continuity (ICA 1887 and Sherman Act 1890 weakly enforced)
Two-party system → continuity (Populist challenge absorbed by 1896)
Women's federal vote → continuity (none; only a few western states, such as Wyoming and Colorado)
World manufacturing → change (U.S. becomes the leading industrial producer by the 1890s)
Monetary standard → continuity after 1879 (gold kept; free silver defeated 1896)
Subsidies and tariffs → continuity (land grants from 1862, high tariffs through 1897)
cards.h: → label each, then a phrase of reasoning
cards.n: A label without its reason earns nothing on a continuity-and-change task; the reasoning phrase is the scored move.

cards.q: Write a two-sentence contextualization for an essay on the growth of labor unions from 1865 to 1898.
cards.a: After the Civil War, federal land grants, protective tariffs and new technologies such as the Bessemer process let railroads and manufacturers grow into national corporations employing thousands of wage workers, many of them immigrants. As skilled craftsmen lost control of production and wages fell in the depressions after the panics of 1873 and 1893, workers faced long hours, danger and employers far more powerful than any individual, setting the stage for national unions.
cards.h: → broader process + its link to the prompt
cards.n: 'The Gilded Age was a time of industrialization' is a phrase, not a description; the context must describe a process and lead into the topic.

cards.q: Explain why historians treat 1865 as the start of a new era in American economic history even though industrialization began decades earlier.
cards.a: Industry predated 1865, but the war changed its scale and its politics. Secession let Republicans pass railroad subsidies, protective tariffs and national banking; after 1865 a reunited national market and federal support made factory and corporate production the center of the economy, not a regional exception.
cards.h: → pre-1865 industry regional → war removes southern opposition → federal support + national market → industry dominates
cards.n: 'Industrialization started in 1865' is false and earns nothing; the claim is about a change in scale and in federal policy, not a beginning.
o: Before 1865 most Americans farmed and most factories were small; by the 1890s the United States led the world in manufacturing, so 1865 marks the acceleration.
The war built federal fiscal power (bonds, greenbacks, national banks) that later helped finance railroads and industry.

w.a: 1865 is the start because the first American factories were built right after the Civil War.
w.why: false; the Lowell mills and the market revolution came decades earlier

w.a: Ending slavery in 1865 automatically made the whole country industrial.
w.why: asserts a cause with no mechanism, and the South stayed agricultural

w.a: Historians pick 1865 because Andrew Carnegie opened his first steel mill that year.
w.why: invented date; his Edgar Thomson works opened in 1875

cards.q: Explain why the rapid industrial growth of 1865-1898 produced intense political debate about the role of government.
cards.a: Growth created private power no rules governed. Railroads and trusts set rates for regions, the panics of 1873 and 1893 cost workers jobs and sank farmers in debt, and cities filled with immigrants, so farmers, workers and reformers demanded regulation, inflation and honest government; business cried laissez-faire.
cards.h: → industrial growth → new private power + panics + crowded cities → groups demand state action → laissez-faire defense
cards.n: Listing Gilded Age laws is description; the point needs the mechanism from economic change to political demand.
o: Government already promoted business with land grants and tariffs, so critics asked why it should not also protect farmers and workers.
Farmers selling in a world market at falling prices, while paying railroad rates they could not control, turned economic grievance into the Grange and Populist campaigns for regulation.

w.a: There was debate because Gilded Age political parties ignored economic issues entirely.
w.why: false; tariffs and currency were the parties' central fights

w.a: Growth caused debate because everyone became poorer during industrialization.
w.why: overstated; real wages rose, and the conflict was over power and distribution

cards.q: Explain why westward expansion after 1865 can be seen as a continuation of antebellum patterns rather than a break from them.
cards.a: Settlers, federal land policy and the army kept displacing American Indians, as under removal and Manifest Destiny. What changed was speed and finality: railroads and the bison's destruction ended Plains independence within a generation, and ending treaties (1871) and allotment (1887) went further than removal.
cards.h: → same settler-army pattern as removal → faster with railroads and bison slaughter → ends sovereignty, not just moves it
cards.n: Borrows from u4 (removal, Manifest Destiny). A continuity answer should also say what changed; claiming nothing was new earns less.
o: Manifest Destiny's belief in Anglo-American destiny carried straight from the Mexican War era to the Plains wars.
Federal land giveaways to settlers and railroads extended the land policy of the Land Ordinance and preemption laws on a larger scale.

w.a: Westward expansion after 1865 was new because Americans had never moved west before the railroad.
w.why: false; settlement crossed the Appalachians and the Mississippi long before

w.a: Nothing changed after 1865 because all Indians had already been removed in the 1830s.
w.why: removal was east of the Mississippi; Plains nations stayed independent until the 1870s-1880s

cards.q: Identify the transcontinental railroad and how it was built.
cards.a: The first transcontinental line, completed when the Union Pacific, building west from Omaha, and the Central Pacific, building east from Sacramento, met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869. The Pacific Railway Acts of 1862 and 1864 funded it with land grants and federal loans per mile of track. The Central Pacific's workforce was mostly Chinese immigrants; the Union Pacific relied heavily on Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans.
cards.h: → who, where, when, how funded, who built it
cards.n: 'Private enterprise built the railroad' misses KC-6.1.I.A: federal land and loans made it possible, and Chinese labor did much of the hardest work.

cards.q: Date the completion of the first transcontinental railroad and the Interstate Commerce Act.
cards.a: Transcontinental railroad completed 1869 (Promontory Summit, Utah); Interstate Commerce Act 1887. The eighteen years between them trace federal railroad policy: Washington first subsidized the lines with land and loans, then, after farmer protest and Wabash v. Illinois (1886), created the Interstate Commerce Commission to regulate their rates.
cards.h: → two years + what connects them
cards.n: Dating the ICA to 1877, the year of Munn v. Illinois, or putting regulation before completion is the common slip.

cards.q: Identify how the federal government subsidized western railroad construction after the Civil War.
cards.a: Through the Pacific Railway Acts (1862, 1864) and later charters, Congress gave railroads alternating sections of public land along their routes, roughly 130 million acres in federal grants (an estimate; states added more), plus loans of government bonds per mile of track. Railroads sold the land to settlers, advertising as far as Europe, to raise capital, which tied railroad profit to rapid settlement.
cards.h: → land grants + loans + how land became capital
cards.n: Acreage is an estimate. 'The government paid for the railroads' is too loose: the key subsidy was land, sold to settlers to finance construction.

cards.q: Explain the economic grievances of late-nineteenth-century farmers.
cards.a: Farmers were squeezed between falling prices and fixed costs. Mechanization and new land in the U.S. and abroad raised output, so wheat and cotton prices roughly halved between the early 1870s and the mid-1890s (approximate). Deflation made mortgage and crop-lien debts harder to repay, railroads charged high rates where they had no competition, elevator operators and middlemen took a cut, and protective tariffs kept manufactured goods expensive.
cards.h: → prices down + costs fixed + whom farmers blamed
cards.n: 'Farmers were poor' earns nothing; name the mechanism (overproduction and deflation against fixed debts and rates) and whom farmers blamed.

cards.q: Identify the Farmers' Alliance and the Grange.
cards.a: The Grange (Patrons of Husbandry), founded in 1867 by Oliver Kelley, began as a social and educational society, then ran cooperative stores and pushed Midwestern 'Granger laws' regulating railroad and grain-elevator rates. The Farmers' Alliances of the 1880s (Southern, Northwestern, and the Colored Farmers' Alliance) built cooperatives, proposed the subtreasury plan for federal crop-backed loans, and in the 1890s became the base of the Populist Party.
cards.h: → two organizations: dates, methods, what followed
cards.n: Both began as cooperative organizations (KC-6.1.III.B); calling the Grange a political party is wrong, and the Alliances, not the Grange, became the Populists.

cards.q: Identify the technologies that made large-scale Great Plains farming possible.
cards.a: The steel plow (John Deere, 1837) broke tough prairie sod; mechanical reapers, twine binders and steam threshers multiplied what one farmer could harvest; windmills pumped groundwater in a dry region; and barbed wire (Joseph Glidden, 1874) fenced a treeless plain. With railroads to carry the crop, these tools let Plains farming expand quickly and drove output up and prices down (KC-6.1.III.A).
cards.h: → each tool + the problem it solved + the net effect
cards.n: Borrows from u4 for the 1837 plow. Listing tools without the result (more output, lower prices, debt for machines) misses what the KC tests.

cards.q: Identify how Chicago's growth illustrates the new centers of commercial activity created by western expansion.
cards.a: Chicago became the hinge between West and East: railroads converged there, grain elevators and the Board of Trade turned western wheat into graded, tradable commodities, the Union Stock Yards (opened 1865) and packers such as Swift and Armour processed western cattle and hogs, and northern lumber passed through it to Plains farms. Its population rose from about 300,000 in 1870 to about 1.7 million in 1900.
cards.h: → railroads → which trades → growth figure
cards.n: Illustrative city; the KC point is that railroads and resources created commercial centers. Denver or Kansas City, with a mechanism, earns the same point.

cards.q: Describe the long cattle drive and the cow towns it created.
cards.a: After 1865, Texas ranchers drove longhorn herds hundreds of miles north on trails such as the Chisholm Trail to railheads in Kansas, beginning with Abilene in 1867, where cattle were shipped east to Chicago packers. Cow towns such as Abilene and Dodge City boomed on the trade, and many cowboys were Mexican American or Black. The drives faded in the 1880s as railroads reached Texas, farmers fenced the range, and the winter of 1886-1887 struck.
cards.h: → route + railhead + who worked + why it ended
cards.n: Illustrative names. The point is that railroads created the market that made ranching pay; the romantic lone-cowboy image misses the railhead and packer.

cards.q: Identify the closing of the open range in the mid-1880s.
cards.a: The open-range cattle boom, in which herds grazed free on public grassland and were driven to railheads, ended in the mid-to-late 1880s. Barbed wire (patented by Joseph Glidden in 1874) let farmers and ranchers fence the range, overstocking and falling beef prices squeezed ranchers, and the winter of 1886-1887 killed huge numbers of cattle. Ranching shifted to fenced, often corporate-owned spreads.
cards.h: → what the range was + three causes + result
cards.n: Crediting its end to one blizzard misses barbed wire and overstocking; the KC point is that railroads and markets remade the western economy.

cards.q: Identify the Comstock Lode.
cards.a: A rich silver-and-gold deposit found in 1859 near Virginia City, Nevada, which set off a rush and made Virginia City a boomtown; Nevada became a state in 1864. Lone prospectors soon gave way to deep corporate mining financed by San Francisco capital, and the flow of western silver later strengthened the silver lobby behind the free-silver movement of the 1890s.
cards.h: → what, where, when + two effects
cards.n: Borrows from u5 (1859). The KC-6.2.II.A point is that mineral finds built new communities and drew corporate capital, not just lone prospectors.

cards.q: Identify the Oklahoma Land Rush of 1889.
cards.a: On April 22, 1889, the federal government opened about two million acres of 'Unassigned Lands' in Indian Territory, land taken from the Creek and Seminole nations after the Civil War, to homesteaders; tens of thousands raced in at a starting signal, and 'Sooners' who slipped in early gave the future state its nickname. It shows federal policy turning land once promised to American Indians into settler property.
cards.h: → date + what land + how opened + significance
cards.n: Calling it empty land ignores that it was taken from tribal nations; the event links 6.2's land policy to 6.3's broken treaties.

cards.q: Explain why federal land grants were decisive in building railroads across the West.
cards.a: Western lines ran ahead of settlement, so there was no traffic to repay private investors. Land grants solved that: railroads sold or mortgaged the land to raise capital, and selling it to settlers created the farms and towns whose freight later paid for the line.
cards.h: → no traffic yet → investors unwilling → land as collateral and sales → settlers → freight revenue
cards.n: 'The government helped' earns nothing; the point needs the mechanism that turned land into capital and into future customers.
o: Government bonds and land gave investors a security a speculative line lacked, which is why the first transcontinental was built with federal loans.
Railroads became the West's biggest land sellers and colonization agents, advertising in Europe, so subsidy and settlement were one process.

w.a: Land grants were decisive because railroads needed the land to lay their track on.
w.why: confuses the right-of-way with the grants, which were sold to raise capital

w.a: Western railroads were built by entrepreneurs like Leland Stanford using only their own money.
w.why: ignores the federal loans and land that financed the Central Pacific

cards.q: Explain why rising farm output after 1870 left many western and southern farmers worse off.
cards.a: Output outran demand. Mechanization, new Plains land and foreign competition raised supply, so crop prices fell while mortgages, machinery debts and railroad rates stayed fixed in dollars. With deflation each dollar owed took more bushels to repay, so producing more deepened debt.
cards.h: → more output → lower prices + deflation → fixed debts cost more bushels → distress
cards.n: The KC says food prices declined; 'farmers didn't make enough money' with no deflation-and-debt mechanism earns nothing.
o: Farmers sold in a world market, competing with Russia, Argentina and India, but bought in a tariff-protected home market, so they were squeezed from both sides.
Each farmer answered low prices by planting more, which pushed prices lower still.

w.a: Farmers were worse off because the new machines did not work on the Plains.
w.why: the machines worked; the problem was the price effect of more output

w.a: Farmers suffered because food prices rose so high that nobody could buy crops.
w.why: backwards; the KC says food prices declined

w.a: Farmers were worse off because the Homestead Act took their land away.
w.why: confuses the source of land with the source of debt

cards.q: Explain why farmers turned to cooperatives in the 1870s and 1880s.
cards.a: Alone, a farmer had to accept the price set by the local elevator, merchant or railroad, which often had no competitor. Pooling crops and purchases through Grange and Alliance cooperatives let farmers bargain together, skip middlemen and hold grain until prices rose, using consolidation's own logic.
cards.h: → local monopolies set prices → lone farmer powerless → pooling gives bargaining power → middlemen cut out
cards.n: Name what cooperatives answered (consolidation and railroad dependence, KC-6.1.III.B); 'to help each other' earns nothing.
o: Cooperatives answered the same consolidation that produced trusts: farmers copied business combination to match its market power.
When cooperatives failed for lack of credit, the Alliances turned to the subtreasury plan and then to politics, so cooperation was the first stage of protest.

w.a: Farmers created cooperatives because the federal government required them to organize.
w.why: false; they were voluntary, and no economic cause is named

w.a: Farmers joined cooperatives mainly for the dances and picnics.
w.why: the Grange was social at first, but cooperatives answered railroad and middleman power

cards.q: Explain why the transcontinental railroads created new towns and cities across the West.
cards.a: Railroads decided where trade could flow. Towns grew at railheads, junctions and division points because cattle, grain and ore could reach eastern markets there and supplies could arrive; railroads also platted towns on their own land to sell lots, while places the line bypassed withered.
cards.h: → route = market access → towns at railheads and junctions → railroads plat and sell lots → bypassed towns decline
cards.n: Illustrative towns. A causation answer links the railroad to market access and land sales, not just notes that towns appeared.
o: Cheyenne began in 1867 as a Union Pacific division point, and many Kansas and Dakota towns were platted by railroad land companies.
Mining towns rose on ore strikes, but they lasted mainly where rail access made shipping the ore profitable.

w.a: Towns grew along railroads because settlers liked living near the excitement of trains.
w.why: gives no economic mechanism

w.a: The railroads created cities because Congress ordered a town every ten miles.
w.why: invented rule

cards.q: Identify who migrated to the West after 1865 and what drew them.
cards.a: Native-born white farmers from the Midwest and East; European immigrants such as Germans, Scandinavians and Germans from Russia; Chinese laborers on railroads and in mines; African Americans such as the Exodusters; and Mormon settlers, while Mexican Americans already in the Southwest moved within it. They came for land under the Homestead Act and from railroad sales, for mining strikes, and for railroad and ranch work, seeking self-sufficiency and independence.
cards.h: → several groups + what pulled each
cards.n: A list of groups without the draw (land, mines, rail and ranch jobs) misses KC-6.2.II.B; 'people wanted adventure' earns nothing.

cards.q: Compare the main ideas of these two sources. Source 1 (paraphrase of an 1870s railroad land-company pamphlet for European emigrants): Kansas land is fertile, cheap and sold on easy credit; rain follows the plow; a family that works hard will own its farm free of any landlord within a few years. Source 2 (composite of Plains homesteaders' letters from the late 1880s, written for this exercise): drought has burned the wheat two years running; the mortgage and the machinery note fall due in autumn; the railroad's rates take what the weather leaves; neighbors have given up and gone back east.
cards.a: Similarity: both treat the Plains as a place where families sought independence by owning and farming their own land (KC-6.2.II.B). Difference: Source 1 promises easy self-sufficiency and a friendly climate, while Source 2 describes dependence on weather, creditors and railroads. The difference follows from purpose and timing: the pamphlet sells railroad land to raise capital, and the letters record experience after the drought years of the late 1880s.
cards.h: → one similarity + one difference + why they differ
cards.n: Summarizing each source separately earns nothing; a comparison must state the similarity or difference outright. Both sources are composed for practice.

cards.q: Identify the destruction of the American bison and its effect on Plains nations.
cards.a: Tens of millions of bison (estimates vary widely, often 30 million or more) once ranged the Plains; by the late 1880s fewer than about 1,000 survived. Commercial hide hunters, served by new railroads and by tanneries that turned hides into industrial leather, destroyed the southern herd in the 1870s and the northern herd by about 1883, and many army officers welcomed it. Plains nations lost their food, shelter and trade base, which pushed them onto reservations and rations.
cards.h: → numbers before and after + who killed them + effect
cards.n: Figures are estimates. 'Hunters killed the buffalo for sport' misses the hide market and the railroads, and the effect KC-6.2.II.C names.

cards.q: Identify the Indian Appropriations Act of 1871 and what it changed.
cards.a: A rider in the 1871 Indian appropriations law declared that no tribe would thereafter be recognized as an independent nation with which the United States could make a treaty. Existing treaties stayed nominally in force, but Congress now governed American Indians by statute and executive order, clearing the way for reservation rules, allotment and the denial of tribal sovereignty the KC describes.
cards.h: → what it declared + what replaced treaties + effect
cards.n: It did not cancel existing treaties; 'it ended all treaties' is wrong. The point is the end of dealing with tribes as nations (KC-6.2.II.D).

cards.q: Identify the cause and the outcome of each western conflict: Sand Creek (1864) · Red Cloud's War (1866-1868) · Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876) · flight of the Nez Perce (1877) · Rock Springs massacre (1885) · Apache resistance under Geronimo (to 1886) · Las Gorras Blancas (1889-1891) · Wounded Knee (1890)
cards.a:
Sand Creek → militia attacked a peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho camp → about 150 to 200 killed, mostly women, children, elders; Plains wars widen
Red Cloud's War → Lakota fought forts on the Bozeman Trail to Montana gold → Fort Laramie Treaty (1868) guaranteed the Black Hills
Little Bighorn → Black Hills gold (1874) and a broken treaty → Lakota and Cheyenne destroyed Custer's command; U.S. seized the Hills (1877)
Nez Perce → ordered onto a shrunken reservation → Chief Joseph's band fled toward Canada, surrendered in Montana, exiled
Rock Springs → white miners resented Chinese miners hired by the Union Pacific → at least 28 Chinese killed
Geronimo → Chiricahua Apache resisted reservation confinement → surrendered 1886, exiled to Florida
Las Gorras Blancas → Hispano villagers resisted Anglos fencing New Mexico common lands → fence-cutting raids; land loss continued
Wounded Knee → army moved to disarm Lakota Ghost Dancers → roughly 250 to 300 killed; armed Plains resistance ends
cards.h: → cause → outcome, each case
cards.n: Illustrative cases; casualty figures are estimates and Sand Creek is Period 5. Naming battles without the cause (land, gold, resources, broken treaties) misses the KC.

cards.q: Identify the Dawes Severalty Act.
cards.a: The Dawes Severalty Act (1887) broke up reservation land held in common by allotting it to individuals, typically 160 acres to each head of family and smaller parcels to others, held in trust by the government for 25 years. Allottees could become citizens, and 'surplus' land left after allotment was sold to white settlers. Reformers meant it to make American Indians individual farmers; it served settlers' demand for land.
cards.h: → date + mechanism + citizenship + surplus land
cards.n: Calling it a law that gave Indians land misses its purpose: it dissolved communal landholding, the base of tribal sovereignty (KC-6.2.II.D).

cards.q: Explain the intent and the actual effect of the Dawes Act.
cards.a: Intent: reformers such as the 'Friends of the Indian' meant to assimilate American Indians as individual Christian farmers and citizens, ending tribal life. Effect: land passed to white owners through surplus sales and later sales and leases of allotments, so Native landholding fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to about 48 million by 1934; much of what remained was arid, poverty deepened, and tribal governments weakened.
cards.h: → stated intent → actual effect, with figures
cards.n: Intent alone, or effect alone, is half an answer; the classic trap is treating the reformers' benevolent aim as the outcome.

cards.q: Identify the Ghost Dance movement and the massacre at Wounded Knee.
cards.a: The Ghost Dance, spread from 1889 by the Paiute prophet Wovoka, was a religious revival promising that through dance and right living the dead would return, the bison would be restored and whites would disappear. Alarmed agents on Lakota reservations called in the army; Sitting Bull was killed during an arrest on December 15, 1890, and on December 29 the Seventh Cavalry killed roughly 250 to 300 Lakota, many of them women and children, at Wounded Knee Creek, South Dakota.
cards.h: → the movement + why it was feared + the massacre
cards.n: Death toll is an estimate. Calling the Ghost Dance a war dance repeats the agents' misreading; it was a religious revival, a form of cultural preservation.

cards.q: Date the Dawes Act, Wounded Knee, and Turner's Frontier Thesis.
cards.a: Dawes Severalty Act 1887; Wounded Knee massacre 1890; Turner's Frontier Thesis presented 1893. The sequence runs from the legal attack on tribal landholding, to the last major armed clash on the Plains, to the claim, based on the 1890 census, that the frontier had closed.
cards.h: → three years, in order
cards.n: Mixing up 1887 and 1890 is the common slip: allotment came before Wounded Knee, and Turner spoke three years after the census.

cards.q: Identify Helen Hunt Jackson's A Century of Dishonor and its influence.
cards.a: Helen Hunt Jackson's 1881 book documented broken treaties and violence against nations such as the Cheyenne, Nez Perce and Ponca, and she sent a copy to every member of Congress. It built reformers' sympathy for American Indians, but that sympathy flowed into assimilation and the 1887 Dawes Act, which cost Native nations far more land. Her novel Ramona (1884) carried the protest to California's Mission Indians.
cards.h: → author, date, content, effect
cards.n: Illustrative source. The trap is assuming sympathy meant good policy: the reformers she reached backed allotment, which deepened land loss.

cards.q: Identify the Carlisle Indian Industrial School and Richard Henry Pratt's assimilationist motto.
cards.a: Founded in 1879 in Pennsylvania by army officer Richard Henry Pratt, the Carlisle Indian Industrial School was the model for off-reservation boarding schools that separated Native children from their families, cut their hair, banned their languages and religions, and trained them for manual and domestic work, under Pratt's motto 'Kill the Indian in him, and save the man.' Many students nonetheless kept tribal identities and later used schooling to defend their nations.
cards.h: → founder, date, methods, goal
cards.n: The motto aimed at cultural, not physical, destruction; describing Carlisle as an ordinary school misses its assimilation purpose (KC-6.2.II.E).

cards.q: Identify the Buffalo Soldiers.
cards.a: The Black regular-army regiments Congress created in 1866, the 9th and 10th Cavalry and the infantry regiments merged in 1869 into the 24th and 25th, served mostly in the West, fighting Apache, Cheyenne and others, building roads, and guarding mail routes and settlers. The name is usually said to come from Plains peoples who fought them. They show African Americans seeking opportunity in the army while enforcing a policy that confined American Indians.
cards.h: → who, when, where, what they did
cards.n: Illustrative. The complexity point: Black soldiers facing racism at home enforced the conquest of other peoples; 'heroes' or 'villains' alone is thin.

cards.q: Explain how the Dawes Act and boarding schools like Carlisle pursued the same assimilationist goal by different means.
cards.a: Both aimed to dissolve tribal identity into individual American citizenship. The Dawes Act attacked the economic base, replacing communal land with private allotments; boarding schools attacked the cultural base, removing children and erasing language, religion and dress. Together they struck land and culture at once.
cards.h: → shared goal: end tribal identity → Dawes targets land → schools target children and culture → one campaign
cards.n: Describing each policy separately earns little; the answer needs the shared goal and the different target of each.
o: Both assumed Native ways blocked 'civilization', so reformers saw private property and English schooling as two halves of one program.
Both used federal wardship over land and people to reach into family life, which is why historians treat them as one assimilation campaign.

w.a: The Dawes Act and Carlisle had nothing in common because one was about land and one was about school.
w.why: misses the shared assimilation goal

w.a: Both policies were meant to protect Native cultures from white settlers.
w.why: reverses their purpose

cards.q: Explain why the destruction of the bison forced many Plains nations onto reservations.
cards.a: The bison supplied Plains nations' food, shelter, clothing and trade goods. Once hide hunters and railroads cut the herds from millions to almost none by the mid-1880s, bands could no longer feed themselves off the reservation, so hunger, as much as army campaigns, drove them to accept confinement and rations.
cards.h: → bison = subsistence → hide hunting + railroads destroy herds → no food off-reservation → rations mean confinement
cards.n: 'The army defeated them' alone misses the economic cause the KC pairs with violence: the decimation of the bison.
o: Many army officers welcomed the slaughter because it undermined Native independence more surely than battles did.
Dependence on rations gave agents leverage to enforce reservation rules, so economic collapse became political control.

w.a: Plains nations moved to reservations because they preferred farming to hunting.
w.why: invented preference that ignores coercion and hunger

w.a: The bison died out from cattle diseases, so Native people chose to move.
w.why: the main cause was commercial hunting, and the move was not a free choice

cards.q: Explain why violent conflict in the West increased after the Civil War.
cards.a: Railroads and migration brought settlers, miners and ranchers onto lands guaranteed to Plains nations, while the bison's collapse destroyed Native livelihoods. Gold strikes such as the Black Hills (1874) led the U.S. to break treaties, and resistance met a postwar army, so competition for land became war.
cards.h: → migrants + railroads enter treaty lands → bison collapse → gold strikes break treaties → resistance meets postwar army
cards.n: A causation answer names competition for land and resources (KC-6.2.II.C); 'Indians and settlers didn't get along' earns nothing.
o: An army freed from fighting the Confederacy could be sent west, changing the balance of force.
Competition was three-sided in the Southwest: Anglo settlers fenced land Mexican Americans and Native peoples used, provoking resistance such as Las Gorras Blancas.

w.a: Western violence rose because American Indians attacked settlers for no reason.
w.why: ignores treaty violations and competition for land

w.a: Conflict increased because the Civil War moved west after 1865.
w.why: false; the Civil War ended in 1865

cards.q: Explain why many American Indians were able to preserve their cultures and tribal identities despite federal assimilation policies.
cards.a: Assimilation depended on institutions Native people could partly shape. Families kept languages at home and hid children from agents, ceremonies went underground or blended with Christianity, students used English to defend treaty rights, and reservations, though confining, kept kin and communities together.
cards.h: → policy needed Native cooperation → languages, ceremonies kept → schooling turned to defense → communities held
cards.n: 'They refused to change' is too thin; the KC credits active strategies, including new self-sustaining economic practices, not mere survival.
o: Religious movements such as the Ghost Dance, and later the peyote religion, gave new forms to Native identity under reservation conditions.
Some nations built self-sustaining economies, such as reservation cattle herds, turning a policy of dependency to their own use.

w.a: American Indians kept their cultures because the government never tried to change them.
w.why: false; allotment and boarding schools aimed to erase them

w.a: Native cultures survived only because reformers like Helen Hunt Jackson protected them.
w.why: denies Native agency, and the reformers backed assimilation

cards.q: Differentiate New South rhetoric from southern economic reality after 1877.
cards.a: Rhetoric: Henry Grady, editor of the Atlanta Constitution, called for a 'New South' of cotton mills, railroads, iron and diversified farming, reconciled with the North and open to northern capital. Reality: industry did grow (Piedmont textile mills, Birmingham iron and steel, the Duke tobacco business), but it paid low wages, relied on northern investors and employed few southerners; most stayed in sharecropping and tenant farming tied to cotton (KC-6.1.II.D).
cards.h: → what was promised → what happened
cards.n: Describing the rhetoric alone, or 'the South industrialized', earns nothing; the KC's claim is continuity: agriculture stayed the primary activity.

cards.q: Identify the convict lease system.
cards.a: Southern states leased prisoners, overwhelmingly Black men often convicted under new vagrancy and petty-theft laws, to planters, mine operators, railroad builders and turpentine camps, which paid the state and worked them under brutal conditions with high death rates. It gave New South industries such as Alabama's coal mines cheap coerced labor and let states profit from criminalizing Black freedom.
cards.h: → what + who + where they worked + purpose
cards.n: Calling it ordinary prison labor misses its role: a legal route back to coerced Black labor that fed New South industry (KC-6.1.II.D).

cards.q: Identify the holding of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896).
cards.a: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld Louisiana's 1890 Separate Car Act, which required separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers. By a 7-1 vote the Court held that 'separate but equal' facilities did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause; Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented that 'our Constitution is color-blind.' The ruling gave constitutional cover to Jim Crow until Brown v. Board of Education (1954).
cards.h: → law challenged + holding + vote + dissent
cards.n: 'Plessy outlawed segregation' reverses it; and the case turned on a state law and the 14th Amendment, not the 13th or 15th.

cards.q: Define Jim Crow.
cards.a: Jim Crow, named for a minstrel-show caricature, was the system of state laws, local ordinances and customs, spreading from the late 1880s, that segregated Black and white southerners on railroads and streetcars and in schools, hospitals, parks and other public places. It was upheld by courts after Plessy (1896), reinforced by disfranchisement that removed Black political power, and enforced by violence including lynching.
cards.h: → origin of the name + what it covered + how enforced
cards.n: Jim Crow was not one law; calling it a single statute, or only custom, misses its legal base after Plessy.

cards.q: Identify the methods southern states used to disfranchise Black voters without violating the 15th Amendment.
cards.a: Poll taxes, literacy and 'understanding' tests judged by white registrars, long residency requirements, complex registration rules, grandfather clauses exempting men whose ancestors could vote before 1867 (Louisiana, 1898), and white primaries. Because none named race, they evaded the Fifteenth Amendment; Williams v. Mississippi (1898) upheld literacy tests and poll taxes, and Black voting collapsed across the South.
cards.h: → the methods + why legal + result
cards.n: 'They stopped Black people from voting' earns nothing; the point is facially race-neutral laws that evaded the 15th Amendment, backed by violence.

cards.q: Date each step in the rollback of Black political rights in the South and state its effect: Compromise of 1877 · Civil Rights Cases · defeat of the Lodge Federal Elections Bill · Mississippi constitution · Plessy v. Ferguson · Williams v. Mississippi · Louisiana grandfather clause · Wilmington coup
cards.a:
Compromise of 1877 → 1877; last federal troops leave southern statehouses, ending Reconstruction
Civil Rights Cases → 1883; Court strikes down the Civil Rights Act of 1875's ban on discrimination in public accommodations: the 14th Amendment reaches state action only
Lodge Federal Elections Bill → 1890-1891; federal supervision of congressional elections passes the House, dies in the Senate; federal protection of Black voting ends for decades
Mississippi constitution → 1890; poll tax and literacy-understanding test, a model other states copy
Plessy v. Ferguson → 1896; 'separate but equal' upheld
Williams v. Mississippi → 1898; Court upholds poll tax and literacy test as not discriminatory on their face
Louisiana grandfather clause → 1898; registered Black voters fall from about 130,000 (1896) to about 5,000 (1900)
Wilmington coup → 1898; armed white supremacists overthrow North Carolina city's elected biracial government, killing an unknown number of Black residents (estimates vary widely; 60 or more is often cited)
cards.h: → year + effect, each step
cards.n: Registration and death figures are commonly cited estimates. Dating Plessy before the Civil Rights Cases scrambles the sequence; each step narrowed federal protection further.

cards.q: Define the 'scientific' theories of race that African American reformers confronted in the late nineteenth century.
cards.a: Pseudoscientific claims, dressed in the language of Darwin, anthropology and measurement of skulls and bodies, that humanity was divided into biologically ranked races, with Anglo-Saxons at the top and people of African descent near the bottom. Taught in universities and spread by the press, they were used to justify segregation, disfranchisement and imperialism and to explain Black poverty as nature rather than discrimination.
cards.h: → what the theories claimed + what they justified
cards.n: They were not real science; calling them 'the science of the time' without saying they served to justify Jim Crow misses the KC's point.

cards.q: Identify Ida B. Wells and her anti-lynching campaign.
cards.a: Ida B. Wells, a Black journalist and co-owner of the Memphis Free Speech, began investigating lynching after three friends who ran a grocery were lynched in Memphis in 1892. In Southern Horrors (1892) and A Red Record (1895) she used lynching records to show that only about a third of victims were even accused of rape, the usual excuse, and that lynching punished Black economic independence. A mob destroyed her press, and she took the campaign north and to Britain.
cards.h: → who + what set her off + method + finding
cards.n: She exemplifies the KC's reformers who kept fighting; 'she wrote about lynching' without her evidence or argument earns little.

cards.q: Identify Booker T. Washington and the Atlanta Compromise.
cards.a: Booker T. Washington, born enslaved, led Tuskegee Institute in Alabama from 1881. In his 1895 Atlanta Exposition address (the 'Atlanta Compromise') he urged Black southerners to accept segregation for now and set aside agitation for political rights, building economic strength through vocational and agricultural training: 'In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress.'
cards.h: → who + the speech + the strategy + the famous line
cards.n: Accommodation was a public strategy, not approval of Jim Crow: Washington secretly funded court challenges to segregation and disfranchisement.

cards.q: Contrast Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois.
cards.a: Washington (Atlanta, 1895) urged accommodation: accept segregation for now, pursue vocational training and economic self-help, earn rights gradually. Du Bois, in The Souls of Black Folk (1903), rejected that bargain, demanding immediate civil and political rights, liberal-arts education for a 'Talented Tenth' of leaders, and open protest; he helped found the Niagara Movement (1905) and the NAACP (1909). Both sought Black advancement; they split on priorities and tactics.
cards.h: → each man's strategy + the difference + a shared goal
cards.n: Borrows from u7 for Du Bois's 1903-1909 work. Listing views without stating the difference (gradual economic vs immediate political) earns nothing.

cards.q: Differentiate the position of Black southerners in 1870 from their position in 1900.
cards.a: In 1870 Black men in the South voted in large numbers under federal protection, held seats in legislatures and Congress (Hiram Revels entered the Senate that year), and had new schools and civil-rights laws. By 1900 federal troops were gone; poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses had removed most Black voters; Plessy had upheld segregation; lynching had peaked; and most Black families were trapped in sharecropping debt, the Reconstruction amendments unenforced.
cards.h: → position in 1870 → position in 1900 → what changed
cards.n: Borrows from u5. A contrast needs both dates' positions and the mechanism of change; 'things got worse' earns nothing.

cards.q: Define the 'Solid South.'
cards.a: The one-party Democratic control of the South from the end of Reconstruction until the mid-twentieth century. White Democrats built it by disfranchising Black voters, crushing the biracial Populist challenge of the 1890s, and invoking memories of Reconstruction; the South's bloc of electoral votes and senior congressmen made it a powerful force in national Democratic politics.
cards.h: → what + when + how maintained + national effect
cards.n: It was solidly Democratic, not Republican, until the civil-rights era; confusing the parties' regional bases is the classic slip.

cards.q: Explain why Henry Grady's 1886 'New South' speech to a New York audience is limited as evidence of southern economic conditions.
cards.a: Grady spoke to northern businessmen whose capital he wanted, so he stressed reconciliation, new mills and racial peace and left out sharecropping debt, low wages and disfranchisement. The speech shows what southern boosters promised investors, not how most southerners lived.
cards.h: → audience = northern investors → purpose = capital → stresses progress, omits tenancy → shows goals, not conditions
cards.n: Identifying the audience ('he spoke in New York') earns nothing; the point is how audience and purpose limit what the speech can prove.
o: As editor of the Atlanta Constitution and a booster of Atlanta, Grady had a personal and civic stake in portraying the South as modern and stable.
Speaking a decade after Reconstruction, he needed northerners to leave race relations to white southerners, so his claims of racial harmony served a political purpose.

w.a: Grady's speech is reliable because he was a southern editor who knew the South well.
w.why: treats expertise as proof and ignores purpose and audience

w.a: The speech is limited because it was given in 1886.
w.why: names the date without explaining why it matters

cards.q: Explain why sharecropping and tenant farming persisted in the South despite New South industrialization.
cards.a: The South lacked capital, so landowners paid labor with crop shares and merchants lent against the next cotton crop under crop liens. Debt tied families to the land, cotton was the crop lenders accepted, and the mills needed far fewer workers than the fields held, so industry grew beside farming without replacing it.
cards.h: → capital scarce → crop-lien credit demands cotton → debt binds tenants → mills too few to absorb labor → continuity
cards.n: 'The South stayed agricultural' only restates the KC; the answer needs the credit-and-debt mechanism that kept it so.
o: Northern investors took profits out of southern railroads and mills, so industrial growth did not build local capital that could free farmers from debt.
White landowners and legislators used vagrancy laws, convict leasing and disfranchisement to keep Black labor on the land.

w.a: Sharecropping continued because southerners didn't know how to build factories.
w.why: ignores capital, credit and labor control

w.a: Sharecropping ended by 1890 as New South factories hired most farm workers.
w.why: false; the KC says agriculture stayed primary

cards.q: Explain why Plessy v. Ferguson helped mark the end of most of the political gains African Americans made during Reconstruction.
cards.a: Plessy read the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause as permitting state-ordered segregation, so Reconstruction's chief legal tool now shielded Jim Crow. With federal enforcement gone and the Court endorsing 'separate but equal', southern states could segregate and disfranchise unchallenged.
cards.h: → 14th Amendment reinterpreted → segregation constitutional → no federal enforcement → states segregate, disfranchise
cards.n: Plessy concerned segregation, not voting; tie it to the wider collapse of federal protection rather than claiming it ended Black voting itself.
o: Plessy capped a line of retreats, from the Slaughterhouse Cases (1873) to the Civil Rights Cases (1883), that narrowed what the Reconstruction amendments protected.
By giving segregation constitutional sanction, Plessy let states build a legal caste system that lasted until Brown v. Board of Education (1954).

w.a: Plessy ended Reconstruction because it repealed the Fourteenth Amendment.
w.why: courts cannot repeal amendments; it reinterpreted one

w.a: Plessy mattered because it took away Black men's right to vote.
w.why: confuses segregation with disfranchisement

cards.q: Explain why southern states in the 1890s used poll taxes and literacy tests rather than openly racial bans on voting.
cards.a: The Fifteenth Amendment forbade denying the vote by race, so legislators wrote laws that never named race but that most Black men, poor and long denied schooling, could not meet; white registrars applied them selectively and grandfather clauses spared white voters. Courts accepted them as race-neutral.
cards.h: → 15th Amendment bars racial bans → race-neutral tests + selective enforcement + white exemptions → courts uphold
cards.n: 'They were racist' is true but earns nothing alone; the answer needs the constitutional constraint that made the methods indirect.
o: The disfranchising conventions followed the biracial Populist threat, so the laws also removed many poor white voters who might ally with Black farmers.
Williams v. Mississippi (1898) showed the strategy worked: the Court upheld the tests because they were not discriminatory on their face.

w.a: Southern states used literacy tests because they sincerely wanted an educated electorate.
w.why: ignores selective enforcement and the tests' intent

w.a: The states banned Black voting outright, and the Supreme Court approved.
w.why: false; an open racial ban would violate the 15th Amendment

cards.q: Identify Thomas Edison's electric light and Alexander Graham Bell's telephone as symbols of Gilded Age technological change.
cards.a: Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876; Thomas Edison produced a practical incandescent bulb in 1879 and then a whole electric system, opening the Pearl Street Station in lower Manhattan in 1882. Both came from organized invention: Edison's Menlo Park laboratory (1876) treated invention as a business. The telephone sped business communication, and electric light and power let offices, stores and plants run longer and larger (KC-6.1.I.B.i).
cards.h: → inventor + date + how each raised production
cards.n: Naming the gadgets misses the KC: the point is how businesses used them to raise output. Edison's lasting innovation was the research lab and power system.

cards.q: Identify Gustavus Swift's refrigerated railcar and its effect on the meatpacking industry.
cards.a: Gustavus Swift, a Chicago packer, backed practical refrigerated railcars in the late 1870s and 1880s, so cattle could be slaughtered and dressed in huge Chicago plants and shipped chilled across the country instead of sent live to local butchers. Disassembly lines, sale of by-products and national branch houses cut costs, and a few big packers such as Swift and Armour came to dominate the industry.
cards.h: → what he did + how it changed meatpacking
cards.n: The effect, not the gadget, earns the point: centralized mass production by a few firms. Local butchers and some railroads fought the change.

cards.q: Identify the Bessemer process and its effect on American steel production.
cards.a: The Bessemer process, patented in the 1850s, blew air through molten pig iron to burn out carbon and impurities, turning iron into steel in minutes and making it cheap enough for mass use. Andrew Carnegie built his Edgar Thomson Works (1875) around it, and U.S. steel output rose from under 100,000 tons in 1870 to roughly 10 million tons by 1900, feeding rails, bridges, machinery and skyscraper frames.
cards.h: → how it works + who used it + output figures
cards.n: Output figures are approximate. 'Bessemer invented steel' is wrong: steel existed; the process made it cheap and plentiful, which is the KC's point.

cards.q: Identify the natural resources that fed industrial expansion after 1865 and where they came from.
cards.a: Coal from Pennsylvania and the Appalachians fueled steam engines and steel furnaces; iron ore came from Michigan and, from the 1890s, Minnesota's Mesabi Range, shipped across the Great Lakes; oil from western Pennsylvania, first drilled at Titusville in 1859, was refined into kerosene; and copper from mines such as Butte, Montana, wired the electrical age. Railroads made each resource reachable and cheap (KC-6.1.I.B.i).
cards.h: → resource + region + what it fed
cards.n: A list of resources without what they powered misses the KC's link: greater access to resources, through railroads, let businesses raise production.

cards.q: Explain how electric power began to change American cities and factories by the 1890s.
cards.a: Electric power freed work and city life from the limits of daylight, steam and horses. Central stations such as Edison's Pearl Street (1882), and alternating current promoted by George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla, lit streets, stores and offices; electric streetcars (Richmond, 1888) let cities spread outward; and electric elevators helped make tall buildings practical. Most factories still ran on steam, a shift completed after 1900.
cards.h: → claim + three uses + the limit
cards.n: Overstating it earns nothing: most factories still ran on steam in 1898. The KC point is new power raising production and reshaping cities.

cards.q: Identify how each innovation helped businesses increase the production or distribution of goods: Bessemer process · Westinghouse air brake · standard time zones · refrigerated railcar · telephone · typewriter · Bonsack cigarette machine · central electric power station · electric streetcar · steel-frame skyscraper · kerosene refining
cards.a:
Bessemer process → cheap steel for rails, bridges and machines
Air brake (1869) → longer, heavier, faster trains carry more freight safely
Standard time zones (1883) → railroads coordinate national schedules and shipping
Refrigerated railcar → centralized packing ships dressed meat nationwide
Telephone (1876) → instant coordination of offices, plants and suppliers
Typewriter (1870s) → faster paperwork for large firms; new clerical jobs
Bonsack machine (1880s) → about 200 cigarettes a minute; Duke's mass production in the New South
Central power station (1882) → electric light and power for longer, larger operations
Electric streetcar (1888) → workers commute from wider areas; cities spread
Steel-frame skyscraper (1880s) → more office space on costly downtown land
Kerosene refining → cheap lamp oil sold nationally and abroad
cards.h: → innovation → effect on output or reach
cards.n: Dates are approximate and names illustrative. Saying what an invention is without how it raised output or reach is the miss the KC punishes.

cards.q: Explain how railroads transformed the national economy.
cards.a: Railroads created a single national market. Cheap, year-round freight let factories buy and sell across the continent and specialize at huge scale; their demand for rails, coal and locomotives drove heavy industry; and their size forced new corporate finance, salaried managers and even standard time (1883).
cards.h: → cheap freight → national market → mass production + demand for steel and coal → new corporate methods
cards.n: A list of railroad effects earns little; the causal hub is the national market, which made mass production and big business pay.
o: Railroads were the first big business, and their bureaucracies of salaried managers and their stock and bond finance became the model other corporations copied.
By linking western farms, ranges and mines to eastern cities, railroads tied agriculture and resource extraction to national and world markets.

w.a: Railroads mattered mainly because they let tourists travel west.
w.why: trivial effect; misses freight and the national market

w.a: Railroads transformed the economy by making canals and rivers useless.
w.why: overstated, and says nothing about what railroads made possible

w.a: Railroads were run by the federal government, which then controlled the economy.
w.why: false; they were private, though federally subsidized

cards.q: Explain why new technology after 1865 favored large firms over small producers.
cards.a: New machinery such as Bessemer converters, refineries and continuous-process machines was costly and paid off only if run at full capacity for mass markets. Big firms could raise that capital, spread costs over huge output and undersell small rivals, so technology pushed industries toward a few large producers.
cards.h: → costly machines → need huge output → economies of scale → big firms undersell small ones → consolidation
cards.n: The link to 6.6 is the scored move: 'big businesses had better technology' restates it; name capital costs and economies of scale.
o: High fixed costs meant firms kept producing even when prices fell, which set off price wars that ended in pools, trusts and mergers.
Railroad rebates and national distribution let the biggest shippers, such as Standard Oil, cut costs further than any small competitor could.

w.a: Small producers failed because they refused to use machines.
w.why: invented; many mechanized but lacked scale

w.a: Technology favored big firms because the government banned small businesses from holding patents.
w.why: no such ban existed

cards.q: Explain why the Bessemer process and railroad expansion reinforced each other.
cards.a: Each created the other's market. Cheap Bessemer steel gave railroads rails that lasted far longer than iron and carried heavier trains, so lines expanded; that expansion made railroads steel's biggest buyer, letting mills like Carnegie's run at scale and cut prices further.
cards.h: → cheap steel → durable rails, heavier trains → more track → biggest steel customer → larger mills, lower prices
cards.n: Two separate descriptions earn nothing on a connections task; the answer must state the feedback loop between the two industries.
o: Carnegie, a former Pennsylvania Railroad manager, built his steel business on railroad contracts and railroad-style cost accounting.
Railroads also carried the coal and iron ore that steelmaking needed, cutting costs for the industry that supplied them.

w.a: The Bessemer process mattered only for skyscrapers, not railroads.
w.why: rails were steel's main early market

w.a: Railroads and steel grew separately because track was made of wood.
w.why: false; iron and then steel rails

cards.q: Identify Andrew Carnegie's role in industrialization.
cards.a: Andrew Carnegie, a Scottish immigrant who rose through the Pennsylvania Railroad, built the nation's largest steel company. His Edgar Thomson Works (1875) used the Bessemer process, and he pursued vertical integration, controlling coke, iron ore, ore ships and rail lines, plus relentless cost accounting, to undersell rivals. He sold out to J.P. Morgan in 1901 and preached the Gospel of Wealth (1889), giving most of his fortune away.
cards.h: → industry + method + outcome + philanthropy
cards.n: Mixing up his vertical integration with Rockefeller's horizontal integration is the classic MC trap; the 1901 sale falls just past the period.

cards.q: Identify John D. Rockefeller's role in industrialization.
cards.a: John D. Rockefeller founded Standard Oil in Cleveland (1870) and pursued horizontal integration: with secret railroad rebates, price cutting and buyouts he absorbed rival refiners until he controlled roughly 90 percent of U.S. refining by about 1880. He held the combination together through the Standard Oil Trust (1882), later a New Jersey holding company, and added pipelines and barrel-making.
cards.h: → company + method + market share + legal form
cards.n: The 90 percent share is approximate. Calling his method vertical integration is the classic miss; his signature was absorbing competitors at the refining stage.

cards.q: Identify J.P. Morgan's role in industrialization.
cards.a: J. Pierpont Morgan was the leading investment banker, the face of finance capitalism: he raised capital for railroads and industry and reorganized bankrupt railroads in the 1890s ('Morganization'), putting his partners on their boards. He arranged mergers such as General Electric (1892), sold the Treasury gold to shore up its reserve in 1895, and in 1901 formed U.S. Steel, the first billion-dollar corporation.
cards.h: → banker, not producer + consolidation + key deals
cards.n: Morgan made nothing himself; filing him with Carnegie and Rockefeller as a producer misses finance capitalism. U.S. Steel (1901) falls just past the period.

cards.q: Contrast vertical and horizontal integration.
cards.a: Vertical integration controls every stage of one product, from raw materials through transport to sale, to cut costs and escape suppliers: Carnegie owned the ore, coke, ships and railroads that fed his mills. Horizontal integration combines competitors at the same stage to control a market and its prices: Rockefeller bought or crushed rival refiners. One seeks efficiency along a chain, the other monopoly across an industry.
cards.h: → each defined + an example + the difference in aim
cards.n: Defining both without the difference in aim (cost control vs. market control) earns nothing; swapping Carnegie and Rockefeller is the classic MC error.

cards.q: Define a trust as used in the late nineteenth century.
cards.a: A trust was an arrangement in which the stockholders of competing companies handed their shares to a single board of trustees in exchange for trust certificates, so the trustees ran all the firms as one while they stayed legally separate. The Standard Oil Trust (1882), with nine trustees, was the model; 'trust' then became shorthand for any giant combination seeking monopoly.
cards.h: → mechanism + first example + broader meaning
cards.n: 'A company people trust' earns nothing; the mechanism is shares traded for certificates under one board, which evaded state limits on corporations.

cards.q: Define a holding company and explain why it replaced the trust.
cards.a: A holding company is a corporation that owns controlling blocks of stock in other corporations and directs them without merging their operations. From 1889 New Jersey let its corporations own stock in other companies, so when courts attacked trusts (Ohio ordered the Standard Oil Trust dissolved in 1892) and the Sherman Act (1890) loomed, combinations reincorporated as New Jersey holding companies, as Standard Oil did in 1899.
cards.h: → definition + legal change + why firms switched
cards.n: Treating the holding company as the end of consolidation reverses it: the form kept monopoly control legal after trusts came under attack.

cards.q: Identify the new financial and management structures that let businesses grow after 1865.
cards.a: The corporation, with limited liability, let owners sell stock to many investors, and stock exchanges and investment banks such as J.P. Morgan's raised capital on a new scale. Railroads pioneered the management hierarchy: salaried middle managers, separate departments and detailed cost accounting to run operations over thousands of miles. Manufacturers such as Carnegie copied these methods to coordinate mass production (KC-6.1.I.B.ii).
cards.h: → finance tools + management tools + who pioneered
cards.n: Naming 'the corporation' without how it raised capital, or managers without what they coordinated, misses the KC's causal link to higher production.

cards.q: Identify the advances in marketing that helped businesses sell mass-produced goods.
cards.a: National brands with trademarks and packaging (Ivory soap, Quaker Oats, Coca-Cola) and paid advertising in mass-circulation newspapers and magazines built demand. Department stores such as Macy's, Wanamaker's and Marshall Field's sold goods under one roof in cities, and mail-order catalogs, Montgomery Ward from 1872 and Sears from the 1890s, reached rural customers by rail and mail.
cards.h: → three methods + an example of each
cards.n: Brand and store names are illustrative. The KC point is that marketing kept pace with mass production; listing stores without that link earns little.

cards.q: Describe how American businesses extended their reach beyond U.S. borders by the 1890s.
cards.a: American firms sought markets and resources in the Pacific, Asia and Latin America. Sugar planters in Hawaii, favored by an 1875 reciprocity treaty, came to control the islands' economy and led the 1893 overthrow of Queen Liliuokalani; investors put money into Cuban sugar and Mexican railroads and mines; Standard Oil sold kerosene across Europe and Asia; and firms such as Singer built factories and sales networks abroad.
cards.h: → region + business + what it sought
cards.n: Examples are illustrative. Jumping to the 1898 war misses the KC's point that business looked abroad first, for markets and resources, well before annexation.

cards.q: State one contemporary estimate of how concentrated American wealth had become by 1890.
cards.a: The economist Charles B. Spahr estimated in 1896 that about 1 percent of American families held more wealth than the other 99 percent combined, and that seven-eighths of families held only about one-eighth of the national wealth. It is a contemporary estimate built from limited tax and probate data, not a census count, but it shows the concentration of wealth the KC ties to trusts and holding companies.
cards.h: → the estimate + its source + its limits
cards.n: Flag it as an estimate; Spahr is illustrative and quoting his figure as census fact overclaims. The concentration itself is the tested point.

cards.q: Identify how the telegraph and the transatlantic cable expanded business communication after 1865.
cards.a: By 1866 Western Union dominated a national telegraph network strung beside the railroads, and that year the first lasting transatlantic cable, promoted by Cyrus Field, linked the United States and Britain. Prices, orders and news now crossed the continent and the Atlantic in minutes instead of days or weeks, so firms could run distant plants, bankers could move capital, and farm crops were priced in a world market (KC-6.1.I).
cards.h: → network + cable + what speed made possible
cards.n: The KC names expanding international communication networks; describing the cable without what instant prices did for business and markets earns little.

cards.q: Explain why business leaders consolidated corporations into trusts and holding companies.
cards.a: Heavy fixed costs made firms keep producing as prices fell, so competition became ruinous price wars. Pools to share markets were unenforceable in court and banned for railroads in 1887, so leaders combined firms under one control to cut output, fix prices and raise profits, which concentrated wealth.
cards.h: → high fixed costs → price wars → pools fail → combine under one control → stable prices, profit, concentrated wealth
cards.n: 'They were greedy' earns nothing; the KC wants the mechanism: consolidation promised higher profits by ending cutthroat competition.
o: The depressions after 1873 and 1893 drove weak firms under, and survivors or bankers such as Morgan bought them up.
State laws limited what one corporation could own, so leaders invented the trust and then the New Jersey holding company to combine firms legally.

w.a: Businesses formed trusts because the Sherman Act required large corporations.
w.why: reversed; the Sherman Act banned combinations in restraint of trade

w.a: Trusts formed because there were too few companies to compete.
w.why: the problem was too much competition, not too little

cards.q: Explain the extent to which industrial capitalism changed the organization of American business between 1865 and 1898.
cards.a: It changed business greatly. Local partnerships gave way to national corporations run by salaried managers, financed by stock and investment banks and combined into trusts. Yet private ownership, profit and founders such as Carnegie persisted, so the change was in scale and form, not in capitalism itself.
cards.h: → extent claim → changes: scale, corporations, managers, trusts → continuities: private ownership, founders → net
cards.n: An extent claim needs both sides weighed; 'business got bigger' names a change without showing what changed in structure.
o: Most Americans still worked on farms or in small shops in 1898, so the corporate economy dominated railroads and heavy industry but not yet everything.
The change in form also changed labor: workers now faced impersonal corporations instead of an owner they knew.

w.a: Business did not change at all, since companies existed before the Civil War.
w.why: ignores the change in scale and form

w.a: By 1898 nearly every American worked for a giant corporation.
w.why: overstated; most still farmed or worked in small firms

cards.q: Explain why American businesses increasingly looked to markets and resources abroad in the 1880s and 1890s.
cards.a: Industry produced more than the home market could absorb, especially in the depressions after 1873 and 1893, so firms and their political allies sought foreign buyers for surplus goods and foreign supplies of sugar, ore and oil. Rivalry with European empires added urgency: markets not secured might be closed.
cards.h: → overproduction + depressions → surplus needs buyers → resources abroad → European rivals → push outward
cards.n: Name the economic cause the KC stresses; 'Americans wanted an empire' skips the market-and-resource motive and jumps to 1898.
o: Hawaii shows the mechanism: American planters invested in sugar for the U.S. market, then pressed for annexation when tariff changes threatened their profits.
Arguments such as Alfred Thayer Mahan's on sea power (1890) linked overseas markets to naval bases, turning business interest into foreign policy.

w.a: Businesses went abroad because the U.S. had run out of natural resources.
w.why: false; domestic resources were abundant

w.a: Companies looked abroad because the Constitution required foreign trade.
w.why: invented requirement

cards.q: Explain why historians have disagreed about whether Gilded Age industrialists were 'robber barons' or 'captains of industry'.
cards.a: The same record supports both readings. Carnegie and Rockefeller built efficient firms that cut prices for steel and kerosene, but also crushed rivals with rebates, broke strikes and bought influence. Those who weigh efficiency and philanthropy call them builders; those who weigh labor and monopoly call them robbers.
cards.h: → same record → efficiency, low prices, philanthropy vs. monopoly, strikebreaking → different weighting → labels
cards.n: Illustrative historiography. Picking one label and describing it earns less than showing which evidence each side weighs and why.
o: The labels shifted with the historians' own era: Depression-era writers such as Matthew Josephson (The Robber Barons, 1934) stressed exploitation, while later business historians stressed innovation and organization.
Contemporaries split the same way: critics such as Henry George and the Populists saw monopoly, while defenders invoked Social Darwinism and the Gospel of Wealth.

w.a: Historians disagree because no records survive of how these men ran their businesses.
w.why: abundant records exist; the dispute is interpretive

w.a: They were captains of industry because they never broke any laws.
w.why: ignores rebates, bribery and strikebreaking the critics cite

cards.q: Identify the Knights of Labor.
cards.a: The Knights of Labor, founded in 1869 and led from 1879 by Terence Powderly, was an inclusive national union open to skilled and unskilled workers, women and Black workers, though it shut out Chinese workers and 'nonproducers' such as bankers and lawyers. It sought the eight-hour day, an end to child labor, arbitration and producer cooperatives to replace wage labor. It peaked near 700,000 members in 1886, then collapsed after Haymarket and failed strikes.
cards.h: → leader + who it admitted + goals + rise and fall
cards.n: Membership is approximate. Calling it a craft union confuses it with the AFL; its inclusiveness and anti-wage-system goals are the tested traits.

cards.q: Identify the American Federation of Labor and Samuel Gompers.
cards.a: The American Federation of Labor, founded in 1886 and led for decades by Samuel Gompers, was a federation of craft unions of skilled workers. It practiced 'pure and simple', or bread-and-butter, unionism: collective bargaining for higher wages, shorter hours and safer conditions within capitalism, backed by strikes and boycotts, not cooperatives or a new social order. It left out most unskilled workers, most women and most Black workers.
cards.h: → founding + leader + membership + strategy
cards.n: Saying the AFL sought to overthrow capitalism reverses it; its narrow membership and workplace goals are why it survived where the Knights did not.

cards.q: Contrast the Knights of Labor with the American Federation of Labor.
cards.a: The Knights admitted nearly all workers, skilled and unskilled, men and women, Black and white, and aimed to reform society by replacing wage labor with cooperatives. The AFL admitted mainly skilled craftsmen and aimed only at concrete workplace gains, wages and hours, within capitalism. The inclusive, reform-minded Knights collapsed after 1886; the narrow, pragmatic AFL endured.
cards.h: → membership vs. membership + goals vs. goals + outcome
cards.n: Describing each union separately earns nothing; state the differences outright: inclusive vs. exclusive, social reform vs. bread-and-butter gains.

cards.q: Identify the Great Railroad Strike of 1877.
cards.a: In July 1877, in the depression after the Panic of 1873, the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad cut wages again and workers walked out; the strike spread along the rail lines to Pittsburgh, Chicago and St. Louis and halted much of the nation's freight. Governors called out militias, President Hayes sent federal troops, and about 100 people were killed. It was the first nationwide strike and showed the government would side with employers.
cards.h: → cause + spread + government response + significance
cards.n: The death toll is an estimate. Dating it to the 1890s, or calling it a Knights or AFL strike, is the common slip; it spread largely without union direction.

cards.q: Identify the Haymarket affair.
cards.a: On May 4, 1886, during the national eight-hour-day campaign, anarchists held a rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square to protest police killings of strikers at the McCormick works; a bomb thrown at police killed several officers, and police gunfire followed. Eight anarchists were convicted on thin evidence, and four were hanged. The press tied unions to foreign-born radicalism, and the Knights of Labor went into steep decline.
cards.h: → date + setting + violence + trial + effect on labor
cards.n: No one proved who threw the bomb, and the Knights did not plan it. The tested point is the backlash that linked labor and immigrants to anarchism.

cards.q: Identify the Homestead Strike of 1892.
cards.a: At Carnegie's Homestead steel works near Pittsburgh in 1892, manager Henry Clay Frick cut wages and locked out the skilled workers' union, the Amalgamated Association, then brought in about 300 Pinkerton guards by barge. A gun battle on July 6 killed several workers and guards, the governor sent some 8,000 state militia, and strikebreakers restarted the mill. The defeat destroyed the union and left steel largely nonunion for decades.
cards.h: → company + managers + confrontation + outcome
