cards.n: Casualty counts vary. Crediting federal troops is wrong: the Pennsylvania militia broke it. Carnegie was abroad but backed Frick's aim of ending the union.

cards.q: Identify the Pullman Strike of 1894.
cards.a: In 1894, during a depression, the Pullman Palace Car Company cut wages by roughly a quarter without lowering rents in its company town, so workers struck, and Eugene Debs's American Railway Union refused to handle trains carrying Pullman cars, stopping traffic across much of the country. Attorney General Richard Olney won a federal injunction, and President Cleveland sent troops over Illinois governor John Altgeld's objection. The strike collapsed and Debs was jailed.
cards.h: → cause + ARU boycott + injunction + troops + outcome
cards.n: The injunction, not the troops alone, broke the strike; missing that the court order was the new weapon misses why Pullman mattered.

cards.q: Date the four major Gilded Age labor conflicts in order.
cards.a: Great Railroad Strike 1877; Haymarket affair 1886; Homestead Strike 1892; Pullman Strike 1894. The first and last came in depressions, after the panics of 1873 and 1893, and across the sequence government added a new weapon, the court injunction, to troops and militia.
cards.h: → four years in order + one pattern
cards.n: 1886 is also the AFL's founding year. Swapping Homestead (1892, steel, Pennsylvania) and Pullman (1894, railroads, Chicago) is the common slip.

cards.q: Define the company town model of industrial paternalism practiced at Pullman, Illinois.
cards.a: Industrial paternalism meant an employer supplying workers' housing, stores, churches and amenities while controlling their lives. George Pullman built a model town south of Chicago in the early 1880s, with brick homes, parks and a library but no saloons, all owned by the company and rented to workers, with rent taken from pay. When he cut wages in 1894 but not rents, the benevolence turned into grievance and set off the Pullman Strike.
cards.h: → definition + Pullman's town + how it backfired
cards.n: Praising the town's amenities misses the point, which is control: workers could not own their homes, and one owner set both their wages and their rents.

cards.q: Explain how many workers' standards of living improved in the Gilded Age even as the gap between rich and poor grew.
cards.a: Both happened because mass production cut prices faster than it cut pay. Cheaper food, clothing, kerosene and manufactured goods meant that workers' real wages, what their pay could buy, generally rose, and many gained access to new goods and services. But profits and ownership concentrated at the top in trusts and industrial fortunes, so the distance between a Carnegie and a steelworker grew even as the steelworker's purchasing power improved.
cards.h: → prices fall → real wages rise → wealth concentrates
cards.n: 'Workers got poorer' contradicts the KC; the tested nuance is rising real wages alongside widening inequality, plus insecurity from layoffs and injury.

cards.q: Describe how the industrial workforce expanded and child labor increased between 1865 and 1900.
cards.a: Factories, mines and railroads drew millions of rural Americans and immigrants into wage work, and machines that broke skilled trades into simple tasks let employers hire children cheaply in textile mills, coal breakers, glassworks and street trades. The 1900 census counted about 1.75 million children aged 10 to 15 at work, nearly one in five of that age group. Hours commonly ran 10 to 12 a day, six days a week, in dangerous conditions.
cards.h: → who joined the workforce + why children + a figure
cards.n: The census figure is the commonly cited count. Blaming parents alone misses the causes the KC points to: deskilled machine work and low family wages.

cards.q: Explain why organized labor achieved so little in the Gilded Age.
cards.a: Labor faced power it could not match. Employers used lockouts, blacklists, Pinkertons, strikebreakers; courts issued injunctions and governments sent troops; and workers were split by skill, race, ethnicity and sex while immigration kept replacement labor plentiful. By 1900 only a few percent of workers were in unions.
cards.h: → employer weapons + state sides with employers + divided workforce + steady labor supply → weak unions
cards.n: A list of failed strikes is description; the answer needs why they failed. Union shares are estimates, often put near 3 percent around 1900.
o: Public opinion turned against unions after Haymarket, when the press linked strikes to foreign-born anarchists.
The depressions of the 1870s and 1890s left so many unemployed that strikers could be replaced easily.

w.a: Labor achieved little because workers were satisfied with their wages and hours.
w.why: ignores the era's massive strikes

w.a: Unions failed because Congress made strikes illegal in 1877.
w.why: no such law; injunctions came case by case

w.a: Gilded Age workers never tried to form national unions.
w.why: the Knights and the AFL were national unions

cards.q: Explain why the American Federation of Labor outlasted the Knights of Labor.
cards.a: The AFL organized skilled craftsmen who were hard to replace, so its strikes had leverage, and it sought limited wage-and-hour gains employers could grant. The Knights' replaceable mass membership, loose structure and broad goals left it exposed when strikes failed and Haymarket turned opinion against it.
cards.h: → skilled members hard to replace + narrow goals → leverage, survival; Knights broad and exposed → collapse
cards.n: A contrast alone ('one was inclusive, one was not') is not an explanation; link the membership difference to bargaining power.
o: The AFL's federation structure let each craft union keep its own treasury and strike fund, so one defeat did not sink the whole.
The AFL's acceptance of capitalism made it less threatening to employers and the public than the Knights' cooperative vision.

w.a: The AFL lasted longer because it included every worker regardless of skill.
w.why: reversed; the Knights were the inclusive one

w.a: The Knights collapsed because Gompers bought them out in 1886.
w.why: invented event

cards.q: Explain continuity and change in the federal government's response to major strikes from 1877 to 1894.
cards.a: The continuity was federal force on employers' side: Hayes sent troops in 1877 and Cleveland in 1894. The change was the legal weapon: in 1894 Attorney General Olney won an injunction, citing the mails and interstate commerce, so defying it meant jail for contempt, as Debs learned.
cards.h: → continuity: troops for employers (1877, 1894) → change: court injunction (1894) → contempt jails leaders
cards.n: Describing each strike separately earns nothing; a CCOT answer names what stayed the same and what changed, with the injunction as the change.
o: In re Debs (1895) confirmed the change, upholding federal power to enjoin strikes that obstructed interstate commerce or the mail.
Between the two strikes, the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) gave courts another ground to treat union boycotts as conspiracies in restraint of trade.

w.a: The federal government stayed neutral in labor disputes throughout the Gilded Age.
w.why: false; it repeatedly sided with employers

w.a: The change was that by 1894 the government supported strikers.
w.why: reversed; it broke the Pullman Strike

cards.q: Define the new immigration of the late nineteenth century.
cards.a: The new immigration was the shift, from about 1880, toward immigrants from southern and eastern Europe: Italians, Poles and other Slavs, Greeks, Hungarians, and Jews from the Russian Empire and Austria-Hungary, with smaller numbers from Asia. Most were Catholic, Orthodox Christian or Jewish, many were poor peasants or artisans, and most settled in industrial cities and mining towns, filling the expanding workforce (KC-6.2.I.A).
cards.h: → when + from where + religion + where they settled
cards.n: 'Immigrants from Europe' is too vague; the tested shift is from northern and western to southern and eastern Europe, and from farms to cities.

cards.q: Contrast old and new immigration in origin, religion, and reception.
cards.a: Old immigrants, before about 1880, came mainly from northern and western Europe (Britain, Ireland, Germany, Scandinavia); most were Protestant apart from the Irish and many Germans, and many settled on farms. New immigrants came mainly from southern and eastern Europe, were mostly Catholic, Orthodox or Jewish, and crowded into industrial cities. Reception grew harsher: nativists called the newcomers racially inferior and pushed literacy tests.
cards.h: → origin + religion + settlement + reception, paired
cards.n: The Irish and German Catholics were old immigrants and met nativism too; 'old immigrants were welcomed' overstates the difference.

cards.q: Contrast the immigrant experience at Ellis Island with that at Angel Island.
cards.a: Ellis Island, opened in New York Harbor in 1892, processed mostly European arrivals, and most cleared medical and legal inspection within hours; only about 2 percent were turned away. Angel Island, opened in San Francisco Bay in 1910, enforced Chinese exclusion, holding Asian arrivals for weeks or months of interrogation about their family claims. The difference reflects laws that restricted Asians long before Europeans.
cards.h: → each station: who, how long, why the difference
cards.n: Borrows from u7 (Angel Island opened 1910). Treating both as the same welcome misses the point: exclusion laws made Asian entry an ordeal.

cards.q: State the approximate volume of immigration to the United States between 1880 and 1920.
cards.a: Roughly 20 to 25 million immigrants arrived between 1880 and 1920, often given as about 23 million, the largest sustained wave in U.S. history to that time. Most came from southern and eastern Europe and entered through Ellis Island after 1892; perhaps a quarter to a third eventually went home, especially Italian and Balkan 'birds of passage'.
cards.h: → approximate number + main sources + return migration
cards.n: Figures are estimates, and the span runs into Period 7. Confusing the annual peak (over a million in several years after 1905) with the total is the slip.

cards.q: State how the urban share of the U.S. population changed between 1860 and 1900.
cards.a: The urban share of the population roughly doubled, from about 20 percent in 1860 to about 40 percent in 1900, as factories, railroads and immigrants concentrated people in cities. Chicago grew from about 110,000 to about 1.7 million, and New York, consolidated in 1898, passed 3 million.
cards.h: → two percentages + an example city
cards.n: The census counted places of 2,500 or more as urban; the country became majority urban only in the 1920 census, so 'most Americans were urban by 1900' is wrong.

cards.q: Explain how industrial growth reshaped the physical layout of American cities.
cards.a: Industrial growth pushed cities up, out and apart. Steel frames and elevators raised skyscrapers downtown; streetcars and elevated railways let the middle class move to outlying neighborhoods and early suburbs; and workers and immigrants who could not afford to commute crowded into tenements near factories and docks, such as New York's dumbbell tenements, with little light, air or plumbing. Cities sorted by class and ethnicity as never before.
cards.h: → up + out + packed tenements → sorted by class
cards.n: 'Cities got bigger' is not a layout; name the vertical, outward and segregating changes. Jacob Riis's How the Other Half Lives (1890) is the classic evidence.

cards.q: Identify the Exodusters.
cards.a: The Exodusters were Black southerners who left Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas and other states for Kansas, above all in 1879, seeking land and escape from violence, debt and the collapse of Reconstruction; several thousand came that spring and perhaps 20,000 or more by 1880. Promoters such as Benjamin 'Pap' Singleton invoked the biblical Exodus. Many met poverty in Kansas, but the movement shows African Americans migrating out of the South to escape limited opportunity.
cards.h: → who + when + where + why + significance
cards.n: Numbers are estimates. Calling it the Great Migration is wrong: that came after 1910 to northern cities; this was a smaller movement to western farmland.

cards.q: Identify the push factors that drove Gilded Age immigrants from their home countries.
cards.a: In southern Italy, poverty, overpopulation, falling crop prices and heavy taxes drove peasants out; in the Russian Empire, the pogroms of 1881-1882 and the May Laws of 1882 persecuted Jews; in Austria-Hungary and Russian Poland, land shortages pushed Slavic peasants; and in China's Guangdong province, poverty and upheaval sent laborers abroad. Cheap steamship passage and letters from relatives already in America turned these pressures into migration.
cards.h: → place + push factor, for several groups + what enabled it
cards.n: The KC names poverty, religious persecution and limited mobility; pull factors alone, or a push tied to the wrong group (pogroms for Italians), miss it.

cards.q: Describe how urban ethnic neighborhoods provided new cultural opportunities for immigrants.
cards.a: Neighborhoods such as New York's Lower East Side and Little Italy, San Francisco's Chinatown and Chicago's Polish districts let newcomers live among people who shared their language and faith. They built parishes, synagogues and temples, foreign-language newspapers, mutual aid and burial societies, theaters such as the Yiddish stage, social clubs and ethnic shops, which offered jobs, credit and a familiar culture while easing adjustment to American life.
cards.h: → example neighborhoods + institutions + what they offered
cards.n: Portraying enclaves only as slums misses the KC's point that they created new cultural opportunities; name institutions, not just crowding.

cards.q: Compare the main ideas of these two sources. Source 1 (paraphrase of an 1890s letter from a Polish steelworker in Pittsburgh to his family, composed for this exercise): the work is hard and hot and the hours long, but I earn in a day what took a week at home; send my brother, there is a job for him. Source 2 (composite of a New York reformer's 1890s report on a tenement district, written for this exercise): families of eight share two dark rooms; the air shafts reek; children work in sweatshops; sickness spreads through the block.
cards.a: Similarity: both describe hard conditions for immigrant workers in industrial cities. Difference: Source 1 judges them worth enduring because wages far exceed those at home, and it invites more migration, while Source 2 sees only danger and misery that call for reform. The difference comes from point of view: the migrant measures America against his homeland, and the reformer measures the tenement against middle-class standards.
cards.h: → one similarity + one difference + why they differ
cards.n: Both sources are composed for practice. Summarizing each separately earns nothing; state the similarity and difference outright, then explain them.

cards.q: Explain why the main sources of immigration to the United States shifted to southern and eastern Europe after 1880.
cards.a: Push and pull both shifted. Industrializing Britain and Germany now absorbed more of their own labor, while in southern Italy, Austria-Hungary and Russia rural poverty and, for Jews, pogroms pushed millions out. Steamships cut the crossing to a week or two, and U.S. industry's hunger for unskilled labor drew them in.
cards.h: → old sources industrialize → new pushes: poverty, pogroms → steamships cheapen crossing → U.S. factory jobs pull
cards.n: Pull factors alone ('America had jobs') don't explain a shift in origin; the answer needs why the sending regions changed.
o: Chain migration compounded the change: early migrants sent passage money and news, so each village's first arrivals drew relatives after them.
Chinese migration, the main Asian stream, was cut off by the 1882 Exclusion Act, tilting the new immigration further toward Europe.

w.a: Immigration shifted because the U.S. banned northern Europeans after 1880.
w.why: no such ban; only Chinese laborers were barred

w.a: Southern Europeans came mainly for free Homestead Act farms.
w.why: most settled in cities as wage workers

cards.q: Explain why many immigrants settled in ethnic neighborhoods in industrial cities.
cards.a: Newcomers had little money, spoke little English and needed work at once, so they went where relatives and townsfolk already were. Chain migration, cheap housing near factories, and ethnic churches, shops and aid societies made the neighborhood the place to find jobs, credit and a familiar culture.
cards.h: → poverty + language + urgent need for work → chain migration → housing near jobs → ethnic institutions hold it together
cards.n: 'They wanted to be with their own kind' is too thin; name the economic and practical mechanism behind clustering (KC-6.2.I.B).
o: Discrimination in housing and hiring, especially against Chinese and Jewish immigrants, pushed groups together as much as choice drew them.
Labor agents such as Italian padrones recruited workers by group and placed them in the same industries and districts.

w.a: Immigrants lived in ethnic neighborhoods because the law required them to.
w.why: no such law for European immigrants

w.a: Immigrants clustered because they refused to take factory jobs.
w.why: most of them worked in factories

cards.q: Explain the extent to which immigration from 1865 to 1898 marked a change from immigration before the Civil War.
cards.a: It changed a great deal in origin and destination but little in motive and reception. New immigrants came from southern and eastern Europe and settled in industrial cities; yet like the Irish and Germans before them they fled poverty or persecution for wage work and met nativist hostility.
cards.h: → change: origins, religions, urban industrial jobs → continuity: push-pull motives, nativism → extent
cards.n: Borrows from u4 (Irish and German migration). A CCOT answer that lists only differences, without weighing a continuity, earns less.
o: The Chinese stream shows change within continuity: it began in the 1850s, like mass Irish migration, but became the first group barred by nationality in 1882.
Scale changed as well: arrivals reached nearly 800,000 in 1882 alone, far above any antebellum year.

w.a: Immigration changed completely because almost no one immigrated before 1865.
w.why: false; millions came before the Civil War

w.a: Nothing changed, since immigrants came from the same countries as before.
w.why: ignores the shift to southern and eastern Europe

cards.q: Identify the Chinese Exclusion Act.
cards.a: The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) suspended the immigration of Chinese laborers for ten years and barred Chinese immigrants from naturalized citizenship. West Coast workers, rallied by Denis Kearney's Workingmen's Party in California, blamed Chinese labor for low wages in the 1870s depression, and racism made the Chinese easy targets. It was the first federal law to bar a group by nationality; renewed in 1892 and made permanent in 1902, it was repealed only in 1943.
cards.h: → date + what it barred + why + significance
cards.n: It barred laborers, not all Chinese (merchants, students and diplomats could enter); 'banned all immigration' confuses it with the 1920s quota laws.

cards.q: Identify the Geary Act of 1892.
cards.a: The Geary Act (1892), named for California congressman Thomas Geary, extended Chinese exclusion for another ten years and required Chinese residents to carry a certificate of residence or face arrest and deportation. Chinese American organizations urged mass refusal to register and challenged the law in court, but the Supreme Court upheld it in Fong Yue Ting v. United States (1893).
cards.h: → what it extended + what it added + resistance + Court
cards.n: Illustrative; the tested idea is escalating exclusion. Confusing Geary with the 1882 act misses what it added: surveillance of Chinese already living here.

cards.q: Date the Chinese Exclusion Act, the opening of Ellis Island, and the founding of Hull House.
cards.a: Chinese Exclusion Act 1882; Hull House founded 1889; Ellis Island opened 1892. Together they show the period's contrasting responses to immigration: exclusion of the Chinese in the West, and the processing and Americanizing of Europeans in the East.
cards.h: → three years in order + what links them
cards.n: Putting Ellis Island before 1882 is the common slip; New York's earlier station, Castle Garden, handled arrivals until 1890.

cards.q: Identify the settlement house movement and Jane Addams.
cards.a: Settlement houses were centers in poor immigrant neighborhoods where educated, mostly female reformers lived among their neighbors and offered kindergartens, English and citizenship classes, clubs, health care and job training, helping immigrants adapt to U.S. language and customs. Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founded Chicago's Hull House in 1889 on the model of London's Toynbee Hall, and Addams used its research to push for child-labor and sanitation laws.
cards.h: → what they were + what they offered + Addams + Hull House
cards.n: Settlement workers lived in the neighborhood; calling them charities handing out relief misses the method and the Americanizing aim the KC names.

cards.q: Identify Lillian Wald and the Henry Street Settlement.
cards.a: Lillian Wald, a nurse, founded the Henry Street Settlement on New York's Lower East Side in 1893, sending nurses into immigrant tenements to treat the sick at home. She coined the term 'public health nurse', built a visiting nurse service, and later pressed for school nurses and the federal Children's Bureau (1912).
cards.h: → who + where + when + public health innovation
cards.n: Illustrative example of KC-6.3.II.B.i; the Children's Bureau is Period 7. The point here is women reformers serving immigrant neighborhoods.

cards.q: Identify the American Protective Association.
cards.a: The American Protective Association, founded in Clinton, Iowa, in 1887, was a secret anti-Catholic society whose members pledged not to vote for Catholics, not to hire them when a Protestant was available, and not to strike alongside them. It warned that the Pope was plotting to control America through Catholic immigrants and claimed a large membership in the mid-1890s before fading.
cards.h: → date + target + tactics + fate
cards.n: The APA targeted Catholics, not Asians, echoing the Know-Nothings of the 1850s. Its own membership claims were inflated, so treat numbers as unreliable.

cards.q: Identify the Immigration Restriction League and its proposed literacy test.
cards.a: Founded in Boston in 1894 by Harvard-educated men such as Prescott Hall, the Immigration Restriction League argued that southern and eastern Europeans were racially inferior and lobbied for a literacy test to cut their numbers. Congress passed the test repeatedly, but Cleveland (1897), Taft and Wilson vetoed it until it became law over Wilson's veto in 1917.
cards.h: → founders + argument + proposal + fate
cards.n: Borrows from u7 for 1917. The trap is dating the test's passage to the 1890s; Cleveland vetoed it. It aimed at new European immigrants, not the Chinese.

cards.q: Name the main nativist organizations in order from the 1850s through the 1920s: Know-Nothings, APA, Immigration Restriction League, and the second Klan.
cards.a: Know-Nothings (American Party), 1850s: anti-Catholic party politics aimed at Irish and German immigrants. American Protective Association, from 1887: anti-Catholic secret society. Immigration Restriction League, from 1894: elite lobby for a literacy test against southern and eastern Europeans. Second Ku Klux Klan, 1920s: mass organization against Catholics, Jews, immigrants and Black Americans. Anti-Catholicism runs through all four.
cards.h: → four groups in order + each one's target
cards.n: Borrows from u5 and u7. The pattern, not the list, earns credit: each wave of immigration brought a new nativist organization.

cards.q: Identify the Statue of Liberty and Emma Lazarus's 'The New Colossus.'
cards.a: The Statue of Liberty, France's gift celebrating American liberty and the two nations' republican friendship, was dedicated in New York Harbor in 1886. Emma Lazarus's sonnet 'The New Colossus' (1883), written to raise money for the pedestal, recast it as a 'Mother of Exiles' welcoming 'your tired, your poor'; the poem went on a plaque in the pedestal in 1903 as the statue became a symbol of welcome to immigrants.
cards.h: → origin + date + the poem + how its meaning changed
cards.n: The statue was not built to welcome immigrants; that meaning, from Lazarus, took hold even as nativists pushed restriction, a contrast worth stating.

cards.q: Define Social Darwinism.
cards.a: Social Darwinism applied a crude version of 'survival of the fittest', Herbert Spencer's phrase, to society: competition sorted people and races by fitness, so great wealth proved merit and poverty proved unfitness. William Graham Sumner and others argued that government aid or regulation interfered with this natural process. It justified the success of those at the top as both appropriate and inevitable, and it fed racial arguments for immigration restriction.
cards.h: → core idea + who + policy conclusion + uses
cards.n: Darwin did not apply his theory to society, so crediting him misattributes it; Spencer coined 'survival of the fittest'. The KC point is justification of the elite.

cards.q: Describe how many immigrants negotiated compromises between the cultures they brought and the culture they found in the United States.
cards.a: Many kept their faith, language and customs at home and in ethnic institutions while adopting American ways in public. Catholic parishes built parochial schools that taught English and American history alongside the faith; foreign-language newspapers explained American politics; children learned English in public schools and translated for parents; and families anglicized names, joined unions and political machines, and took up American holidays and sports.
cards.h: → what was kept + what was adopted + examples
cards.n: Choosing only 'they assimilated' or 'they refused to' misses the KC's word, compromise; show something kept and something adopted.

cards.q: Explain a key difference between how Social Darwinists and settlement house reformers explained urban poverty.
cards.a: Social Darwinists blamed heredity and character: the poor were unfit, and aid only preserved weakness, so government should stay out. Settlement reformers such as Jane Addams blamed environment, meaning tenements, low wages and unsafe work, so they built services and pushed for laws to change conditions.
cards.h: → Social Darwinists: poverty = unfitness → no aid; settlement workers: poverty = environment → services + laws
cards.n: Describing each group without naming the difference in cause (heredity vs. environment) and remedy (none vs. reform) earns nothing.
o: Both assumed immigrants should adopt American ways, but Social Darwinists doubted some races could, while settlement workers believed education could make citizens of anyone.
The difference set up the Progressive Era: settlement research on tenements and child labor became evidence for regulation, rejecting laissez-faire.

w.a: Social Darwinists and settlement workers agreed that the poor deserved no help.
w.why: settlement workers built services for the poor

w.a: Settlement workers blamed immigrants' laziness, while Social Darwinists blamed factories.
w.why: reverses the two positions

cards.q: Explain why Chinese immigrants faced federal exclusion decades before restrictions targeted European immigrants.
cards.a: Race, law and economics set the Chinese apart. Naturalization law barred them as non-white, so they could not vote to defend themselves; western workers in the 1870s depression blamed Chinese labor for low wages; and both parties, in close national elections, courted western votes by promising exclusion.
cards.h: → no citizenship, no votes → western labor rivalry in the 1870s depression → both parties court votes → exclusion
cards.n: A comparison needs why the Chinese differed from Europeans, not just 'people were racist': name citizenship, labor politics and race theory.
o: European immigrants could naturalize and vote, so eastern machines courted them, while the Chinese had no electoral power.
Chinese workers were concentrated in California, where Denis Kearney's Workingmen's Party made 'The Chinese must go!' a rallying cry.

w.a: The Chinese were excluded first because they outnumbered every European group.
w.why: false; far more Europeans arrived

w.a: Europeans were never targeted because nativists liked them.
w.why: the APA and the IRL targeted Europeans

cards.q: Explain why public debates over assimilation and Americanization intensified in the 1880s and 1890s.
cards.a: The new immigrants were more numerous and visibly different: mostly Catholic, Orthodox or Jewish, non-English-speaking and crowded into cities. Haymarket, the 1890s depression and race theories drawn from Social Darwinism convinced many native-born Americans that newcomers threatened jobs and democracy.
cards.h: → scale + religious and language difference → urban crowding → Haymarket, 1890s depression → race theories → debate
cards.n: 'Americans didn't like immigrants' earns nothing; name what changed about immigration and what events turned difference into perceived threat.
o: Reformers answered the same fears differently, arguing that settlement houses and public schools could Americanize newcomers rather than exclude them.
The census report of 1890 that the frontier line had closed fed anxiety that the nation could no longer absorb newcomers as before.

w.a: Debates intensified because immigrants refused to learn any English.
w.why: overstated; many learned it, especially children

w.a: Americanization debates began only after World War I.
w.why: they were intense by the 1880s and 1890s

cards.q: Identify Carnegie's Gospel of Wealth.
cards.a: In 'Wealth' (1889), soon called 'The Gospel of Wealth', Andrew Carnegie argued that great fortunes were a natural result of competition, but that the rich were trustees for society and should give their wealth away during their lifetimes: 'The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.' He favored libraries, universities, concert halls and parks that helped people help themselves over alms he thought bred dependence.
cards.h: → author + date + core claim + what to fund
cards.n: It defends inequality as natural while demanding philanthropy; calling it a plea for government redistribution misses that it rejected state action.

cards.q: Identify the causes of the growth of a distinctive middle class in the late nineteenth century.
cards.a: Large corporations needed managers, accountants, salesmen and male and female clerical workers to run their offices; cities needed engineers, teachers, doctors and lawyers; and more high schools, colleges and professional schools trained people for these salaried white-collar jobs. Steady incomes, streetcar suburbs and growing leisure time gave the new middle class a distinctive home life, consumption and respectability (KC-6.2.I.E).
cards.h: → corporate jobs + professions + education → lifestyle
cards.n: The KC names corporations' need for managers and clerks plus access to education; 'people got richer' skips the specific cause and earns nothing.

cards.q: Describe how the growth of corporate offices opened new work to women.
cards.a: Corporate paperwork exploded, and the typewriter, marketed from 1874, created jobs as typists and stenographers that employers filled with young, educated, mostly native-born women at lower pay than men. Women also became telephone operators, department-store clerks, bookkeepers and teachers; by 1900 women held about three-quarters of stenographer and typist jobs. Office work offered respectability and some independence but rarely promotion.
cards.h: → technology + new jobs + who filled them + limits
cards.n: The share is an approximate census figure. Treating clerical work as equality misses the limits: lower pay, no promotion, pressure to quit on marriage.

cards.q: Identify how access to education expanded in the late nineteenth century.
cards.a: Public high schools multiplied, and enrollment more than doubled in the 1890s, from roughly 200,000 to 500,000; land-grant colleges under the Morrill Acts (1862, 1890) taught agriculture and engineering; research universities such as Johns Hopkins (1876) opened, along with endowed ones such as Stanford (1891) and the University of Chicago (founded 1890); and women's colleges and state universities admitted women. Schooling became the ladder into the middle class.
cards.h: → high schools + colleges + who gained access
cards.n: Enrollment figures are approximate. Black students were often shut out or segregated; the 1890 Morrill Act funded separate Black land-grant colleges.

cards.q: Identify examples of philanthropy by Gilded Age business leaders that enhanced educational opportunities and urban environments.
cards.a: Andrew Carnegie paid for public libraries, starting in the 1880s in his Scottish hometown and his Pennsylvania mill towns (more than 1,600 in the U.S. in all, most built after 1900), and for Carnegie Hall (1891). John D. Rockefeller endowed the University of Chicago (1890); Leland Stanford founded Stanford University (1891); and wealthy donors built museums and concert halls in growing cities.
cards.h: → donor + gift + what it improved
cards.n: Most Carnegie libraries came after 1900. Listing gifts without the Gospel of Wealth's idea of helping people help themselves misses the KC's link.

cards.q: Identify vaudeville as a form of Gilded Age mass entertainment.
cards.a: Vaudeville was a variety stage show of comedy, songs, dancing, acrobats and novelty acts, organized from the 1880s by managers such as Tony Pastor and B.F. Keith into 'clean' family entertainment and national theater circuits. It drew mixed working- and middle-class urban audiences who spent growing leisure time on a cheap ticket, and it dominated popular entertainment until movies displaced it.
cards.h: → what it was + who organized it + who watched
cards.n: Illustrative example of KC-6.2.I.E. Much of its comedy ran on ethnic and blackface caricature, so 'harmless fun' misses how it spread stereotypes.

cards.q: Identify Coney Island as a symbol of Gilded Age commercialized leisure.
cards.a: Coney Island, a Brooklyn beach resort, grew by the 1890s into a huge amusement district of roller coasters, sideshows, dance halls and bathing pavilions, with enclosed parks such as Steeplechase (1897). Cheap streetcar and railroad fares let working- and middle-class New Yorkers spend a day off there, making it a symbol of leisure sold as a commodity.
cards.h: → where + what it offered + who went + what it symbolized
cards.n: Illustrative. 'A beach people liked' misses the KC point: cheap transit, a little free time and commercial amusement made leisure a mass market.

cards.q: Identify the founding of professional baseball's National League in 1876.
cards.a: The National League, formed in 1876, organized professional baseball as a business: owners controlled franchises in growing cities, standardized rules and schedules, and later bound players with the reserve clause. Baseball became the leading spectator sport, spread by newspapers' new sports pages, and a color line drawn in the 1880s shut out Black players.
cards.h: → date + how organized + what it became + who was excluded
cards.n: Illustrative example of commercial leisure. Treating it as amateur sport misses the point: city spectators paying for entertainment.

cards.q: Identify the Chautauqua movement.
cards.a: The Chautauqua movement began in 1874 at Lake Chautauqua, New York, as a summer training camp for Methodist Sunday school teachers and grew into adult education for the middle class: lectures, concerts, home-study courses and, later, traveling tent circuits that brought speakers to small towns. It joined self-improvement, religion and leisure.
cards.h: → where + when + what it offered + who went
cards.n: Illustrative. Calling it a religious revival misses its broader role as education and respectable leisure for a growing middle class.

cards.q: Explain why a distinctive middle class grew in the late nineteenth century.
cards.a: Corporations and cities created salaried white-collar work for managers, clerks, salesmen, engineers and teachers. Wider schooling trained people for it, and steady salaries, streetcar suburbs and more leisure let them build a shared way of life that set them apart from both manual workers and the very rich.
cards.h: → corporate and urban growth → white-collar jobs → schooling → steady pay, suburbs, leisure → shared identity
cards.n: 'The economy grew' earns nothing; the KC names corporations' demand for managers and clerks and wider access to education as the causes.
o: Professional associations, such as the American Bar Association (1878), set standards and credentials that marked middle-class status.
Department stores and magazines taught a middle-class style of consumption, making the class as much a culture as an income.

w.a: The middle class grew because factory workers' wages rose until they became managers.
w.why: few manual workers rose; the growth came from new white-collar jobs

w.a: A middle class appeared because the government created clerical jobs.
w.why: most new jobs were in private corporations

cards.q: Explain why commercial leisure and consumer culture expanded in Gilded Age cities.
cards.a: Industrial cities concentrated millions of people with a little spare time and money. Shorter hours for some workers, rising real wages and cheap streetcar fares created a mass market that entrepreneurs filled with vaudeville, amusement parks, professional baseball and department stores.
cards.h: → dense cities + some free time + real wages up → cheap transit → mass market → vaudeville, parks, sports, stores
cards.n: Listing amusements is description; the KC's cause is growing leisure time, plus money and transit, turning leisure into something bought.
o: Mass-circulation newspapers and advertising publicized these amusements and taught readers to see leisure as something to buy.
Leisure sorted by class: the rich had resorts and opera, the middle class Chautauqua, workers the saloon, dance hall and ballpark.

w.a: Leisure expanded because factories gave workers months of paid vacation.
w.why: paid vacations were rare; the gain was shorter hours

w.a: Consumer culture spread because Americans stopped working long hours.
w.why: most still worked ten-hour days

cards.q: Explain how Carnegie's Gospel of Wealth both defended and qualified laissez-faire capitalism.
cards.a: It defended capitalism by calling concentrated wealth the natural, beneficial result of competition, so no state redistribution was needed. It qualified it by insisting fortunes were a public trust: the rich owed society libraries, schools and parks, conceding that great inequality needed a moral justification.
cards.h: → defends: wealth natural, no state role → qualifies: rich as trustees → duty to fund uplift → inequality justified
cards.n: Describing the essay alone earns little; set it against Social Darwinism: both justify inequality, but only the Gospel imposes a duty.
o: Carnegie rejected almsgiving and favored institutions that let the able rise, so his philanthropy still expressed faith in individual effort.
Critics saw the 1892 Homestead lockout as proof that his gifts came from wealth squeezed out of low wages.

w.a: The Gospel of Wealth argued that government should tax the rich to aid the poor.
w.why: Carnegie opposed state redistribution

w.a: Carnegie said the rich should keep everything they earned.
w.why: closer to Social Darwinism; he demanded giving

cards.q: Contrast Social Darwinism with the Gospel of Wealth and the Social Gospel.
cards.a: All three answered industrial inequality but reached opposite conclusions. Social Darwinism (Spencer, Sumner) held that the poor were unfit and that aid or regulation defied natural law. The Gospel of Wealth (Carnegie) accepted inequality but obliged the rich to fund libraries and schools for self-help. The Social Gospel (Gladden, Rauschenbusch) held that Christianity required reforming the social conditions that caused poverty.
cards.h: → each view of poverty + remedy, then the dividing line
cards.n: Three definitions side by side earn little; state the split: the first two justify inequality, and only the Social Gospel attacks its causes.

cards.q: Identify Walter Rauschenbusch and the Social Gospel movement.
cards.a: Walter Rauschenbusch, a Baptist minister who served a German immigrant congregation in New York's Hell's Kitchen from 1886, became the leading theologian of the Social Gospel, which held that Christians must fight the social sins of slums, child labor and unsafe work, not only save individual souls. Washington Gladden preached the same message from the 1880s; Rauschenbusch's Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907) made it famous and fed Progressive reform.
cards.h: → who + setting + core idea + influence
cards.n: Borrows from u7 for the 1907 book. Confusing the Social Gospel with the Gospel of Wealth is the classic trap: one reforms society, the other justifies fortunes.

cards.q: Identify the Woman's Christian Temperance Union and Frances Willard's 'Do Everything' policy.
cards.a: The Woman's Christian Temperance Union, founded in 1874, became the largest women's organization of the era. Under Frances Willard, its president from 1879, it adopted a 'Do Everything' policy that linked temperance to woman suffrage (a 'home protection' ballot), kindergartens, labor and prison reform and public health, drawing churchgoing middle-class women into public life.
cards.h: → founding + leader + policy + significance
cards.n: Calling it only an anti-alcohol group misses the KC point: voluntary organizations became women's route into reform and suffrage politics.

cards.q: Date the founding of the WCTU and the merger that created the National American Woman Suffrage Association.
cards.a: WCTU founded 1874; the National and American woman suffrage associations, split since 1869, merged in 1890 to form the National American Woman Suffrage Association. By then the temperance union, under Willard, was far larger than the suffrage movement and was itself endorsing votes for women.
cards.h: → two years + what links them
cards.n: Dating NAWSA to the 1848 Seneca Falls convention, or to 1869, the year of the split, is the common slip.

cards.q: Identify the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA) and its founding year.
cards.a: The National American Woman Suffrage Association formed in 1890 when Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony's National association merged with Lucy Stone's American association, ending the split of 1869. Led by Stanton, then Anthony, it pursued suffrage state by state and through a federal amendment; western states such as Wyoming (1890) and Colorado (1893) granted the vote, and under Carrie Chapman Catt it later won the Nineteenth Amendment (1920).
cards.h: → year + merger + strategy + later result
cards.n: Borrows from u7 for 1920. Crediting NAWSA with national suffrage in the 1890s is wrong; only a few western states had it by 1898.

cards.q: Identify Susan B. Anthony's 1872 arrest for voting.
cards.a: In November 1872 Susan B. Anthony and more than a dozen other women voted in Rochester, New York, claiming that the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of citizenship included the vote. She was arrested, and at her 1873 trial the judge directed a guilty verdict and fined her 100 dollars, which she refused to pay. In Minor v. Happersett (1875) the Supreme Court ruled that citizenship did not carry a right to vote.
cards.h: → what she did + legal claim + outcome + Court ruling
cards.n: Borrows from u5 (1872-1875). Her claim rested on the 14th Amendment, not the 15th, which bars only racial discrimination in voting.

cards.q: Identify Dwight L. Moody and his urban revival campaigns.
cards.a: Dwight L. Moody, a Chicago shoe salesman turned evangelist, led huge revival campaigns in American and British cities from the 1870s to the 1890s with the singer Ira Sankey, using businesslike organization, advertising and simple gospel hymns. He preached individual conversion rather than social reform, and he founded the Chicago training school that became the Moody Bible Institute (1886).
cards.h: → who + method + message + legacy
cards.n: Illustrative. Moody buttressed the social order; filing him with the Social Gospel misses that he stressed personal salvation, not social change.

cards.q: Identify Nellie Bly and her stunt journalism.
cards.a: Elizabeth Cochrane, writing as Nellie Bly for Joseph Pulitzer's New York World, feigned insanity to enter the women's asylum on Blackwell's Island and exposed its cruelty in 'Ten Days in a Mad-House' (1887), which helped win more funding for the city's asylums. In 1889-1890 she circled the globe in 72 days. Her stunt journalism opened reporting careers to women and anticipated muckraking.
cards.h: → who + employer + exposé + effect
cards.n: Illustrative. The exposé, not the race around the world, ties her to KC-6.3.II.B.ii: a woman using journalism to promote reform.

cards.q: Identify Henry George's Progress and Poverty (1879) and its proposed remedy.
cards.a: Henry George's Progress and Poverty (1879) asked why poverty deepened as wealth grew and blamed private ownership of land: landowners pocketed rising land values that society, not they, created. His remedy was a 'single tax' on the unearned value of land, replacing other taxes. The book became one of the era's best sellers, and George ran second in New York City's 1886 mayoral race on a labor ticket, ahead of Theodore Roosevelt.
cards.h: → author + question + diagnosis + single tax
cards.n: George was not a socialist: he would tax land values, not abolish private capital. Calling his single tax an income tax is the classic slip.

cards.q: Identify Edward Bellamy's Looking Backward (1888) and the movement it inspired.
cards.a: In Edward Bellamy's utopian novel Looking Backward: 2000-1887 (1888), a Bostonian falls asleep in 1887 and wakes in 2000 to find competition replaced by a cooperative society: the nation owns all industry, every citizen serves in an industrial army and receives an equal share, and poverty and class conflict are gone. It became one of the century's best-selling novels and inspired 'Nationalist' clubs across the country.
cards.h: → author + plot device + vision + following
cards.n: Utopian fiction, not a program: treating it as a Populist or AFL platform is the slip, though many Nationalists later joined the Populists.

cards.q: Identify the socialist movement in Gilded Age America.
cards.a: Socialists, many of them German and Jewish immigrants, argued that capitalism itself caused exploitation and that workers should collectively own the means of production. The Socialist Labor Party (so named from 1877), led in the 1890s by Daniel De Leon, ran candidates and tried to win over unions; Eugene Debs turned to socialism after his 1895 imprisonment and helped found the Socialist Party (1901). Socialists stayed a small minority in this period.
cards.h: → claim + party + leaders + influence
cards.n: Borrows from u7 (Socialist Party, 1901). Lumping socialists with Populists misses the difference: Populists wanted to regulate capitalism, socialists to replace it.

cards.q: Describe how women sought greater equality through education and voluntary organizations in the late nineteenth century.
cards.a: Women's colleges such as Vassar (opened 1865), Smith and Wellesley (1875) and Bryn Mawr (1885), and coeducational state universities, admitted growing numbers of women, who made up about a third of college students by 1900. Women's clubs, linked nationally in the General Federation of Women's Clubs (1890) and, for Black women, the National Association of Colored Women (1896), moved from study to civic reform: libraries, schools, sanitation and child welfare.
cards.h: → colleges + clubs + what they did
cards.n: The college share is approximate. Calling women's clubs social teas misses how the KC ties education and clubs to reform and public life.

cards.q: Explain why the Social Gospel movement arose in the late nineteenth century.
cards.a: Protestant ministers in industrial cities saw slums, child labor and violent strikes their churches were not reaching. Concluding that poverty came from social conditions, not only personal sin, they preached that Christianity required reforming wages, housing and work.
cards.h: → urban poverty + labor strife → churches losing workers → poverty seen as social → Christianity demands reform
cards.n: 'Religious people wanted to help the poor' is too thin; name what in industrial cities pushed ministers from individual to social salvation.
o: The Social Gospel rejected Social Darwinism's claim that poverty proved unfitness, offering a Christian alternative to both laissez-faire and socialism.
Ministers such as Rauschenbusch lived among immigrant workers in Hell's Kitchen, so direct experience shaped their theology.

w.a: The Social Gospel arose because churches wanted to justify industrialists' wealth.
w.why: that describes the Gospel of Wealth

w.a: It began because the government required churches to run welfare programs.
w.why: no such requirement existed

cards.q: Explain why many middle-class women joined voluntary reform organizations in the late nineteenth century.
cards.a: More women had schooling, smaller families and some leisure, yet were barred from voting and most professions. Organizations such as the WCTU and women's clubs let them act in public by claiming to protect homes and children, so civic housekeeping became a route into politics and suffrage.
cards.h: → education + leisure → shut out of the vote and professions → home-protection claim → clubs, WCTU → politics, suffrage
cards.n: 'They were bored' earns nothing; name why women's energy took the voluntary form: exclusion from formal politics plus the language of domesticity.
o: Industrial cities made alcohol, tenements and child labor visible problems that seemed to threaten families directly.
Black women formed their own clubs, joined in the National Association of Colored Women (1896), because white groups excluded them and lynching and segregation demanded a response.

w.a: Women joined reform groups to use the vote they already had.
w.why: most women could not vote before 1920

w.a: Women's organizations formed mainly to oppose woman suffrage.
w.why: most, like the WCTU, came to support it

cards.q: Explain how the form of Edward Bellamy's Looking Backward (1888) both limits and strengthens its use as evidence about Gilded Age society.
cards.a: As a utopian novel set in an imagined year 2000, it cannot show how Americans actually lived or what policy was adopted. But its critique of competition, and its huge sales, show what troubled many middle-class readers in 1888: class conflict, waste and insecurity.
cards.h: → purpose: fiction imagining the future → no proof of conditions → but reveals anxieties + sales show reach
cards.n: 'It is fiction, so it is useless' earns nothing; a sourcing answer explains what the form limits and what it can still show.
o: Its audience matters: Bellamy wrote for middle-class readers frightened by strikes, so his orderly, peaceful socialism reflects their fear of revolution.
The Nationalist clubs it inspired give historians firmer evidence of its influence than the novel's own claims.

w.a: Looking Backward is reliable because it describes America in 2000.
w.why: that future is imagined

w.a: The novel is useless because Bellamy was not a historian.
w.why: misses what it shows about 1888 anxieties

cards.q: Define laissez-faire and explain how consistently it was practiced.
cards.a: Laissez-faire was the doctrine that government should leave the economy to competition and markets, neither regulating business nor aiding the poor. It was practiced selectively: Washington refused relief and resisted regulation, but it subsidized railroads with land grants, protected manufacturers with high tariffs, kept the gold standard creditors wanted, and used troops and injunctions against strikes.
cards.h: → definition + where it held + where it was ignored
cards.n: Calling the Gilded Age a time of no government role earns less; the strongest answers show intervention on business's behalf.

cards.q: Identify the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 and its early record.
cards.a: The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) outlawed every contract, combination or conspiracy 'in restraint of trade' in interstate commerce, but vague terms and weak enforcement made it nearly useless against business in the 1890s. In United States v. E.C. Knight Co. (1895) the Supreme Court ruled that a sugar trust controlling most U.S. refining was engaged in manufacturing, not commerce, and so beyond the law's reach. Courts applied it more readily against unions.
cards.h: → what it banned + weakness + E.C. Knight + use on labor
cards.n: 'It broke up the trusts' is wrong for this period; serious trust-busting came under Theodore Roosevelt after 1901.

cards.q: Identify the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887.
cards.a: The Interstate Commerce Act (1887), passed after farmer and shipper protests and after Wabash v. Illinois (1886) barred states from regulating interstate rates, required railroad rates to be 'reasonable and just', banned rebates, pools and higher charges for short hauls than long ones, and created the Interstate Commerce Commission, the first federal regulatory agency. The ICC could not set rates, and courts overturned most of its early rulings.
cards.h: → causes + what it required + ICC + weakness
cards.n: Its significance is precedent, not results: calling it effective regulation overstates it, but calling it meaningless misses the new federal role.

cards.q: Contrast the holdings of Munn v. Illinois and Wabash v. Illinois.
cards.a: Munn v. Illinois (1877) upheld an Illinois Granger law setting grain-elevator rates, ruling that private property 'affected with a public interest' may be regulated by the state. Wabash v. Illinois (1886) struck down an Illinois law regulating rates on an interstate railroad route, holding that only Congress may regulate interstate commerce. The shift moved regulation from the states to Washington and led directly to the Interstate Commerce Act.
cards.h: → each holding + the shift + consequence
cards.n: The contrast is about which government may regulate, not whether any may; saying Wabash banned all regulation misreads it.

cards.q: Identify In re Debs (1895) and its significance for organized labor.
cards.a: In re Debs (1895) unanimously upheld the federal injunction against the Pullman boycott and Eugene Debs's six-month jail sentence for contempt. The Court ruled that the national government could go to court to remove obstructions to interstate commerce and the mail, resting on those powers rather than the Sherman Act. It made the injunction employers' chief legal weapon against strikes until the Norris-LaGuardia Act of 1932.
cards.h: → case + holding + legal basis + long-term effect
cards.n: The Court relied on commerce and postal power, not the Sherman Act (the lower court cited both); either way it put government on employers' side.

cards.q: Identify the Panic of 1893.
cards.a: The Panic of 1893, set off by the failure of overbuilt, overborrowed railroads, a drain on the Treasury's gold and bank collapses, began the worst depression to that time: about 15,000 businesses and hundreds of banks failed, and unemployment reached perhaps 12 to 18 percent. President Cleveland defended the gold standard, won repeal of the Sherman Silver Purchase Act and refused federal relief, splitting his Democrats and feeding the free-silver revolt of 1896.
cards.h: → causes + scale + government response + political effect
cards.n: Unemployment figures are estimates. The KC point is that policymakers opposed intervention in a downturn; describing only the crash misses it.

cards.q: Identify Coxey's Army.
cards.a: In 1894 Ohio businessman Jacob Coxey led several hundred unemployed men, 'Coxey's Army', on a march to Washington to demand that the federal government create jobs through public works such as road building, financed with 500 million dollars in paper money. Coxey was arrested for walking on the Capitol grounds, and the march dispersed without result. It was an early national protest asking Washington to fight unemployment.
cards.h: → who + when + demand + outcome + significance
cards.n: Its significance is the demand for federal jobs relief, rejected under laissez-faire; calling it a strike or a riot misreads a peaceful petition.

cards.q: Contrast Coxey's Army with the Pullman Strike as responses to the depression of the 1890s.
cards.a: Coxey's Army was a peaceful, symbolic march that petitioned Congress for federal public-works jobs; the Pullman Strike was a mass work stoppage and boycott that halted rail traffic to force a private employer to restore wages. The government answered Coxey with arrests for trespass and Pullman with an injunction and troops. Both showed the depression driving workers to seek national remedies, and both failed in the short run.
cards.h: → method vs. method + target vs. target + response
cards.n: Listing both events without the differences in method (petition vs. strike) and target (Congress vs. employer) is not a contrast.

cards.q: Contrast the Greenback Party's currency demands with the postwar push to resume specie payments.
cards.a: Greenbackers, organized as the Greenback Party from the mid-1870s, wanted the government to keep and expand the paper greenbacks issued during the Civil War, inflating prices to ease the debts of farmers and workers. Hard-money advocates, backed by bankers and creditors, won the Specie Resumption Act (1875), which made greenbacks redeemable in gold from 1879 and held down the money supply. The fight over inflation then moved to silver.
cards.h: → Greenbackers' aim + resumption's aim + who benefited
cards.n: Borrows from u5 (Civil War greenbacks). Leaving out who gained (debtors from inflation, creditors from sound money) turns a contrast into two definitions.

cards.q: Identify Alfred Thayer Mahan's argument in The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890).
cards.a: Naval officer Alfred Thayer Mahan argued that great nations rose through sea power: a large battleship navy to protect foreign trade, overseas coaling stations and bases, and a canal across Central America. Widely read by policymakers such as Theodore Roosevelt and Henry Cabot Lodge, the book reinforced the naval buildup begun under the Naval Act of 1890 and the push for Hawaii and other Pacific bases.
cards.h: → author + claim + what it called for + influence
cards.n: Mahan argued for trade and naval power, not mass colonization; calling it a plan to settle Asia misses the markets-and-bases logic of KC-6.1.I.E.ii.

cards.q: Identify how each step extended U.S. influence over markets or resources abroad: purchase of Alaska · annexation of Midway · reciprocity treaty with Hawaii · Pearl Harbor naval rights · first Pan-American Conference · Naval Act of 1890 · overthrow of Queen Liliuokalani · Venezuela boundary crisis · annexation of Hawaii
cards.a:
Purchase of Alaska (1867) → Seward's 7.2-million-dollar deal: fish, furs, later gold, and a North Pacific foothold
Midway (1867) → Pacific islands claimed as a coaling stop on the route to Asia
Hawaii reciprocity (1875) → duty-free Hawaiian sugar ties the islands' economy to American planters and the U.S. market
Pearl Harbor rights (1887) → the treaty's renewal grants a U.S. naval station
Pan-American Conference (1889) → Secretary of State Blaine courts Latin American trade and arbitration
Naval Act (1890) → first modern battleships to protect commerce
Overthrow of Liliuokalani (1893) → American planters, aided by U.S. marines, depose the queen; Cleveland refuses annexation
Venezuela crisis (1895) → Secretary of State Olney invokes the Monroe Doctrine against Britain, claiming U.S. primacy in the hemisphere
Annexation of Hawaii (1898) → a joint resolution makes the islands U.S. territory during the war with Spain
cards.h: → step + year + what it gained
cards.n: Several steps are illustrative. The KC stresses markets and resources; listing dates without the economic or strategic gain misses the point.

cards.q: Explain how the Sherman Antitrust Act was turned against labor unions.
cards.a: The act banned combinations 'in restraint of trade', and judges read strikes and boycotts that stopped interstate shipments as exactly that. Courts cited it to enjoin strikes, notably the 1894 Pullman boycott, while E.C. Knight (1895) shielded manufacturing trusts, so a law aimed at monopoly hit unions hardest.
cards.h: → vague 'restraint of trade' → strikes read as conspiracies → injunctions (Pullman) → trusts shielded (E.C. Knight)
cards.n: In re Debs itself rested on commerce and postal power, not the Sherman Act; cite the lower-court injunction, or later cases, for the Sherman link.
o: The irony reflects the courts' laissez-faire outlook: judges treated unions as illegitimate combinations but corporations as property to protect.
In Loewe v. Lawlor (1908) the Court held a union boycott liable under the act, which is why labor sought an exemption in the Clayton Act (1914).

w.a: The Sherman Act was written to outlaw labor unions.
w.why: it targeted trusts; courts turned it on unions

w.a: Unions were prosecuted under the act because they formed holding companies.
w.why: confuses unions with corporate forms

cards.q: Explain the extent to which the federal government's role in the economy changed from 1865 to 1898.
cards.a: It changed only modestly. Washington kept promoting business through tariffs, land grants and the gold standard and refused relief in depressions, but the Interstate Commerce Act (1887) and Sherman Act (1890) set the principle of federal regulation, even though courts and weak enforcement blunted both.
cards.h: → continuity: promote business, no relief → change: ICA and Sherman set a precedent → blunted by courts → modest change
cards.n: An extent answer must weigh both; 'the government did nothing' ignores subsidies and the new laws, and 'it regulated business' overstates them.
o: Troops and injunctions against strikes show the government intervening, but on business's side, a continuity beneath the laissez-faire rhetoric.
The ICC became the model for the stronger regulation of the Progressive Era, so the change mattered more later than at the time.

w.a: The government's role did not change, since laissez-faire meant Congress passed no economic laws.
w.why: ignores the ICA and the Sherman Act

w.a: By 1898 the federal government closely regulated all large businesses.
w.why: overstated; enforcement was weak

cards.q: Explain why President Cleveland and many other policymakers opposed federal relief during the depression of the 1890s.
cards.a: They held laissez-faire views: depressions corrected themselves, and federal aid would waste money, weaken self-reliance and exceed the Constitution's limits on national power. Defending the gold standard to restore business confidence mattered more to them than jobs programs such as Coxey's.
cards.h: → laissez-faire → depressions self-correct → aid breeds dependence, exceeds federal power → protect gold, not jobs
cards.n: 'Cleveland did not care about the poor' earns nothing; the KC wants the argument opponents of intervention made: long-run growth through competition.
o: Cleveland had vetoed a small seed-relief bill for drought-stricken Texas farmers in 1887, saying the people should support the government, not the government the people.
Bankers and business leaders, including the Democrats' pro-gold wing, saw inflation or federal spending as a threat to property and credit.

w.a: Cleveland opposed relief because the Treasury had no money at all.
w.why: the issue was principle and the gold reserve

w.a: Policymakers saw no need for relief because unemployment stayed low.
w.why: unemployment was severe

cards.q: Explain why U.S. policymakers increasingly looked outside U.S. borders for markets and influence in the late 1880s and 1890s.
cards.a: Industrial output outgrew the home market, and the depression of the 1890s made foreign markets seem vital. Mahan's sea-power arguments, the 1890 census report that the frontier had closed and rivalry with European empires carving up Africa and Asia persuaded leaders to build a navy and seek bases.
cards.h: → surplus output + 1890s depression → need markets → Mahan, closed frontier, European rivals → navy, bases, influence
cards.n: Jumping straight to the 1898 war skips the KC's point that the push for markets and bases began earlier, as policy, in the 1880s and 1890s.
o: Ideas of Anglo-Saxon superiority, drawn from Social Darwinism, framed expansion as a racial mission.
American planters in Hawaii and investors in Cuba pressed Washington to protect their property, linking private interests to policy.

w.a: Policymakers looked abroad because the Constitution required colonies.
w.why: invented requirement

w.a: Expansion began because the U.S. had no manufactured goods to sell.
w.why: reversed; it had a surplus

cards.q: Identify political machines and Tammany Hall.
cards.a: Political machines were urban party organizations run by bosses that traded jobs, food, coal and help with naturalization, police and landlords for the votes of immigrants and the poor, paid for with graft from city contracts and franchises. New York's Tammany Hall, the Democratic machine, reached its most notorious form under William 'Boss' Tweed, whose ring stole tens of millions of dollars through padded contracts before his conviction in 1873.
cards.h: → what machines did + how funded + Tammany + Tweed
cards.n: Tweed's theft totals are estimates. The KC point is services for votes where access to power was unequal; 'corrupt politicians' alone misses it.

cards.q: Identify the Pendleton Civil Service Act.
cards.a: The Pendleton Civil Service Act (1883), passed after President James Garfield was assassinated in 1881 by a disappointed office seeker, created a bipartisan Civil Service Commission and required competitive exams for a share of federal jobs, at first about a tenth, which presidents could expand. It began replacing the spoils system with merit hiring and, by banning forced contributions from officeholders, pushed parties toward business donors.
cards.h: → year + trigger + what it required + effect
cards.n: It covered only a minority of jobs at first, so 'it ended patronage' overstates it. The KC names reformers' charge that self-interest corrupted government.

cards.q: Identify the Populist Party and the Omaha Platform.
cards.a: The People's (Populist) Party, formed by Farmers' Alliance leaders and labor allies, adopted the Omaha Platform in 1892. It demanded free and unlimited coinage of silver at 16 to 1, a graduated income tax, government ownership of railroads, telegraph and telephone, the subtreasury plan for farm credit and postal savings banks, and it endorsed the secret ballot, direct election of senators and shorter hours. Its candidate, James Weaver, won over a million votes.
cards.h: → founding + platform planks + 1892 result
cards.n: The KC point is a stronger government role in the economy; listing planks without that theme misses it. Several planks became law in the Progressive Era.

cards.q: Define free silver and explain who wanted it.
cards.a: Free silver was the demand that the government coin all silver brought to the mint at a ratio of 16 ounces of silver to 1 of gold, expanding the money supply and ending deflation. Indebted farmers of the South and West wanted the inflation to raise crop prices and ease debts, and western silver miners wanted a market; bankers, creditors and eastern business defended the gold standard as sound money.
cards.h: → definition + who wanted it + who opposed and why
cards.n: By the 1890s silver was worth far less than 1/16 of gold on the market, which is why creditors opposed it; 'more coins for everyone' misses inflation.

cards.q: Identify William Jennings Bryan and the Cross of Gold speech.
cards.a: William Jennings Bryan, a 36-year-old former Nebraska congressman, electrified the 1896 Democratic convention by defending free silver and farmers against eastern finance: 'You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold.' The speech won him the Democratic nomination, and the Populists nominated him too, with their own vice-presidential candidate, Tom Watson.
cards.h: → who + speech + key line + result
cards.n: Bryan was a Democrat whom the Populists endorsed, not a Populist nominee first; the speech is about currency, not religion or tariffs.

cards.q: Identify the outcome of the election of 1896.
cards.a: Republican William McKinley defeated Bryan, 271 electoral votes to 176 and about 51 to 47 percent of the popular vote. Backed by Mark Hanna's record fund-raising from business, McKinley campaigned from his front porch for the gold standard, protective tariffs and prosperity for workers, and carried the industrial Northeast and Midwest; Bryan carried the South and most of the West.
cards.h: → winner + margin + campaign + regional pattern
cards.n: Bryan's appeal to farmers did not reach urban immigrant workers, many of whom feared that inflation would cut real wages; that is the key to the result.

cards.q: Explain the significance of the election of 1896.
cards.a: The 1896 election ended two decades of partisan stalemate and began a generation of Republican dominance. It settled the currency question for gold (the Gold Standard Act followed in 1900), broke the Populists as an independent party after fusion, and redrew politics along urban-industrial versus rural lines rather than purely Civil War sectional ones. Hanna's organization and spending made it the first modern campaign.
cards.h: → claim + three consequences
cards.n: 'McKinley won' is an outcome, not significance; the point needs what changed after 1896: realignment, gold, and the end of Populism.

cards.q: Define 'waving the bloody shirt' as a Gilded Age political tactic.
cards.a: Waving the bloody shirt was the Republican tactic of reminding northern voters that Democrats had been the party of secession and rebellion, blaming them for Civil War deaths to win elections long after 1865. Together with Union veterans' pensions and the Grand Army of the Republic, it kept northern voters loyal through memory rather than current economic issues.
cards.h: → what it was + who used it + effect
cards.n: It was a Republican tactic against Democrats, not the reverse, and it appealed to the Civil War divisions the KC names, not to economic policy.

cards.q: Identify the Ocala Demands of 1890.
cards.a: The Ocala Demands, adopted by the Southern Farmers' Alliance and its allies at Ocala, Florida, in December 1890, called for the subtreasury plan (federal warehouses lending farmers money against stored crops), free coinage of silver, a graduated income tax, direct election of senators, and strict regulation or, failing that, government ownership of railroads. They became the core of the Populists' Omaha Platform (1892).
cards.h: → who + when + demands + what followed
cards.n: The subtreasury plan never passed, but the income tax and direct election of senators became the 16th and 17th Amendments (1913), a Period 7 link.

cards.q: Identify the positions of the Republican and Democratic parties on the tariff and on currency in the Gilded Age.
cards.a: Tariff: Republicans championed high protective tariffs to shelter industry and wages, peaking in the McKinley Tariff (1890); Democrats, led by Cleveland, called for lower rates to cut consumer prices and the Treasury surplus, winning only a modest cut in the Wilson-Gorman Tariff (1894). Currency: Republicans stood for gold; Democrats split between Cleveland's gold wing and southern and western silverites until Bryan's nomination in 1896.
cards.h: → each party on tariffs + each on money
cards.n: Treating Democrats as free-silver throughout is the slip: Cleveland's wing defended gold until 1896. The KC names tariffs and currency as the main fights.

cards.q: Explain why political machines were so durable despite their corruption.
cards.a: Machines traded services for votes when no government agency or charity did the job: jobs on city payrolls, coal and food in hard times, help with naturalization, police and courts. Immigrants and the poor, shut out elsewhere, rewarded that personal help with loyal votes, so graft went on because the exchange worked.
cards.h: → unmet needs of immigrants and poor → machine supplies jobs, relief, favors → votes in return → graft tolerated
cards.n: 'Voters were bribed' or 'voters were ignorant' misses the KC: machines thrived by providing social services where access to power was unequal.
o: Rapid urban growth fed the machines: contracts for streets, sewers and streetcar franchises supplied the graft that paid for their favors.
Ward bosses spoke immigrants' languages and came to their weddings and funerals, while reformers were often native-born elites who looked down on them.

w.a: Machines lasted because elections were not held in Gilded Age cities.
w.why: elections were held; machines won them

w.a: Machines survived because no one ever exposed their corruption.
w.why: Nast and others exposed Tweed, yet machines endured

cards.q: Explain why Gilded Age national politics accomplished so little.
cards.a: Power was too evenly split to act. Presidential elections were decided by tiny margins, control of Congress was usually divided, and voters were held by Civil War memory, religion and ethnicity more than policy. Both parties largely shared laissez-faire assumptions, so they fought mostly over tariffs and patronage.
cards.h: → close elections + divided Congress → no mandate → war-memory, ethnic loyalty → shared laissez-faire → little action
cards.n: 'Presidents were weak and lazy' earns nothing; name the structural causes: partisan balance, identity-based loyalty and shared laissez-faire.
o: Turnout often near 80 percent outside the South (an estimate) shows voters cared; the stalemate came from balance, not apathy.
The vacuum at the national level is why reform appeared first in states, cities and third parties such as the Populists.

w.a: National politics accomplished little because few Americans bothered to vote.
w.why: turnout was very high

w.a: Congress passed no laws at all between 1877 and 1898.
w.why: it passed the Pendleton, Interstate Commerce and Sherman Acts

cards.q: Explain why the Populist Party's 1896 fusion with the Democrats ultimately destroyed the party.
cards.a: Fusion traded independence for a chance to win. Endorsing Bryan narrowed Populism to free silver, the Democrats' issue, and dropped demands such as railroad ownership. When Bryan lost, Populist voters had already learned to vote Democratic, and the party had no separate program or base left.
cards.h: → endorse Bryan → program narrowed to silver → identity merged with Democrats → Bryan loses → nothing distinct left
cards.n: 'The Populists lost the election' is not enough; explain why fusion itself, not just defeat, dissolved the party's identity and base.
o: In the South, fusion meant allying with the party of white supremacy that had fought Populism with fraud, splitting biracial Populist coalitions.
Rising farm prices after 1897, helped by new gold discoveries, eased the distress that had fed the movement.

w.a: Fusion destroyed the party because Bryan was a Republican.
w.why: Bryan was the Democratic nominee

w.a: The Populists disappeared because they won in 1896 and had nothing left to do.
w.why: they lost in 1896

cards.q: Explain one similarity and one difference between the Republican and Democratic parties during the Gilded Age.
cards.a: Similarity: both largely accepted laissez-faire and courted business, living on patronage and Civil War loyalties. Difference: Republicans backed high protective tariffs and drew Union veterans, northern Protestants and Black voters; Democrats wanted lower tariffs and drew the white South and urban Catholics.
cards.h: → similarity: laissez-faire, business ties, patronage → difference: tariffs + voter bases
cards.n: LO 6.K asks for both. Listing each party's traits without naming the similarity and the difference outright earns nothing.
o: Both parties split internally over currency, with gold Democrats such as Cleveland against southern and western silverites until 1896.
Both relied on machines and patronage until civil service reform, which reformers such as the Mugwumps blamed for corruption in each.

w.a: The parties differed because Democrats wanted to regulate business and Republicans did not.
w.why: neither party pursued much regulation

w.a: The two parties were identical in every way.
w.why: ignores tariffs and their different voter bases

cards.q: Explain how the McKinley Tariff (1890), the Sherman Silver Purchase Act (1890) and Cleveland's 1887 message against high tariffs modify the claim that Gilded Age parties ignored economic issues.
cards.a: They show the parties fought hard over economic policy, just not over regulating industry. Cleveland made tariff reduction his cause, Republicans answered with the record-high McKinley Tariff, and silver purchases were a bargain with inflationists, so tariffs and currency were the central partisan issues.
cards.h: → claim: no economic issues → tariffs and currency central → yet little regulation → claim modified, not refuted
cards.n: Refuting the claim outright overreaches; the evidence modifies it: parties fought over tariffs and money while avoiding regulation of business.
o: The evidence matches the KC's wording that the parties 'contended over tariffs and currency issues', economic questions of the first rank.
Western senators' support for the McKinley Tariff was widely linked to passage of the silver purchase act, showing economic bargaining drove Congress.

w.a: These laws prove the parties had no differences on economic issues.
w.why: the tariff fight shows sharp differences

w.a: The evidence shows Gilded Age parties built a welfare state.
w.why: anachronistic; no welfare programs

cards.q: Identify Frederick Jackson Turner's Frontier Thesis.
cards.a: In 'The Significance of the Frontier in American History' (1893), historian Frederick Jackson Turner argued that the frontier of free land had shaped American democracy, individualism and self-reliance, and that the 1890 census's report that no continuous frontier line remained marked the end of the first period of American history. The thesis voiced anxieties about what would replace the frontier, later tied to overseas expansion.
cards.h: → author + date + claim + significance
cards.n: Turner's thesis is an interpretation, not a fact: 'the frontier closed in 1890' is the census's claim, and the land was never empty of Native nations.

cards.q: Differentiate Populism from the Progressivism that followed it.
cards.a: Populism (1890s) was mainly a movement of indebted southern and western farmers with some labor allies, demanding inflation through silver, government ownership of railroads and farm credit, through a third party.
