cards.n: Traditional, revisionist, and post-revisionist interpretations argue over blame; the exam wants mutual misperception plus real conflicts of interest.

cards.q: Explain NSC-68 and how it changed containment.
cards.a: The 1950 National Security Council report, written after the Soviet atomic test and the communist victory in China, portrayed a global struggle and called for a massive permanent military buildup and a quadrupled defense budget. Korea provided the justification to implement it.
cards.h: → document + policy shift
cards.n: It converts Kennan's selective, largely political containment into militarized, global containment.

cards.q: Explain the significance of the Berlin blockade and airlift.
cards.a: When Stalin cut off ground access to West Berlin in 1948, Truman refused to withdraw or force the issue and instead supplied the city by air for eleven months. The USSR backed down, Germany was permanently divided into two states, and NATO was created the next year.
cards.h: → event + consequences
cards.n: It showed containment could work without war and made West Berlin a symbol reused through the 1961 Wall.

cards.q: Explain why the Second Red Scare gained such force after 1949.
cards.a: The fall of China, the Soviet atomic bomb, the Hiss and Rosenberg spy cases, and the Korean War made subversion look plausible. Truman's own loyalty program legitimized the hunt, and politicians found accusations electorally profitable. It collapsed once McCarthy attacked the Army on live television.
cards.h: → causes + how it ended
cards.n: Compare with the First Red Scare of 1919-1920: fear of foreign ideology plus domestic political payoff.

cards.q: Explain the significance of Sputnik (1957) for U.S. policy.
cards.a: The first Soviet satellite implied missiles that could reach America and shattered assumptions of U.S. technological superiority. Congress responded with NASA (1958) and the National Defense Education Act, funding science, math, and foreign language instruction; talk of a missile gap shaped the 1960 election.
cards.h: → event + policy responses
cards.n: Neat example of Cold War competition reshaping domestic institutions, especially schools.

cards.q: Explain why the United States escalated its involvement in Vietnam.
cards.a: Containment logic and the domino theory held that losing Vietnam would topple Southeast Asia; leaders feared looking weak after China and Korea; commitments piled up from Truman's aid to France through Kennedy's buildup; and the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution let Johnson escalate without a declaration of war.
cards.h: → causes + mechanism
cards.n: Emphasize incrementalism: no single decision, but a chain each president found harder to reverse.

cards.q: Explain why the Tet Offensive was a turning point despite being a military failure for the communists.
cards.a: It contradicted official assurances that the enemy was nearly beaten, widening the credibility gap. Walter Cronkite declared the war a stalemate, Johnson's approval fell, he halted bombing and withdrew from the 1968 race, and majority opinion turned against the war.
cards.h: → contrast + consequences
cards.n: Media and public opinion as a factor of war: the classic causation prompt for Period 8.

cards.q: Explain the significance of Brown v. Board of Education and the limits of its enforcement.
cards.a: Brown destroyed the legal foundation of Jim Crow. But Brown II's all deliberate speed invited delay: Southern officials signed the Southern Manifesto and closed schools, Eisenhower had to send troops to Little Rock in 1957, and most Southern Black students remained in segregated schools a decade later.
cards.h: → significance + limits
cards.n: Court victories need executive enforcement and mass pressure; that argument organizes many civil rights essays.

cards.q: Explain why nonviolent direct action was effective from 1955 to 1965.
cards.a: Boycotts imposed economic costs, and disciplined nonviolence in the face of dogs, hoses, and beatings created televised images that shocked national opinion, isolated segregationists, and generated pressure on presidents and Congress to act. It also claimed moral and religious authority that opponents could not match.
cards.h: → mechanism + outcome
cards.n: The tactic depended on television and on federal willingness to intervene; it worked poorly against Northern de facto segregation.

cards.q: Explain why the civil rights movement fragmented after 1965.
cards.a: Once legal segregation and voting barriers fell, the remaining problems were economic and structural: poverty and Northern housing and school segregation, which laws did not reach. Younger activists rejected nonviolence, urban uprisings frightened white allies, Vietnam split the coalition, and King was killed in 1968.
cards.h: → causes of fragmentation
cards.n: Change over time: from legal equality to economic justice, a far harder goal with far less white support.

cards.q: Explain the causes of 1970s stagflation.
cards.a: Deficit spending on Vietnam and the Great Society without tax increases fed inflation; the 1971 abandonment of the gold standard weakened the dollar; the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks raised prices across the economy; and rising foreign competition plus deindustrialization slowed growth and cut manufacturing jobs.
cards.h: → causes listed
cards.n: Stagflation discredited Great Society liberalism and opened the door to supply-side conservatism.

cards.q: Explain the significance of Watergate for American politics.
cards.a: It forced the first presidential resignation, confirmed that the president is subject to judicial process, and produced reforms in campaign finance, war powers, and government transparency. Combined with Vietnam, it drove a lasting collapse of public trust in the federal government.
cards.h: → effects on institutions + trust
cards.n: The distrust Watergate created is a key precondition for Reagan's argument that government is the problem.

cards.q: Contrast containment with rollback.
cards.a: Containment sought to hold the line against further Soviet expansion through aid, alliances, and limited war, accepting the existing communist sphere. Rollback, urged by critics such as MacArthur and by 1952 Republican rhetoric about liberation, meant actively freeing territory already under communist control.
cards.h: → two strategies compared
cards.n: Truman's firing of MacArthur is the moment containment beats rollback and civilian control is affirmed.

cards.q: Contrast the Truman Doctrine with the Marshall Plan.
cards.a: The Truman Doctrine was a military and political commitment to aid governments resisting communist takeover, framed in urgent ideological terms. The Marshall Plan was economic reconstruction aid designed to make Western Europe prosperous, and thus resistant to communism, while creating markets for U.S. goods.
cards.h: → military vs economic
cards.n: Both are containment; the difference is the instrument, hard commitment versus economic prevention.

cards.q: Contrast massive retaliation with flexible response.
cards.a: Eisenhower's massive retaliation threatened overwhelming nuclear reprisal for aggression, cheaper than large conventional forces (more bang for the buck) but credible only against major threats. Kennedy's flexible response built conventional and counterinsurgency forces for limited wars, making intervention easier.
cards.h: → two doctrines compared
cards.n: The shift helps explain escalation in Vietnam: more usable options meant more temptation to use them.

cards.q: Contrast the approaches of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X.
cards.a: King preached nonviolent direct action, integration, and appeals to Christian conscience and federal power. Malcolm X, in his Nation of Islam years, rejected integration and nonviolence, urging Black separatism, self-defense by any means necessary, and racial pride; after Mecca he sought broader alliances.
cards.h: → two philosophies compared
cards.n: Both diagnosed the same injustice; the difference is over means, and Malcolm X spoke more directly to Northern urban conditions.

cards.q: Contrast the strategies of the NAACP, SCLC, and SNCC.
cards.a: The NAACP litigated for legal change through the courts. King's SCLC mobilized Black churches for staged nonviolent campaigns aimed at national media and federal action. SNCC organized students for grassroots direct action and voter registration, and moved after 1966 toward Black Power.
cards.h: → three organizations compared
cards.n: Movement, not monolith: knowing the division of labor prevents a vague one-leader essay.

cards.q: Contrast the Civil Rights Act of 1964 with the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
cards.a: The 1964 act attacked segregation and discrimination in public accommodations and employment, using federal funding leverage and the EEOC. The 1965 act targeted political exclusion, suspending literacy tests and placing federal registrars and preclearance requirements over states with histories of disfranchisement.
cards.h: → social vs political rights
cards.n: 1964 addresses access to public life, 1965 addresses power; Selma is the event that produces the second.

cards.q: Contrast de jure and de facto segregation.
cards.a: De jure segregation is separation required by law, as in the Jim Crow South, and can be struck down by courts and statutes. De facto segregation arises from private practice and policy, including redlining, restrictive covenants, and white flight, and persisted in Northern cities after the laws changed.
cards.h: → definitions + where each existed
cards.n: This distinction explains why the movement's Northern campaigns after 1965 largely failed.

cards.q: Compare the New Deal and the Great Society.
cards.a: Both expanded federal responsibility for economic security under liberal Democrats with large majorities. The New Deal answered mass unemployment with relief, jobs, and social insurance for workers; the Great Society, in a time of prosperity, targeted poverty, health care, education, civil rights, and quality of life.
cards.h: → continuity + differences
cards.n: Great Society is New Deal liberalism extended to groups the New Deal excluded, especially African Americans.

cards.q: Compare first-wave and second-wave feminism.
cards.a: The first wave, from Seneca Falls to 1920, concentrated on legal rights, above all suffrage. The second wave, after 1963, targeted workplace discrimination, equal pay, reproductive rights, and cultural and domestic roles, arguing that legal equality alone left women subordinate.
cards.h: → continuity + change
cards.n: Both drew organizers and tactics from contemporaneous reform movements: abolition then, civil rights now.

cards.q: Compare U.S. Cold War policy in the late 1940s with policy in the early 1970s.
cards.a: Late 1940s: confrontation, refusal to recognize communist China, alliance building, and a rapid arms buildup. Early 1970s: detente, arms control through SALT I, recognition of the Soviet sphere at Helsinki, and Nixon's opening to China, exploiting the Sino-Soviet split.
cards.h: → change over time
cards.n: The continuity is the goal, containing Soviet power; the change is negotiation replacing confrontation as the method.

cards.q: Contrast 1950s mainstream culture with the 1960s counterculture.
cards.a: 1950s culture stressed suburban domesticity, corporate conformity, religious observance, and consumer abundance, with dissent confined to figures like the Beats. The 1960s counterculture rejected those norms for personal authenticity, communal living, sexual freedom, and open political protest.
cards.h: → two cultures compared
cards.n: Note the continuity: both rest on postwar affluence, which gave youth the leisure and means to opt out.

cards.q: Date the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan.
cards.a: The Truman Doctrine was announced in March 1947; the Marshall Plan was proposed in June 1947 and funded in 1948.
cards.h: → year only
cards.n: 1947 is the standard start date for open Cold War in most exam framings.

cards.q: Date the Berlin airlift, the founding of NATO, the Soviet atomic test, and the communist victory in China.
cards.a: The Berlin airlift ran from June 1948 to May 1949. NATO was founded in April 1949, the USSR tested an atomic bomb in August 1949, and Mao's communists won China in October 1949.
cards.h: → cluster of years
cards.n: 1949 is the hinge: the loss of the atomic monopoly and of China drives NSC-68 and the Second Red Scare.

cards.q: Date the Korean War.
cards.a: 1950 to 1953. It began with the North Korean invasion in June 1950 and ended with an armistice, not a peace treaty, in July 1953.
cards.h: → two years
cards.n: No formal peace treaty exists; the war explains the permanent U.S. military presence in Asia.

cards.q: Date Brown v. Board of Education and the Montgomery Bus Boycott.
cards.a: Brown was decided in May 1954. The Montgomery Bus Boycott ran from December 1955 to December 1956.
cards.h: → two years
cards.n: Chronology trap: Brown comes first and helps make the boycott legally plausible.

cards.q: Date the Cuban Missile Crisis.
cards.a: October 1962, thirteen days of confrontation resolved by the Soviet withdrawal of missiles from Cuba.
cards.h: → month and year
cards.n: It follows the failed Bay of Pigs (1961) and the building of the Berlin Wall (1961).

cards.q: Date the Civil Rights Act and the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution.
cards.a: Both came in 1964, the Civil Rights Act in July and the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in August, months before Johnson's landslide election.
cards.h: → same year, two laws
cards.n: Same president, same summer: the Great Society and Vietnam escalation start together and then compete for money.

cards.q: Date the Tet Offensive, the assassinations of King and Robert Kennedy, and Nixon's election.
cards.a: All in 1968: Tet in January and February, King in April, Robert Kennedy in June, and Nixon's victory in November on a law-and-order and peace-with-honor platform.
cards.h: → year + events
cards.n: 1968 is the pivot of Period 8: liberal coalition fractures and conservative realignment begins.

cards.q: Date Nixon's resignation and the fall of Saigon.
cards.a: Nixon resigned in August 1974; Saigon fell to North Vietnamese forces in April 1975, ending the war.
cards.h: → two dates
cards.n: Within nine months the U.S. loses both a president to scandal and the war, deepening the crisis of confidence.

cards.q: Identify Executive Order 9981 and give its year.
cards.a: President Truman's 1948 order declaring equal treatment and opportunity in the U.S. armed forces regardless of race, which led to the desegregation of military units over the following several years, ahead of most civilian institutions.
cards.h: → 1948 + Truman + desegregates military
cards.n: An early Cold War civil rights move: Truman worried segregation embarrassed the U.S. in its propaganda contest with the Soviets.

cards.q: Identify the Little Rock Nine and the 1957 crisis at Central High School.
cards.a: Nine Black students who integrated Little Rock Central High School in Arkansas in 1957 despite Governor Orval Faubus using the National Guard to block them. President Eisenhower federalized the Guard and sent Army troops to enforce the integration order.
cards.h: → 9 students + governor blocks + Eisenhower sends troops
cards.n: Shows the federal government's willingness, if reluctantly, to enforce Brown with military force.

cards.q: Identify the Eisenhower Doctrine and give its year.
cards.a: A 1957 policy pledging U.S. military and economic aid to any Middle Eastern nation resisting communist aggression or subversion, extending containment into a region destabilized by the Suez Crisis and declining British and French influence.
cards.h: → 1957 + region (Middle East) + pledge
cards.n: It grew out of the 1956 Suez Crisis and was invoked once, to land Marines in Lebanon in 1958.

cards.q: Identify the U-2 incident of 1960.
cards.a: The Soviet Union shot down an American U-2 spy plane over its territory and captured pilot Francis Gary Powers. Eisenhower's initial denial was embarrassed by Soviet proof, and the incident wrecked a planned Paris summit and worsened Cold War tensions.
cards.h: → spy plane shot down + failed cover story
cards.n: Eisenhower's denial collapsed because the Soviets had Powers alive; he was later swapped for Soviet spy Rudolf Abel in 1962.

cards.q: Explain why East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961.
cards.a: Hundreds of thousands of East Germans were fleeing to the West through Berlin's open border each year, draining the East German economy of skilled workers. East Germany, backed by the Soviet Union, built a concrete wall in 1961 to seal the border and stop the exodus.
cards.h: → mass exodus west → wall seals the border
cards.n: It became the Cold War's most visible physical symbol of a divided Europe.

cards.q: Identify the Peace Corps.
cards.a: A federal volunteer program created by President Kennedy in 1961 that sent young Americans abroad to work on education, agriculture, and health projects in developing nations, combining humanitarian goals with a soft-power effort to counter Soviet influence.
cards.h: → 1961 + Kennedy + volunteers abroad
cards.n: Pair it with the Alliance for Progress in Latin America: both are the soft-power half of Kennedy's flexible response strategy.

cards.q: Identify the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947.
cards.a: A law passed over Truman's veto that curbed union power gained under the Wagner Act, banning the closed shop, allowing states to pass 'right-to-work' laws, and letting the president order an 80-day cooling-off period to delay strikes threatening national health or safety.
cards.h: → 1947 + rolls back Wagner Act + right-to-work
cards.n: Labor called it the 'slave labor act'; it marked the start of organized labor's postwar decline.

cards.q: Identify Truman's Fair Deal.
cards.a: Truman's postwar domestic program proposing an extension of New Deal liberalism, including national health insurance, an increased minimum wage, and civil rights legislation. A conservative coalition in Congress blocked most of its ambitious elements.
cards.h: → New Deal extension + what passed vs. blocked
cards.n: A higher minimum wage, expanded Social Security, and the 1949 Housing Act did pass; the blocking coalition had formed against FDR back in 1938.

cards.q: Explain why Congress passed the National Defense Education Act in 1958.
cards.a: The Soviet Union's 1957 Sputnik launch convinced American leaders the U.S. was falling behind in science and technology. The 1958 act funneled federal funding into science, math, and foreign language education and student loans to close the perceived gap.
cards.h: → Sputnik shock → federal funding for STEM education
cards.n: It broke the taboo on federal money for schools, the precedent Johnson's 1965 education act expanded far beyond science and languages.

cards.q: Identify the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965.
cards.a: A Great Society law providing the first major federal funding for K-12 public education, targeted especially at schools serving low-income students, greatly expanding the federal government's role in a policy area traditionally left to states and localities.
cards.h: → 1965 + first major federal K-12 funding
cards.n: Aid followed low-income students rather than schools, which is how Johnson got past the church-state fight that had killed earlier school bills.

cards.q: Identify the Clean Air Act of 1970.
cards.a: A federal law, strengthened during the environmental movement's peak, that set national air quality standards and required states to reduce industrial and vehicle pollution, enforced by the newly created Environmental Protection Agency.
cards.h: → 1970 + national air standards + enforced by EPA
cards.n: Nixon, no environmentalist, signed it and created the EPA because the first Earth Day in 1970 made the issue too popular to resist.

cards.q: Identify the holding of United States v. Nixon (1974).
cards.a: The Supreme Court unanimously ruled that executive privilege was not absolute and ordered President Nixon to turn over White House tape recordings sought in the Watergate investigation, a decision that led directly to his resignation.
cards.h: → rejects absolute executive privilege → tapes released
cards.n: A landmark check on executive power, decided unanimously even by Nixon's own appointees.

cards.q: Explain why Nixon's 1972 visit to China mattered for Cold War diplomacy.
cards.a: By opening relations with Communist China after more than two decades of hostility, Nixon exploited the growing Sino-Soviet split to gain diplomatic leverage over the Soviet Union, a striking example of detente-era pragmatism from a longtime anticommunist.
cards.h: → opens China relations + exploits Sino-Soviet split → leverage over USSR
cards.n: A striking reversal from the anticommunist Nixon of the 1950s Red Scare era.

cards.q: Identify Title IX and give its year.
cards.a: A 1972 federal law banning sex discrimination in any education program receiving federal funding, which dramatically expanded women's and girls' access to school athletics and professional and graduate programs over the following decades.
cards.h: → 1972 + bans sex discrimination in education + athletics impact
cards.n: It came in the Education Amendments the same year Congress sent the ERA to the states, and athletics was not what its drafters had in mind.

cards.q: Contrast the legislative fate of Truman's Fair Deal with Lyndon Johnson's Great Society.
cards.a: A conservative coalition of Republicans and southern Democrats blocked most of the Fair Deal in a closely divided Congress. Johnson, with huge Democratic majorities after 1964 and the political momentum from JFK's assassination, pushed most of the Great Society into law.
cards.h: → mostly blocked vs. mostly enacted + why (majorities)
cards.n: The window was short: the 1966 midterms cut those majorities back and Vietnam spending crowded out the rest of Johnson's domestic agenda.

cards.q: Explain why Eisenhower relied on covert CIA operations as a Cold War tool.
cards.a: Covert action, such as CIA-backed coups that overthrew elected governments in Iran (1953) and Guatemala (1954), let the U.S. remove leaders viewed as pro-Soviet without the cost, casualties, or diplomatic fallout of open military intervention.
cards.h: → cheap + deniable + examples: Iran 1953, Guatemala 1954
cards.n: Both coups had long-term backlash: Iran's 1979 revolution and decades of anti-U.S. sentiment in Latin America.

cards.q: Date Executive Order 9981, Brown v. Board of Education, and the Little Rock crisis in order.
cards.a: Executive Order 9981 desegregated the armed forces in 1948, Brown v. Board of Education struck down school segregation in 1954, and the Little Rock Nine integrated Central High School amid federal troop enforcement in 1957.
cards.n: Eisenhower privately disliked Brown but sent the 101st Airborne to Little Rock; the issue for him was federal authority, not civil rights.

cards.q: Identify Jack Kerouac's On the Road and Allen Ginsberg's Howl as Beat critiques of 1950s conformity.
cards.a: Kerouac's 1957 novel On the Road celebrated spontaneous cross-country travel over stable careers, while Ginsberg's 1956 poem Howl attacked consumerism and conformity in raw, confrontational language. Both defined the Beat movement's rejection of mainstream 1950s values.
cards.h: → Kerouac's travel novel + Ginsberg's confrontational poem
cards.n: Howl's 1957 obscenity trial ended in an acquittal that widened literary free speech, and the Beats prefigure the 1960s counterculture.

cards.q: State the central argument of Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963).
cards.a: Friedan argued that postwar culture trapped educated, middle-class suburban women in an idealized housewife role that left many secretly unfulfilled, a feeling she called 'the problem that has no name,' and urged women to seek identity and work outside the home.
cards.h: → 'problem that has no name' + suburban housewife
cards.n: Friedan's book focused almost entirely on white, educated, suburban women; critics note it largely ignored working-class and Black women, who were rarely full-time homemakers by choice.

cards.q: Explain how rock and roll emerged from Black rhythm and blues to become a symbol of 1950s youth culture.
cards.a: Rock and roll fused Black rhythm-and-blues traditions with country music, popularized by artists like Chuck Berry and by white performers such as Elvis Presley who brought Black musical styles to segregated white audiences, alarming parents and giving teenagers a distinct identity through music.
cards.h: → R&B roots + Presley crossover to white teens
cards.n: Presley's crossover success also raised uncomfortable questions about who profited from Black musical innovation.

cards.q: Identify David Riesman's The Lonely Crowd and William Whyte's The Organization Man.
cards.a: Both 1950s bestsellers criticized suburban conformity: Riesman's 1950 book argued Americans had become 'other-directed,' anxiously conforming to peer approval, while Whyte's 1956 book warned that corporate bureaucracy was replacing individualism with team-player conformity.
cards.h: → two sociological critiques of conformity
cards.n: Pair them with Harrington's The Other America (1962), which attacked invisible poverty rather than conformity in the same affluent decade.

cards.q: Identify the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act of 1975.
cards.a: A law that formally ended termination policy, allowing tribes to administer their own federal programs, such as schools and health services, under contracts with the government, marking a shift toward tribal self-governance.
cards.h: → 1975 + ends termination, tribal self-rule
cards.n: It followed a decade of activism: the Alcatraz occupation of 1969 and the AIM standoff at Wounded Knee in 1973.

cards.q: Define termination policy of the 1950s.
cards.a: A federal policy ending recognition of certain tribes as sovereign nations, withdrawing reservation trust status and federal services, and relocating Native people to cities, all aimed at ending tribal identity by dissolving tribes' legal existence.
cards.h: → ends tribal recognition + urban relocation
cards.n: Around a hundred tribes lost recognition, and the urban relocation it pushed created the city communities that later produced AIM.

cards.q: Identify the 1973 occupation at Wounded Knee.
cards.a: Members of the American Indian Movement occupied the town of Wounded Knee, South Dakota, for 71 days in 1973 to protest corrupt tribal leadership and demand treaty rights, drawing national attention back to the site of the 1890 massacre.
cards.h: → AIM's 71-day occupation, 1973
cards.n: Do not confuse with the 1890 Wounded Knee massacre; this is a Red Power protest eighty-three years later at the same site.

cards.q: Differentiate the counterculture from the New Left.
cards.a: The counterculture rejected mainstream values through lifestyle, drugs, music, and communal living, largely apolitical in its goals. The New Left, centered on groups like Students for a Democratic Society, pursued explicit political change through campus activism, civil rights work, and opposition to the Vietnam War.
cards.h: → lifestyle rebellion vs organized political activism
cards.n: AP exam essays often wrongly treat the counterculture and New Left as one movement; graders reward students who separate them.

cards.q: Identify the Port Huron Statement and Students for a Democratic Society.
cards.a: SDS, founded in 1960, issued the Port Huron Statement in 1962, a manifesto calling for 'participatory democracy' and criticizing Cold War liberalism, corporate power, and racial injustice. It became the New Left's founding document.
cards.h: → SDS 1960 + 1962 manifesto
cards.n: The group split apart by 1969, when the Weather Underground turned to bombings, ending the New Left's mass-organizing phase.

cards.q: Explain the demographic consequences of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965.
cards.a: By abolishing the national-origins quota system and prioritizing family reunification and job skills, the act shifted the source of immigration away from Europe toward Latin America and Asia, reshaping U.S. demographics far more than Congress anticipated.
cards.h: → ends quotas, shifts source to Latin America/Asia
cards.n: Its sponsors promised the ethnic mix would not change, and the law also imposed the first numerical cap on Western Hemisphere migration.

cards.q: Identify Jerry Falwell and the rise of televangelism in the late 1970s.
cards.a: Falwell built a national following through his televised Old-Time Gospel Hour and founded the Moral Majority in 1979, using cable and satellite broadcasting to mobilize evangelical Christians into a conservative political voting bloc.
cards.h: → TV ministry + Moral Majority founder
cards.n: Its organizing spark was as much federal pressure on segregated Christian academies as abortion, though abortion became the public issue.

cards.q: Explain the immediate effect of Title IX (1972) on women's college athletics.
cards.a: By barring sex discrimination in any federally funded education program, Title IX forced colleges to fund women's sports comparably to men's, producing a rapid multi-fold increase in female collegiate athletic participation over the following decade.
cards.h: → funding parity + participation surge
cards.n: One unintended effect: as women's programs merged into men's athletic departments, the share of women coaching those teams fell sharply.

cards.q: Name the major antipoverty programs created under the Economic Opportunity Act of 1964.
cards.a: The act created Head Start (early childhood education), the Job Corps (job training for youth), and VISTA (Volunteers in Service to America, a domestic counterpart to the Peace Corps), among other community action programs.
cards.h: → Head Start, Job Corps, VISTA
cards.n: Its maximum feasible participation rule let poor residents run local programs, which enraged big-city Democratic mayors and doomed community action.

cards.q: Explain the United Farm Workers' use of consumer boycotts under Cesar Chavez.
cards.a: Chavez and the UFW organized a nationwide boycott of California table grapes during the Delano strike beginning in 1965, pressuring growers by turning ordinary consumers into economic allies rather than relying on strikes alone, winning contracts by 1970.
cards.h: → grape boycott + consumers as allies
cards.n: Farm workers were excluded from the 1935 Wagner Act, so they had no legal right to bargain; the boycott was a way around that gap.

cards.q: Identify Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign.
cards.a: Schlafly led a grassroots campaign arguing the Equal Rights Amendment would strip women of protections like alimony and exemption from the military draft while undermining traditional family roles, helping stall ratification three states short of the required 38.
cards.h: → traditional-roles argument, blocks ratification
cards.n: The amendment had passed Congress overwhelmingly in 1972 and looked certain, which makes her campaign the standard example of backlash politics.

cards.q: Identify court-ordered busing as a tool for school desegregation in the 1970s.
cards.a: Federal courts ordered busing students across district lines to integrate schools after Brown's slow enforcement, most controversially in Boston starting in 1974, provoking violent white resistance and accelerating white flight to suburbs.
cards.h: → 1970s court-ordered busing + Boston backlash
cards.n: Swann approved busing in 1971, but Milliken v. Bradley in 1974 barred crossing city-suburb lines, which locked segregation in by district.

cards.q: Explain how a complexity move could connect Cold War containment to earlier American foreign policy.
cards.a: You might note that containment's premise — that the U.S. must actively counter a rival ideology beyond its own hemisphere — echoed and extended Wilson's post-war vision of American-led collective security, showing continuity of ambition even as alliances and foreign aid were new tools.
cards.h: → link containment's logic back to Wilsonian internationalism
cards.n: This earns complexity inside Analysis and Reasoning. There is no separate synthesis row: it was removed from both rubrics in 2017-18, so a dedicated "synthesis paragraph" chases a point that does not exist.

cards.q: State the developments the College Board identifies as central to Period 8.
cards.a: The Cold War's domestic and international effects, the growth of federal power and the welfare state, and the postwar struggle to extend civil rights and equality to groups still excluded from full citizenship.
cards.h: → Cold War + federal power/welfare state + civil rights struggle
cards.n: Treat these three as the contextualization menu for any Period 8 essay: open with the Cold War frame and narrow from there.

cards.q: Identify Billy Graham and postwar religious revival.
cards.a: Evangelist Billy Graham drew huge crowds to his 'crusades,' broadcast on radio and television starting in the late 1940s, becoming an informal spiritual adviser to Cold War presidents. Congress added 'under God' to the Pledge of Allegiance in 1954 amid the era's civic religious revival.
cards.h: → Graham's crusades + adviser to presidents + 'under God' 1954
cards.n: Ties Cold War anti-communism to a religious revival, since atheism was closely associated with communism.

cards.q: Identify the 1960 Kennedy-Nixon televised debates.
cards.a: The first televised presidential debates let a young, telegenic Kennedy outshine a pale, sweating Nixon on screen, even though radio listeners judged the debate closer. It marked television's arrival as the dominant force in American political campaigns.
cards.h: → first TV debate + Kennedy looks better on screen + TV era begins
cards.n: The claim that radio listeners preferred Nixon rests on one small survey, so use it carefully; the safe point is that image became a campaign asset.

cards.q: Explain how highway construction and urban renewal affected Black urban neighborhoods after 1956.
cards.a: Interstate highways and 'slum clearance' projects were often routed directly through thriving Black neighborhoods, demolishing homes and businesses, displacing residents, and cutting off communities from downtown jobs, while the new highways simultaneously enabled white flight to the suburbs.
cards.h: → highways/renewal demolish Black neighborhoods + fuel white flight
cards.n: Complements the Interstate Highway Act and Levittown cards already in the deck with the era's environmental-justice cost.

cards.q: Identify the Army-McCarthy hearings of 1954.
cards.a: Televised Senate hearings into Joseph McCarthy's accusations against the U.S. Army let millions of Americans watch his bullying tactics firsthand. Army counsel Joseph Welch's rebuke, 'Have you no sense of decency,' helped turn public opinion against McCarthy, who was censured by the Senate that December.
cards.h: → televised hearings + Welch's rebuke + Senate censure
cards.n: McCarthy fell, but the machinery outlived him: loyalty boards and HUAC kept working for years after his censure.

cards.q: Identify the Three Mile Island accident (1979).
cards.a: A partial nuclear reactor meltdown at a Pennsylvania power plant released small amounts of radioactive gas and triggered a mass evacuation scare. It became the worst commercial nuclear accident in U.S. history and stalled new nuclear plant construction for decades.
cards.h: → PA nuclear plant + partial meltdown 1979 + halts new construction
cards.n: The film The China Syndrome had opened twelve days earlier, so the public already had a script in mind for what it was hearing.

cards.q: Identify the Clean Water Act of 1972.
cards.a: Passed over Nixon's veto, the act set national goals for eliminating water pollution and required permits for discharging pollutants into waterways, extending the regulatory reach the Clean Air Act had established for air two years earlier.
cards.h: → passed over veto + regulates water pollutant discharge
cards.n: The Cuyahoga River catching fire in 1969 gave the cause its image; Nixon signed other environmental laws but balked at this one's cost.

cards.q: State the developments the College Board identifies as central to Period 9.
cards.a: Three key concepts define Period 9. (1) A newly ascendant conservative movement achieved major political and policy goals in the 1980s and kept shaping public debate afterward (KC-9.1). (2) The nation went through significant technological, economic and demographic change moving into the 21st century (KC-9.2). (3) The end of the Cold War and new challenges, above all terrorism after 2001, forced the United States to redefine its foreign policy and role in the world (KC-9.3).
cards.h: → three key concepts, one clause each
cards.n: Listing events (Reagan, 9/11, 2008) is not naming the developments; each needs its process: conservatism, economic and demographic change, a redefined world role.

cards.q: Date the opening year of AP Period 9 and explain which development makes that year a sensible boundary.
cards.a: 1980. Ronald Reagan's election that November brought the conservative movement to national power (KC-9.1.I.A), ending the liberal dominance of federal policy that ran from the New Deal through the Great Society. The same moment also saw the Cold War revive after the 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and deindustrialization reshape the economy, so several Period 9 stories start there.
cards.h: → the year + the development that justifies it
cards.n: '1980 because a new decade began' earns nothing; the boundary is justified by Reagan's election and the conservative turn it marks.

cards.q: Differentiate a complexity move from a contextualization paragraph, using Reagan-era conservatism as the example.
cards.a: Contextualization describes the broader setting of the prompt in several sentences and earns its own point (Row B): for Reagan's rise, the 1970s stagflation, Watergate, the Iran hostage crisis and the backlash against busing and Roe v. Wade. Complexity is a quality of the argument (Row D): e.g., explaining that Reagan cut taxes and deregulated yet left Social Security and Medicare intact, or connecting his pro-business program to Gilded Age laissez-faire, with evidence.
cards.h: → what each is + where each scores
cards.n: A single line comparing Reagan to the Gilded Age earns neither point: context needs a described setting, complexity an explained connection that drives the argument.

cards.q: Describe the domestic context of the 1970s that a contextualization paragraph on the rise of conservatism after 1980 should establish.
cards.a: The 1970s undermined confidence in liberal government. Stagflation, with double-digit inflation by 1979-1980 after the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks, defied Keynesian remedies; Vietnam and Watergate eroded trust in Washington; tax revolts such as California's Proposition 13 (1978) showed homeowners turning against taxes. Busing, Roe v. Wade (1973), the ERA and rising crime mobilized religious and suburban conservatives, while population shifted to the more conservative Sunbelt.
cards.h: → economic, political and cultural strands, tied to prompt
cards.n: 'The 1970s were a troubled decade' is a phrase; the point needs described developments linked to the conservative turn.

cards.q: Describe the international context in 1980 that shaped Reagan's foreign policy.
cards.a: Detente had collapsed. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 led Carter to announce the Carter Doctrine, embargo grain sales and boycott the 1980 Moscow Olympics; revolutions in Iran and Nicaragua (1979) had removed U.S. allies; and Iranian militants held 52 Americans hostage from November 1979 until January 1981. Many Americans felt the Vietnam defeat had left the nation weak, which Reagan promised to reverse with rearmament.
cards.h: → Soviet moves + lost allies + hostages, tied to Reagan
cards.n: Context that starts with Reagan's own policies describes the topic, not its setting; the point needs the late-1970s events he was responding to.

cards.q: Describe the economic changes already under way by 1980 that set the context for Period 9's changing economy.
cards.a: Deindustrialization had begun: manufacturing employment peaked at about 19.6 million in 1979, as steel and auto plants in the Northeast and Midwest lost ground to Japanese and West German competitors and to automation. The oil shocks and stagflation of the 1970s squeezed wages, service-sector jobs were growing faster than factory jobs, and the first personal computers (the Apple II of 1977, then the IBM PC of 1981) hinted at the digital economy to come.
cards.h: → three trends, each with an example
cards.n: Dating deindustrialization to NAFTA (1994) is a common error; the factory decline was well under way by the late 1970s.

cards.q: Describe the demographic trends from Period 8 that continued into Period 9.
cards.a: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 had ended national-origins quotas, so immigration from Latin America and Asia kept rising and made the population steadily more diverse. Americans kept moving to the Sunbelt of the South and West, drawn by jobs, defense spending, lower taxes and air conditioning. The baby boom generation was aging, and more married women worked for wages, changing family life.
cards.h: → immigration + regional shift + family change
cards.n: Treating Period 9 immigration as new misses the continuity: it follows from the 1965 law and earlier Sunbelt migration (borrowed from u8).

cards.q: Identify one continuity and one change between Period 8 and Period 9 in debates over the federal government's role.
cards.a: Continuity: Americans kept arguing over the size and purpose of federal power, as liberals defended New Deal and Great Society programs and conservatives attacked them, and Social Security and Medicare survived. Change: after 1980 conservatives held power and set the terms, cutting top tax rates, deregulating, and pushing even a Democratic president, Clinton, to declare that 'the era of big government is over' (1996).
cards.h: → one continuity + one change, each with evidence
cards.n: Naming a change without evidence, or calling Reagan's program a complete reversal of the New Deal, loses the point; the programs' survival is the continuity.

cards.q: Explain how a response earns the contextualization point on a prompt about U.S. foreign policy after the September 11, 2001, attacks.
cards.a: It must describe, in more than a phrase, developments before 2001 that bear on the prompt and link them to it. For example: the Soviet collapse left the United States the sole superpower, with troops stationed in Saudi Arabia after the Gulf War, a grievance Osama bin Laden cited; al-Qaeda had already bombed U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (1998) and the USS Cole (2000). Those developments explain why the attacks came and why policy turned to terrorism.
cards.h: → describe earlier developments + link to the prompt
cards.n: 'After 9/11 America fought terrorism' restates the prompt and earns nothing; context must come from outside the prompt's own events.

cards.q: Explain how the end of the Cold War serves as context for U.S. domestic politics in the 1990s.
cards.a: With the Soviet threat gone, voters and politicians turned inward. Defense spending fell as a share of the economy (the 'peace dividend'), helping produce budget surpluses by 1998; the 1992 election turned on the economy rather than foreign policy; and anticommunism no longer held conservatives together, so taxes, spending and culture-war issues such as abortion and gay rights dominated the Republican agenda.
cards.h: → Cold War ends → three domestic effects
cards.n: Describing the fall of the Soviet Union without linking it to domestic politics is narrative, not context for the prompt.

cards.q: Explain how the civil rights and women's movements of Period 8 set the context for the culture wars of Period 9.
cards.a: Period 8 movements changed law and custom: the Civil Rights Act (1964), affirmative action, feminism and the ERA, gay liberation after Stonewall (1969) and Roe v. Wade (1973) expanded rights and altered gender roles. Religious and social conservatives organized against these changes, as in Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA and the Moral Majority (1979), so Period 9's fights over abortion, gay rights, affirmative action and family structure continued arguments begun in Period 8.
cards.h: → Period 8 rights gains → backlash → Period 9 fights
cards.n: Borrows from u8. Listing Period 8 movements without showing the backlash that carried their issues into Period 9 does not explain the context.

cards.q: State how Period 9 content can appear on the May 2027 AP U.S. History exam.
cards.a: Unit 9 carries 4 to 6 percent of the exam weighting, so expect only a few of the 55 multiple-choice questions. The three short-answer questions cover 1491 to 2001, each from a different period, so a Period 9 short answer can reach 1980 to 2001 but no later. The document-based question is drawn from 1754 to 1980, so it never centers on Period 9. The long essay covers about half the course's chronology, so Period 9 can supply it or its later evidence.
cards.h: → one line per exam section
cards.n: Skipping Period 9 is a mistake: it still supplies multiple-choice questions, short-answer content through 2001, and evidence for complexity connections across periods.

cards.q: Classify each development of 1980-2020 as mainly a CONTINUITY from earlier periods or a CHANGE, with one phrase of reasoning: Reagan's cuts in top income tax rates · survival of Social Security and Medicare · U.S. military interventions abroad · the Soviet Union as the main U.S. rival · manufacturing employment · union membership · nativist arguments against immigrants · the main enemy after 2001 · limits on civil liberties in wartime · population movement to the South and West · daily communication through the internet and smartphones · evangelical Christians as an organized political bloc
cards.a:
Top tax rate cuts → change (top rate fell from 70 percent to 28 percent, reversing decades of high rates)
Social Security and Medicare → continuity (New Deal and Great Society core survived conservative attacks)
Military interventions → continuity (interventionism runs from the Cold War through the Gulf War, Balkans and war on terror)
Soviet rival → change (USSR dissolved in 1991)
Manufacturing employment → change (long decline from a 1979 peak as services grew)
Union membership → change (fell from about 20 percent of workers in 1983 to about 10 percent)
Nativist arguments → continuity (echo the Know-Nothings and the 1920s quotas)
Enemy after 2001 → change (nonstate terrorist networks instead of a rival state)
Wartime civil liberties → continuity (PATRIOT Act fits the pattern of Sedition Acts, Red Scares, internment)
Sunbelt migration → continuity (growth since World War II kept going)
Internet and smartphones → change (new ways to work, shop, organize and get news)
Evangelical bloc → change (evangelicals organized as a Republican constituency from about 1980)
cards.h: → label each, then the one-phrase reason
cards.n: Labeling without the reason earns nothing on a continuity-and-change task; say what the development continues from or breaks with.

cards.q: Explain the rise of modern conservatism by 1980.
cards.a: Liberalism lost credibility as conservatives built a movement. Stagflation and Watergate discredited federal management; backlash against busing, Roe and the ERA mobilized evangelicals; Sunbelt growth shifted votes; and think tanks, direct mail and churches organized these voters for Reagan.
cards.h: → stagflation + Watergate discredit liberalism → backlash mobilizes evangelicals → Sunbelt + organization → Reagan wins
cards.n: Listing grievances without saying how they became votes earns nothing; the chain from liberalism's failures to an organized movement is the point.
o: Goldwater's 1964 defeat built the activist network, including Reagan's own debut speech 'A Time for Choosing,' that captured the Republican Party by 1980.
Tax revolts such as California's Proposition 13 (1978) showed middle-class homeowners turning against taxes and spending before Reagan ran on the same theme.

w.a: Conservatism rose in 1980 because Americans suddenly became religious.
w.why: asserts a sudden change without evidence and ignores economic causes

w.a: Reagan won because he was a famous actor who looked good on television.
w.why: personal appeal, no structural cause or movement

w.a: Conservatism rose because the Great Society was repealed in the 1970s.
w.why: false; Medicare, Medicaid and most programs survived

cards.q: Explain why 1980 marks a turning point in U.S. political history rather than a continuation of the 1970s.
cards.a: Reagan's win put an organized conservative coalition in power with a program to cut taxes, deregulate and rearm, reversing the New Deal assumption that Washington should manage the economy. Yet it built on the 1970s: Carter had begun deregulation, and tax revolts and Cold War revival predated Reagan.
cards.h: → conservative coalition takes power → new program reverses New Deal premise → but builds on 1970s trends
cards.n: Asserting 'Reagan changed everything' earns less than a claim that names what turned and what carried over.
o: Republicans also won the Senate in 1980 for the first time since the 1952 elections, giving conservatives the votes to pass the 1981 tax cut.
The coalition assembled in 1980, economic conservatives, evangelicals and white Southern and blue-collar former Democrats, held together for decades.

w.a: 1980 is a turning point because it began a new decade.
w.why: a calendar fact, not a historical development

w.a: 1980 is a turning point because Reagan ended all New Deal programs.
w.why: false; Social Security and Medicare survived

w.a: 1980 is a turning point because the Cold War ended that year.
w.why: wrong date; the Cold War ended in 1989-1991

cards.q: Explain why the end of the Cold War changed the context of U.S. foreign policy after 1991.
cards.a: With the Soviet Union gone, containment lost its organizing enemy and the United States became the sole superpower. Policy turned to regional conflicts, humanitarian crises and trade, as in the Gulf War, Somalia and the Balkans, while the habit of intervention continued.
cards.h: → USSR dissolves → containment loses its enemy → sole superpower → new missions, same interventionism
cards.n: Describing the Soviet collapse without saying what it did to U.S. goals and missions is narrative, not explanation.
o: Debates over when to use force replaced the Cold War consensus: Somalia made leaders wary, while Kosovo brought action without UN approval.
The 'peace dividend' let defense spending fall as a share of the economy even as U.S. forces stayed deployed around the world.

w.a: After 1991 the United States withdrew from world affairs.
w.why: false; it intervened in the Gulf, Somalia, Haiti and the Balkans

w.a: The end of the Cold War changed nothing because America stayed strong.
w.why: ignores the lost enemy and the new kinds of missions

cards.q: Explain why deindustrialization that began in the 1970s is essential context for the economic inequality of Period 9.
cards.a: Factory jobs had given workers without college degrees unionized, middle-class wages. As plants closed or moved from the 1970s on, those workers shifted to lower-paid service jobs and unions shrank, so income gains flowed mainly to the college-educated and to owners of capital.
cards.h: → union factory jobs lost → workers move to lower-paid services → unions shrink → gains go to educated and wealthy
cards.n: Saying 'jobs were lost' without the link to wages and bargaining power does not explain inequality.
o: Manufacturing employment peaked in 1979 at about 19.6 million, so Period 9's wage stagnation starts from a labor market already losing its best-paid blue-collar jobs.
Unions had raised wages even for nonunion workers who competed with them, so their decline removed a force that had narrowed inequality.

w.a: Inequality grew because workers in the 1980s stopped working hard.
w.why: a moral judgment with no economic mechanism

w.a: Deindustrialization began with NAFTA in 1994.
w.why: wrong date; the decline was under way by the 1970s

cards.q: Explain why historians disagree over whether 1980, 1991, or 2001 is the sharpest turning point in recent U.S. history.
cards.a: Each date marks a different kind of change. 1980 transformed domestic politics and economic policy with the conservative ascendancy; 1991 transformed the world order by ending the Cold War; 2001 transformed security policy and civil liberties. Which is sharpest depends on the theme measured.
cards.h: → each date changes a different theme → the choice of theme decides the turning point
cards.n: Picking one date and praising it earns less than comparing what kind of change each date brought.
o: A political or economic historian favors 1980, when tax, regulatory and labor policy changed direction, while a diplomatic historian favors 1991.
Periodization is an argument: choosing 2001 stresses the war on terror, while choosing 1980 stresses continuity from Reagan into the 2000s.

w.a: 2001 is the turning point because 9/11 was the worst attack in American history.
w.why: asserts one date without comparing kinds of change

w.a: Historians disagree because they do not know the facts yet.
w.why: the disagreement is interpretive, not factual

cards.q: Identify the New Right coalition that elected Reagan in 1980.
cards.a: The New Right coalition joined economic conservatives who wanted tax cuts and deregulation, evangelical and other religious conservatives mobilized against abortion, the ERA and secular schooling, anticommunist hawks who wanted rearmament, and white Southern and Sunbelt voters leaving the Democrats, plus blue-collar Northern 'Reagan Democrats.' Stagflation and the Iran hostage crisis pushed swing voters to Reagan, who carried 44 states.
cards.h: → the coalition's groups + what each wanted
cards.n: Naming only 'conservatives' earns nothing; the point is that distinct groups, economic, religious and anticommunist, voted together, several of them former Democrats.

cards.q: Define supply-side economics and identify Reagan's core domestic policies.
cards.a: Supply-side economics holds that cutting tax rates, especially on high incomes and investment, raises the incentive to work, save and invest, so growth widens the tax base; its boldest claim (the Laffer curve) was that lower rates could even raise revenue. Reagan's core domestic policies: the 1981 tax cut (top rate 70 to 50 percent) and the 1986 reform (to 28 percent), deregulation, cuts in domestic social spending, and a military buildup.
cards.h: → definition by mechanism + list of policies
cards.n: 'Trickle-down' is a label, not a definition; name the mechanism (incentives to invest). Claiming the cuts raised revenue is the trap: deficits soared.

cards.q: Identify the Moral Majority and the culture wars.
cards.a: The Moral Majority, founded in 1979 by the Baptist minister Jerry Falwell, organized evangelical and fundamentalist Christians into a Republican voting bloc against abortion, the ERA and gay rights and for school prayer. The culture wars were the conflicts that followed from the 1980s on between traditionalists and progressives over abortion, sexuality, family, religion in public life and school curricula.
cards.h: → organization + founder + goals; then the wider conflict
cards.n: Treating the culture wars as a single law or event earns little; name the issues and the organized religious right that pressed them.

cards.q: Identify the AIDS crisis and the activist response.
cards.a: AIDS was first reported in 1981 and killed hundreds of thousands of Americans by the mid-1990s, hitting gay men hardest amid stigma. Critics charged federal neglect: Reagan gave no major speech on AIDS until 1987. Activists, above all ACT UP (1987), used direct action to demand research money and faster drug approval, and won both; the crisis pushed gay rights to the center of the culture wars.
cards.h: → what + when + federal response + activist response
cards.n: Illustrative: the KCs do not name AIDS. Use it as evidence for debates over sexuality and the federal role, not as a list of medical facts.

cards.q: Identify the Contract with America and the domestic politics of the Clinton years.
cards.a: The Contract with America was the House Republicans' 1994 platform, led by Newt Gingrich: votes on a balanced-budget amendment, tax cuts, term limits, crime and welfare reform. Republicans won both houses for the first time in 40 years. Clinton 'triangulated': he fought GOP cuts through the 1995-96 shutdowns yet signed welfare reform (1996) and reached balanced budgets by 1998. The House impeached him in 1998; the Senate acquitted.
cards.h: → the platform + the 1994 result + Clinton's response
cards.n: The Contract was a campaign pledge, not a law, and many of its items never became law; its significance is the GOP Congress that pushed Clinton to the center.

cards.q: Identify Barack Obama's presidency and the Affordable Care Act.
cards.a: Barack Obama, elected in 2008 during the financial crisis, was the first African American president (2009-2017). His signature law, the Affordable Care Act (2010), passed with no Republican votes; it expanded coverage through subsidized private-insurance exchanges and Medicaid expansion, barred denial for preexisting conditions and required most people to carry insurance. It became the central fight over the scope of the safety net.
cards.h: → who + when + what the law did + why it mattered
cards.n: Calling the ACA 'government-run health care' is wrong: it worked through private insurers. The KC point is the debate over the safety net's scope.

cards.q: Contrast New Deal liberalism with Reagan-era conservatism.
cards.a: New Deal liberalism held that an active federal government should secure economic security: regulating business, providing social insurance, spending in downturns, taxing progressively and protecting unions. Reagan-era conservatism held that government was 'the problem': it cut top tax rates, deregulated, trimmed domestic programs, confronted unions (PATCO) and stressed traditional morality, while raising military spending. Yet Social Security and Medicare survived.
cards.h: → point-by-point contrast + one continuity
cards.n: Two lists of traits are not a contrast; pair them point by point (regulate vs deregulate, tax vs cut taxes) and note that the core programs survived.

cards.q: Identify the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993.
cards.a: The Family and Medical Leave Act (1993), the first major bill Bill Clinton signed, guarantees eligible workers at employers with 50 or more employees up to 12 weeks a year of unpaid, job-protected leave for a birth or adoption or for their own or a close family member's serious illness. George H. W. Bush had vetoed it twice.
cards.h: → what the law guarantees + who signed and who vetoed
cards.n: The leave is unpaid; saying the act created paid leave is the classic error. Use it as evidence of debates over gender roles and family structures.

cards.q: Identify the 'Don't Ask, Don't Tell' policy and give its year.
cards.a: 1993. 'Don't Ask, Don't Tell' was the Clinton-era compromise, written into law by Congress, that let gay, lesbian and bisexual Americans serve in the military only if they kept their orientation hidden: commanders were not to ask, and those who disclosed it were discharged. Clinton had promised to end the ban outright but retreated under military and congressional opposition. Congress repealed it in December 2010, effective 2011.
cards.h: → year + what it allowed and forbade + its end
cards.n: Calling it a ban on gay service misreads it: it allowed service in secrecy, and more than 13,000 people were still discharged under it.

cards.q: Identify the Defense of Marriage Act and give its year.
cards.a: 1996. The Defense of Marriage Act, signed by Clinton, defined marriage for all federal purposes as the union of one man and one woman and let states refuse to recognize same-sex marriages performed elsewhere. It passed by large bipartisan margins before any state allowed same-sex marriage. The Supreme Court struck down its federal definition in United States v. Windsor (2013).
cards.h: → year + the two provisions + its fate
cards.n: DOMA did not ban same-sex marriage in the states; it denied federal recognition and freed states from recognizing other states' marriages.

cards.q: Identify the Tea Party movement.
cards.a: The Tea Party was a grassroots conservative movement that arose in 2009 against the bank and auto bailouts, the stimulus and the Affordable Care Act, demanding lower spending and taxes and a strict reading of the Constitution. Its activists backed primary challengers and helped Republicans gain 63 House seats and control of the House in 2010, pushing the party right on fiscal policy.
cards.h: → when + what it opposed + its political effect
cards.n: Treating the Tea Party as a third party is wrong: it worked inside the Republican Party, mostly through primaries.

cards.q: Identify Obergefell v. Hodges and give its year.
cards.a: 2015. In Obergefell v. Hodges the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4, in Justice Anthony Kennedy's opinion, that the Fourteenth Amendment's due process and equal protection clauses guarantee same-sex couples the right to marry, striking down the remaining state bans nationwide. It capped a rapid shift from DOMA (1996) through Massachusetts (2004) and Windsor (2013).
cards.h: → year + holding + constitutional basis
cards.n: Calling Obergefell a law passed by Congress earns nothing; it is a Court ruling resting on the Fourteenth Amendment.

cards.q: Contrast supply-side economics with Keynesian demand-side economics.
cards.a: Keynesian (demand-side) policy holds that recessions come from too little spending, so government should boost demand by spending more or cutting consumers' taxes, accepting deficits. Supply-side policy holds that growth comes from production, so government should cut marginal tax rates on high earners and investment and reduce regulation to raise the incentive to work and invest. Postwar administrations had leaned Keynesian; Reagan adopted supply-side ideas.
cards.h: → each theory's cause of growth + its remedy
cards.n: Saying Keynesians never cut taxes is wrong: both may; the difference is whose taxes (consumers vs investors) and why (demand vs incentives).

cards.q: Identify the 1992 'Year of the Woman' in Congress.
cards.a: The 1992 elections sent a record number of women to Congress: elected women senators rose from two to six, including Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman senator, and women in the House rose from 28 to 47. The surge followed anger at the all-male Senate Judiciary Committee's handling of Anita Hill's sexual-harassment testimony against Clarence Thomas in 1991, and many open seats.
cards.h: → what happened + the numbers + the trigger
cards.n: Illustrative: the KCs do not name it. Use it as evidence of changing gender roles tied to the Thomas-Hill hearings, not as a stand-alone fact.

cards.q: Identify the savings and loan crisis of the late 1980s.
cards.a: More than 1,000 savings and loan associations failed between the mid-1980s and early 1990s after deregulation, especially the Garn-St Germain Act of 1982, let them make risky real estate and commercial loans while their deposits stayed federally insured. The 1989 bailout law created the Resolution Trust Corporation, and the cleanup cost taxpayers roughly 124 billion dollars.
cards.h: → what failed + why + the federal cost
cards.n: It is evidence of deregulation's costs; confusing it with 2008 (banks and mortgage securities, rescued by TARP) loses the point.

cards.q: Identify Sandra Day O'Connor's 1981 Supreme Court appointment.
cards.a: In 1981 Reagan named Sandra Day O'Connor, an Arizona appeals judge and former state senator, the first woman on the Supreme Court, keeping a campaign pledge; the Senate confirmed her 99 to 0. She became a moderate conservative and often the swing vote, notably co-writing the Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992) opinion that preserved Roe's core holding.
cards.h: → who + when + significance on the Court
cards.n: Illustrative. The point is not a trivia 'first' but the tension it shows: Reagan courted women voters while some social conservatives opposed her record on abortion.

cards.q: Contrast the abortion-rights battle in Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992) with the marriage-equality battle resolved in Obergefell v. Hodges (2015).
cards.a: Casey (1992) was a partial, defensive outcome: it kept Roe's core right to abortion before viability but let states impose restrictions that did not create an 'undue burden,' so the fight moved to state legislatures. Obergefell (2015) was a decisive expansion: it set one national right to same-sex marriage and struck down every state ban. Both rested on Fourteenth Amendment liberty; Dobbs (2022) overturned Casey and left Obergefell standing.
cards.h: → each outcome + how settled + shared basis
cards.n: Saying both simply 'expanded rights' misses the contrast: Casey loosened Roe's protection even as it kept it, while Obergefell settled its issue nationally.

cards.q: Identify the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Act (welfare reform, 1996).
cards.a: The 1996 welfare law, passed by the Republican Congress and signed by Clinton after he vetoed two earlier versions, ended Aid to Families with Dependent Children, a federal entitlement dating from 1935, and replaced it with Temporary Assistance for Needy Families: block grants to states, work requirements and a five-year lifetime limit on federal aid. It fulfilled Clinton's pledge to 'end welfare as we know it.'
cards.h: → what it ended + what replaced it + who signed
cards.n: Calling it a Republican-only law misses the point: a Democratic president signing it shows how far conservative ideas about welfare had moved the center.

cards.q: Identify Massachusetts's 2004 legalization of same-sex marriage.
cards.a: In Goodridge v. Department of Public Health (November 2003) the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court held that the state constitution required marriage equality, and in May 2004 Massachusetts became the first state to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples. Eleven states answered with constitutional bans that November, but other states followed Massachusetts until Obergefell (2015) made same-sex marriage national.
cards.h: → the ruling + the first licenses + the reaction
cards.n: Saying the Massachusetts legislature legalized it is wrong: a state court ruling did, which is why opponents attacked 'activist judges.'
x: Goodridge v. Department of Public Health

cards.q:
Compare the arguments of the two described sources about the federal government's role.
Source 1: Ronald Reagan, First Inaugural Address, January 1981: 'In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.' He calls for cutting federal spending and taxes and returning power to the states and the people.
Source 2 (a labeled composite paraphrase of liberal critics, 1982-1984): the administration's cuts fall on school lunches, food stamps and job training while its tax cuts go mostly to the wealthy, so federal programs, not their removal, protect ordinary families.
cards.a: Similarity: both treat the federal budget as the tool that decides who bears the costs of the economic crisis. Difference: Source 1 claims government itself caused the crisis, so shrinking spending, taxes and federal power will restore growth; Source 2 claims federal programs protect ordinary families and the cuts shift burdens onto the poor while tax cuts favor the rich. The clash is KC-9.1.I.B's debate over the scope of government.
cards.h: → one similarity + one difference, each explicit
cards.n: Summarizing each source separately is not a comparison; the point needs an explicit similarity or difference between their claims.

cards.q: Identify three examples of federal deregulation between 1978 and 1988 and state what each changed.
cards.a: Airline Deregulation Act (1978, Carter): ended federal control of fares and routes. Motor Carrier Act (1980, Carter): opened trucking to competition. Garn-St Germain Act (1982, Reagan): let savings and loans make riskier loans. The FCC's repeal of the Fairness Doctrine (1987): ended the rule that broadcasters air contrasting views on public issues. Reagan also cut enforcement budgets at agencies such as the EPA.
cards.h: → law or rule + year + what it changed, three times
cards.n: Crediting deregulation to Reagan alone misses the KC's word 'continue': Carter deregulated airlines and trucking first.

cards.q: Identify two conservative efforts after 1980 to cut or restructure popular federal programs that failed or were scaled back, and state the outcome of each.
cards.a: Social Security, 1981-1983: Reagan's 1981 plan to cut early-retirement benefits drew a 96-0 Senate vote against it, and the 1983 bipartisan rescue raised payroll taxes and slowly lifted the retirement age to 67 instead of cutting the program. Social Security, 2005: George W. Bush's plan for private accounts never reached a vote in Congress. Both failed because older voters turn out heavily and the program is popular.
cards.h: → effort + year + outcome, twice
cards.n: Claiming Reagan 'dismantled the welfare state' is the trap: KC-9.1.I.B stresses inertia and liberal opposition, and the largest programs kept growing.

cards.q: Identify the Dodd-Frank Act (2010) and the debate over financial regulation it continued.
cards.a: The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, signed by Obama in July 2010 after the 2008 crisis, tightened bank capital and stress-test rules, limited banks' speculative trading (the Volcker Rule), regulated derivatives and created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Supporters called it overdue reform after decades of deregulation; Republicans called it costly overreach and in 2018 eased its rules for mid-size banks.
cards.h: → what the law did + both sides of the debate
cards.n: Confusing Dodd-Frank with the 2008 bailout (TARP) is common; TARP rescued the banks, Dodd-Frank regulated them afterward.

cards.q: Identify California's Proposition 209 (1996) and the national debate over affirmative action it reflected.
cards.a: Proposition 209, approved by California voters in 1996, banned racial and gender preferences in state hiring, contracting and public university admissions. It reflected conservative arguments that affirmative action was reverse discrimination, against defenders who saw it as a remedy for past and present discrimination. The Supreme Court allowed limited race-conscious admissions in Grutter v. Bollinger (2003) but ended them in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023).
cards.h: → what it banned + the two sides + the Court's path
cards.n: Illustrative: the KC names 'diversity' debates, not Prop 209. Do not confuse it with Proposition 187 (1994), which targeted services for undocumented immigrants.

cards.q:
Compare the two described sources on the 1996 welfare law.
Source 1 (a labeled paraphrase of President Clinton's remarks on signing it, August 1996): the law turns welfare from a way of life into a path to work and frees states to design their own programs; its flaws, such as cuts in aid to legal immigrants, can be fixed later.
Source 2 (a labeled composite paraphrase of critics, among them Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan, 1995-1996): ending the federal guarantee of cash aid will push large numbers of children into poverty, and states will compete to cut benefits.
cards.a: Similarity: both treat the law as a decisive break with the federal guarantee of cash aid created in 1935. Difference: Source 1 claims the break is healthy, turning aid into a route to work and freeing states to innovate; Source 2 claims ending the guarantee will impoverish children and set off a race to the bottom among states. The clash is KC-9.1.I.C's debate over the scope of the safety net.
cards.h: → shared premise + the point of conflict
cards.n: Quoting each source without naming the shared premise and the point of conflict earns nothing; the comparison must be explicit.

cards.q: Explain the economic effects of Reagan's policies.
cards.a: The effects were mixed. Tight money from the Federal Reserve and a deep recession broke inflation by 1983, and a long expansion followed; but tax cuts plus a military buildup roughly tripled the national debt, and deregulation and pressure on unions came with falling union membership and widening inequality.
cards.h: → Fed tight money + tax cuts → inflation broken, growth → but deficits and inequality rise
cards.n: One-sided praise or blame earns less than weighing growth against deficits and inequality; note that the Fed, not Reagan, set tight money.
o: The supply-side promise failed on revenue: with top rates cut from 70 to 28 percent and defense spending up, the deficit reached about 6 percent of GDP in 1983.
Deregulation's costs showed in the savings and loan collapse, whose cleanup cost taxpayers roughly 124 billion dollars.

w.a: Reagan's tax cuts paid for themselves and balanced the budget.
w.why: false; deficits and debt soared

w.a: Reagan's policies caused a great depression in the 1980s.
w.why: the 1981-82 recession ended in 1982 and growth followed

w.a: Reagan's policies had no effect because Congress was Democratic.
w.why: ignores the 1981 tax cut and budget cuts Congress passed

cards.q: Explain why the election of 1980 is considered a realigning election.
cards.a: It rearranged party coalitions for decades. White Southerners, evangelicals and many blue-collar Northern Democrats voted Republican alongside economic conservatives, and the GOP won the Senate. That coalition won three straight presidential elections and slowly turned the South Republican.
cards.h: → stagflation + hostages sink Carter → new groups shift to GOP → durable coalition + Senate
cards.n: Reagan won just under 51 percent (Anderson ran third), so argue from the lasting shift in who voted Republican, not from the popular-vote margin.
o: The election broke the New Deal coalition's hold, since white Southerners and many union households, its pillars since the 1930s, split away.
The shift outlasted Reagan: George H. W. Bush won in 1988 with much the same coalition, and the South kept moving Republican in Congress through 1994.

w.a: 1980 was a realigning election because Reagan won every state.
w.why: false; Carter won six states and D.C.

w.a: 1980 was realigning because Democrats never won the presidency again.
w.why: false; Clinton won in 1992

w.a: 1980 was realigning because Reagan won a huge popular vote.
w.why: under 51 percent; realignment is about coalitions

cards.q: Explain how the Christian Coalition extended the religious right's political influence after the Moral Majority.
cards.a: It moved religious-right power from national TV preachers into precinct politics. Founded by Pat Robertson in 1989 as the Moral Majority folded, and run by Ralph Reed, it distributed church voter guides and trained local activists, and it helped Republicans win Congress in 1994.
cards.h: → Moral Majority folds → Coalition organizes locally (voter guides, school boards) → GOP gains 1994
cards.n: Saying it simply 'continued' the Moral Majority earns less than naming the change: grassroots organizing inside the Republican Party.
o: By targeting school boards and state party conventions, the Coalition made evangelicals a permanent Republican constituency rather than a movement led by a few preachers.
Its voter guides, handed out in churches before elections, turned congregations into get-out-the-vote networks, continuing the mobilization begun in 1979.

w.a: The Christian Coalition extended the religious right by founding the Moral Majority in 1989.
w.why: reverses the two; Falwell founded the Moral Majority in 1979

w.a: The Christian Coalition won influence by electing Pat Robertson president in 1988.
w.why: false; Robertson lost the nomination

cards.q: Explain why many New Deal and Great Society programs survived the conservative ascendancy after 1980.
cards.a: They had large, organized constituencies. Social Security and Medicare served nearly every older voter, and older voters turn out heavily, so cuts were punished; Democrats held the House until 1995; and conservatives shifted to trimming growth instead of repeal, as in the 1983 Social Security rescue.
cards.h: → universal programs build voting blocs → cuts politically costly → trimming replaces repeal
cards.n: 'Reagan chose to keep them' names no cause; KC-9.1.I.B credits inertia, liberal opposition and the programs' popularity with voters.
o: Programs tied to work and age were seen as earned, not charity, so voters defended them even while backing cuts to 'welfare.'
When Gingrich's Congress sought large Medicare savings in 1995, the government shutdowns that followed hurt Republicans and helped Clinton win in 1996.

w.a: The programs survived because conservatives agreed with the New Deal.
w.why: ignores repeated efforts to cut them

w.a: The programs survived because the Supreme Court ruled they could not be cut.
w.why: no such ruling; Congress sets benefits

cards.q: Explain why Bill Clinton's presidency showed continuity with Reagan-era conservatism rather than a return to Great Society liberalism.
cards.a: Clinton governed as a 'New Democrat' on terms Reagan had set. He balanced the budget, signed welfare reform with work requirements and time limits, backed NAFTA and bank deregulation, and declared 'the era of big government is over,' while defending Medicare.
cards.h: → Reagan moves the center → Clinton triangulates → budget, welfare, trade, deregulation follow
cards.n: 'Clinton was a liberal Democrat' earns nothing; the continuity claim needs Clinton policies that followed conservative premises.
o: The 1999 repeal of the Glass-Steagall wall between commercial and investment banking, signed by Clinton, continued the deregulation Reagan had championed.
The collapse of Clinton's 1993-94 health plan and the 1994 Republican sweep show the limits voters put on any renewed liberal expansion.

w.a: Clinton continued Reagan's policies because he was a Republican.
w.why: false; Clinton was a Democrat

w.a: Clinton reversed Reagan by raising taxes, so there was no continuity.
w.why: ignores welfare reform, NAFTA and balanced budgets

cards.q: Explain why law and public opinion on same-sex marriage changed so rapidly between 1996 and 2015.
cards.a: Visibility and litigation moved together. As more gay Americans came out, most people knew someone gay; state court wins such as Massachusetts (2004) made married couples familiar; and younger voters backed equality, so Gallup support rose from 27 percent (1996) to 60 percent (2015).
cards.h: → more visibility + state court wins → generational shift in opinion → DOMA to Obergefell
cards.n: Crediting the Supreme Court alone reverses the sequence: opinion and state law shifted first, and the Court ruled after majorities had changed.
o: Generational replacement mattered: Americans who grew up with openly gay peers backed marriage equality by wide margins, so each electorate was more supportive.
After Windsor (2013), federal courts struck down state bans one after another, so by early 2015 same-sex marriage was already legal in most states.

w.a: Opinion changed because Congress legalized same-sex marriage in 2004.
