w.why: false; a Massachusetts court ruling did, in one state

w.a: Opinion never changed; the Supreme Court forced marriage equality on the public.
w.why: polls showed majority support by 2011

cards.q: Explain why the Affordable Care Act continued rather than ended the long debate over the federal role in health care.
cards.a: It extended an old pattern of partial federal coverage without settling it. Like Medicare (1965), it widened coverage through a mix of public programs and private insurers, stopping short of a national system; opponents attacked it as Truman's plan had been attacked, and repeal efforts went on.
cards.h: → ACA widens coverage by mixed design → stops short of universal system → opposition renews debate
cards.n: Calling the ACA the first federal health program ignores Medicare and Medicaid (1965); the continuity claim needs that earlier evidence.
o: The repeal fight shows continuity: House Republicans voted dozens of times to repeal it, and a 2017 Senate repeal bill failed 49 to 51.
The Supreme Court's 2012 ruling that made the Medicaid expansion optional left a patchwork of state choices, keeping the debate alive state by state.

w.a: The ACA ended the debate because it created one government insurance plan for everyone.
w.why: false; it relies on private insurers

w.a: The ACA continued the debate because the Supreme Court struck it down in 2012.
w.why: false; the Court upheld it

cards.q: Identify the Reagan Doctrine and the Strategic Defense Initiative.
cards.a: The Reagan Doctrine was the policy of arming and funding anticommunist insurgents fighting Soviet-backed governments, among them the mujahideen in Afghanistan, the Contras in Nicaragua and UNITA in Angola, to roll back Soviet influence rather than only contain it. The Strategic Defense Initiative (1983), mocked as 'Star Wars,' proposed a space-based shield against nuclear missiles; it was never built, but Soviet leaders feared a costly technology race.
cards.h: → each policy: what it was + its purpose
cards.n: Calling SDI a working missile shield is the trap: it stayed research. Its effect came through Soviet fears, which historians still weigh.

cards.q: Identify the Iran-Contra affair.
cards.a: In 1985-1986 Reagan administration officials secretly sold arms to Iran, despite an arms embargo, hoping to free American hostages in Lebanon, and National Security Council aide Oliver North diverted profits to the Contras fighting Nicaragua's Sandinista government, though the Boland Amendment barred such aid. Exposed in November 1986, it led to congressional hearings and convictions of aides (some overturned or pardoned); Reagan was not charged.
cards.h: → the two secret deals + the law broken + the fallout
cards.n: It belongs with the Reagan Doctrine (covert aid to anticommunist rebels). The issue is defying a law Congress passed, not a Watergate-style burglary.

cards.q: Identify Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms.
cards.a: Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet leader from 1985, launched glasnost (openness), which relaxed censorship and allowed public criticism, and perestroika (restructuring), which added limited market mechanisms to the stagnant planned economy. He also cut military commitments, signed the INF Treaty (1987), pulled Soviet troops out of Afghanistan (1988-1989), and in 1989 refused to use force to keep Eastern Europe's communist governments in power.
cards.h: → the two named reforms + his foreign-policy moves
cards.n: Glasnost and perestroika are not interchangeable: one is political openness, the other economic restructuring. Mixing them up costs the point.

cards.q: Identify the fall of the Berlin Wall and the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
cards.a: In 1989 communist governments in Eastern Europe fell one after another, mostly peacefully, beginning with Poland's partly free election won by Solidarity; East Germany opened the Berlin Wall on November 9, 1989, and Germany reunified in October 1990. After hard-liners' failed coup against Gorbachev in August 1991, the Soviet republics broke away, and the USSR dissolved into 15 independent states in December 1991.
cards.h: → 1989 revolutions + the Wall + the 1991 collapse
cards.n: Treating the Wall's fall and the Soviet collapse as one event is the trap: Eastern Europe broke free in 1989, the USSR itself ended two years later.

cards.q: Identify the Persian Gulf War (1991).
cards.a: After Iraq under Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990, George H. W. Bush built a UN-authorized coalition of about 35 nations; Operation Desert Storm, a five-week air campaign followed by a 100-hour ground war (January-February 1991), drove Iraqi forces out with few U.S. casualties. Bush stopped short of Baghdad, leaving Saddam in power, and U.S. forces stayed in Saudi Arabia.
cards.h: → cause + coalition + result + what was left undone
cards.n: It is the first large post-Cold War intervention, not a Cold War proxy war: the Soviet Union voted for the UN resolution authorizing force.

cards.q: Compare U.S. foreign policy during the Cold War with policy after 1991.
cards.a: Similarity: in both eras the United States kept a global military presence, alliances such as NATO and a readiness to intervene abroad. Difference: Cold War policy was organized around containing one rival state, the Soviet Union, through deterrence, alliances and proxy conflicts; after 1991 the sole superpower intervened in regional wars and humanitarian crises (Gulf War, Somalia, the Balkans) and, after 2001, against nonstate terrorist networks.
cards.h: → one similarity + one difference, stated explicitly
cards.n: Describing each era separately is not a comparison; state the similarity (intervention) and the difference (the kind of enemy) outright.

cards.q: Date the fall of the Berlin Wall and the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
cards.a: The Berlin Wall opened on November 9, 1989; the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, when Gorbachev resigned on December 25. Between them came German reunification (October 1990) and the failed hard-line coup of August 1991.
cards.h: → two dates + what came between
cards.n: Swapping the dates is a common multiple-choice error: Eastern Europe's revolutions come first, the USSR's own collapse second.

cards.q: Identify the U.S. invasion of Panama (1989).
cards.a: In December 1989 George H. W. Bush sent some 26,000 troops into Panama (Operation Just Cause) to remove General Manuel Noriega, who had been indicted in the United States on drug-trafficking charges and had annulled an election; officials also cited threats to Americans and the canal. Noriega surrendered in January 1990 and was convicted in a U.S. court.
cards.h: → who ordered it + target + reasons + outcome
cards.n: Noriega had long worked with U.S. intelligence, so the invasion shows a Cold War asset becoming a liability, not an anticommunist mission.

cards.q: Identify the 1992-93 U.S. intervention in Somalia.
cards.a: In December 1992 George H. W. Bush sent U.S. troops to Somalia to protect famine relief amid civil war. Under Clinton the UN-led mission widened into a hunt for the warlord Mohamed Farrah Aidid, and in the Battle of Mogadishu (October 1993) 18 Americans were killed. Clinton withdrew U.S. forces by March 1994.
cards.h: → humanitarian start + mission creep + withdrawal
cards.n: The lesson leaders drew, reluctance to risk troops in humanitarian missions, is the point; it helps explain inaction in Rwanda in 1994.

cards.q: Identify U.S. intervention in the Balkans during the 1990s.
cards.a: As Yugoslavia broke apart, Clinton backed NATO air strikes against Bosnian Serb forces in 1995 and brokered the Dayton Accords (1995), which ended the Bosnian war and put U.S. troops in a NATO peacekeeping force. In 1999 he led a 78-day NATO bombing campaign against Serbia to stop the ethnic cleansing of Albanians in Kosovo, without UN Security Council authorization.
cards.h: → Bosnia + Dayton + Kosovo, each with its method
cards.n: It shows KC-9.3.I.C's 'peacekeeping interventions' and the debate over force without UN approval; calling it a Cold War action is wrong.

cards.q: Identify two speeches in which Reagan asserted U.S. opposition to communism, with the message of each.
cards.a: 'Evil empire' speech (March 1983, to the National Association of Evangelicals): called the Soviet Union an 'evil empire' and rejected a nuclear freeze, framing the Cold War as a moral struggle. Brandenburg Gate speech (June 1987, West Berlin): challenged the Soviet leader, 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!', daring him to prove his reforms by opening the Berlin Wall.
cards.h: → speech + year + audience + message, twice
cards.n: Quoting the line is not enough; name the purpose: a moral rejection of detente in 1983, a public test of Gorbachev's reforms in 1987.

cards.q: Identify the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty of 1987.
cards.a: Signed by Reagan and Gorbachev in Washington in December 1987, the INF Treaty eliminated all U.S. and Soviet ground-launched missiles with ranges of about 500 to 5,500 kilometers, the first treaty to abolish a whole class of nuclear weapons, and it allowed on-site inspections. It followed the failed Reykjavik summit (1986) and marked Reagan's turn from confrontation to negotiation.
cards.h: → who + when + what it eliminated + why new
cards.n: Calling it an arms limitation like SALT misses what was new: it eliminated a class of weapons and allowed inspections.

cards.q: Identify two limited military interventions of the Reagan years and the outcome of each.
cards.a: Lebanon (1982-1984): Marines joined a multinational peacekeeping force in Beirut; after a suicide truck bomb killed 241 U.S. service members in October 1983, Reagan withdrew them in early 1984. Grenada (October 1983): U.S. forces invaded the Caribbean island after a Marxist coup, citing danger to American medical students, and installed an interim government. Libya (April 1986): air strikes answered a terrorist bombing of a Berlin nightclub.
cards.h: → place + year + purpose + outcome, twice
cards.n: 'Limited' is the KC's word: short, small operations, not wars. Confusing Grenada with the Contra war, a covert proxy effort, loses the point.

cards.q: Describe the military buildup of the Reagan years.
cards.a: Defense spending rose from about 134 billion dollars in 1980 to about 300 billion by 1989 (current dollars), from about 5 to about 6 percent of GDP at its mid-1980s peak. The buildup revived the B-1 bomber, deployed MX and Pershing II missiles (the Pershings in Western Europe from 1983), expanded the Navy toward 600 ships and funded SDI research, largely with borrowed money.
cards.h: → scale with numbers + what it bought + how it was paid for
cards.n: Crediting the increase to Reagan alone misses that Carter began raising defense spending after 1979; and deficits, not cuts elsewhere, paid for it.

cards.q: Identify the U.S. response to the 1994 genocide in Rwanda and what it shows about post-Cold War debates over American power.
cards.a: The United States did not intervene while Hutu extremists killed an estimated 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in about 100 days in 1994; wary after Somalia, the Clinton administration avoided the word 'genocide' and backed shrinking the UN force there. Clinton later apologized for the inaction. It shows the post-Cold War debate over when humanitarian crises justify force, answered differently in Bosnia and Kosovo.
cards.h: → what happened + U.S. response + what it shows
cards.n: Non-intervention is still evidence: KC-9.3.I.C is about the debate over using power, and Rwanda is the case where the answer was no. Death tolls are estimates.

cards.q: Classify each U.S. action as COLD WAR (anticommunist) or POST-COLD WAR (collective security, humanitarian or peacekeeping), with its purpose in a phrase: aid to the Afghan mujahideen (1980s) · aid to the Contras (1980s) · invasion of Grenada (1983) · Pershing II deployment in Europe (1983) · Operation Desert Storm (1991) · Somalia mission (1992-93) · restoring President Aristide in Haiti (1994) · Dayton Accords peacekeeping (1995) · Kosovo air war (1999) · NATO admission of Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic (1999)
cards.a:
Afghan mujahideen → Cold War (Reagan Doctrine: bleed the Soviet occupation)
Contras → Cold War (Reagan Doctrine: pressure Nicaragua's Sandinistas)
Grenada → Cold War (remove a Marxist regime tied to Cuba)
Pershing II → Cold War (counter Soviet SS-20 missiles aimed at Europe)
Desert Storm → post-Cold War (UN-backed collective security: reverse Iraq's conquest of Kuwait)
Somalia → post-Cold War (humanitarian: protect famine relief)
Haiti → post-Cold War (restore an elected president)
Dayton peacekeeping → post-Cold War (NATO peacekeeping in Bosnia)
Kosovo → post-Cold War (humanitarian air war against ethnic cleansing)
NATO expansion → post-Cold War (new diplomatic ties with former Soviet-bloc states)
cards.h: → label + purpose phrase, each case
cards.n: Labeling by date alone earns nothing; the purpose phrase (anticommunist vs humanitarian or collective security) is what the task tests.

cards.q: Explain why the Cold War ended.
cards.a: Soviet weakness and Soviet choices ended it, with U.S. pressure adding weight. A stagnant command economy, falling oil prices and the Afghan war drained the USSR; Gorbachev loosened control and refused to use force in 1989; Reagan's buildup raised costs and his diplomacy made arms deals possible.
cards.h: → Soviet economy fails + Gorbachev reforms, no force in 1989 + U.S. pressure and diplomacy → bloc collapses
cards.n: Crediting Reagan alone, or Soviet collapse alone, earns less; KC-9.3.I.B names U.S. actions and Soviet and East European changes together.
o: Movements inside the bloc, from Poland's Solidarity to the crowds in Leipzig and Berlin in 1989, dissolved communist rule from below once Moscow would not intervene.
Nationalism inside the Soviet Union, from the Baltic republics to Ukraine, broke the union apart after the failed August 1991 coup.

w.a: The Cold War ended because the United States defeated the Soviet Union in a war.
w.why: there was no direct war; the USSR collapsed internally

w.a: The Cold War ended because Star Wars made Soviet missiles useless.
w.why: SDI was never built

w.a: The Cold War ended when the Berlin Wall was built.
w.why: the Wall went up in 1961 and opened in 1989

cards.q: Explain why historians disagree about how much Reagan's military buildup contributed to ending the Cold War.
cards.a: The evidence supports two causal stories. The buildup and SDI raised the cost of competing for a Soviet economy already failing, pushing leaders toward reform; yet Soviet stagnation began earlier, and Gorbachev's own choices, not U.S. arms, decided to let Eastern Europe go.
cards.h: → buildup raises Soviet costs vs Soviet decline predates Reagan → relative weight of causes contested
cards.n: Picking a side without weighing the other earns less; KC-9.3.I.B calls U.S. spending and Soviet and East European problems 'all important.'
o: Some historians credit Reagan's diplomacy more than his arms: his readiness to deal with Gorbachev at Reykjavik and in the INF Treaty let the Soviet leader cut military spending safely.
Others argue confrontation strengthened Soviet hard-liners during the 1983 war scare, so the buildup alone did not produce reform.

w.a: Historians agree the buildup alone bankrupted the Soviet Union.
w.why: overstates; there is no consensus

w.a: The buildup did not matter because the Soviets spent little on their military.
w.why: false; Soviet defense spending was enormous

cards.q: Explain why Gorbachev's reforms hastened rather than prevented the collapse of Soviet power.
cards.a: Reforms meant to save the system loosened what held it together. Glasnost let citizens and nationalities air grievances openly; perestroika disrupted the planned economy without building a market; and his refusal to use force in 1989 told East Europeans and Soviet republics they could leave.
cards.h: → glasnost frees criticism + perestroika disrupts economy + no force in 1989 → satellites and republics break away
cards.n: 'Gorbachev wanted to end communism' earns nothing; he aimed to reform it, and the point is the unintended effect.
o: Partly free elections in 1989-1990 gave nationalist movements in the Baltics and Ukraine platforms to demand independence.
Shortages worsened as perestroika weakened central planning, costing the reformers support and emboldening the hard-liners whose failed 1991 coup finished the union.

w.a: Gorbachev's reforms failed because he was a hard-line Stalinist.
w.why: false; he was a reformer

w.a: Gorbachev's reforms at once created a full free-market economy.
w.why: perestroika added only limited market mechanisms

cards.q: Explain why the Iran-Contra affair became a constitutional scandal and not only a foreign-policy failure.
cards.a: Officials used executive power to defy Congress. The Boland Amendment barred aid to the Contras, yet NSC staff secretly funded them with arms-sale profits, bypassing Congress's power of the purse, and then shredded documents, so, like Watergate, it raised whether a president's aides were above the law.
cards.h: → Congress bans Contra aid → NSC funds it secretly → power of the purse evaded → constitutional clash
cards.n: Calling it a scandal about 'selling weapons' misses the point: the constitutional issue is evading a law Congress passed.
o: It continues the struggle over war powers from Vietnam on: after the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Congress again tried to limit covert executive action.
Selling arms to Iran also broke the administration's public refusal to bargain with hostage-takers, which damaged Reagan's credibility at home.

w.a: Iran-Contra was a constitutional scandal because Reagan was impeached for it.
w.why: false; Reagan was never impeached

w.a: Iran-Contra was illegal because presidents cannot make foreign policy.
w.why: they can; the problem was defying a specific law

cards.q: Explain why the end of the Cold War led to new U.S. military and peacekeeping interventions rather than a retreat from world affairs.
cards.a: Removing the Soviet check freed the United States to act. As sole superpower with forces already worldwide, it could send troops without risking war with Moscow, and regional aggression and ethnic wars that the Cold War had frozen, in Kuwait, Somalia and the Balkans, now drew it in.
cards.h: → Soviet check removed → sole superpower with forces in place → new regional crises → interventions
cards.n: 'America wanted to rule the world' is an assertion, not a cause; name the mechanism: no Soviet check on action plus new crises.
o: The UN Security Council, deadlocked through the Cold War, could now authorize force, as it did against Iraq in 1990, making coalition interventions easier.
Leaders justified new missions as humanitarian, stretching American purpose from containing communism to stopping famine and ethnic cleansing.

w.a: The U.S. intervened after 1991 to keep fighting the Soviet Union.
w.why: the Soviet Union no longer existed

w.a: After 1991 the U.S. retreated into isolationism as in the 1920s.
w.why: false; it intervened in the Gulf, Somalia, Haiti and the Balkans

cards.q: Explain why the 1991 Gulf War created problems that shaped later U.S. policy in the Middle East.
cards.a: It won the war but left the region unsettled. Saddam Hussein stayed in power under sanctions and no-fly zones, which kept U.S. forces committed for a decade, and U.S. troops remained in Saudi Arabia, which Osama bin Laden cited as a grievance; both paths led toward 2001 and 2003.
cards.h: → Saddam survives + troops stay in Saudi Arabia → sanctions, no-fly zones, al-Qaeda grievance → 2001 and 2003
cards.n: Calling the Gulf War a failure misreads it: its stated goal, freeing Kuwait, was met. The causal point is its unfinished aftermath.
o: Bush's decision not to march on Baghdad, taken to hold the coalition together, left the regime-change question that his son's administration answered in 2003.
The quick, low-casualty victory bred confidence in high-tech American power, which shaped expectations for the 2003 invasion.

w.a: The Gulf War caused 9/11 because Iraq planned the attacks.
w.why: false; al-Qaeda, not Iraq, carried them out

w.a: The Gulf War removed Saddam Hussein, so it had no later effects.
w.why: false; Saddam ruled until 2003

cards.q: Explain how the end of the Cold War produced new diplomatic relationships for the United States.
cards.a: With the Soviet bloc gone, former enemies could become partners. Arms treaties with Moscow (START I, 1991) cut arsenals; NATO admitted Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic in 1999; the U.S. normalized relations with Vietnam in 1995; and trade with China grew without the anti-Soviet logic.
cards.h: → Soviet threat ends → former rivals become partners → arms cuts, NATO expansion, ties with Vietnam and China
cards.n: Listing treaties without linking them to the end of the Soviet threat is description, not causation.
o: NATO's eastward expansion, sought by Central Europeans wanting security, was also criticized for antagonizing Russia, part of the debate over American power in KC-9.3.I.C.
The United States and Russia cooperated to secure former Soviet nuclear weapons under the Nunn-Lugar program (1991), a partnership unthinkable before.

w.a: After the Cold War the United States formed an alliance with the Soviet Union.
w.why: the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991

w.a: The end of the Cold War ended NATO.
w.why: false; NATO expanded

cards.q: Identify NAFTA and the digital revolution as forces of globalization.
cards.a: NAFTA, in effect from January 1994, phased out most tariffs among the United States, Canada and Mexico; trade among the three grew several-fold, with supply chains, especially in autos, running across borders. The digital revolution (personal computers, the internet, later smartphones) let firms coordinate production and services worldwide, raising productivity and U.S. participation in global markets. Both brought cheaper goods and new jobs, and cost factory jobs.
cards.h: → each force: what it was + how it globalized
cards.n: 'Globalization' alone is a label; name each force's mechanism (tariff cuts, digital coordination) and both kinds of effect.

cards.q: Identify the 2008 financial crisis and the government response.
cards.a: A housing bubble built on subprime mortgages, packaged into securities held worldwide, collapsed in 2007-2008; Lehman Brothers failed in September 2008, credit froze and the Great Recession followed, with unemployment reaching 10 percent in 2009. The response: the 700-billion-dollar TARP bank rescue (2008), near-zero interest rates and bond buying by the Fed, the auto bailout, the 2009 stimulus (about 800 billion) and Dodd-Frank (2010).
cards.h: → cause + collapse + effects + federal response
cards.n: Listing the response without the cause (mortgage securities, leverage) earns half. TARP was signed by Bush, so the rescue was bipartisan.

cards.q: Compare the federal response to the Great Depression with the response to the 2008 recession.
cards.a: Similarity: both times Washington rescued the financial system and pumped money into the economy, and each crisis produced new financial regulation (the SEC and FDIC in the 1930s; Dodd-Frank in 2010). Difference: the 2008 response came within weeks, relied on the Federal Reserve and bank rescues on a vast scale and on existing safety nets, while the New Deal came after more than three years of collapse and built lasting programs and direct federal jobs such as the WPA.
cards.h: → one similarity + one difference, each with evidence
cards.n: The comparison needs a stated similarity and difference; noting that New Deal institutions (FDIC, unemployment insurance) cushioned 2008 adds continuity.

cards.q: Date the financial crisis, Obama's election, and the Affordable Care Act.
cards.a: The financial crisis peaked in September 2008 (Lehman Brothers failed on September 15); Obama was elected on November 4, 2008; and he signed the Affordable Care Act on March 23, 2010.
cards.h: → three dates in order
cards.n: The chain matters: the crisis helped elect Obama, and the large Democratic majorities it brought passed the ACA before the 2010 midterms ended them.

cards.q: Identify the PATCO strike of 1981.
cards.a: In August 1981 about 13,000 members of the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization, federal employees barred by law from striking, walked out for higher pay and shorter hours. Reagan fired more than 11,000 who ignored his order to return and barred them from federal rehiring, and the union was decertified. Private employers read it as license to replace strikers, and strikes and union membership fell afterward.
cards.h: → who struck + Reagan's response + the signal it sent
cards.n: PATCO is a symbol, not the whole cause: union decline also came from deindustrialization and global competition.

cards.q: Identify the World Trade Organization and give its founding year.
cards.a: 1995. The World Trade Organization replaced the GATT framework (1947) as the body that sets rules for international trade and settles disputes among members; the United States helped create it in the Uruguay Round talks. China's admission in 2001 greatly expanded U.S. imports, and the WTO's 1999 meeting in Seattle drew mass protests by unions, environmentalists and anti-globalization activists.
cards.h: → year + what it does + what it replaced
cards.n: The WTO is not a U.S. agency or a regional free-trade zone like NAFTA; it is a global rule-making body that replaced the GATT.

cards.q: Date the founding of the WTO, NAFTA's implementation, and the 2008 financial crisis in order.
cards.a: NAFTA took effect on January 1, 1994; the World Trade Organization began on January 1, 1995; the financial crisis struck in 2008, peaking that September. The order runs from trade liberalization to the worst downturn since the Great Depression.
cards.h: → three dates in order
cards.n: NAFTA's start date is the trap: it was signed in 1992 under George H. W. Bush and approved in 1993 under Clinton, but took effect in 1994.

cards.q: Explain the debate over NAFTA's effects on American manufacturing jobs.
cards.a: Critics, among them Ross Perot, who in 1992 warned of a 'giant sucking sound' of jobs going south, and most labor unions, argued NAFTA would move factories to low-wage Mexico and cut U.S. manufacturing jobs and wages. Supporters argued it would lower prices, expand exports and integrate North American production. Most economists find modest net effects, with real losses concentrated in some industries and towns; Clinton passed it with more Republican than Democratic votes.
cards.h: → critics' claim + supporters' claim + the evidence
cards.n: Blaming NAFTA for all factory job loss is the trap: automation and later Chinese imports mattered more, and the decline began in 1979.

cards.q: Identify the Telecommunications Act of 1996.
cards.a: The Telecommunications Act of 1996, the first major rewrite of communications law since 1934, deregulated the industry: it let telephone, cable and broadcast companies enter each other's markets and loosened limits on media ownership, which led to rapid consolidation, especially in radio. Its Section 230 shielded online platforms from liability for users' posts, a legal foundation of the later internet economy.
cards.h: → what it deregulated + two effects
cards.n: Illustrative: the KCs do not name it. Link it to deregulation and the internet's growth, not only to media mergers.

cards.q: Explain how the internet and social media reshaped American news consumption after 2000.
cards.a: The internet moved news from print and broadcast schedules to constant online feeds. Advertising shifted to Google and Facebook, so newspaper revenue fell and newsroom jobs dropped by more than half from 2008 to 2020 (Pew), closing many local papers; social media let people choose sources that fit their views, and algorithms rewarded outrage. Many scholars link this to deeper polarization and misinformation, though the size of the effect is debated.
cards.h: → shift + economic effect on papers + effect on audiences
cards.n: 'People got their news online' describes; the explanation needs the mechanism: lost ad revenue, closed papers, self-selected and algorithmic feeds.

cards.q: State how manufacturing employment and union membership changed between about 1980 and 2020.
cards.a: Manufacturing jobs fell from a peak of about 19.6 million in 1979 to about 11.5 million in 2010, recovering only to about 12.8 million by 2019, while service jobs in health care, retail, finance and technology grew to more than four in five jobs. Union membership fell from 20.1 percent of wage and salary workers in 1983 to about 10 percent by the early 2020s, and about 6 percent in the private sector.
cards.h: → two trends, each with numbers
cards.n: BLS figures, rounded. Saying 'manufacturing output collapsed' is wrong: output kept rising for decades while jobs fell, largely because of automation.

cards.q:
Interpret the data. Union membership as a percentage of U.S. wage and salary workers (Bureau of Labor Statistics, rounded to whole percents):
Year · Percent
1983 · 20
1990 · 16
2000 · 13
2010 · 12
2020 · 11
Identify the pattern and explain one cause of it.
cards.a: Pattern: union membership fell steadily, roughly halving from about 20 percent in 1983 to about 11 percent in 2020, fastest in the 1980s. Cause: deindustrialization moved jobs from unionized factories into service work that was harder to organize, and employers, emboldened after Reagan fired the PATCO strikers in 1981, more often hired replacements and resisted organizing drives.
cards.h: → pattern with numbers + one cause with mechanism
cards.n: The 2020 figure rose from about 10.3 in 2019 only because many low-paid nonunion workers lost jobs in the pandemic; do not read it as a union revival.

cards.q: Describe the pattern of real wages and income inequality in the United States from 1980 to about 2015.
cards.a: Real wages for most workers barely grew: Pew Research found in 2018 that the average hourly wage bought about what it had 40 years earlier, even as productivity kept rising. Gains went to the top: the richest 1 percent's share of national income roughly doubled, from about 10 percent around 1980 to over 20 percent by the 2010s (Piketty-Saez estimates), and real median household income was lower in 2012 than in 1999.
cards.h: → wages vs productivity + the top's share, with data
cards.n: Estimates vary by method (Piketty-Saez run high). 'Everyone got poorer' is wrong: average income rose, but gains concentrated at the top.

cards.q: Identify three technological innovations after 1980 that transformed daily life, with the change each brought.
cards.a: Personal computer (IBM PC, 1981; common by the 1990s): moved word processing, spreadsheets and games into offices and homes. World Wide Web (public from 1991, commercial internet by the mid-1990s): email, online shopping (Amazon, 1994) and instant access to information. Smartphone (iPhone, 2007): put the internet, maps and social media (Facebook, 2004) in every pocket, creating new social networks, gig work and constant connection.
cards.h: → innovation + date + change, three times
cards.n: Naming gadgets earns little; KC-9.2.I.B asks what changed: access to information, new social behaviors and networks.

cards.q: Identify the Rust Belt and the effects of deindustrialization on it after 1980.
cards.a: The Rust Belt is the old industrial region of the Northeast and Midwest, from Pennsylvania and Ohio through Michigan to Illinois and Wisconsin, where steel, auto and other plants closed or shed workers from the late 1970s on. Towns such as Youngstown, Flint and Gary lost jobs, tax revenue and population, and many residents moved to the Sunbelt. Its discontent later shaped national politics, as in the 2016 election.
cards.h: → where + what happened + effects on people and politics
cards.n: The Rust Belt is a region, not a policy; tie it to plant closures and to out-migration to the Sunbelt (KC-9.2.II.A).

cards.q: Identify China's entry into the World Trade Organization (2001) and its effect on U.S. manufacturing.
cards.a: After Congress granted China permanent normal trade relations in 2000, China joined the WTO in December 2001, and U.S. imports of Chinese goods surged. Economists call the result the 'China shock': one widely cited study (Acemoglu, Autor, Dorn, Hanson and Price, 2016) estimated that Chinese import competition cost 2.0 to 2.4 million U.S. jobs from 1999 to 2011, concentrated in furniture, textile and electronics towns.
cards.h: → what happened + when + estimated effect
cards.n: The job figure is one study's estimate and is debated. Do not date this to NAFTA: the steepest factory job losses came after 2000.

cards.q: Explain the causes of the 2008 financial crisis.
cards.a: Cheap credit and loose lending built a housing bubble; banks packaged risky subprime loans into securities that ratings agencies called safe; lightly regulated, highly leveraged firms held them. When home prices fell in 2007, defaults spread, firms like Lehman collapsed and credit froze.
cards.h: → cheap credit + subprime lending → bubble → securitized risk + leverage → prices fall → defaults cascade
cards.n: 'Greedy bankers' names no mechanism; the chain from lending to securities to leverage to the freeze earns the point.
o: Deregulation mattered: the 1999 repeal of Glass-Steagall and a 2000 law exempting most derivatives from oversight let risk build outside supervision.
Global demand for U.S. mortgage securities, from European banks and Asian savings, fed the bubble and spread the crash worldwide.

w.a: The 2008 crisis was caused by the September 11 attacks.
w.why: no causal link; the bubble burst in 2007

w.a: The 2008 crisis happened because the stock market crashed as in 1929.
w.why: the stock fall was an effect of the credit crisis

w.a: The crisis was caused by Obama's health care law.
w.why: the ACA passed in 2010, after the crisis

cards.q: Explain the rise and collapse of the dot-com bubble.
cards.a: Investors bid up internet start-ups in the late 1990s on hopes of future growth, pushing the tech-heavy NASDAQ from about 1,000 in 1995 to over 5,000 in March 2000, far beyond earnings. When profits failed to appear, many firms folded; by late 2002 the index had lost about three-quarters of its value.
cards.h: → web hype + easy capital → prices outrun earnings → firms fail → 2000-02 crash
cards.n: The crash began in March 2000, before 9/11; saying the attacks caused it is a common error.
o: Its aftermath links it to 2008: the Federal Reserve cut interest rates sharply in 2001, and cheap credit helped inflate the housing bubble.
The bubble left lasting infrastructure: fiber-optic networks built in the boom, and survivors such as Amazon and Google, became the core of the digital economy.

w.a: The dot-com bubble burst because the internet stopped working in 2000.
w.why: the internet kept growing; stock prices fell

w.a: The dot-com crash was caused by the 9/11 attacks.
w.why: it began in March 2000

cards.q: Explain why union membership declined in the United States after 1980.
cards.a: Unions lost the jobs and leverage that sustained them. Unionized factory jobs disappeared through automation, imports and relocation to the South and abroad; new service jobs were harder to organize; and after PATCO (1981), employers replaced strikers and fought organizing drives more openly.
cards.h: → union factory jobs vanish + service jobs hard to organize + employers bolder after PATCO → membership falls
cards.n: 'Workers no longer wanted unions' asserts without a mechanism; name the structural and political causes.
o: Firms moved plants to Sunbelt right-to-work states, where laws allowed since the Taft-Hartley Act (1947) made organizing harder.
Global competition let employers threaten to move production abroad, weakening unions' bargaining power even where plants stayed.

w.a: Unions declined because Reagan made unions illegal.
w.why: false; he broke one federal strike

w.a: Unions declined because wages rose so fast workers no longer needed them.
w.why: wages stagnated in this period

cards.q: Explain why real wages stagnated for working- and middle-class Americans after 1980 even as productivity rose.
cards.a: Workers lost bargaining power while gains flowed elsewhere. Unions shrank; trade and automation held down pay for workers without degrees; the minimum wage lost value to inflation; and tax cuts and rising returns to capital and top salaries sent productivity gains to the wealthy.
cards.h: → unions shrink + trade and automation press wages + minimum wage erodes → gains go to the top
cards.n: 'The economy was bad' ignores the pattern: the economy grew; the point is who captured the growth.
o: The college wage premium widened as computers raised the value of skilled work, so graduates' wages rose while those of high-school graduates stalled.
Rising health-insurance costs absorbed much of employers' spending on compensation, leaving less for take-home pay.

w.a: Real wages stagnated because the economy did not grow after 1980.
w.why: false; GDP and productivity grew

w.a: Wages stagnated because immigrants took all the jobs.
w.why: one overstated cause with no mechanism or evidence

cards.q: Explain how improvements in digital communications increased American participation in the world economy after 1990.
cards.a: Cheap, instant communication let firms work across borders. Companies could manage suppliers and factories abroad in real time, move call centers and software work to India, trade financial assets around the clock, and sell online worldwide, raising productivity and exposing more jobs to global competition.
cards.h: → cheap instant data → global supply chains, offshored services, 24-hour finance → productivity up, jobs exposed
cards.n: Naming 'the internet' without the mechanism, coordination at a distance, does not explain KC-9.2.I.A.
o: Container shipping plus digital inventory tracking let retailers such as Walmart build global supply chains that cut consumer prices.
Digital finance tied U.S. markets to the world, so Asian savings flowed into U.S. assets, a link that also spread the 2008 crisis.

w.a: Digital technology increased trade because the internet was invented in China.
w.why: false; it grew from U.S. research networks

w.a: Digital communications ended manufacturing because computers built everything.
w.why: overstates automation and ignores trade

cards.q: Explain why employment shifted from manufacturing to services after 1980.
cards.a: Two forces cut factory jobs while demand grew elsewhere. Automation let plants make more with fewer workers, and imports, above all from Asia after 2000, replaced domestic production; meanwhile an aging, richer society spent more on health care, education, finance and retail, adding millions of jobs.
cards.h: → automation + imports shrink factory jobs → rising demand for health, finance, retail → services grow
cards.n: Treating manufacturing as dead is the trap: output kept rising; employment fell because of productivity gains and trade.
o: Health care became one of the largest employers as Medicare, private insurance and an aging population expanded demand for care.
Information technology created new service industries, from software to online retail, employing many college-educated workers.

w.a: Jobs shifted to services because Americans stopped buying manufactured goods.
w.why: false; purchases of goods rose, many of them imported

w.a: Service jobs grew because the government banned factories.
w.why: no such policy

cards.q: Identify the demographic changes and immigration debates of the 1990s and 2000s.
cards.a: Immigration, mostly from Latin America and Asia after the 1965 act, doubled the foreign-born population from about 20 million in 1990 to about 40 million in 2010; Latinos became the largest minority group in the early 2000s and Asian Americans the fastest-growing. Debates centered on unauthorized immigrants (11 to 12 million by the late 2000s), border enforcement, public services and a path to citizenship, from Proposition 187 (1994) to failed reform bills and DACA (2012).
cards.h: → the demographic change + the debate's main issues
cards.n: Listing groups without the debate earns half; the KC pairs demographic change with its cultural and political consequences.

cards.q: Compare immigration debates of the 1920s with those of the 2000s.
cards.a: Similarity: in both decades, immigration provoked nativist claims that newcomers took jobs, resisted assimilation and threatened national identity, with demands for restriction. Difference: the 1920s produced sweeping federal law, the national-origins quotas of 1921 and 1924 that ranked Europeans by ethnicity and barred most Asians; the 2000s debate centered on unauthorized immigration, border enforcement and legal status, and Congress failed to pass comprehensive reform.
cards.h: → one similarity + one difference, each with evidence
cards.n: Nativism is the continuity; the comparison earns credit only when it also names the difference in target (ethnic quotas vs legal status) and in outcome.

cards.q: Identify the Mariel Boatlift of 1980.
cards.a: Between April and October 1980 Fidel Castro let about 125,000 Cubans leave from the port of Mariel, most on boats sent by Cuban Americans in Florida, and included some prisoners and mental patients. The influx strained South Florida and hurt Carter politically; unlike earlier Cuban exiles welcomed as Cold War refugees, the 'Marielitos' met a cooler reception. It shows foreign crises driving new migration at the start of Period 9.
cards.h: → who + when + how many + reception
cards.n: Illustrative. Do not present most arrivals as criminals: only a small minority had criminal records.

cards.q: Identify California's Proposition 187 (1994).
cards.a: Proposition 187, approved by 59 percent of California voters in 1994 amid recession, barred undocumented immigrants from public schools, non-emergency health care and other state services and required officials to report suspected undocumented people. Federal courts blocked most of it as conflicting with federal power and Plyler v. Doe (1982), and the state dropped its appeal in 1999. Governor Pete Wilson won reelection backing it, but it pushed Latinos toward the Democrats.
cards.h: → what it did + its legal fate + political effect
cards.n: Do not confuse 187 (1994, services for undocumented immigrants) with 209 (1996, affirmative action); citing 187 as enforced law is wrong.

cards.q: Identify the Immigration Act of 1990.
cards.a: Signed by George H. W. Bush, the Immigration Act of 1990 raised the annual ceiling on legal immigration (to 700,000 for 1992-1994, then 675,000), expanded employment-based visas, created the H-1B visa for skilled workers and set up the diversity visa lottery for countries with low recent immigration. It shows the expansionist side of the debate, favoring legal and skilled immigrants.
cards.h: → who signed + what it raised + what it created
cards.n: It expanded legal immigration; mixing it up with IRCA (1986), which dealt with unauthorized immigrants, is the classic error.

cards.q: State how the size of the U.S. immigrant population changed between 1970 and 2010.
cards.a: The foreign-born population rose from about 9.6 million (4.7 percent of Americans) in 1970, the lowest share on record, to about 40 million (about 13 percent) in 2010, roughly quadrupling in number and nearly tripling as a share of the population. Its main sources shifted from Europe to Latin America and Asia after the 1965 Hart-Celler Act.
cards.h: → start and end figures + the shift in sources
cards.n: Census figures, rounded. The 2010 share was still below the 1890 record of about 14.8 percent, so 'the highest ever' needs that qualification.

cards.q: Identify the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986.
cards.a: Signed by Reagan, the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 (Simpson-Mazzoli) offered legal status to undocumented immigrants who had lived in the United States continuously since before 1982, and to certain farmworkers, about 2.7 million people in all, and for the first time penalized employers who knowingly hired undocumented workers. Weak enforcement of those penalties let unauthorized immigration keep growing.
cards.h: → who signed + the two halves of the bargain + result
cards.n: Opponents later called it 'amnesty'; the trap is forgetting it was a bipartisan bargain: legalization in exchange for enforcement.

cards.q: Identify Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA, 2012).
cards.a: DACA was a 2012 Obama executive action, taken after Congress failed to pass the DREAM Act, that deferred deportation and granted renewable work permits to undocumented immigrants brought to the United States as children (the 'Dreamers'); about 800,000 people enrolled. Trump moved to end it in 2017, but the Supreme Court blocked the repeal on procedural grounds in 2020 (DHS v. Regents).
cards.h: → who + how + whom it covered + its legal fate
cards.n: DACA is neither a law nor a path to citizenship; it is temporary relief by executive action, which is why it stayed vulnerable in court.

cards.q: State how the Latino and Asian American populations changed between 1990 and 2020.
cards.a: The Latino population nearly tripled, from about 22 million (9 percent) in 1990 to about 62 million (about 19 percent) in 2020, and Latinos passed African Americans as the largest minority group in the early 2000s. Asian Americans grew fastest of any major group, from about 7 million to about 20 million, and by 2010 Asia had passed Latin America as the largest source of new immigrants.
cards.h: → each group: start, end, and one milestone
cards.n: Census figures, rounded. Most Latino growth after 2000 came from U.S. births, not new immigration; treating every Latino as an immigrant is the trap.

cards.q: Identify the population shift to the South and West after 1980 and one measure of its political effect.
cards.a: Americans kept moving to the Sunbelt, drawn by jobs, lower taxes and living costs, weaker unions, retirement and air conditioning, and most new immigrants settled there too. California grew from about 24 million people in 1980 to about 37 million in 2010, Texas from about 14 million to about 25 million. Political effect: after the 2010 census Texas gained four House seats and Florida two, while New York and Ohio lost two each.
cards.h: → the shift + why + one measurable political effect
cards.n: Measure influence with evidence (House seats, electoral votes), not 'more people moved there.' Rust Belt out-migration is the other half.

cards.q: Describe how the political influence of the South and West grew after 1980.
cards.a: Every president elected from 1980 through 2004 came from the Sunbelt: Reagan (California), George H. W. Bush and George W. Bush (Texas) and Clinton (Arkansas). The white South moved to the Republican Party, which in 1994 won a majority of Southern House seats for the first time since Reconstruction, and Southerners such as Speaker Newt Gingrich (Georgia) led Congress. Growing Latino populations later made Nevada and Arizona swing states.
cards.h: → presidents + party shift + congressional leaders
cards.n: Population growth alone is not influence; name the political result: presidents, congressional leadership and a Republican South.

cards.q: Describe two ways new immigrants from Latin America and Asia affected American culture after 1980.
cards.a: Language and media: Spanish-language networks such as Univision and Telemundo grew into national broadcasters, and bilingual signs and services spread. Religion and food: immigrants filled Catholic parishes and built Hindu and Buddhist temples and mosques, widening American religious life, while Mexican, Chinese, Vietnamese, Korean and Indian foods became everyday fare. Fights over bilingual education followed, as in California's Proposition 227 (1998).
cards.h: → two cultural areas, each with examples
cards.n: 'They brought diversity' is too vague to earn credit; name specific cultural areas and examples.

cards.q: Describe the role of immigrants in the U.S. labor force after 1990.
cards.a: Immigrants supplied a growing share of workers, about 17 percent of the civilian labor force by 2019 (BLS). Less-educated immigrants, many undocumented, filled often low-paid jobs in agriculture (a large share of hired farmworkers), construction, meatpacking, landscaping, cleaning and restaurants; highly educated immigrants, many on H-1B visas, filled technology, engineering and medical jobs, keeping those industries growing as the native-born workforce aged.
cards.h: → overall share + low-skill and high-skill roles
cards.n: Describing immigrants only as low-wage workers misses the skill split; KC-9.2.II.B calls them 'an important labor force' across the economy.

cards.q:
Explain how the purpose of the source described below limits its usefulness as evidence of immigration patterns, and what it is better evidence of.
Source (a labeled paraphrase): a 1994 television advertisement for the reelection of California's governor. Grainy black-and-white footage shows people running between cars at the San Diego border crossing while a narrator says, 'They keep coming,' claims two million illegal immigrants live in California, and blames Washington for making the state pay for them.
cards.a: As a campaign ad meant to win votes by creating alarm, it chose dramatic footage and an unsourced figure, so it is weak evidence of how many migrants came or how they crossed. It is strong evidence of political attitudes in recession-hit 1994 California: candidates believed fear of unauthorized immigration and anger at federal costs would move voters, the mood that passed Proposition 187 that year.
cards.h: → purpose → what it distorts → what it reliably shows
cards.n: 'The ad is biased' earns nothing; the point is how its purpose shapes its content and what that makes it good or bad evidence for.

cards.q:
Explain the significance of the audience and purpose of the source described below.
Source (described): a news photograph from Los Angeles, March 25, 2006. A crowd of several hundred thousand fills downtown streets to protest a House bill (H.R. 4437, passed December 2005) that would have made unlawful presence in the country a federal felony. Many marchers wave U.S. flags and carry signs reading 'We are America' and 'Today we march, tomorrow we vote.'
cards.a: The marchers addressed a national audience of voters and Congress, not only fellow immigrants, so their purpose was to present immigrants as loyal, working members of American society rather than criminals; the U.S. flags and 'we vote' signs rebut the bill's framing and warn of electoral consequences. The photo is strong evidence of Latino political mobilization in 2006, weaker evidence of what all immigrants or Americans thought.
cards.h: → audience → purpose → how flags and slogans serve it
cards.n: Describing the photo ('people marching with flags') earns nothing; explain why the flags and slogans served the marchers' purpose with their audience.

cards.q: Identify two federal measures between 1994 and 2006 that tightened border or immigration enforcement.
cards.a: Operation Gatekeeper (1994): added agents, lights and fencing near San Diego, pushing crossings into deserts and mountains, where migrant deaths rose. Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (1996): expanded deportation for crimes, sped removals and barred re-entry for 3 or 10 years after unlawful presence. Secure Fence Act (2006): authorized about 700 miles of border fencing.
cards.h: → measure + year + what it did, twice
cards.n: Enforcement rerouted migration more than it stopped it; claiming these laws ended unauthorized immigration is wrong, as it peaked around 2007.

cards.q: Explain the push and pull factors behind Latin American and Asian immigration after the 1965 Hart-Celler Act.
cards.a: Push factors: civil wars in El Salvador, Guatemala and Nicaragua, economic crises in Mexico, and war's aftermath in Southeast Asia. Pull factors: the 1965 act's family-reunification preferences, which let each immigrant sponsor relatives, U.S. demand for labor, and refugee programs under the Refugee Act of 1980.
cards.h: → wars and poverty push + family preferences, jobs, refugee law pull → chain migration from Latin America and Asia
cards.n: A list of pushes and pulls earns less than a chain: the 1965 act's family preferences multiplied each arrival through sponsorship.
o: U.S. Cold War policy helped create the push: refugees came from Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia after 1975 and from Central American wars Washington funded in the 1980s.
Mexico's 1982 debt crisis and 1994-1995 peso collapse cut wages there while U.S. jobs in construction and agriculture paid several times more.

w.a: Immigrants came after 1965 because the act allowed unlimited immigration.
w.why: false; it set numerical caps

w.a: Asian immigration grew because the 1965 act kept the old national-origins quotas.
w.why: reverses it; the act abolished them

cards.q: Explain why the population and political influence of the South and West grew after 1980.
cards.a: Jobs and costs pulled people south and west. Defense, energy, tech and service industries grew there; lower taxes, cheaper housing, weaker unions and air conditioning drew firms and retirees; and immigrants settled there. More people meant more House seats and electoral votes, and a Sunbelt outlook shaped both parties.
cards.h: → jobs, low costs, climate, immigrants → population grows → more seats and electoral votes → political weight
cards.n: 'People like warm weather' is one pull, not an explanation; connect the migration to the political result (seats, votes, leaders).
o: Deindustrialization pushed workers out of the Rust Belt at the same time, so the shift was a push from the Northeast and Midwest as well as a pull to the Sunbelt.
Federal spending on military bases and aerospace since World War II had built the Sunbelt economy that kept attracting migrants after 1980.

w.a: The South grew because the Civil Rights Act made people move there.
w.why: the law relocated no one

w.a: The West grew mainly because of the Gold Rush.
w.why: a nineteenth-century cause

cards.q: Explain why the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 failed to stop unauthorized immigration.
cards.a: It legalized people already here but barely changed the incentives for new arrivals. Employer sanctions were weakly enforced and evaded with false documents, U.S. demand for low-wage labor stayed strong, and Mexico's economic crises pushed workers north, so the undocumented population reached about 12 million by 2007.
cards.h: → weak employer sanctions + forged papers + strong labor demand + Mexican crises → migration continues
cards.n: 'The border was open' is not an explanation; say why the law's enforcement side failed while the economic pull persisted.
o: Newly legalized immigrants anchored family and job networks that helped later migrants, including unauthorized ones, find work and housing.
Heavier border enforcement after 1994 made crossing costly, so many migrants stayed permanently instead of moving back and forth, raising the resident undocumented population.

w.a: IRCA failed because it banned all immigration from Mexico.
w.why: false; it did no such thing

w.a: IRCA failed because Reagan vetoed it.
w.why: false; Reagan signed it

cards.q: Explain why immigration became an intensely contested political issue in the 1990s and 2000s.
cards.a: Rapid, visible change met economic anxiety. The immigrant population doubled from 1990 to 2010 and spread from gateway cities to new Southern and Midwestern towns; recessions and stagnant wages sharpened fears about jobs and public costs; and after 9/11 border control became a security issue.
cards.h: → fast growth spreads to new places + wage stagnation, recessions + post-9/11 security fears → contested issue
cards.n: 'People are prejudiced' is an assertion; the answer needs causes with mechanisms: scale, new destinations, economic fear, security.
o: An undocumented population of about 11 to 12 million made legal status, not national origin, the center of the debate, and neither party could pass reform.
Growing Latino and Asian electorates raised the stakes, since both parties calculated how immigration policy would affect future voters.

w.a: Immigration became controversial because immigration fell sharply in the 1990s.
w.why: false; it rose

w.a: Immigration was debated only because of the 1924 quota law.
w.why: wrong period; those quotas ended in 1965

cards.q: Explain how immigrants after 1980 affected the U.S. economy.
cards.a: They filled labor gaps at both ends. Less-educated immigrants kept farming, construction, meatpacking and services staffed at low wages, and skilled immigrants filled tech and medical jobs; as native-born workers aged, they added workers, consumers and new businesses, though they may have held down some low-end wages.
cards.h: → labor gaps at both ends + aging native workforce → immigrants fill jobs, start firms → growth, some wage pressure
cards.n: Claiming immigrants 'took jobs' or 'helped the economy' without a mechanism earns nothing; KC-9.2.II.B stresses their role as a labor force.
o: Immigrant entrepreneurs founded firms at high rates, from corner groceries to Silicon Valley technology companies, creating jobs as well as filling them.
Economists debate small wage effects: most find little overall impact, with possible pressure on earlier immigrants and workers without a high-school diploma.

w.a: Immigrants hurt the economy because most of them did not work.
w.why: false; their labor-force participation was high

w.a: Immigrants after 1980 worked only in farming.
w.why: ignores construction, services and skilled jobs

cards.q: Explain why Proposition 187 shifted Latino voters in California toward the Democratic Party.
cards.a: Many Latinos, citizens included, saw the measure as an attack on their community. It spurred record naturalization and voter registration, Republicans were identified with it through Governor Wilson, and California's growing Latino electorate swung Democratic, helping make the state a Democratic stronghold.
cards.h: → 187 seen as attack on Latinos → naturalization and registration surge → GOP linked to it → Latinos swing Democratic
cards.n: 'Latinos are always Democrats' ignores the change; the point is the cause-and-effect link from 1994 to the shift.
o: The measure's backers made unauthorized immigration a Republican issue, so later GOP candidates in California inherited its unpopularity among fast-growing Latino and Asian electorates.
Latino civic groups and unions organized against 187, building networks that later ran naturalization and registration drives.

w.a: Latinos turned Democratic because Proposition 187 gave them free health care.
w.why: reverses it; 187 cut off services

w.a: Latinos voted Democratic because Governor Wilson was a Democrat.
w.why: false; Wilson was a Republican

cards.q: Identify the September 11 attacks and the War on Terror.
cards.a: On September 11, 2001, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers crashed airliners into the World Trade Center towers and the Pentagon; a fourth plane crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. Nearly 3,000 people died. President George W. Bush declared a 'war on terror' against al-Qaeda and states that harbored terrorists, invaded Afghanistan in October 2001, created new homeland-security agencies and later invaded Iraq (2003).
cards.h: → the attacks + toll + the policy response
cards.n: The war on terror is a policy framework, not one war; naming only Afghanistan misses its global and domestic sides (KC-9.3.II.A-B).

cards.q: Identify the USA PATRIOT Act and the Department of Homeland Security.
cards.a: The USA PATRIOT Act (October 2001), passed by lopsided margins (98 to 1 in the Senate), widened federal power to conduct surveillance, obtain business and library records, track money flows and share intelligence among agencies. The Department of Homeland Security (2002) combined 22 agencies, among them the Coast Guard, customs, immigration services and the new TSA, in the largest reorganization since 1947. Critics said both traded liberty for security.
cards.h: → what each did + year + the criticism
cards.n: The PATRIOT Act did not create Guantanamo or authorize torture; tie it to surveillance and the wartime civil-liberties pattern (Sedition Act, internment).

cards.q: Identify the Iraq War (2003).
cards.a: In March 2003 the United States and a smaller coalition, led by Britain, invaded Iraq without UN Security Council authorization, citing Saddam Hussein's supposed weapons of mass destruction and ties to terrorism under the Bush Doctrine of preemption. Baghdad fell within weeks, but no WMD stockpiles were found, and insurgency and sectarian civil war followed. Nearly 4,500 U.S. troops and far more Iraqis died before U.S. forces left in December 2011.
cards.h: → when + justification + course + cost
cards.n: Saying Iraq was behind 9/11 is the trap: no link was found. The controversy rests on the missing WMD and the long occupation. Iraqi death estimates vary widely.

cards.q: Date the September 11 attacks and the invasion of Iraq.
cards.a: The attacks came on September 11, 2001; the United States invaded Afghanistan on October 7, 2001, and Iraq on March 20, 2003, about eighteen months later.
cards.h: → two dates, with Afghanistan between
cards.n: Keep the order straight: Afghanistan was the direct response to 9/11; Iraq was a separate war begun in 2003 on different grounds.

cards.q: Identify the Oklahoma City bombing (1995).
cards.a: On April 19, 1995, Timothy McVeigh, an army veteran tied to the antigovernment militia movement and enraged by the deadly 1993 federal siege at Waco, Texas, set off a truck bomb at the Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City, killing 168 people, including 19 children. It remains the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in U.S. history and led to the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996.
cards.h: → who + when + motive + toll + result
cards.n: Illustrative: it predates the war on terror and the KCs do not name it. Use it as evidence that domestic security debates began before 9/11.

cards.q: Identify the Kyoto Protocol (1997).
cards.a: The Kyoto Protocol (1997) committed industrialized nations to binding cuts in greenhouse-gas emissions, about 7 percent below 1990 levels for the United States by 2008-2012, while exempting developing nations such as China and India. The Clinton administration signed it in 1998 but never sent it to a Senate that had voted 95 to 0 against any such treaty, and George W. Bush rejected it in 2001, citing costs and the exemptions.
cards.h: → what it required + U.S. response
cards.n: Saying the United States ratified Kyoto is wrong: it signed but never ratified. The debate set climate concerns against economic costs (KC-9.3.II.C).

cards.q: Identify the Paris Agreement (2015).
cards.a: The Paris Agreement (2015), negotiated under Obama, had nearly every nation set its own voluntary emission targets to hold warming well below 2 degrees Celsius. Because it set no binding targets, Obama joined without Senate ratification. Trump withdrew (announced 2017, effective 2020), Biden rejoined in 2021, and Trump ordered a second withdrawal in 2025.
cards.h: → what it asked + how the U.S. joined + in and out
cards.n: The back-and-forth is the point: an executive agreement shifts with each president, showing how partisan the climate debate became.

cards.q: Identify the killing of Osama bin Laden (2011).
cards.a: On May 2, 2011 (local time), U.S. Navy SEALs acting on Obama's order killed Osama bin Laden, al-Qaeda's leader and the planner of 9/11, in a raid on his compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, nearly ten years after the attacks. The raid was carried out without informing Pakistan, straining relations, and the Afghan war went on until 2021.
cards.h: → who + when + where + what followed
cards.n: The raid ended neither the war on terror nor the Afghan war; using it as an end point is the trap.

cards.q: Identify Edward Snowden and the 2013 NSA surveillance revelations.
cards.a: In June 2013 Edward Snowden, a National Security Agency contractor, leaked classified documents showing that the NSA collected the phone records of millions of Americans in bulk and gathered internet communications through programs such as PRISM. The revelations set off a debate over security and privacy, and Congress ended the NSA's bulk phone-records collection in the USA Freedom Act (2015). Snowden fled and received asylum in Russia.
cards.h: → who + what he revealed + the response
cards.n: Whistleblower or leaker, the exam point is the debate: KC-9.3.II.B's question of security versus civil liberties.

cards.q: Identify Hurricane Katrina (2005) and its political fallout.
cards.a: Hurricane Katrina struck the Gulf Coast in August 2005; federally built levees failed and flooded about 80 percent of New Orleans, and more than 1,800 people died, disproportionately poor and Black residents without means to evacuate. The slow, disorganized federal response (FEMA) badly damaged the Bush administration's standing. The storm also shut Gulf oil production and refineries, pushing gasoline above 3 dollars a gallon.
cards.h: → what happened + who suffered + political damage
cards.n: Illustrative: the KCs do not name Katrina. It fits debates over government capacity, race and poverty, and energy vulnerability, not the war on terror.

cards.q: Identify the Bush Doctrine.
cards.a: The Bush Doctrine, set out in speeches and the 2002 National Security Strategy, held that the United States would act preemptively, alone if necessary, against terrorists and hostile states seeking weapons of mass destruction before they could strike, would treat states that harbored terrorists as enemies, and would promote democracy abroad. It justified the 2003 invasion of Iraq.
cards.h: → its principles + where stated + what it justified
cards.n: Preemption, striking before being attacked, is the new element; confusing it with Cold War containment or deterrence misses the change.

cards.q: Identify the debate over Guantanamo Bay and 'enhanced interrogation' in the war on terror.
cards.a: From 2002 the Bush administration held suspected terrorists as 'enemy combatants' without trial at the Guantanamo Bay naval base in Cuba, and the CIA used 'enhanced interrogation' methods, including waterboarding, that critics called torture; photos of abuse at Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq (2004) caused outrage. The Supreme Court upheld detainees' right to challenge detention (Rasul, 2004; Boumediene, 2008). Obama banned the harsh methods in 2009 but could not close the prison.
cards.h: → the practices + the outcry + the responses
cards.n: Keep the actors straight: the courts limited detention and Obama banned the harsh methods; KC-9.3.II.B is about human rights and civil liberties.

cards.q: Identify the end of the U.S. war in Afghanistan in 2021.
cards.a: Under a 2020 agreement between the Trump administration and the Taliban, U.S. forces were to leave Afghanistan; Biden completed the withdrawal in August 2021. The U.S.-backed government collapsed, the Taliban retook Kabul on August 15, and a suicide bombing at the Kabul airport killed 13 U.S. service members during the evacuation. The nearly 20-year war, the longest in U.S. history, cost about 2,400 American military lives.
cards.h: → agreement + withdrawal + collapse + cost
cards.n: The war did not end with bin Laden's death in 2011; it lasted another decade, which is why its end fed debate over the limits of American power.

cards.q: Describe the debate over U.S. dependence on fossil fuels in the early 21st century.
cards.a: Net oil imports peaked at about 60 percent of U.S. petroleum use in 2005, and Middle East wars and gasoline above 4 dollars a gallon in 2008 fed calls for 'energy independence.' One side urged more domestic drilling ('drill, baby, drill,' 2008) and pipelines such as Keystone XL; the other urged conservation, fuel-economy rules and renewable energy to curb climate change. Fracking made the U.S. the world's top oil producer by 2018.
cards.h: → the problem + both sides + what changed
cards.n: Treat it as a debate between security and cost on one side and climate on the other; describing only gas prices misses KC-9.3.II.C's link to consumption and the environment.

cards.q:
Explain how the historical situation and audience of the source described below shape its message and limit its use as evidence.
Source: President George W. Bush, address to a joint session of Congress, broadcast nationally, September 20, 2001, nine days after the attacks: 'Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists.' He announces that the war on terror 'begins with al Qaeda, but it does not end there,' and tells Americans to expect 'a lengthy campaign.'
cards.a: Delivered nine days after 9/11 to Congress, a grieving nation and foreign governments, the speech aimed to rally unity and warn other states to choose sides, so its stark 'with us or against us' framing reflects wartime persuasion, not a detailed policy plan. It is strong evidence of how the administration framed the war on terror, weaker evidence of how the war was actually fought or of Americans' later doubts.
cards.h: → situation + audiences → framing → evidential limits
cards.n: 'The speech is biased' earns nothing; explain how the moment and the audiences shaped its absolutes, and what that makes it good evidence for.

cards.q: State two measures showing that the United States remained the world's leading superpower in the early 21st century.
cards.a: Military: the United States accounted for close to 40 percent of world military spending in the early 2020s (SIPRI), more than the next several countries combined, with bases and alliances on every continent. Economic: it produced about a quarter of world output at market exchange rates, and the dollar remained the main reserve and trade currency. Challenges came from China's rise, Russian aggression in Ukraine (2014, 2022) and the costs of the Iraq and Afghan wars.
cards.h: → one military and one economic measure + a challenge
cards.n: SIPRI and IMF figures, rounded. KC-9.3.II.D says 'despite' challenges: name at least one, or the claim of dominance is one-sided.

cards.q: Explain how the September 11 attacks changed American government and society.
cards.a: They expanded the security state and reordered priorities. Congress passed the PATRIOT Act and created DHS and the TSA; surveillance and detention powers grew; foreign policy turned to preemptive war in Afghanistan and Iraq; and at home early unity gave way to debates over liberty and anti-Muslim discrimination.
cards.h: → attacks expose vulnerability → new agencies and powers + preemptive wars → security vs liberty debate
cards.n: A list of changes is description; the explanation links the attacks' shock to each new power and to the debate it provoked.
o: Airport screening, watch lists and ID rules made security part of daily life, so the change reached ordinary routines, not only policy.
The pattern echoes earlier wars: as with the Sedition Act, the Red Scares and Japanese internment, security fears narrowed liberties and later drew pushback.

w.a: 9/11 changed nothing because the United States was already at war with al-Qaeda.
w.why: ignores the new agencies, laws and wars

w.a: After 9/11 Congress repealed the Bill of Rights.
w.why: false; it expanded surveillance powers

cards.q: Explain why the United States invaded Afghanistan in October 2001.
cards.a: Al-Qaeda planned the attacks from bases in Afghanistan, whose Taliban rulers refused to hand over Osama bin Laden. Congress authorized force within days, and U.S. forces, with NATO allies and Afghan militias, invaded in October 2001 to destroy al-Qaeda's haven and topple the Taliban.
cards.h: → al-Qaeda plans 9/11 from Afghanistan → Taliban shelter bin Laden → invasion to destroy the haven
cards.n: Confusing the Afghan war with Iraq is the trap: Afghanistan was the direct response to 9/11; Iraq came in 2003 on separate grounds.
o: NATO invoked its mutual-defense clause, Article 5, for the first time, so allies treated the attack on the United States as an attack on all.
Congress's authorization, passed with a single dissenting vote, covered those responsible for 9/11 and was later stretched to justify operations far beyond Afghanistan.

w.a: The U.S. invaded Afghanistan because it had weapons of mass destruction.
w.why: confuses it with the Iraq justification

w.a: The U.S. invaded Afghanistan to end the Soviet occupation.
w.why: that ended in 1989

cards.q: Explain why the Iraq War became controversial at home and abroad.
cards.a: Its justification collapsed and its costs mounted. No weapons of mass destruction or al-Qaeda link was found; the invasion went ahead without UN approval over allies' objections; and the occupation brought insurgency, civil war and Abu Ghraib, killing thousands of Americans and far more Iraqis.
cards.h: → WMD claims fail + no UN approval + insurgency and abuse + mounting deaths → opposition grows
cards.n: 'It was a war for oil' asserts a motive without evidence; the controversy is explained by failed justifications and mounting costs.
o: The 2007 troop surge reduced violence but did not settle Iraq's politics, and U.S. forces left in 2011 only to return against ISIS in 2014, feeding debate over the war's results.
Opposition to the war helped Democrats win Congress in 2006 and helped Obama, who had opposed it, win in 2008.

w.a: The war was controversial because Iraq had carried out the 9/11 attacks.
w.why: false; no such link was found

w.a: The war was controversial because the U.S. lost the initial invasion.
w.why: false; Baghdad fell within weeks

cards.q: Explain why the war on terror raised questions about civil liberties and human rights.
cards.a: It fought a hidden enemy by expanding secret power. Surveillance of Americans' communications grew under the PATRIOT Act and NSA programs; suspects were held without trial at Guantanamo and some were tortured; and Muslim Americans faced profiling, so security gains came at liberty's expense.
cards.h: → hidden, stateless enemy → surveillance, indefinite detention, harsh interrogation → liberties questioned
cards.n: 'The government violated rights' earns little; name the policy and the right at stake (privacy, due process, freedom from torture).
o: The pattern continues earlier wartime restrictions, from the Alien and Sedition Acts to Japanese internment, in which security fears narrowed liberties.
Courts and Congress pushed back, as in Boumediene (2008) on detainees' rights and the 2015 USA Freedom Act ending bulk phone-records collection.

w.a: The war on terror raised no liberty questions because it was fought only overseas.
w.why: ignores domestic surveillance and profiling

w.a: The PATRIOT Act suspended the Constitution.
w.why: overstated; it expanded surveillance powers

cards.q: Explain why Middle East conflicts and climate concerns intensified debate over U.S. dependence on fossil fuels after 2000.
cards.a: Both made oil use a national question. Wars and instability in the oil-rich Middle East tied energy imports to security and pushed gas prices up, while growing evidence of climate change tied burning fuel to environmental harm; the two concerns produced rival answers, more drilling or cleaner energy.
cards.h: → Middle East wars → oil as security risk + climate science → fuel as environmental risk → drill vs renewables
cards.n: Naming two concerns without showing how each raised the stakes of oil consumption is listing, not causation.
o: The fracking boom cut imports after 2008, turning the debate from dependence on foreign oil toward pipelines, drilling on public land and emissions.
Gas prices above 4 dollars in 2008 made energy a campaign issue, with 'drill, baby, drill' on one side and green-jobs plans on the other.

w.a: The debate grew because the United States produced no oil of its own.
w.why: false; it was a major producer

w.a: Climate concerns began only after Hurricane Katrina.
w.why: the debate predates 2005, as Kyoto shows

cards.q: Explain why the United States remained the world's leading superpower despite economic and foreign policy setbacks after 2001.
cards.a: Its foundations outlasted the setbacks. It kept the largest economy, the dominant reserve currency and unmatched military reach with worldwide alliances, and it recovered from the 2008 crisis faster than many rivals, so the Iraq and Afghan wars and China's rise dented but did not end its primacy.
cards.h: → largest economy + dollar + military and alliances → setbacks absorbed → still the leading power
cards.n: 'America is the greatest' earns nothing; KC-9.3.II.D asks why primacy held despite named challenges.
o: Alliances such as NATO, which added members after 2001 and revived after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, multiplied American influence in ways rivals could not match.
Technology firms and universities kept the United States central to the digital economy, a source of power beyond the military.

w.a: The U.S. stayed a superpower because it won every war after 2001.
w.why: ignores the Iraq and Afghan setbacks

w.a: The U.S. stopped being a superpower after 2008.
w.why: contradicts KC-9.3.II.D

cards.q: Explain why the war in Afghanistan lasted nearly twenty years.
cards.a: Quick victory became a war without a clear end. The Taliban fell in 2001 but regrouped from havens in Pakistan; attention and troops shifted to Iraq after 2003; and the U.S.-backed Afghan government stayed corrupt and dependent, so no president could leave without risking its collapse, which came in 2021.
cards.h: → Taliban toppled but regroup in Pakistan + Iraq diverts resources + weak Afghan state → no exit until 2021
cards.n: 'The Afghans were hard to defeat' is too vague; name the mechanisms: sanctuary, diverted resources, a weak partner state.
o: Mission creep turned a counterterrorism strike into nation-building, which needed far more time and troops than destroying al-Qaeda's camps.
Obama's 2009 surge raised troop levels to about 100,000 but came with a withdrawal timeline, and the Taliban could wait it out.

w.a: The war lasted twenty years because the Soviet Union kept helping the Taliban.
w.why: the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991

w.a: The war lasted so long because bin Laden was never found.
w.why: he was killed in 2011

cards.q: Identify Bush v. Gore (2000).
cards.a: Bush v. Gore (December 2000) was the Supreme Court decision that ended Florida's contested recount in the presidential election. With George W. Bush ahead by a few hundred votes out of about 6 million, the Court held 7 to 2 that the recount's varying standards raised equal-protection problems and ruled 5 to 4 that no new recount could finish in time, so Bush won Florida and the presidency, though Al Gore won the national popular vote.
cards.h: → what the Court decided + its effect on the election
cards.n: Illustrative: the KCs do not name it. Use it as evidence of partisan division and distrust of institutions, not as a verdict on who 'really' won.

cards.q: Explain the specific controversy behind the Bush v. Gore (2000) Florida recount.
cards.a: The controversy was over how to count disputed ballots and who should decide.
